### Κεφ. ε'. 5.

Καὶ ἦλθον εἰς τὸ πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης, εἰς τὴν χώραν τῶν Γαδαρηνῶν.

2 Καὶ ἐξελθόντι αὐτῷ ἐκ τοῦ πλοίου, εὐθέως ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ ἐκ τῶν μνημείων ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ·

3 Ὅς τὴν κατοίκησιν εἶχεν ἐν τοῖς μνημείοις, καὶ ἁλύσεσιν οὐδεὶς ἠδύνατο αὐτὸν δῆσαι·

4 Διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν πολλάκις πέδαις καὶ ἁλύσεσι δεδέσθαι, καὶ διεσπάσθαι ὑπ' αὐτοῦ τὰς ἁλύσεις, καὶ τὰς πέδας συντετρίφθαι· καὶ οὐδεὶς αὐτὸν ἴσχυε δαμάσαι.

5 Καὶ διαπαντὸς νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσι καὶ ἐν τοῖς μνήμασιν ἦν κράζων, καὶ κατακόπτων ἑαυτὸν λίθοις·

6 Ἰδὼν δὲ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ μακρόθεν, ἔδραμε, καὶ προσεκύνησεν αὐτῷ·

7 Καὶ κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ, εἶπε· Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοὶ Ἰησοῦ υἱὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου; ὁρκίζω σε τὸν Θεὸν, μή με βασανίσῃς.

8 (Ἔλεγε γὰρ αὐτῷ· Ἔξελθε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἀκάθαρτον ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου·)

9 Καὶ ἐπηρώτα αὐτόν· Τί σοι ὄνομα; Καὶ ἀπεκρίθη, λέγων· Λεγεὼν ὄνομά μοι· ὅτι πολλοί ἐσμεν.

10 Καὶ παρεκάλει αὐτὸν πολλὰ ἵνα μὴ αὐτοὺς ἀποστείλῃ ἔξω τῆς χώρας.

11 Ἦν δὲ ἐκεῖ πρὸς τὰ ὄρη ἀγέλη χοίρων μεγάλη βοσκομένη.

12 Καὶ παρεκάλεσαν αὐτὸν πάντες οἱ δαίμονες, λέγοντες· Πέμψον ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς χοίρους, ἵνα εἰς αὐτοὺς εἰσέλθωμεν.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>to one another: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

### Chap. 5.

And they came to the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes.

2 And when he had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit,

3 Who had his dwelling among the tombs; and no one could bind him, not even with chains:

4 Because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him, and the shackles smashed to pieces; and no one was strong enough to tame him.

5 And constantly, night and day, in the mountains and in the tombs, he was crying out and cutting himself with stones.

6 But seeing Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him,

7 And crying out with a loud voice, he said: What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.

8 (For he said to him: Come out of the man, you unclean spirit.)

9 And he asked him: What is your name? And he answered, saying: My name is <term>Legion</term> <gloss>a Roman military unit of thousands</gloss>, because we are many.

10 And he pleaded with him earnestly not to send them out of the country.

11 Now there was there, near the mountains, a great herd of pigs feeding.

12 And all the demons pleaded with him, saying: Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter into them.

<summary>Jesus arrives in the country of the Gadarenes and encounters a severely demon-possessed man whom no one could restrain. The demons, calling themselves Legion, beg Jesus not to banish them from the region but to send them into a nearby herd of pigs.</summary>
<keywords>Gospel of Mark, Jesus, Gadarenes, exorcism, unclean spirit, Legion, demons, herd of pigs</keywords>

<header>PROCLUS BY MARINUS.</header>

But if I should wish likewise to recount and detail every single matter regarding his intimacy with Pan, the son of Mercury <note>original: "Pane Mercurii Filio"</note>, concerning the frequent proofs of benevolence and the manifold assistance which that deity deigned to bring to Proclus at Athens; and moreover concerning that truly singular kind of good fortune which fell to him from the Mother of the Gods, and in which he was especially accustomed to triumph and rejoice: perhaps I shall seem to readers to say many things rashly, and to utter what is incredible to others. For many and great things were done and spoken each day by the Goddess toward him, which, since they are innumerable and unheard of, I myself do not now hold in precise memory. But if anyone desires to know what sort of man he was even in these matters, he ought to study his book on the Mother of the Gods, from which he will understand that the Philosopher brought to light the entire Theology of that Goddess not without divine aid—

<column-break/>

<margin>CHAPTER XXXIII.</margin>
But if I should thus wish to go through all things and to tell of his friendship with Pan, the son of Hermes, and the great goodwill and deliverance which he met with at Athens from the God; and furthermore to narrate at length all the good fortune he obtained from the Mother * of the Gods, in which he indeed especially exulted and took great delight: I might perhaps seem to my readers to talk idly, and to some even to speak incredible things. For many and great were the things done and spoken toward him daily by the Goddess, of which, on account of their multitude and unexpected nature, I, the author, do not even now possess a fully articulated memory. But if anyone longs to discern this aptitude of his as well, let him take into his hands his book on the Mother <note>original: "μητρωακὴν αὐτοῦ βίβλον"</note>. For you will see that not without divine † possession <note>original: "κατακωχῆς"</note> <gloss>inspiration</gloss> did he set forth the Theology concerning the—

---

* Above, page 36. Marinus had recorded that Proclus assiduously purified himself with the rites of the Mother of the Gods each month.
† Suidas repeats these words verbatim from Marinus under Proclus <note>original: "Πρόκλῳ"</note>.

<summary>Marinus recounts Proclus's intimate divine friendship with Pan and the daily favor shown to him by the Mother of the Gods. Readers seeking a complete account of these divine mysteries are referred to Proclus's own treatise on the Mother of the Gods.</summary>

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>a violent earthquake fell upon them; but Emperor Antoninus restored even these through excessive expenditure and eagerness for their rebuilding. Now as to all his gifts of money both to Greeks and to those barbarians who requested them, and the construction of public works in Greece, throughout Ionia, around Carthage, and in the land of the Syrians, others have recorded these things with the greatest accuracy. But this emperor left behind also another deed worthy of memory. As many of his subjects as were Roman citizens, while their children were reckoned as Greeks, these parents were faced with either distributing their property to those unrelated to them or augmenting the emperor's wealth according to a certain law; Antoninus, however, permitted even these citizens to bestow the inheritance upon their own children, preferring to appear benevolent rather than to uphold a law profitable in terms of money. The Romans called this emperor <term>Pius</term> <gloss>Dutiful or Pious</gloss>, because he was seen especially to practice honour toward the divine; in my judgment he might also bear the title of Cyrus the elder, being called the Father of Mankind. He also left behind to inherit the empire a son of the same name; and this second Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius, adopted son and successor of Antoninus Pius</note> went out to take vengeance upon the Germans, the most warlike and numerous of the barbarians in Europe, and also the nation of the Sauromatae <note>Sarmatians</note>, who had initiated war and wrongdoing.

The remaining portion of our Arcadian account: there is a road leading out from Megalopolis to Pallantium and to Tegea, which runs as far as the place called the Dyke <note>Choma</note>.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>music in some way appears to be related to another, being a certain relation and harmony of things completely unlike and in otherness. But geometry corresponds to the <term>triad</term> <gloss>the number three</gloss>, not only because it is occupied with the three-dimensional and its parts and forms, but also because it is peculiar to this teacher always to name surfaces, which indeed they used to call colors, as geometry reaching its term, since geometry is concerned primarily with the plane surface. And the most elementary plane surface consists in a triad of either angles or sides, from which, as if from a certain base toward a single point when depth is added, the most elementary of solid bodies, the pyramid, is in turn constituted. It is bounded by the minimum of four angles or lines, fitted together by three equal intervals, after which no other body exists naturally in solid space. And spherical science <note>astronomy</note> is fitted to the <term>tetrad</term> <gloss>the number four</gloss>; for of all bodies the sphere is naturally the most complete, the most encompassing of all others, and superior in countless other respects. It is an enclosure of four things: center, diameter, circumference, and solid volume, that is to say, resistance to touch. Because it is of such a nature, the men used to swear by Pythagoras through it, obviously admiring and singing his praises for the discovery, just as Empedocles also says somewhere:

> "No, by him who handed down to our generation the <term>tetractys</term> <gloss>the sacred quaternary</gloss>,  
> fountain holding the roots of ever-flowing nature."

<margin>A</margin> we must do so. From where, then, do you wish us to begin our investigation? Since we have entered upon a certain model, so that we may see whether the names themselves will guide us in our inquiry, or whether everything is merely accidental and haphazard, or if they possess a certain correctness. Now, names given to heroes and men might perhaps deceive us. For many are given to them after the surnames of their ancestors, which have no relation to them, as we were saying at the beginning; and men often bestow names as though expressing a wish, such as <term>Eutychides</term> <gloss>son of good fortune</gloss>, <term>Sosias</term> <gloss>savior</gloss>, <term>Theophilus</term> <gloss>beloved of God</gloss>, and many others. Such names, then, it seems to me we ought to dismiss.
<margin>B</margin> It is most likely that we shall find names rightly established in those things that are eternal and naturally existing. For it is especially fitting that earnest care was taken concerning the imposition of names there. Perhaps some of them were even established by a power more divine than that of mortal humans. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak well, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Is it not just, then, to begin from the gods, examining how this very name, the gods, was rightly called? **HERMOGENES:** It is reasonable. **SOCRATES:** Here is what I suspect. It appears to me that the earliest inhabitants of Greece considered those to be the only gods whom many of the barbarians still revere today: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the sky. Seeing that all these were always running in motion and running swiftly <note>original: "θέοντα"</note>, from this nature of running <note>original: "θεῖν"</note> they called them
<margin>C</margin> <margin>gods</margin> gods <note>original: "θεούς"</note>. Later, learning of the rest, they addressed all of them by this name. Does what I say seem like the truth, or not at all? **HERMOGENES:** It seems entirely like the truth. **SOCRATES:** What, then, should we investigate after this? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly both daimones, heroes, and men. **SOCRATES:** Daimones? And indeed, Hermogenes, what might the name daimones ever mean? Consider whether you think I am saying anything sound. **HERMOGENES:** Only speak. **SOCRATES:** Do you know, then, whom Hesiod says the daimones are? **HERMOGENES:** I do not call it to mind. **SOCRATES:** Nor that he says the golden race of men came first into being? **HERMOGENES:** That I do know. **SOCRATES:** He says of it, then: "Yet when fate covered this generation, they are called holy daimones dwelling upon the earth, noble, deliverers from evil, guardians
<margin>D</margin> of mortal men." **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** I believe he calls it the golden race not because it was made of gold, but because it was good and noble. My evidence is that he says we are an iron race. **HERMOGENES:** You speak truly. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think, then, that if someone living today were good, Hesiod would say that he belongs to that golden race? **HERMOGENES:** It is likely. **SOCRATES:** And are the good anything other than wise? **HERMOGENES:** Wise. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it seems to me, he calls them daimones above all because they were wise and knowledgeable <term>daēmones</term> <gloss>knowing ones</gloss>; he named them daimones, and in our ancient language the name itself coincides. Both he and many other poets speak well, all who
<margin>E</margin> say that whenever a good man dies, he obtains a great destiny and honor, and becomes a daimon, according to the surname of wisdom. In this way I myself also hold that every knowledgeable man who is good is daemonic <gloss>divinely inspired</gloss>, both living and dead, and is rightly called a daimon. **HERMOGENES:** I believe, Socrates, that I am entirely in agreement with you on this point. But what might a hero be? **SOCRATES:** That is not very difficult to grasp. For their name has been slightly altered, showing their birth from love <term>erōs</term> <gloss>love</gloss>. **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that heroes are demigods? **HERMOGENES:** What of it? **SOCRATES:** All of them were surely born from a god falling in love with a mortal woman, or a mortal man with a goddess. If you examine this according to the ancient Attic dialect, you will understand better. For it will show you that from the name of love <term>erōs</term> <gloss>love</gloss>, whence the heroes were born, it is slightly altered for the sake of the name.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>from love</margin> And either it calls them heroes for this reason, or because they were wise, and rhetoricians, and skilled, and dialecticians, being capable of questioning <note>original: "ἐρωτᾶν"</note>. For to speak <note>original: "εἴρειν"</note> means to utter words. Just as we were saying just now, when called heroes in the Attic tongue, they turn out to be rhetoricians, questioners, and lovers, so that the heroic race becomes a family of rhetoricians and sophists. But this is not difficult to understand. Rather, regarding that of men, can you tell why men are called <term>anthrōpoi</term> <gloss>human beings</gloss>? **HERMOGENES:** How could I, good sir? Even if I were somehow able to discover it, I would not exert myself, because I believe you will be able to discover it better than I. **SOCRATES:** You seem to place your trust in the inspiration of Euthyphro. **HERMOGENES:** Evidently. **SOCRATES:** And you trust rightly. For even now I seem to have thought of it cleverly, and there is a danger, unless I take care, that I shall become wiser today than is proper. Consider what I say. First,
<margin>G</margin> one must understand this about names: that we often insert letters and remove others, naming them as we wish, and we change the pitch accents. For instance, <term>Dii philos</term> <gloss>dear to Zeus</gloss>; so that this might become a single name for us instead of a phrase, we removed one iota from it, and instead of an acute accent on the middle syllable, we pronounced it with a grave accent. With others, on the contrary, we insert letters, and pronounce acute syllables more gravely. **HERMOGENES:** You speak truly. **SOCRATES:** In my view, this is the very thing that has happened to the name of men. For from a phrase it has become a name, with one letter, alpha, being removed,
<margin>he who examines what he has seen</margin> and the ending made grave. **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** In this manner: this name, human being <term>anthrōpos</term> <gloss>man, human</gloss>, signifies that while other beasts inspect none of the things they see, nor do they reflect or look up and examine <term>anathrei</term> <gloss>examines closely</gloss>—

<margin>A</margin> is entirely to be done. Whence, then, do you judge we should especially begin? Now that we have prescribed a certain rule, so that we may learn whether the names themselves also bear witness to us that they were not made by chance, but contain a certain correctness. The names of heroes and men might perhaps deceive us; for many of these are given according to the surnames of ancestors, and often do not agree at all, just as we said at the beginning. Moreover, men often assign names as though wishing, such as <term>Eutychides</term> <gloss>fortunate</gloss>, <term>Sosias</term> <gloss>safe</gloss>, <term>Theophilus</term> <gloss>beloved of God</gloss>, and very many others.
<margin>B</margin> Therefore, I judge that such names ought to be passed over. For it is most fitting and appropriate that we discover those that are rightly given to things everlasting and established in the order of nature. For concerning those things it is most proper to have taken great care in establishing names. Perhaps some of them were established by a divine power rather than a human one. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak excellently, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Is it not right to begin from the gods themselves, and investigate the reason why they are called gods <note>original: "θεοὶ"</note>? **HERMOGENES:** Truly. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, I infer it thus. It seems to me that the ancients of the Greeks thought those alone were gods whom even in these times most barbarians consider: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, the sky. Seeing therefore that all these were perpetually
<margin>C</margin> <margin>gods, from running</margin> in course, from this nature of running swift <note>original: "θεῖν"</note> they seem to have named them gods <note>original: "θεοὺς"</note>, and then, observing the others, they called them all by the same name. Does what I say have any likelihood, or not? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly does. **SOCRATES:** What should be investigated after this? **HERMOGENES:** It is clear that we must inquire about daimones, heroes, and men. **SOCRATES:** About daimones? And certainly the matter stands thus, Hermogenes. What then does the name daimones mean? Pay attention to whether I say anything of worth. **HERMOGENES:** Speak now. **SOCRATES:** Do you know whom Hesiod says are daimones? **HERMOGENES:** No. **SOCRATES:** Nor even that he says in the verses of his work *Works and Days* that a golden race of men existed in the beginning? **HERMOGENES:** This indeed I know. **SOCRATES:** For he says that from this race, after the destinies of this present life,
<margin>D</margin> holy, earthly, excellent daimones come to be, expellers of evils, and guardians of men. **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** Truly I judge that he calls it a golden race not because it was formed from gold, but because it was good and distinguished; which I infer from the fact that he says our race is of iron. **HERMOGENES:** You tell true things. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think that if someone from our people now were good, he would be judged by Hesiod to belong to that golden race? **HERMOGENES:** It is consistent. **SOCRATES:** But are the good anything other than prudent? **HERMOGENES:** Prudent. **SOCRATES:** On that account, as I judge, he calls them daimones especially because they were wise and knowing <note>original: "δαίμονες"</note>. And from our ancient language that name exists.
<margin>E</margin> For which reason both he and very many other poets speak excellently, whosoever say that after some good man has died, he obtains the greatest dignity and reward, and becomes a daimon, according to the surname of wisdom. Thus I also assert that every man who is good is knowing <note>original: "δάϊμονα"</note>, that is, wise, and that he is daemonic, that is, blessed, both living and departed, and is rightly called a daimon. **HERMOGENES:** I seem to myself, Socrates, to agree with you completely in this. But what does hero <note>original: "ἥρως"</note> signify? **SOCRATES:** That is by no means difficult to discover, for the name of heroes differs little from its origin, indicating that their generation flowed
<margin>from love</margin> from love <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔρωτος"</note>. **HERMOGENES:**
<margin>F</margin> By what reason do you say that? **SOCRATES:** Are you ignorant that heroes are demigods? What then? **SOCRATES:** All heroes were certainly born either from the love of gods toward human women, or from the love of men toward goddesses. Moreover, if you consider this according to the ancient language of the Attics, you will understand more. For you will find that it was changed a little for the sake of the name from love <note>original: "ἔρωτος"</note>, whence heroes were born; or that either from this the name of heroes was derived, or from the fact that they were wise and rhetoricians, eloquent and most prompt in questioning and disputing. For to speak <note>original: "εἴρειν"</note> is to utter words. Wherefore, as we were saying just now, in the Attic voice heroes appear as certain rhetoricians, disputers, and lovers. Whence the heroic offspring exists as a race of rhetoricians and sophists. But that is not difficult to know; rather, that is more obscure, for what cause
<margin>G</margin> men are called <term>anthrōpoi</term> <gloss>human beings</gloss>. Do you have anything to offer yourself? **HERMOGENES:** Whence would I have it, good man? Even if I were able to discover it in any way, I would not try, because I hope that you will discover it better and more easily than I. **SOCRATES:** You seem to me to rely on the inspiration of Euthyphro. **HERMOGENES:** Without doubt. **SOCRATES:** And deservedly indeed do you rely on it. For I seem to myself to have thought of it altogether too neatly, and there is danger, unless I take care, lest today I turn out wiser than is proper. Attend to the things I shall say. First of all, one ought to observe this concerning names: that we often add letters, often also remove them, while we name at our pleasure, and we frequently alter acute accents, as when we say "beloved of Zeus" <note>original: "Διὶ φίλος"</note>; that this might be a single name for you, we removed the second iota, and in place of the acute middle syllable, we pronounced a grave one. In certain other names we insert letters, and pronounce others more gravely. **HERMOGENES:** You report the truth. **SOCRATES:** This also happens in human being <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος"</note>, as it seems to me.

<meta>catchword: For from</meta>

---

For from a verb a noun was formed, one alpha being removed, and the end made grave. **HERMOGENES:** How do you say that? **SOCRATES:** Thus: that name of man signifies that other animals do not examine what they see, nor do they reflect upon it, nor contemplate it;

<summary>Socrates investigates the correctness of names by examining terms for eternal things, gods, daimones, heroes, and human beings, demonstrating how word origins reflect divine qualities, wisdom, love, or reflective contemplation.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Cratylus, Socrates, Hermogenes, etymology, gods, daimones, heroes, human beings, Hesiod, language</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>...wealth is found; but when many search, the silver-bearing ore appears in much greater quantity. Thus in this enterprise alone of those that I know, no one envies those who establish additional operations. 

Furthermore, all those who own land could tell how many yokes of oxen and how many laborers are sufficient for an estate. If someone puts to work more than the adequate number, they reckon it as a financial loss. But in silver-mining operations, everyone says they are in need of workers. 

For indeed, it is not as when coppersmiths become numerous and, because copper wares become cheap, the coppersmiths are ruined, and ironworkers likewise; and whenever much grain and wine are produced, because the produce is cheap, agricultural ventures become unprofitable, so that many abandon working the land and turn to maritime trade, retail, and moneylending. Rather, the more silver-bearing ore appears and the more silver is produced, the more people come to this work. 

Moreover, when someone acquires enough furniture for their house, they do not buy much more. But no one has ever acquired so much silver as to no longer need more. If any obtain an immense quantity, they take no less pleasure in burying what is surplus than in using it. 

Furthermore, whenever cities prosper, people have a strong need for silver. For men desire to spend on fine armor, good horses, and magnificent houses and furnishings, while women turn their spending toward luxurious clothing and gold jewelry. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>the four pillars:

The <term>sighah</term> <gloss>contractual formula</gloss> is an expression indicating the assumption of an obligation towards a right. In its meaning is what was previously discussed under <term>daman</term> <gloss>guaranty</gloss>, such as a person saying: "Zayd has against me" or "with me such-and-such." Excluded by his saying "to Zayd against me or with me" is what he says to him alone without specifying a right, so it is not an acknowledgment unless the acknowledged object is specified, such as "this garment," in which case it is an acknowledgment. 

The expressions "against me" <note>original: "alā"</note> or "in my liability" <note>original: "fī dhimmatī"</note> apply to debt, because that is what is understood from them, and this holds when stated without qualification, not absolute release. Similar to "against me" in admitting clarification <note>original: "taballī al-tafsīr"</note> and in "against me" regarding a <term>wadi'ah</term> <gloss>safekeeping deposit</gloss>, and similar to "against me" in the mother/origin, while "with me" <note>original: "ma'ī"</note> or "at my possession" <note>original: "'indī"</note> are for an identified item; thus if he claims that it was a safekeeping deposit and that it perished, or that it was a pledge, his word is accepted with his oath. My phrasing with "or" in both places is preferable to his phrasing with "and" in both of them.

The reply to "You owe me" or "Is it against you to me?" or "Yes," or "I returned it," or "I acknowledge it," and similar expressions—whether phrased as a denial or an undertaking—constitutes an acknowledgment, because that is what is understood from it. It is like responding to the question "Pay the thousand that you owe me" with "Yes," or with his words "I will lend you," or "Advance me a loan," or "Until I open the purse," or "Until I find the goods," for example, or similar phrases like "Come to take it" or "Wait until you receive it," for indeed that is an acknowledgment of it. 

Conversely, answering that with "Weigh it," or "Take it," or "Judge him," or "Put it into your purse," or "I acknowledge" or "I confess it," and similar expressions, as well as "Valid coins or bad coins," does not constitute an acknowledgment of the thousand, but rather of other than it.

<summary>This text explains the legal formula for acknowledgment in Islamic jurisprudence, distinguishing valid expressions that establish debt or property liability from ambiguous replies that do not constitute an admission of debt.</summary>
<keywords>sighah, contractual formula, iqrar, acknowledgment, daman, guaranty, dhimmah, legal liability, wadi'ah, safekeeping deposit, debt confession, fiqh</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>then it is an imperfect verb <term>fiʿl muḍāriʿ</term>.

**Preliminary Note:** If a word indicates a past event and does not accept the feminine *tāʾ* suffix <note>original: "al-tāʾ li-thintān"</note>, or if it indicates a second occurrence in the present and future but does not accept *lam*, such as *awwah* <gloss>an interjection of sighing or pain</gloss>, it is also considered a verbal noun. The author stated this in his work *al-ʿUmdah*.

This is the chapter on the inflected <term>al-muʿrab</term> and the uninflected <term>al-mabnī</term>.

The noun is partly flexible <term>mutamakkin</term>, which is the inflected form representing the original default state <note>original: "al-aṣl"</note>. Its other part is non-flexible <term>ghayr mutamakkin</term>, which is the uninflected form, established contrary to the default state.

The noun is made uninflected due to its resemblance to particles <term>shabah al-ḥarf</term>. This relates to his statement that it is uninflected, meaning an explanation for its lack of inflection. Another view was claimed regarding what deviates from the uninflected state, which concerns cases where inflection is required by a counteracting factor, such as *ayy* <gloss>which / whichever</gloss> in interrogation and conditional clauses. For although it resembles the particle in meaning, this resemblance is countered by its obligatory state of annexation <term>iḍāfah</term>.

A single aspect of resemblance to a particle is sufficient to make a noun uninflected. This contrasts with the prohibition of full inflection or nunation <term>manʿ al-ṣarf</term> <gloss>diptote status</gloss>, where resemblance to a verb from two aspects is strictly required. Ibn al-Ḥājib justified this in his *Amālī* by stating that a single resemblance to a particle places the noun into a different genus and brings close that between which and the particle there is no shared affinity, except in the broadest category, which is being a word. By contrast, the resemblance of a noun to a verb, even if it is another distinct class, does not share the same extreme distance from the noun as the particle does.

From the author's restriction of the cause of indeclinability exclusively to resemblance to the particle, it is understood that other factors are not considered. Abū al-Fatḥ <note>Ibn Jinnī</note> and others preceded him in this view, even if it has been said otherwise.

<summary>This page explains the criteria distinguishing verbal nouns, introduces the chapter on inflected and uninflected nouns, and examines the theoretical basis for noun indeclinability through resemblance to particles versus diptote inflection.</summary>
<keywords>imperfect verb, mudari, verbal noun, ism fil, inflected, murab, uninflected, mabni, flexible noun, mutamakkin, particle resemblance, shabah al-harf, diptote, man al-sarf, Ibn al-Hajib, Abu al-Fath, Ibn Jinni</keywords>

translation:
For reports explicitly state that the disobedient will be punished, as in God Almighty's words: "There is none of you but will pass through it" <note>Qur'an 19:71</note>, which is unequivocal that this must occur for everyone, since no believer is free from committing a sin. And as for His words: "None shall burn therein except the most wretched" <note>Qur'an 92:15</note>, He meant a specific group thereby, just as He intended a specific individual by "the most wretched." And His words: "Every time a group is cast into it" <note>Qur'an 67:8</note> means a group from among the disbelievers. The contextual restriction of such general expressions is straightforward, unlike interpretations that reduce speech to poetic hyperbole.

A group among the speculative theologians denied the very validity of general forms of speech, holding that these verses must be suspended until some accompanying contextual indicator clarifies their meaning. As for the <term>Mu'tazilites</term> <gloss>an early rationalist theological school that asserted the absolute necessity of punishment for unrepentant grave sinners</gloss>, their doubt rests on God Almighty's words: "And indeed, I am most forgiving toward him who repents, believes, and works righteousness" <note>Qur'an 20:82</note>; and His words: "By the declining day, indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds" <note>Qur'an 103:1-3</note>; and His words: "There is none of you but will pass through it," followed immediately by: "Then We will save those who feared God" <note>Qur'an 19:71-72</note>; and His words: "And whoever disobeys God and His messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell" <note>Qur'an 72:23</note>. Thus His speech explicitly conjoins righteous action with faith. They also point to His words: "And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell" <note>Qur'an 4:93</note>.

Yet these general texts are likewise restricted, by virtue of the evidence in His words: "And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" <note>Qur'an 4:48</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to affirm for Him a divine will in the forgiveness of sins other than <term>shirk</term> <gloss>polytheism or attributing partners to God</gloss>. In the same way, there is the tradition: "Whoever has in his heart even the weight of a speck of dust of faith shall be brought out of the Fire"; and His words: "Indeed, God does not cause the reward of those who do good to be lost" <note>Qur'an 9:120</note>. How then

Pay no heed to what is said that demonstrative syllogisms <term>al-burhāniyyah</term> <gloss>demonstrative arguments</gloss> are necessary, dialectical syllogisms <term>al-jadaliyyah</term> <gloss>dialectical arguments</gloss> are majority-possible, rhetorical syllogisms <term>al-khiṭābiyyah</term> <gloss>rhetorical arguments</gloss> are equally possible <note>Apparatus a: Manuscript D reads "equal".</note> having neither inclination nor rarity, and poetic syllogisms <term>al-shiʿriyyah</term> <gloss>poetic arguments</gloss> are false and impossible. Regard is not given to that, nor did the Master of Logic <note>original: "ṣāḥib al-manṭiq", referring to Aristotle</note> point to it. As for sophistical syllogisms <term>al-sūfasṭāʾiyyah</term> <gloss>sophistical arguments</gloss> <note>Apparatus b: Manuscript D reads "and they are".</note>, they are those that use fallacious resemblances <term>al-mushabbahah</term> <gloss>fallacious semblance premises</gloss> <note>Apparatus c: Manuscript F reads "uses them".</note>, and in this they share with tested and trial premises on the method of misleading. If the resemblance is to necessary premises and the manner of their application, its practitioner is called a sophist <term>sūfasṭāʾī</term> <gloss>sophist</gloss>. If it is to generally accepted propositions <term>al-mashhūrāt</term> <gloss>widely received opinions</gloss>, its practitioner is called a disputant <term>mushāghib</term> <gloss>eristic contentious arguer</gloss> <note>Apparatus d: Manuscript D reads "a contentious arguer".</note> and an obstinate wrangler <term>mumārrī</term> <gloss>caviler</gloss>. The disputant <note>Apparatus e: Manuscript F reads "and the disputant".</note> stands opposite the dialectician <note>Apparatus f: Manuscript B reads "to dialectic".</note>, and the sophist stands opposite the philosopher <term>al-ḥakīm</term> <gloss>sage / philosopher</gloss> <note>Apparatus g: Manuscript D contains a variant reading.</note>.

Pointers to Demonstrative Syllogisms and Problems <note>original: "ishārah ilā al-qiyāsāt wa-l-maṭālib al-burhāniyyah"</note>. Just as inquiries in the sciences may concern a necessity in the judgment, they may also concern a possibility in the judgment, or they may concern an absolute non-necessary existence, as is known concerning the conjunctions and disjunctions of celestial bodies. Each genus is specialized with its own premises and conclusion. The demonstrator deduces <note>Apparatus g: Manuscript D contains a variant reading.</note> the necessary from the necessary, and the non-necessary from the non-necessary, whether in combination or purely. Do not pay attention to the one who says that he uses only necessities and majority possibilities to the exclusion of others. Rather, if he intends to produce the truth of a minority possible <note>Apparatus h: Manuscript B reads "more appropriate".</note>, he employs the minority possible, and he uses in every domain what is suitable for it. The fourth category is the blood offering of valuation and estimation <term>dam al-tamtīʿ wa-al-taqdīr</term> <gloss>an expiatory sacrifice determined by flexible appraisal within set statutory bounds, also known as the blood offering of choice and estimation</gloss>, and its meaning has already been explained.

Its causes are eight: shaving <term>al-ḥalq</term>, clipping the hair <term>al-qaṣr</term>, wearing sewn garments <term>al-labs</term>, oiling or bleeding <term>al-dam</term> <note>medical treatments or applying oil</note>, applying perfume <term>al-ṭīb</term>, sexual foreplay <term>muqaddimat jimāʿ</term>, contracting a marriage <term>ʿaqd al-nikāḥ</term>, and intercourse after an initial invalidating intercourse <term>al-jimāʿ baʿd al-jimāʿ al-mufsid</term>.

In every one of these eight violations, the required expiation according to the legal school is either a sheep, or charity given to six poor persons <term>masākīn</term> with half a measure <term>ṣāʿ</term> <gloss>a traditional dry volume measure</gloss> to each poor person, or fasting three days.

Then an expiation is also due for one who performs the pilgrimage manual's obligations...

<note>Vocabulary: <term>tamtīʿ</term> <gloss>enjoyment or estimated compensation</gloss>, <term>ḥalq</term> <gloss>shaving the head</gloss>, <term>qaṣr</term> <gloss>trimming the hair</gloss>, <term>jimāʿ</term> <gloss>intercourse</gloss>, <term>nikāḥ</term> <gloss>marriage contract</gloss>, <term>masākīn</term> <gloss>poor persons</gloss>, <term>ṣāʿ</term> <gloss>a volumetric measure roughly equivalent to four mudd</gloss>.</note>

<summary>This page defines the fourth category of expiation, known as the sacrifice of valuation and estimation. It enumerates the eight specific infractions of pilgrimage prohibitions, such as shaving, wearing clothing, applying perfume, and foreplay, and details the penalty of choosing between sacrificing a sheep, feeding six poor persons half a sa', or fasting for three days.</summary>

translation:
...having fully gathered the sphere of the body, and being established having attained the sphere of nothingness, that which is non-dual and immovable, that is the supreme. 

Since there is also the cessation of the mental formations, the Tathagata, having understood that it exists, turns away from it, and looks upon it as peaceful, looking upon it as the definite exit. Monks, that is gross, conditioned, intentional, and dependent origination. Just as when there are mental formations, there is also their cessation, so the Tathagata, having understood that it exists, turns away from it, and looks upon it as peaceful, and remains looking upon the definite exit. Monks, regarding that, those Shramanas and Brahmanas who say there is no consciousness, they say that henceforth the self becomes without consciousness. ...it is the fruit. Consciousness is the sting. This, the cessation of consciousness, is peace. This is the supreme, so they think. They also know them exactly as they are. 

Monks, regarding that, those Shramanas and Brahmanas who say that one is neither with consciousness nor without consciousness, they say that henceforth the self becomes neither with consciousness nor without consciousness. And those Shramanas and Brahmanas who speak of consciousness, they argue against and despise those who say that henceforth the self becomes with consciousness. And they think this: Consciousness is a disease. Consciousness is a boil. Consciousness is a sting. Consciousness is also totally deluded. The sphere of neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness is peace. This is the supreme, so they think. The Tathagata, regarding the Shramanas and Brahmanas who say that one is neither with consciousness nor without consciousness..."

<meta>continues from previous page: ...with practitioners of mantra and with</meta> the wise who are the wise, with the wise who have attained the wise, with those who are becoming the wise who have attained, the self is the self, the self is. One should not become a reciter while remaining in a place, nor should one become a wise one who has attained. One should not remain in a place,

in order to make oneself beautiful, one should not wear garlands or colors. One should completely abandon leaping, jumping, running, tearing up roots, and taking up the bad states that arise from the body. Remaining in the truth of the <term>dharma</term> <gloss>teachings of the Buddha</gloss>, one should abandon harsh, changing, and rough speech, as well as divisive words, and one should not engage in meaningless chatter. One should not reside with or argue with <term>tirthikas</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist ascetics</gloss>, and one should not make noise while reciting <term>mantras</term> in the presence of <term>candala</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss> or other low-caste individuals. When the intelligent one is performing recitation, except for a single <term>mantra</term> assistant, one should not have joy or make noise together with others without necessity. One should not smear the body with oils, nor should one eat sesame seeds. Those who desire <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>spiritual accomplishment</gloss> should completely abandon radishes, garlic, hot spices, various types of sour fermented alcohol, <term>junglen</term> <gloss>a type of legume</gloss>, lentils, likewise <term>masha</term> <gloss>black gram</gloss> beans, and various <term>junglen</term> made of sesame. One should abandon all food from <term>mara</term> <gloss>demonic forces</gloss>, all food from <term>torma</term> <gloss>ritual offering cakes</gloss>, <term>krisara</term> <gloss>a dish of rice and sesame</gloss>, and <term>okthuk</term> <gloss>a type of gruel</gloss>.

translation:
...the inconceivable knowledge of becoming, the inconceivable knowledge of the explanation of becoming, the inconceivable knowledge of the defiled becoming, and the inconceivable knowledge of the purified becoming; these are the four. Youth, these are the four knowledges of entities of the Bodhisattvas; what are the four? The inconceivable knowledge of entities of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of entities of the explanation of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of entities of the defiled, and the inconceivable knowledge of entities of the purified; these are the four. Youth, these are the four knowledges of persons of the Bodhisattvas; what are the four? The inconceivable knowledge of persons of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of persons of the explanation of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of persons of the defiled, and the inconceivable knowledge of persons of the purified; these are the four. Youth, these are the four knowledges of objects of the Bodhisattvas; they are inconceivable, and the four teachings that are inconceivable; they are not to be taught as ultimate states.

Whatever desire there is for the knowledge of phenomena, that is called the perfect knowledge of the individual definitions of words. This means teaching, explaining, applying, demonstrating, elevating, analyzing, and correctly differentiating phenomena knowledge; it is making it clear, having unobstructed words, having words that are not cast away, not stammering, not being confused, and having words without hesitation; this, Youth, is called the perfect knowledge of individual oratorical power. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

As many as are the wisdoms of the Buddhas,
So many are the designations of form.
As many as are the designations of form,
So many are the names spoken of form.
As many as are the spoken names of form,
So many are the names of morality.
As many as are the names of morality,
So many are the names of the Buddhas.
As many as are the names of the Buddhas,
So many are the names of sentient beings.
The names of a single sentient being,
I have explained as being that many.
Names and speech are infinite;
Those which I have previously explained,
The names of morality and the names of the Buddhas,
The names of sentient beings are equivalent to them.
As many as are the faults of the conditioned,
So many are the praises of nirvana.

Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva looks at all beings like water in a mirage. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva looks at all beings like the sound of an echo. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva looks at all beings like a mass of clouds in the sky. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva looks at all beings like the origin of foam. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva investigates all beings, like the appearance and disappearance of bubbles in water. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva investigates all beings, like the essence of a plantain tree. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva investigates all beings, like the flash of lightning. Mañjuśrī, it is like this: just as a bodhisattva investigates all beings according to the five elements."

qua que Hierosme Roy de Sicile perdit son estat, & fut cruellement tué auec tous ses parents & amis, pour auoir mesprisé le Senat sans rien luy communiquer³: & par le moyen duquel son ayeul auoit gouuerné l'estat cinquante ans & plus, ayant empieté la souueraineté. Cesar fit la mesme faute, gouuernant la Republique sans l'aduis du Senat, & la principale occasion qu'on print pour le tuer, fut par ce qu'il ne daigna se leuer deuant le Senat, à la suasion de son flatteur Cornelius Balbus. Et pour mesme cause les Rommains auoyent tué le premier, & chassé le dernier Roy, d'autant que l'vn mesprisoit le Senat, faisant tout à sa teste: l'autre le vouloit abolir du tout supprimant les Senateurs par mort. Et pour ceste cause le Roy Louys XI. ne voulut pas que son fils Charles VIII. sceust plus de trois mots de Latin, qu'on a rayés de l'histoire de Philippe de Commines, à fin qu'il se gouuernast par conseil, congnoissant bien que ceux qui ont bonne opinion de leur suffisance, ne font rien que de leur cerueau: ce qui auoit reduit Louys XI. à vn doigt pres de sa ruine, comme il confessa depuis. Aussi est-il certain que le sçauoir d'vn Prince, s'il n'est accompli d'vne bien rare & singuliere vertu, est vn dangereux cousteau en la main d'vn furieux: & n'y a rien plus à craindre qu'vn sçauoir accompagné d'iniustice, & armé de puissance. Il ne s'est point trouué de Prince, hors le faict des armes, gueres plus ignare que Traian, ny quasi plus sçauant que Neron: & toutesfois cestuy-cy n'eust onques son pareil en cruauté, ny cestuy-là en bonté: l'vn mesprisoit, l'autre reueroit le Senat. Puis donc que le Senat est vne chose si vtile en la monarchie, & si necessaire és estats populaires & aristocratiques, qu'ils ne peuuent subsister, disons en premier lieu des qualités requises aux senateurs, puis du nombre d'iceux: & s'il doit y auoir plus d'vn conseil, & les choses qu'on y doit traitter, & en dernier lieu quelle puissance on doit dõner au Senat. I'ay dit que le Senat est vne assemblee legitime: cela s'entend de la puissance qui leur est donnee du souuerain, de s'assembler en temps & lieu ordonné. Quant au lieu, il ne peut chaloir où soit, car bien souuent l'occasion le presente où les affaires se doiuent executer. translation:
<margin>3 Livy, on Hieronymus: "While Hiero reigned, there had been a public council; after his death they were neither summoned nor consulted on any matter."</margin>
that Hieronymus, King of Sicily, lost his state and was cruelly killed together with all his relatives and friends, for having scorned the Senate and shared nothing with it. Yet it was by means of that Senate that his grandfather <note>Hiero II of Syracuse</note> had governed the state for fifty years and more, after seizing sovereignty. Caesar made the same mistake, governing the Commonwealth without the advice of the Senate. The chief pretext taken for killing him was that he did not deign to rise before the Senate, at the urging of his flatterer Cornelius Balbus. For the same cause the Romans had killed their first King and driven out their last, since the one scorned the Senate and did everything as he pleased, while the other wished to abolish it altogether by putting the Senators to death. <note>Romulus and Tarquin the Proud.</note> For this reason King Louis XI did not want his son Charles VIII to know more than three words of Latin, a detail that has been struck from the history of Philippe de Commynes. He wanted him to govern by counsel, knowing well that those who think highly of their own ability do nothing except by their own heads. This had brought Louis XI within a finger's breadth of ruin, as he later confessed. It is certain too that the learning of a Prince, unless it is joined to a very rare and singular virtue, is a dangerous knife in the hand of a madman. Nothing is more to be feared than learning joined to injustice and armed with power. Apart from the business of arms, there was hardly a Prince more ignorant than Trajan, nor almost any more learned than Nero. Yet the latter never had his equal in cruelty, nor the former in goodness: the one scorned the Senate, the other revered it. Since, then, the Senate is so useful in a monarchy, and so necessary in popular and aristocratic states that they cannot survive without it, let us speak first of the qualities required in senators, then of their number, whether there should be more than one council, what matters should be dealt with there, and lastly what power should be given to the Senate. I have said that the Senate is a lawful assembly. This means the power given to its members by the sovereign to assemble at an appointed time and place. As for the place, it matters little where it is, for very often the occasion itself presents the place where affairs must be carried out. **Figures from the Saint-Marc manuscript.**

I will first give the oldest figures, those of the Saint-Marc manuscript <note>the 11th-century Greek alchemical manuscript held in the Library of Saint Mark in Venice</note>, namely:

The <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <gloss>gold-making</gloss> of Cleopatra, made up of several parts related to one another, some of a practical nature and others of a mystical or magical nature: this is figure 11. <note>The Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra is a famous diagram attributed to "Cleopatra the Alchemist," including the ouroboros serpent and drawings of distillation apparatus.</note>

Figure 12 is a crude (partial) imitation of it, taken from manuscript 2325, and figure 13, taken from manuscript 2327, derives from the same type, with considerable and characteristic variations.

Figures 14 and 14 *bis* reproduce the alembic with two receivers (*dibikos*), already drawn in the preceding figures, but with various variations.

Figure 15 is that of the alembic with three receivers (*tribikos*).

Figure 16 represents a distilling apparatus without an upper dome or condenser, and fitted with a single receiver.

Figure 17 is that of the tribikos, according to manuscript 2325.

Figure 18 has the appearance of a distilling boiler.

Figure 19, barely sketched, seems to be the head of a similar apparatus.

Figures 20 and 21 are digestion apparatus, in the form of cylinders.

Figure 22 is a water bath with <term>kerotakis</term> <gloss>a palette for softening metals</gloss>. <note>The kerotakis was a closed vessel in which metals placed on a palette were exposed to rising vapors, such as those of mercury or sulfur.</note>

Figure 23 is a reproduction of it, according to manuscript 2325.

Figure 24 is another water bath with kerotakis.

*Tah* means: would that, if only.

11° Le manuscrit 2325 ne renferme pas les poètes; ceux-ci devaient donc former à l'origine une collection à part.

12° Le manuscrit 2325 ne renferme aucun traité de vieil auteur important, qui ne soit dans le manuscrit de Saint-Marc.

Il contient en moins le traité d'Ostanès, les chapitres de Zosime à Théodore, le serment de Pappus, le traité de Cléopâtre (poids et mesures) et quelques autres articles; articles qui manquent également dans le manuscrit 2327.

La liste des signes offre certaines confusions et diversités (v. pages 97 et 98 du présent volume).

Le manuscrit 2325 ne contient aucune trace des traités de Comarius.

Il contient en plus, par rapport à Saint-Marc, certains traités techniques, tel que celui de l'arabe Salmanas sur les perles, et la fabrication des émeraudes et autres pierres colorées, d'après le livre du Sanctuaire. La Chrysopée de Cosmas est ajoutée à la suite, d'une écriture plus moderne et presque effacée.

Dans le manuscrit 2325, l'ordre relatif est absolument, et du commencement à la fin, le même que celui du manuscrit 2327. Ce dernier dérive évidemment d'un type commun, mais complété par des intercalations et additions considérables.

Au contraire, l'ordre relatif est très différent entre ces deux manuscrits et le manuscrit de Saint-Marc : on y reviendra.

13° Examinons les traités qui manquent dans le manuscrit de Saint-Marc et qui existent dans le manuscrit 2327. Parlons d'abord de ceux qui portent des noms d'auteurs.

Le manuscrit 2327 débute par la lettre de Psellus adressée à Xiphilin. Dans certains manuscrits, cette lettre est adressée à Michel Cérularius; l'identité complète des deux lettres aurait besoin d'être vérifiée.

Le traité de Comarius se trouve dans le manuscrit 2327, sous sa forme la plus complète.

Je signalerai encore :

Le traité de Jean l'archiprêtre, qui manque dans le 2325;

Le traité de Salmanas et celui des émeraudes, qui s'y trouvent au contraire, ainsi que la Chrysopée de Cosmas, transcrite à la suite et à une époque postérieure dans le 2325;

Les livres de Sophé (Chéops);

La lettre d'Isis à Horus;

Le livre de Démocrite à Leucippe;

Le traité d'Agathodémon sur l'oracle d'Orphée;

La coction excellente de l'or, avec les procédés de Jamblique;

La chimie domestique de Moïse;

The name of Sergius, to whom some treatises of the Christian Philosopher are addressed, calls for similar remarks, since it does not appear in all the manuscripts.

11° Manuscript 2325 does not contain the poets; these must therefore originally have formed a separate collection.

12° Manuscript 2325 contains no treatise by an important early author that is not also in the Saint Mark manuscript. <note>The Saint Mark manuscript is the famous codex Marcianus in the Library of Saint Mark in Venice, the oldest and most important manuscript of the Greek alchemists.</note>

It lacks the treatise of Ostanes, the chapters of Zosimos to Theodore, the oath of Pappus, the treatise of Cleopatra (weights and measures) and a few other articles; these articles are likewise missing from manuscript 2327.

The list of signs shows certain confusions and variations (see pages 97 and 98 of the present volume).

Manuscript 2325 contains no trace of the treatises of Comarius.

Compared with Saint Mark, it contains in addition certain technical treatises, such as that of the Arab Salmanas on pearls, and the making of emeralds and other colored stones, according to the Book of the Sanctuary. The <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <gloss>art of making gold</gloss> of Cosmas is added afterward, in a more modern and almost faded hand.

In manuscript 2325, the relative order is exactly the same as that of manuscript 2327, from beginning to end. The latter clearly derives from a common type, but one completed by considerable insertions and additions.

By contrast, the relative order differs greatly between these two manuscripts and the Saint Mark manuscript: we will return to this.

13° Let us examine the treatises that are missing from the Saint Mark manuscript but present in manuscript 2327. First, let us discuss those that bear authors' names.

Manuscript 2327 opens with the letter of Psellus addressed to Xiphilinus. <note>Michael Psellus (11th century) was a leading Byzantine scholar; John Xiphilinus was his contemporary and later Patriarch of Constantinople.</note> In some manuscripts, this letter is addressed to Michael Cerularius; whether the two letters are wholly identical would need to be verified.

The treatise of Comarius is found in manuscript 2327 in its most complete form.

I will also point out:

The treatise of John the Archpriest, which is missing from 2325;

The treatise of Salmanas and that on emeralds, which on the contrary are found there, as is the Chrysopoeia of Cosmas, copied afterward and at a later period in 2325;

The books of Sophe (Cheops); <note>Sophe is a Greek form of the name of the pharaoh Khufu, known to the Greeks as Cheops.</note>

The letter of Isis to Horus;

The book of Democritus to Leucippus;

The treatise of Agathodaimon on the oracle of Orpheus;

The excellent cooking of gold, with the procedures of Iamblichus;

The domestic chemistry of Moses;

14° Finally, among the anonymous articles missing from the Saint Mark manuscript and present in manuscript 2327, one may cite:

The list of the gold-makers (missing from 2325).

Toutefois si la lettre *u* se trouve précédé d'un *Q*, elle n'a pas plus de son par elle même qu'elle n'en aurait p. ex, dans l'Espagnol *Quebrado* ou le français *quérir*. Ainsi l'on prononcera *quel*, pierre plate ; *quem*, toile, tisser, comme s'il y avait *gkel* ou *kkel*, *gkem* ou *kkem*. Parfois le E qui suit est marqué d'un tréma, pour indiquer que le son de cette lettre ne se confond point avec celui dela précédente ou peut-être qu'il est ouvert. We shall not detain the reader here with the barred *Y* of the Mayas. It is simply a spelling abbreviation for the preposition *yetel*, "by, with." This sign could be compared to the barred *K* of Lower Breton, which stands for the particle *Ker*, "at the home of, near." <note>Lower Breton is the Breton spoken in western Brittany.</note>

As for the half-vowel OU, in Quiché it is rendered by *v* or *u* before another vowel; for example in *vatch*, "face," pronounced *ouatch*. However, if the letter *u* is preceded by a *Q*, it has no more sound of its own than it would have, for example, in the Spanish *Quebrado* or the French *quérir*. Thus one will pronounce *quel*, "flat stone," and *quem*, "cloth, to weave," as if they were written *gkel* or *kkel*, *gkem* or *kkem*. Sometimes the following E is marked with a diaeresis, to show that the sound of this letter does not merge with that of the preceding one, or perhaps that it is open. Such is the case, for example, with *quëh*, "deer," pronounced *gkeh* or better *ghèc'h* (in Maya *Ceh*). Let us add that most often this silent *u* after Q is left out, for example in *qax*, "sorrow"; *qel*, "parakeet"; *qil*, "brother"; *qop*, "to cut," etc., etc.

In Maya, U sometimes has a value like that of English W in *William*, *well*, when it is followed by another vowel; for example in *uah*, "to nail," and *uinic*, "man," pronounced *wac'h*, *winik*. But most often, even in this case, it has an <term>interflatile</term> <gloss>breathed or glided</gloss> sound, which we shall deal with when discussing the consonants. We have already seen that sometimes, even when followed by another vowel, it remains a vowel itself.

V does not exist in Maya, at least in Beltrán and the authors who followed him. As will be seen shortly, it is replaced by B. The use of V in Tzeltal seems much the same as in Quiché. One must therefore pronounce *Valum*, *Votan* as if they were written *Waloum*, *Wotan* or *Wotane* (with silent *e*). <note>Votan was a culture hero in Tzeltal tradition, much discussed by 19th-century scholars.</note> Galindo renders this same semivowel V either by W or by U in Cakgi; for example in *wakki*, "six," and *vukú*, "seven" (pronounced *woukoú*).

# Third Instruction ( 122 )

### Root: Afterwards, one should perform the Bellows <term>Bhastrika</term> and quickly awaken the <term>Kundalini</term>. || 15 ||
### One should perform the contraction of the sun and then move the <term>Kundalini</term>. Even if one has entered the mouth of death, why should there be any fear of death? || 16 ||
### By moving the śakti fearlessly for the duration of two <term>muhurtas</term> <gloss>approximately 96 minutes</gloss>, it is drawn slightly upward, having arisen in the <term>Sushumna</term> <gloss>the central channel</gloss>. || 17 ||
### By that movement, the <term>Kundalini</term> certainly leaves the mouth of the <term>Sushumna</term>. Therefore, this life-breath <term>prana</term> enters the <term>Sushumna</term> on its own. || 18 ||

->|| Commentary ||<-

The word "afterwards" means having performed the previous actions. After the practice of moving the śakti <term>Shakti-chalana</term>, one should perform the <term>breath-retention</term> <gloss>kumbhaka</gloss> known as the Bellows <term>Bhastrika</term>. In this way, one should quickly awaken the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. Although the Thunderbolt Pose <term>Vajrasana</term> was already prescribed for the process of moving the śakti, it is mentioned again here to establish a rule: the Thunderbolt Pose must be maintained specifically for the Bellows breath following the energy movement. || 15 ||

Regarding the sun: One should perform the contraction of the sun, which is located in the region of the navel. This contraction of the sun occurs by the contraction of the navel itself. Then, from that contraction of the sun, one should move the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. For a man who performs this, even if he has reached the mouth of death, where is the fear of death or the fear of time? The meaning is that there is no fear at all. || 16 ||

Regarding two <term>muhurtas</term>: For a period of two <term>muhurtas</term>, which consists of two pairs or four <term>ghatikas</term> <gloss>a ghatika is 24 minutes</gloss>, the energy is moved fearlessly and without doubt. Through this, the energy arises in the <term>Sushumna</term> and is drawn slightly upward. || 17 ||

Regarding "by that": By that upward drawing, the <term>Kundalini</term> leaves the mouth—the entrance—of the well-known <term>Sushumna</term>...

->|| Vernacular Language ||<-

After performing the gesture for moving the śakti, one should perform the breath-retention named Bellows. By this method, one should quickly awaken the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. || 15 ||

Regarding the sun: One should contract the sun situated in the navel region. By contracting the navel, the sun is contracted. Following the contraction of the sun, one should move the <term>Kundalini</term> energy. Then a man who has reached the mouth of death will have no fear of time. || 16 ||

Regarding two <term>muhurtas</term>: By moving the śakti fearlessly for four <term>ghadis</term> <gloss>units of 24 minutes</gloss>, this energy rises in the <term>Sushumna</term> and is pulled slightly upward. || 17 ||

Regarding "by that": By pulling it upward, the <term>Kundalini</term> certainly <note>original: "निश्चय" meaning "certainly" or "with certainty"</note> clears its own path of entry into the <term>Sushumna</term>...

<summary>This page describes the transition from moving the Kundalini energy to performing the Bhastrika breath-retention while seated in the Thunderbolt Pose. These practices aim to clear the entrance of the central channel so the life-breath can enter and rise, effectively conquering the fear of death.</summary>

शक्तिप्रथः स्वयं भूत्वा परं शिवेन सङ्गमम् ।
नानासुखं विहारञ्च चिन्तयेत् परमं सुखम् ॥ ४० ॥
शिवशक्तिसमायोगादेकान्तं भुवि भावयेत् ।
आनन्दमानसो भूत्वा अहं ब्रह्मेति संभवेत् ॥ ४१ ॥
योनिमुद्रा परा गोप्या देवानांमपि दुर्लभा ।
सकृत्तु लाभसिद्धिः समाधिस्थः स एव हि ॥ ४२ ॥

10.—YONIMUDRA.

37—42. Sitting in Siddhâsana, close the two ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the index fingers, the nostrils with the middle fingers, the upper lip with the fore fingers, and the lower lip with the little fingers. Draw in the Prâna-Vâyu by Kâkî-mudrâ, (as in verse 86) and join it with the Apâna-Vâyu; contemplating the six chakras in their order, let the wise one awaken the sleeping serpent-Kundalinî, by repeating the mantra Hun (हुं), and Hansa (हंसः), and raising the Sakti (Force-kundali) with the jîva, place them at the thousand-petalled lotus. Being himself full of Sakti, being joined with the great Siva, let him think of the various pleasures and enjoyments. Let him contemplate on the union of Siva (spirit) and Sakti (force or energy) in this world. Being himself all bliss, let him realise that he is the Brahma. This Yoni-mudrâ is a great secret, difficult to be obtained even by the Devas. By once obtaining perfection in its practice, one enters verily into Samâdhi.

अथ योनिमुद्राफलकथनम् ।
ब्रह्महा भ्रूणहाचैव सुरापी गुरुतल्पगः ।
एतैः पापैर्न लिप्येत योनिमुद्रानिबन्धनात् ॥ ४३ ॥
यानि पापानि घोराणि उपपापानि यानि च ।
तानि सर्वाणि नश्यन्ति योनिमुद्रानिबन्धनात् ।
तस्मादभ्यसनं कुर्याद्यदि मुक्तिं समिच्छति ॥ ४४ ॥

*Its benefits.*

43—44. By the practice of this Mudrâ, one is never polluted by the sins of killing a Brâhmana, killing a fœtus, drinking liquor, or polluting the bed of the Preceptor. All the mortal sins and the venal sins are completely destroyed by the practice of this Mudrâ. Let him therefore practise it, if he wishes for emancipation.

अथ वज्रोलीमुद्राकथनम् ।
अरामवत्थ्य करयोस्तलाभ्यां क्षिपेत्पादयुगं शिरः ।
शक्तिप्रबोधाय चिरजीयनाय वज्रोलीमुद्रां मुनयो वदन्ति ॥ ४५ ॥

With the crow-beak, draw in the Prâna and join it to the Apâna.
Thinking of the six chakras in order, with the mantra Hun and Hansa, the wise one— 38.
Should awaken the sleeping goddess, the serpent-Kundalinî.
Raising the Force <note>Sakti-Kundali</note> along with the Jîva, place it at the lotus of the thousand petals. 39.
Being himself the manifestation of Sakti, he unites with the supreme Siva.
One should meditate on the various pleasures, enjoyments, and the supreme bliss. 40.
Contemplate the union of Siva and Sakti in this world.
Having become blissful in mind, he realizes "I am Brahman." 41.
This Yoni-mudrâ is a great secret, difficult even for the gods.
By obtaining perfection in it once, one is verily established in Samâdhi. 42.

10.—YONIMUDRA.

37—42. Sitting in <term>Siddhâsana</term> <gloss>adept's posture</gloss>, close the two ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the index fingers, the nostrils with the middle fingers, the upper lip with the fore fingers, and the lower lip with the little fingers. Draw in the <term>Prâna-Vâyu</term> <gloss>the in-breath</gloss> by <term>Kâkî-mudrâ</term> <gloss>crow-beak seal</gloss>, (as in verse 86) and join it with the <term>Apâna-Vâyu</term> <gloss>the downward breath</gloss>; contemplating the six <term>chakras</term> <gloss>energy centers</gloss> in their order, let the wise one awaken the sleeping serpent-<term>Kundalinî</term> <gloss>coiled spiritual energy</gloss>, by repeating the mantra Hun (हुं), and Hansa (हंसः), and raising the <term>Sakti</term> <gloss>Force-kundali</gloss> with the <term>jîva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss>, place them at the thousand-petalled lotus. Being himself full of Sakti, being joined with the great <term>Siva</term> <gloss>supreme consciousness</gloss>, let him think of the various pleasures and enjoyments. Let him contemplate on the union of Siva (spirit) and Sakti (force or energy) in this world. Being himself all bliss, let him realise that he is the <term>Brahma</term> <gloss>the Absolute</gloss>. This Yoni-mudrâ is a great secret, difficult to be obtained even by the Devas. By once obtaining perfection in its practice, one enters verily into <term>Samâdhi</term> <gloss>absorbed meditative state</gloss>.

Now the statement of the benefits of Yoni-mudra.
One who has killed a Brahmin, killed a foetus, drank liquor, or approached the guru's bed,
Is not stained by these sins through the power of Yoni-mudra. 43.
Whatever terrible sins or lesser sins exist,
All are destroyed by the power of Yoni-mudra.
Therefore, one should practise it if one desires emancipation. 44.

*Its benefits.*

43—44. By the practice of this Mudrâ, one is never polluted by the sins of killing a Brâhmana, killing a fœtus, drinking liquor, or polluting the bed of the Preceptor. All the mortal sins and the venal sins are completely destroyed by the practice of this Mudrâ. Let him therefore practise it, if he wishes for emancipation.

Now the description of Vajroli-mudra.
Throw the feet over the head like a bow.
The sages say Vajroli-mudra is for the awakening of Sakti and for longevity. 45.

## Commentary (Sayana)
विश्वायुः सर्वान्नः सर्वत्र गमनशीलो वायुः । वकारलोपश्चान्दसः । वायुः । यद्वा । छन्दसीण इत्युण्प्रत्यये वृद्धौ च कृतायां रूपं । गन्ता वायुस्त्वा त्वाँ परि पासति । परिपातु । पूषानुज्ञया परितो रक्षतु ॥ पा रक्षणे । लेटि सिब्यडागमः ॥ प्रपथे प्रकृष्टे मार्गे स्वर्गे पुरस्तात्सर्वेषां प्रथममेव वर्तमानः पूषा स्वयमेव त्वा त्वाँ प्रमितं यजमानं पातु । रक्षतु । सुकृतः पुण्यकर्माणो यत्र यस्मिन्देश आसते तिष्ठन्ति यत्र वा ते सुकृतो ययुः प्राप्तास्तत्र तस्मिन्स्थाने देवो दीप्यमानः सविता सर्वस्य स्वस्वकर्मणि प्रेरक एतन्नामको देवस्त्वा त्वाँ दधातु । निदधातु ॥

एकादशिनस्य पौष्णस्य पशोर्हविषः पूषेमा इत्यनुवाक्या । पूषेमा आशा अनु वेद सर्वाः शुक्रं ते अन्यद्यजतं ते अन्यत् । आ० ३. ९. । इति हि सूचितं ॥

## Commentary (Sayana)
पूषा देव इमा सर्वा आशाः प्राच्याद्या दिशोऽनु वेद । आनुपूर्व्येण जानाति । इमाः सुखेन गन्तव्या अमुखेनेति वैवमनुक्रमेण जानातीत्यर्थः । एवं सत्यस्मान् ।

## Hymn Text

May Āyu, who goes everywhere, protect you <note>original: "āyur viśvāyuḥ"; Sāyaṇa takes it as Vāyu, the wind</note>; may Pushan protect you on the distant path ahead.
Where the righteous dwell, where they have gone, may the god Savitr place you there. 4

**Padapatha:**
Life | all-pervading life | around | protect | you | Pushan | you | protect | on the distant path | in front |
Where | dwell | the righteous | where | they | have gone | there | you | god | Savitr | place | 4

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

The all-pervading one (viśvāyu) is the Wind (<term>vayu</term>), who moves everywhere—the elision of the 'va' is Vedic—may this Wind protect you on all sides; may he protect you with the permission of Pushan. On the distant path, the path to heaven, standing first of all, may Pushan himself protect you, the sacrificer. Where the righteous, those who have done good deeds, dwell, or where those righteous ones have gone, may the god Savitr—the shining one, the impeller of all in their respective tasks—place you there.

For the animal sacrifice of the <term>ekashina</term> <gloss>a rite involving eleven victims</gloss> dedicated to Pushan, the verse "Pusha ima" is the <term>yajya</term> <gloss>offering verse</gloss>. It is noted: "Pusha ima asha anu veda sarvah, shukram te anyadyajatam te anyat." <note>Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 3.9</note>

## Hymn Text

Pushan knows all these quarters of the sky; may he lead us on the safest path.
The giver of welfare, the glowing one, the lord of all heroes, may he go ahead without faltering, knowing the way. 5

**Padapatha:**
Pushan | these | quarters | after | knows | all | he | us | by the safest | lead |
Welfare-giver | glowing one | lord of all heroes | without faltering | ahead | go | knowing | 5

## Commentary (Sayana)

The god Pushan knows all these quarters, from the east onwards. He knows them in order, knowing which ones are to be traveled easily and which are not. Being so, may he lead us on the safest path, the path entirely free from fear. How? As the giver of welfare, as one who possesses heat <note>a reference to the sun's rays</note>, as the lord of all heroes—meaning he is accompanied by all the priests capable of performing the rite—and as one who does not falter, without negligence, knowing our fruits of action, may he go ahead. May he move in front of us.

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chapter of the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā, moving from the necessity of the Guru's grace to the specific internal states of the yogi when the Kuṇḍalinī is awakened. It elaborates on the transition from physical and mental activity to the "Natural State" (Sahajāvasthā) and the eventual destruction of all past actions (karma).</meta>

### ON THE HAṬHA YOGA PRADĪPIKĀ

**Root Text:**
**For the yogi whose awareness of the Power <note>the Kuṇḍalinī</note> has arisen, and who has abandoned all actions without exception, the Natural State <term>Sahajāvasthā</term> arises spontaneously. (11)**
**When the breath <term>prāṇa</term> flows through the Suṣumṇā and the mind enters the Void, then the knower of Yoga uproots all karmas. (12)**

->|| COMMENTARY ||<-

[Continuing from the previous verse:] When sleep occurs, the breath—the air—dissolves into the Void, the "Opening of Brahman" <term>Brahmarandhra</term>; it reaches a state of dissolution. The dissolution of the breath is simply the absence of its activity. (10)

**Regarding Verse 11 ("For the yogi whose awareness..."):** "Arisen" means born. The "awareness of the Power" refers to the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī. For that yogi by whom all actions—the entirety of them—have been abandoned or discarded. By means of physical posture <term>āsana</term>, physical activities are abandoned, yet activity remains in the breath and the senses. When mental activities are abandoned through withdrawal <term>pratyāhāra</term>, concentration <term>dhāraṇā</term>, meditation <term>dhyāna</term>, and cognitive absorption <term>samprajñāta-samādhi</term>, activity still remains in the intellect <term>buddhi</term>. This is because the pure Self <term>puruṣa</term> is unchanging and "is indeed unattached" <note>original Sanskrit: *asaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣaḥ*, a famous Upanishadic quote</note>, whereas the intellect, which is composed of the quality of purity <term>sattvaguṇa</term>, is subject to change. (11)

Through highest dispassion <term>paravairāgya</term> or through the long-term practice of cognitive absorption <term>samprajñāta-samādhi</term>, once the activities of the intellect are abandoned, one remains in a state of unchanging self-nature. That itself is the Natural State <term>Sahajāvasthā</term>, the Fourth State <term>Turyāvasthā</term>, and Liberation While Living <term>Jīvanmukti</term>. It manifests spontaneously, without any further effort. This is supported by the scripture: "By that which you renounce, renounce that as well; one should become unattached through wisdom." <note>This suggests a total letting go, even of the tool of renunciation itself.</note> **Regarding Verse 12 ("When the breath..."):** When the breath—the air—is flowing in the Suṣumṇā, the middle channel...

->|| VERNACULAR EXPLANATION ||<-

Through various types of Great Seals <term>mahāmudrā</term> and other practices, when the Great Power—the Kuṇḍalinī—is awakened, the breath then dissolves into the Void of the "Opening of Brahman" <term>Brahmarandhra</term>. (10)

**Regarding Verse 11:** For the yogi in whom the awareness of the Kuṇḍalinī has arisen and who has removed all karmas: through the practice of posture <term>āsana</term>, the activities of the body are removed. However, activity still resides in the breath and senses. Through withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and cognitive absorption, the activities of the mind are removed. At that point, activity remains only in the intellect, and the intellect becomes pure <term>sattvic</term>. Through dispassion and the long practice of absorption, the activities of the intellect are also removed. Then, one is established in the unchanging self-nature. This is called the Natural State <term>Sahajāvasthā</term>. This is also called the Fourth State <term>Turyāvasthā</term>. In this state, the yogi attains Liberation While Living <term>Jīvanmukti</term> spontaneously, without needing to make further effort. (11)

**Regarding Verse 12:** And when the breath begins to move in the Suṣumṇā, which is the middle channel, then the internal faculty <term>antaḥkaraṇa</term> enters the Void of Brahman. At that time, the knower of yoga uproots all those karmas that were destined to be experienced <term>prārabdha karma</term>. (12)

<summary>This page describes how the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī leads a yogi from physical and mental stillness to the "Natural State" (Sahajāvasthā), where effort ceases and all past karmas are destroyed. It explains the hierarchy of stillness, moving from the body to the senses, then the mind, and finally the intellect.</summary>

# J

## CLXXVII

### Jagüey

( Véase el artículo *Chagüite.*)

## CLXXVIII

### Jaltepeque

*Jaltepeques* llaman nuestros salineros á los cerritos de *arena dulce* que se forman en las salinas con los residuos que quedan después de extraer la sal á la arena bañada por el mar. Recuerdo que estando yo en el puerto del Triunfo, y tratando de encontrar un punto desde el cual pudieran verse los volcanes de San Vicente y de San Miguel, me dijo un individuo: "tal vez señor, desde esos *jaltepeques* pudiera Ud. ver esos picos." (1)

El sustantivo *jaltepeque* se deriva de la lengua nahuatl: se compone de *xalli* (*jal-li*)="arena," y de *tepetl*= "cerro;" significa, pues, "cerro de arena."

Estos vocablos *xalli* y *tepetl* son de origen quiché: el primero de ellos se compone de *tza*="cosa salobre," y de *lil*, raíz de *litil*="llano, plano;" de

---

(1) En la hermosa bahía que está al Sur de Zacatecoluca se ha trabajado la sal desde hace muchísimos años, y probablemente á los numerosos montones de arena que fueron formándose en los bordes de la bahía, se daba el nombre de *Jaltepeque*, ó "Bahía de los *jaltepeques*" con que la conocemos.

De *xalli* se deriva *xaxalteyo*="pedregoso, lugar de piedras menudas."

# J

## CLXXVII

### Jagüey

(See the article *Chagüite*.)

## CLXXVIII

### Jaltepeque

Our salt-makers call *jaltepeques* the little mounds of *fresh sand* <note>original: "arena dulce," that is, sand from which the salt has been removed</note> that form in the salt works from the leftovers that remain after the salt is extracted from sand soaked by the sea. I remember that once, when I was at the port of El Triunfo trying to find a spot from which the volcanoes of San Vicente and San Miguel could be seen, a man said to me: "Perhaps, sir, you might see those peaks from those *jaltepeques*." (1)

The noun *jaltepeque* derives from the Nahuatl language. It is made up of *xalli* (*jal-li*), "sand," and *tepetl*, "hill"; it therefore means "hill of sand."

These words *xalli* and *tepetl* are of K'iche' origin. The first is made up of *tza*, "brackish thing," and *lil*, root of *litil*, "plain, flat"; so

---

(1) In the beautiful bay south of Zacatecoluca, salt has been worked for a great many years. Probably the many heaps of sand that gradually formed along the shores of the bay were called *Jaltepeque*, whence the name "Bay of the *jaltepeques*" by which we know it.

From *xalli* derives *xaxalteyo*, "stony, a place of small stones."

Antes de hacerlas nos asaltó la duda en el argumento que nos hicimos de no tenerse noticias en Yucatán, ni aun en América, del caballo que supusieron los aborígenas parte integrante del ginete, cuando en el Egipto prestaban sus servicios tan útiles cuadrúpedos en los carros de guerra.

Consultamos la historia, hallando en la Sagrada, que Salomón mandó comprar caballos al Egipto un mil años antes de J. C. Sin otro antecedente para un cálculo retrospectivo que debía datar de muchas centurias, pues de la venta no podía deducirse sino que ya existían y de ningún modo la fecha de su importación al país de Misraim, las notas del sabio alemán citado nos hacen saber que los caballos y coches no se importaron al Egipto sino antes del tercer milenario de nuestra Era.
