<meta>continues from previous page</meta>upon their strokes, once mysterious and undecipherable. The famous German Egyptologist already mentioned, Mr. Ebers, gives an account of them in the most interesting notes to *An Egyptian Princess* <note>original: "La hija del rey de Egipto"</note>, which we have consulted in our study, as well as the no less important work of Don Ramiro Fernández de Valbuena entitled *Assyria and Egypt Resurrected* <note>original: "La Asiria y el Egipto resucitados"</note>, which we have also had before us as a basis for our assertions.

<note>Ebers's historical novel *Eine ägyptische Königstochter* (1864) was published with extensive scholarly notes. Ramiro Fernández Valbuena was a Spanish priest and writer on biblical archaeology.</note>

Before making these assertions, a doubt assailed us in an objection we raised to ourselves: that nothing was known in Yucatán, nor even in America, of the horse, which the natives supposed to be part of the rider himself, whereas in Egypt these very useful quadrupeds served in the war chariots.

<note>The author refers to accounts that Indigenous peoples, on first seeing mounted Spaniards, took horse and rider for a single creature.</note>

We consulted history, finding in Sacred History that Solomon ordered horses to be bought from Egypt a thousand years before Christ. There was no other antecedent for a retrospective calculation, which would have to reach back many centuries, since from that purchase one could only deduce that horses already existed there, and in no way the date of their importation into the land of Mizraim. But the notes of the learned German just cited tell us that horses and chariots were not imported into Egypt until before the third millennium of our era.

<note>See 1 Kings 10:28–29. The author's phrase is confusing; Ebers placed the introduction of the horse into Egypt in the period of the Hyksos, in the second millennium BC.</note>

...where feet agree in a simple to double ratio, I pronounce the verse, I do not offend the judgment of your sense with any deceit. And yet that sound which is produced by shorter and, as it were, more fleeting syllables cannot occupy more time than it sounds. But if those judicial numbers were held by the bond of time in as much space as these sounding ones are arranged, they would not be able to attain the judgment of those sounding ones which are produced a little more lengthily by the same iambic law. Therefore, the delay of times does not hold those (numbers) which preside over judging. But if they were held by nothing, however much more lengthily I might utter sounds in iambic rhythm with suitable and mutually corresponding intervals, nevertheless they would be used for judging. But now, if I were to utter one syllable with the delay (not to say much) of three steps of someone walking, and another (syllable) with double (that delay), and thus in sequence I were to arrange such long iambs of simple and double (ratios), that law would nevertheless be preserved; yet we would not be able to apply that natural judgment to approving these dimensions. Therefore, those judicial (numbers) are also held by certain limits of temporal spaces, which they cannot exceed in judging; and whatever exceeds these spaces, they do not attain so as to judge. Yet these temper individual actions. For that which restrains and checks us in any attention of doing something with the limbs of the body from unequal movements – whether walking with unequal steps, or striking with unequal intervals of blows, or eating with unequal movements of the jaws, and finally scratching with unequal movements of the nails – and tacitly commands a certain equality, that very thing is a certain judicial something, which causes humans to have a sense and appreciation of beauty and decorum more than beasts, who rush to any of their impulses for the sake of appeasing bodily passion, and are not attracted by the grace and desire for beauty. Hence horses do not choose a more beautiful mare to love, but are drawn to any (mare) with equal frenzy. But that judicial (something) suggests God as the creator of animals, whom it certainly befits to believe as the author of all suitability and harmony. Furthermore, numbers, both those that are in sound and those that are made in sensing—I say, then, memory can preserve their intervals—to that extent they are offered to those judicial (numbers) for judging and are judged. ### *De Quæstionibus Astronomiæ.*

PRincipia Astronomiæ quæ sunt ? Solutio. Vade ad rubricam antedictam. Astronomus considerat ante in sole habitum caloris quam lucis? Solutio. Nullus habitus appropriatus est ita considerabilis sicut habitus proprius. Astronomus quomodo facit iudicium? Solutio. Astronomus considerat respectum, quem vnum signū habet cum alio, & quem habet cum vna planeta per respectum lineæ diametricæ, & facit iudicium de hominibus qui nascuntur in illa linea, aut qui in illa faciunt, petitiones quos iudicat secundum conditiones signi & planetæ. Et valde ad rubricam virtutis. Quare scientia astronomiæ magis incerta est quam alia ? Solutio. de nulla scientia est ita grauis experientia sicut de astronomia, nec aliqua scientia est ita positiua sicut illa.

**Chapitre XXVI. — Des actes raisonnables de quelques animaux.**

Les actes de certains animaux qui paraissent attester une inspiration de la raison, comme, entre mille, ceux-ci, qui sont les plus connus : le gouvernement des abeilles, la prévoyance des fourmis, l'habileté de l'araignée à tendre ses filets, sont-ils l'œuvre d'une raison propre à ces animaux ? Cette raison serait alors ou supérieure, ou inférieure, ou égale à celle de l'homme. Mais si ces animaux avaient une raison plus éclairée que la nôtre, dans toutes ou presque toutes les circonstances ils agiraient mieux que l'homme, et il est visible que le plus souvent ils restent au-dessous de lui. Si cette raison était inférieure, chacun d'eux ne s'attacherait pas exclusivement à un seul ouvrage pour le porter presque à la perfection ; car il semble que ce soit le propre d'une intelligence accomplie et supérieure à celle de l'homme de s'appliquer toujours à un seul ouvrage pour le rendre le plus parfait possible. Si enfin leur esprit était égal à celui de l'homme, il ne se concentrerait pas ainsi sur un seul travail, pour se montrer ensuite dans tout le reste inférieur aux œuvres humaines. Il est donc évident que les animaux obéissent, non pas à une raison individuelle, mais à l'influence de cette âme qui gouverne notre monde, et des intelligences abstraites qu'elle fait présider à chacun de ces êtres et auxquelles elle attache chacun

TREATISE ON THE LAWS, II.

81

**Chapter XXVI. On the rational acts of certain animals.**

Consider the acts of certain animals that seem to show the inspiration of reason. Among a thousand examples, take these best-known ones: the government of bees, the foresight of ants, and the skill of the spider in spreading its nets. Are these the work of a reason belonging to these animals themselves? If so, this reason would be either superior, inferior, or equal to that of man. But if these animals had a reason more enlightened than ours, they would act better than man in all or nearly all circumstances; and it is plain that most of the time they fall short of him. If this reason were inferior, each of them would not devote itself exclusively to a single work and bring it almost to perfection; for it seems to be the mark of an accomplished intelligence, superior to man's, always to apply itself to a single work so as to make it as perfect as possible. Finally, if their mind were equal to man's, it would not concentrate in this way on a single task, only to show itself inferior to human works in everything else. It is therefore evident that animals obey, not an individual reason, but the influence of that soul which governs our world, and of the abstract intelligences <note>the "separate intelligences" of the Greek text, immaterial minds standing apart from bodies</note> which it sets over each of these beings, and to which it attaches each

# ON SPIRIT.

What is the duration of the innate spirit <term>pneuma</term> <gloss>breath, spirit</gloss>, and what is its growth? We see that it becomes greater and stronger both according to changes in age and the condition of the body. Or is it like other parts, with something added to it? Nourishment is added to living things, so we must consider what kind it is and where it comes from. There are two ways through which it occurs: either through respiration, or through the digestion that accompanies the intake of food, just as in other things. Perhaps it would not seem less likely that it is through food, for body is nourished by body, and the spirit is a body. What then is the method? It is clearly through the vein by some sort of suction and digestion, for blood is the final nourishment and the same for all. Just as it takes nourishment into its vessel and into that which is contained, it takes it into the heat. The air acts by creating energy, that is, digestive energy; by adding to itself, it grows and nourishes. Perhaps there is nothing strange in this very thing, but that it first comes from nourishment. For what is innate to the soul is purer, unless one says that the soul also comes later, as the seeds are separated and move toward nature. If it is the residue of all nourishment, how is it transmitted? It is not reasonable to say through expiration, for it immediately perceives. It remains clear that it is through the pores of the artery. That which is secreted is either thinner or thicker. In both cases, it is strange if this is to be the purest of all. If it were thicker, there would be larger pores. But if it takes in and sends out through the same ones, this itself is irrational and strange. Such is the growth and duration from nourishment.

<margin>2</margin> The growth from respiration, as Aristogenes thinks (for he thinks the spirit also is nourished by being digested, not by air being in the spirit; but that this is distributed into the vessels, and the residue is sent back out), involves more difficulties. For by what is the digestion performed? It is likely by itself, just as the others are. But this itself is strange, unless it differs from the outside air; in that case, the heat would be doing the digesting. And indeed, it is reasonable for it to be thicker, being with the moisture from the vessels and the whole mass, so that the digestion would be into the bodily. But that the residue becomes thinner is not plausible. The speed of the digestion is also irrational. For expiration occurs immediately after inspiration. What then is the thing that changes and alters it so quickly? One might most likely suppose the heat, and sensation bears witness to how; for the air being breathed out is hot. If the digestion is in the lung and the artery, the power of the heat is in these, which they do not say, but rather that the food is heated by the movement of the spirit. But if it is drawn from somewhere else, or received while moving, that is more wonderful. At the same time, it is the first thing that moves. But if respiration is only up to the lung, as they themselves say, while the innate spirit is throughout the whole body, and if it is distributed from this down to the lower parts and to the others, how is the digestion so quick? This is more wonderful and greater; for it would have to transmit this air to the lower parts immediately upon being digested. And yet this might seem necessary if digestion happens in the lung, with both the respiration and the lower parts participating. But the outcome is even greater and more paradoxical; for digestion happens only by way of passage and contact. This is also irrational and less logical if the same account applies to the nourishment and the residue. If it is through some other internal part, the same arguments apply as before, unless one says that not all nourishment and not for everyone does digestion occur...

<summary>This page explores the source and nature of the innate pneuma, debating whether it is nourished by respiration or by digestion, and critiquing the theories of Aristogenes regarding the speed and mechanism of these processes.</summary>

μίτιδος non autem παρθενίου. Neque inde tamen nobis facile persuadebitur hanc non esse veram genuinamque Clementis nostri vocem. Nulli siquidem dubitamus ab illo sensum potius Platonis quam verba exhiberi. Quapropter si nullus ibi ipsius memoriæ lapsus fuerit, vocem παρθενίου potius quam κεραμίτιδος ab eo usurpatam credimus, tum quia utraque vox idem significat, quando quidem creta est terra, qua nemo unquam usus fuit; tum quia ea vox ad suum de sacra Scriptura, quam ille, ut infra dicetur, cum Virgine Deipara alibi componit, propositum magis faciebat. Has porro voces παρθενίου γῆς, quas Hervetus nullibi se legisse dicit, ab alio in suis ad Clementis nostri opera scholiis scite observatur in Nicandri *Alexipharmacis* reperiri. Addamus obiter, si velis, alio sensu virginem terram a Tertulliano accipi pro terra nec pluviis rigata, nec imbribus fecundata, ex qua Adam et Christus plasmati sunt: « Utique, inquit, illa terra virgo, nondum pluviis rigata, nec imbribus fecundata, ex qua homo tunc primum plasmatus est, ex qua nunc Christus secundum carnem ex virgine natus est ¹⁶. »

*Stromatum* suorum argumenta ubi paulo post Clemens explicat, ex illis unum sic proponit: Καὶ τούτοις ἀντερεῖ πάνθ' ὅσα προοικονομηθῆναι καθήκει τῆς κατὰ **140** τὴν ὑποπτικὴν θεωρίαν γνώσεως ¹⁷. Quod in ultima editione sic Latine redditum est: « Et adversus ea dicet, quæcunque ante propheticam contemplationem prius dispensata esse oportet. » Atque ita quidem Hervetus se prius ex Clementis Græcis Latina olim fecisse aperte declarat. Sed re maturius expensa, pro ὑποπτικὴν legendum esse ait ἐποπτικὴν θεωρίαν, hoc est « inspectivam seu speculatoriam contemplationem. » Vult enim Clementem ibi alludere ad mysteria Græcorum, quibus ea cum aspicere liceret, tunc, ut infra dicemus ¹⁸, hi ἐπόπται vocabantur. Qui tamen posteriori horum *Stromatum* editioni præfuerunt, spreta illa Herveti correctione, quæ sensui auctoris omnino consentanea ipsis forsitan non videbatur, verbum Græcum ὑποπτικὴν, et Latinum « propheticam » censuerunt esse retinendum. Et vero in Græco nostro manuscripto codice idem verbum habetur. Nihil ergo in textu Græco, nisi accedat major alterius cujusdam manuscripti auctoritas, quidquam mutandum est. Vox autem ὑποπτικὴ quid ibi significet si roges, tibi respondebimus ὕποπτος, teste Julio Polluce, non solum idem ac « suspectus, » sed quandoque « inspiciens, » significare. Quamobrem illius interpres verbum ὕποπτοι Latine « inspectores » reddidit. Atqui vox ὑποπτικὴ si eo significatu accipi possit, hic Clementis locus in Latinum sermonem ita convertendus est: « Atque (sermo noster) ea indicabit quæcunque aut dispensari convenit ante inspicientis seu inspectricis contemplationis cognitionem, γνώσεως. » Verbum enim ἀντέρω interdum « renuntio, denuntio et indico » significare certum est. Eo porro significatu illud, atque ipso, quo diximus, sensu vocem ὑποπτικὴν ibi a Clemente usurpari ex his, quæ continuo ille subtexuit, et ipsismet, quæ in toto opere pertractat, argumentis haud obscure colligitur. Si quis vero aliam veriorem horum verborum interpretationem, aliumque sincerum illorum sensum assecutus fuerit, hunc nobis si suggerere voluerit, maximas sane et debitas ei gratias referemus.

Notat porro Hervetus alibi Clementis textui tenebras perquam densissimas offundi, atque in illo librariorum oscitantia aliquid depravatum vel hiulcum et mutilum esse, ubi Mosaicæ legis benignitate eo demonstrata argumento, quia arbores nuper plantatas tribus annis ali et foveri, quartoque anno eas Deo consecrari jubet, hæc Clemens subjunxit:

<column-break/>

« Quarto anno, quoniam tempore quoque opus est ei, qui stabiliter per catechesin instituitur, quaternio virtutum Deo consecratur, cum tertia jam sola subjungatur cum quarta Domini hypostasi; sacrificium autem laudis super holocausta. » Τῷ τε γὰρ τετάρτῳ ἔτει, ἐπεὶ καὶ χρόνου χρεία τῷ κατηχουμένῳ βεβαίως, ἡ τετρὰς τῶν ἀρετῶν καθιεροῦται τῷ Θεῷ τῆς τρίτης ἤδη μόνης συναπτούσης ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου τετάρτην ὑπόστασιν. Θυσία δὲ αἰνέσεως ὑπὲρ ὁλοκαυτώματα ¹⁹. Hervetus itaque hæc se non intelligere fatetur. Conjicit tamen, « ex hoc intelligi, » ita ille loquitur, « perfectam illam esse fidem, quæ tres complectitur hypostases, seu personas, quarum tertia, nempe Filii hypostasis, sola conjungitur cum quarta hypostasi Domini, nempe cum humana natura. » Quæ quidem cum ante susceptam a Filio carnem, ab ejus persona esset separata, videtur aliqua ratione dici posse quarta hypostasis, tametsi reapse in Christo, humana carne induto, una tantum divina persona sit. Quocirca nos serio ea de re monitos esse vult, ne inde in Nestorii errorem imprudentes prolabamur.

Sed tantum abest ut hac explicatione obscura hujus loci discutiatur caligo; quin ei potius longe major aspergatur. Quis enim facile sibi persuadeat Clementem ibi de triplici Dei persona, et de quarta improprie dicta humanitatis Christi hypostasi fuisse locutum? Quomodo in illum de divinis personis, de quibus nihil plane neque prius, neque posterius dicit vel insinuat, sermonem delapsus est? Qua denique ratione Hervetus probabit ibi Clementem verbo ὑπόστασις personam, seu, ut aiunt, personalitatem intellexisse. Neminem certe fugit ab antiquis scriptoribus, qui ante et post Clementis ætatem scripserunt, illud nomen ad naturam, seu idem atque οὐσία, significandum sæpissime adhiberi. Quin etiam si Hieronymo credamus: « Tota sæcularium litterarum schola nihil aliud hypostasin, nisi usiam novit ²⁰. »

Nobis ergo Clementem non de divinis personis, sed de quaternione virtutum, quas vulgo cardinales nuncupant, loqui facilius probabitur. Vox enim ὑπόστασις ibi nihil aliud significare videtur, quam id quod stat et subsistit, seu firmum rei alicujus semperque immobilem consistendi statum. Quamobrem verum Clementis sensum hunc esse putamus: quaternio virtutum Deo consecratur, tertia sola, nimirum justitia, hominem quartæ Domini ὑποστάσει, hoc est firmo nec mutationis amplius obnoxio Domini statui conjungente. Vult enim doctus ille vir, hac quaternione virtutum hominem Christianum Deo, quoad ejus fieri potest, assimilari, ac quiescentibus animi perturbationibus, ad permanentem nullique mutationi obnoxium Dei statum, quantum fieri licet, accedere, pervenire ac ipsi inhærere. Hanc porro esse Clementis mentem ea plane demonstrant, quæ ille dixerat de quatuor illis virtutibus, atque ibidem de « gnostico, » seu perfecto Christiano addidit: « Hic est enim, inquit, ad Dei imaginem et similitudinem gnosticus, qui Deum imitatur, quoad ejus fieri potest, nihil prætermittens eorum, quæ faciunt ad eam, quæ contingere potest, similitudinem, continens, sustinens, juste vivens, imperans animi perturbationibus, ea quæ habet impartiens, pro viribus benefaciens et verbo et opere. » Subsequentia porro verba: « Sacrificium laudis super holocausta, » quomodo cum superioribus cohæreant, etiamsi dictu difficillimum esse fateamur, eorum tamen is sensus dici potest: Hanc virtutum quaternionem qui adeptus fuerit, ab illo sacrificium, holocautomatis longe præstantius, ipsimet Deo offerri. Si quis nihilominus aliam ostendat fuisse auctoris nostri mentem, huic manus dabimus, atque nos ab eo vinci lubenter patiemur.

Cæterum nulli certe mirum videri debet quatuor

---

<meta>continues from previous page: the discussion concerns whether Clement wrote "κεραμίτιδος" (of potter's clay) or "παρθενίου" (virgin) earth in his paraphrase of Plato. The source language of this page is Latin with embedded Greek, not Greek alone. Column section letters A, B, C, D and the bold earlier-edition page number 140 are noted in the OCR.</meta>

of potter's clay <note>original: "κεραμίτιδος"</note>, not "virgin" <note>original: "παρθενίου"</note>. Yet this will not easily persuade us that the latter is not the true and genuine word of our Clement. For we have no doubt at all that he is giving the sense of Plato rather than his exact words. Therefore, unless his memory slipped at this point, we believe that he used the word "virgin" rather than "of potter's clay." First, because both words mean the same thing, since chalk is earth that no one has ever used. Second, because that word better served his purpose with regard to Sacred Scripture, which, as will be said below, he elsewhere compares with the Virgin Mother of God <note>original: "Virgine Deipara"</note>. Moreover, these words "virgin earth" <note>original: "παρθενίου γῆς"</note>, which Hervetus says he never read anywhere, are shrewdly observed by another scholar, in his notes on the works of our Clement, to be found in the *Alexipharmaca* of Nicander. <note>Gentian Hervet (Hervetus) was a sixteenth-century French humanist who translated Clement into Latin. Nicander of Colophon wrote the Alexipharmaca, a Greek poem on poisons and their antidotes.</note> Let us add in passing, if you like, that Tertullian takes "virgin earth" in another sense: earth not yet watered by rains nor made fruitful by showers, from which Adam and Christ were formed. "Certainly," he says, "that earth was a virgin, not yet watered by rains nor made fertile by showers, from which man was then first formed, just as now Christ according to the flesh was born of a virgin ¹⁶."

Where Clement, a little later, sets out the subjects of his *Stromata*, he proposes one of them as follows: "And it will speak in reply to all those things which ought to be arranged beforehand for the knowledge that belongs to the **140** 'hypoptic' contemplation ¹⁷." <note>original: "Καὶ τούτοις ἀντερεῖ πάνθ' ὅσα προοικονομηθῆναι καθήκει τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὑποπτικὴν θεωρίαν γνώσεως"</note> In the most recent edition this was rendered into Latin thus: "And it will speak against those things which must first be arranged before prophetic contemplation." Hervetus openly declares that he had once made this Latin version from Clement's Greek. But after weighing the matter more maturely, he says that instead of *hypoptikēn* one should read *epoptikēn theōrian*, that is, "inspective or speculative contemplation." He holds that Clement is alluding here to the mysteries of the Greeks: those who were permitted to behold them were then called *epoptai* <gloss>beholders, the highest grade of initiates</gloss>, as we shall explain below ¹⁸. Those who oversaw the later edition of these *Stromata*, however, rejected Hervetus's correction, which perhaps did not seem to them fully consistent with the author's meaning. They judged that the Greek word *hypoptikēn* and the Latin "prophetic" should be kept. And indeed the same word is found in our Greek manuscript. Nothing in the Greek text should therefore be changed, unless the greater authority of some other manuscript is brought forward.

If you ask what the word *hypoptikē* means here, we will answer that *hypoptos*, according to Julius Pollux, means not only "suspected" but sometimes also "one who inspects." <note>Julius Pollux was a second-century Greek grammarian whose Onomasticon is a thesaurus of Greek vocabulary.</note> For this reason his translator rendered the word *hypoptoi* in Latin as "inspectors." Now, if *hypoptikē* can be taken in that sense, this passage of Clement should be turned into Latin as follows: "And (our discourse) will set forth all those things that ought to be arranged before the knowledge <note>original: "γνώσεως"</note> of inspecting, or observing, contemplation." For it is certain that the verb *anterō* sometimes means "I announce, declare, and indicate." That Clement uses the verb in this meaning, and the word *hypoptikē* in the sense we have given, can be gathered quite clearly from what he immediately adds, and from the very subjects he treats throughout the whole work. But if anyone arrives at another, truer interpretation of these words and their genuine sense, and is willing to suggest it to us, we shall give that person the greatest and most deserved thanks.

Hervetus further notes that elsewhere very thick darkness is cast over Clement's text, and that through the carelessness of copyists something in it has been corrupted, left gaping, or mutilated. This is the passage where Clement shows the kindness of the Mosaic Law by the argument that it commands newly planted trees to be nourished and tended for three years, and in the fourth year consecrated to God. <note>See Leviticus 19:23–25.</note> To this Clement added the following:

<column-break/>

"In the fourth year, since time is also needed by one who is being firmly instructed through catechesis, the foursome of the virtues is consecrated to God, the third alone now joining with the fourth hypostasis of the Lord; and the sacrifice of praise is above burnt offerings." <note>original: "Τῷ τε γὰρ τετάρτῳ ἔτει, ἐπεὶ καὶ χρόνου χρεία τῷ κατηχουμένῳ βεβαίως, ἡ τετρὰς τῶν ἀρετῶν καθιεροῦται τῷ Θεῷ τῆς τρίτης ἤδη μόνης συναπτούσης ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου τετάρτην ὑπόστασιν. Θυσία δὲ αἰνέσεως ὑπὲρ ὁλοκαυτώματα"</note> ¹⁹ Hervetus admits that he does not understand this. Still, he conjectures, in his own words, "that from this we are to understand that faith is perfect which embraces three hypostases, or persons, of which the third, namely the hypostasis of the Son, alone is joined with the fourth hypostasis of the Lord, namely with the human nature." Since the human nature was separate from the Son's person before he took on flesh, it seems that in some way it could be called a fourth hypostasis, even though in reality there is only one divine person in Christ, clothed in human flesh. For this reason Hervetus wants us to be seriously warned not to slip unawares into the error of Nestorius. <note>Nestorius, fifth-century bishop of Constantinople, was condemned for teaching what opponents saw as a division of Christ into two persons.</note>

But this explanation is so far from dispelling the darkness of the passage that it rather spreads a much greater darkness over it. Who could easily persuade himself that Clement was speaking here about the three persons of God, and about a "fourth hypostasis," improperly so called, of Christ's humanity? How would he have slipped into a discussion of the divine persons, about which he says or hints nothing at all either before or after? And finally, how will Hervetus prove that Clement here understood by the word *hypostasis* a person, or, as they say, personality? Surely no one is unaware that ancient writers, both before and after Clement's time, very often used that word to mean nature, that is, the same as *ousia* <gloss>essence, substance</gloss>. Indeed, if we believe Jerome: "The whole school of secular learning knows *hypostasis* as nothing other than *ousia* ²⁰."

It will therefore be easier for us to prove that Clement is speaking not of the divine persons but of the foursome of virtues commonly called cardinal. <note>The four cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.</note> The word *hypostasis* here seems to mean nothing other than that which stands and subsists, that is, the firm and ever-immovable state of a thing's existence. We therefore think Clement's true meaning is this: the foursome of the virtues is consecrated to God, while the third alone, namely justice, joins the human being to the fourth *hypostasis* of the Lord, that is, to the firm state of the Lord that is no longer subject to change. For that learned man means that through this foursome of virtues the Christian is made like God, as far as possible, and that, once the passions of the soul are at rest, he approaches, reaches, and clings to the permanent and unchanging state of God, so far as is allowed.

That this is Clement's thought is plainly shown by what he had said about those four virtues, and by what he added in the same place about the "gnostic," that is, the perfect Christian: "For this," he says, "is the gnostic made after the image and likeness of God, who imitates God as far as he can, neglecting nothing that leads to the likeness that is attainable: self-controlled, enduring, living justly, ruling over the passions of the soul, sharing what he has, doing good as far as he is able, both in word and in deed." As for the following words, "the sacrifice of praise is above burnt offerings," we admit it is very hard to say how they connect with what precedes. Yet their sense can be stated thus: whoever has attained this foursome of virtues offers to God himself a sacrifice far more excellent than a burnt offering. If anyone nevertheless shows that our author meant something else, we shall yield to that person and gladly let ourselves be overcome.

For the rest, it certainly ought to seem strange to no one that the four

<summary>The editor defends Clement's reading "virgin earth" and keeps the manuscript reading "hypoptic contemplation" against Hervetus's emendation to "epoptic." He then rejects Hervetus's Trinitarian reading of a difficult passage on the "fourth hypostasis," arguing instead that Clement means the four cardinal virtues uniting the Christian to God's unchanging state.</summary>

They knew him from afar as he drew near,—gathered around him,—and then assailed him with taunts from this side and from that, every man of them,—calling him 'that kinsman of the maniac, of the plotter against the host,'—saying that he should not save himself from being mangled to death by stoning. And so they had come to this, that swords plucked from sheaths were drawn in men's hands; then the strife, when it had run well-nigh to the furthest, was allayed by the soothing words of elders. But where shall I find Ajax, to tell him this? He whom most it touches must hear all the tale.

CH. He is not within; he hath gone forth but now; for he hath yoked a new purpose to his new mood.

**730** *κολεῶν*] *κουλεῶν* r.—*διεπεραιώθη*] The scribe of L wrote *διεπαιρεώθη* (transposing ε and αι): S has corrected ε to αι, but the αι after π has been allowed to remain: a later hand has placed dots over it. **733** *πού στιν* L, with the mark of aphaeresis (') just over π, not in front of σ: a curious error, suggestive of mechanical copying. **735 f.** Nauck, objecting to *ἐγκαταζεύξας*, would write, *οὐκ ἔνδον ἀνήρ, ἀλλὰ φροῦδος ἀρτίως, | βουλὰς νέας νέοισιν ἁρμόσας τρόποις.*

---

dying: schol. *ὡς οὐκ ἀρκέσοι ἑαυτῷ τὸ μὴ λιθόλευστος γενέσθαι.* Cp. Aesch. *P. V.* 918 *οὐδὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ ταῦτ' ἐπαρκέσει τὸ μὴ οὐ | πεσεῖν ἀτίμως.* For the fut. optat., cp. 313.—**καταξανθείς**, carded (like wool), torn to shreds; Eur. imitates this (*Suppl.* 503) *πέτροις καταξανθέντες ὀστέων ῥαφάς.* Cp. Ar. *Ach.* 319 *τί φειδόμεσθα τῶν λίθων, ὦ δημόται, | μὴ οὐ καταξαίνειν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον εἰς φοινικίδα;*

**729 f.** **ὥστ'** ('and so') has been suspected on account of the second **ὥστε**: but the latter, going with **τοσοῦτον**, does not offend the ear, since its sense is different and subordinate; cp. *Ant.* 735 *ὁρᾷς τόδ' ὡς εἴρηκας ὡς ἄγαν νέος*; *Tr.* 1241 *τάχ', ὡς ἔοικας, ὡς νοσεῖς φράσεις.* So in Xen. *Anab.* 2. 2. 17 *κραυγὴν.. ἐποίουν,.. ὥστε καὶ τοὺς πολεμίους ἀκούειν· ὥστε οἱ μὲν ἐγγυτάτω.. ἔφυγον*: where the first *ὥστε* = 'so that,' while the second = 'and so.'

**κολεῶν.. ξίφη.** The swords **διεπεραιώθη** *κολεῶν*, were drawn through (and out of) the scabbards, **ἐρυστά**, by a sharp, quick pull,—*i.e.* with angry haste.—Not, 'swords plucked from the sheaths were *crossed*': as if Teucer actually crossed swords with one or more of his assailants. The whole scene has been suggested by that in the first book of the *Iliad*, as the schol. in L saw:—*ἐκ τῆς Ἀχιλλέως δὲ πρὸς Ἀγαμέμνονα ἀρχῆς* (read *ὀργῆς*) *παραγέγραπται.* There, Achilles was drawing his sword—*ἕλκετο δ' ἐκ κολεοῖο μέγα ξίφος*—when Athena came to him

<column-break/>

(*Il.* 1. 194): *ἂψ δ' ἐς κουλεὸν ὦσε μέγα ξίφος* (*ib.* 220).—Some of the later MSS. here have **κουλεῶν**, which was a current form in late Greek (Eustathius p. 1604. 58 *τὸ κολεὸν κοινότερον κουλεὸν λέγεται*).

**731 f.** **δραμοῦσα τοῦ προσωτάτω**: for the partitive gen., cp. Xen. *Anab.* 1. 3. 1 *οὐκ ἔφασαν ἰέναι τοῦ πρόσω*: Ar. *Ran.* 174 *ὑπάγεθ' ὑμεῖς τῆς ὁδοῦ.*—**ἐν ξυναλλαγῇ λόγου.. γερόντων**, by means of the conciliatory words of elders: for the double gen., cp. 308 f.: for **ἐν**, denoting the instrument, *Ph.* 60 *ἐν λιταῖς στείλαντες*, *ib.* 1393 *ἐν λόγοις | πείσειν.*

**733 f.** **ἡμὶν**, ethic dat.: *O. C.* 81 *ἦ βέβηκεν ἡμὶν ὁ ξένος;*—**τοῖς κυρίοις**, *i.e.*, Ajax himself, who is the *κύριος* or 'principal person' in this matter, as being most nearly concerned in it. For the poet. plur., cp. Aesch. *Ch.* 688 (Orestes to Clytaemnestra) *εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω | τοῖς κυρίοισι καὶ προσήκουσιν λέγων | οὐκ οἶδα.*

**735 f.** **νέας βουλάς**, his new 'counsels,' in respect of his supposed resolve to propitiate gods and men; **νέοισιν.. τρόποις**, the new 'dispositions,' the character of greater gentleness and docility, which the resolve implies. **ἐγκαταζεύξας**: he has 'harnessed' the new resolve, as it were, to the new character,—brought it under the yoke of his chastened will. The word conveys more than the idea of 'adapting' (Pindar's *ἔργμασιν νικαφόροις ἐγκώμιον ζεῦξαι μέλος*, *N.* 1. 7). It further implies self-conquest.

They knew him from afar as he drew near, gathered around him, and then assailed him with taunts from this side and from that, every man of them, calling him 'that kinsman of the maniac, of the plotter against the host,' saying that he should not save himself from being mangled to death by stoning. And so they had come to this, that swords plucked from sheaths were drawn in men's hands; then the strife, when it had run well-nigh to the furthest, was allayed by the soothing words of elders. But where shall I find Ajax, to tell him this? He whom most it touches must hear all the tale.

CHORUS. He is not within; he hath gone forth but now; for he hath yoked a new purpose to his new mood.

**730** *<term>koleōn</term>* <gloss>from the sheaths</gloss>: some later manuscripts read *<term>kouleōn</term>*.—*<term>dieperaiōthē</term>* <gloss>were drawn through</gloss>: The scribe of L <note>the Laurentian manuscript in Florence, the oldest and most important manuscript of Sophocles</note> wrote *<term>diepaireōthē</term>* (transposing e and ai). S <note>a corrector of L</note> has corrected e to ai, but the ai after p has been allowed to remain; a later hand has placed dots over it. **733** *<term>pou stin</term>* <gloss>where is he?</gloss> in L, with the mark of <term>aphaeresis</term> <gloss>the dropping of an initial vowel</gloss> (') placed just over the p, not in front of the s: a curious error, suggestive of mechanical copying. **735 f.** Nauck, objecting to *<term>enkatazeuxas</term>* <gloss>having yoked</gloss>, would write: "The man is not within, but gone just now, having fitted new counsels to new ways." <note>original: "οὐκ ἔνδον ἀνήρ, ἀλλὰ φροῦδος ἀρτίως, | βουλὰς νέας νέοισιν ἁρμόσας τρόποις."</note>

---

dying: the scholiast explains, "that it would not avail him to escape being stoned." <note>original: "ὡς οὐκ ἀρκέσοι ἑαυτῷ τὸ μὴ λιθόλευστος γενέσθαι."</note> Compare Aeschylus, *Prometheus Bound* 918: "for these things will in no way suffice to save him from falling dishonourably." <note>original: "οὐδὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ ταῦτ' ἐπαρκέσει τὸ μὴ οὐ | πεσεῖν ἀτίμως."</note> For the future optative, compare line 313.—**<term>kataxantheis</term>** <gloss>carded</gloss>, carded like wool, that is, torn to shreds. Euripides imitates this (*Suppliants* 503): "carded by stones in the seams of their bones." <note>original: "πέτροις καταξανθέντες ὀστέων ῥαφάς."</note> Compare Aristophanes, *Acharnians* 319: "Why do we spare our stones, fellow demesmen, instead of carding this fellow into a scarlet rag?" <note>original: "τί φειδόμεσθα τῶν λίθων, ὦ δημόται, | μὴ οὐ καταξαίνειν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον εἰς φοινικίδα;" The "scarlet rag" puns on the red cloak of Athenian soldiers.</note>

**729 f.** **<term>hōst'</term>** <gloss>and so</gloss> has been suspected on account of the second **<term>hōste</term>**. But the latter, going with **<term>tosouton</term>** <gloss>so far</gloss>, does not offend the ear, since its sense is different and subordinate. Compare *Antigone* 735: "Do you see how you have spoken this, like one far too young?" <note>original: "ὁρᾷς τόδ' ὡς εἴρηκας ὡς ἄγαν νέος"</note>; *Trachiniae* 1241: "Soon, it seems, you will show how sick you are." <note>original: "τάχ', ὡς ἔοικας, ὡς νοσεῖς φράσεις."</note> So also in Xenophon, *Anabasis* 2. 2. 17: "they raised a shout... so that even the enemy heard it; and so those nearest... fled." <note>original: "κραυγὴν.. ἐποίουν,.. ὥστε καὶ τοὺς πολεμίους ἀκούειν· ὥστε οἱ μὲν ἐγγυτάτω.. ἔφυγον"</note> Here the first *hōste* means 'so that,' while the second means 'and so.'

**<term>koleōn.. xiphē</term>** <gloss>swords... from the sheaths</gloss>. The swords **<term>dieperaiōthē</term>** *<term>koleōn</term>*, were drawn through and out of the scabbards, **<term>erusta</term>** <gloss>plucked</gloss>, by a sharp, quick pull, that is, with angry haste. The meaning is not 'swords plucked from the sheaths were *crossed*,' as if Teucer actually crossed swords with one or more of his assailants. The whole scene has been suggested by the one in the first book of the *Iliad*, as the scholiast in L saw: "it has been modelled on the anger of Achilles against Agamemnon" <note>original: "ἐκ τῆς Ἀχιλλέως δὲ πρὸς Ἀγαμέμνονα ἀρχῆς"; the manuscript reads <term>archēs</term> <gloss>beginning</gloss>, which Jebb corrects to <term>orgēs</term> <gloss>anger</gloss>.</note>. There, Achilles was drawing his sword, "and he was drawing his great sword from its sheath" <note>original: "ἕλκετο δ' ἐκ κολεοῖο μέγα ξίφος"</note>, when Athena came to him

<column-break/>

(*Iliad* 1. 194): "and back into the sheath he thrust the great sword" <note>original: "ἂψ δ' ἐς κουλεὸν ὦσε μέγα ξίφος"</note> (same book, line 220).—Some of the later manuscripts here have **<term>kouleōn</term>**, which was a current form in late Greek. Eustathius, p. 1604. 58, says: "the sheath, <term>koleon</term>, is more commonly called <term>kouleon</term>." <note>original: "τὸ κολεὸν κοινότερον κουλεὸν λέγεται." Eustathius was a 12th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator on Homer.</note>

**731 f.** **<term>dramousa tou prosōtatō</term>** <gloss>having run to the furthest point</gloss>: for the partitive genitive, compare Xenophon, *Anabasis* 1. 3. 1: "they said they would not go further" <note>original: "οὐκ ἔφασαν ἰέναι τοῦ πρόσω"</note>; Aristophanes, *Frogs* 174: "move along on your way" <note>original: "ὑπάγεθ' ὑμεῖς τῆς ὁδοῦ."</note>—**<term>en xunallagē logou.. gerontōn</term>** <gloss>by the reconciling speech of elders</gloss>, that is, by means of the conciliatory words of the elders. For the double genitive, compare lines 308 f. For **<term>en</term>** <gloss>in, by</gloss> denoting the instrument, compare *Philoctetes* 60: "having sent with entreaties" <note>original: "ἐν λιταῖς στείλαντες"</note>, and the same play, 1393: "to persuade by words" <note>original: "ἐν λόγοις | πείσειν."</note>

**733 f.** **<term>hēmin</term>** <gloss>for us</gloss>, an ethic dative, expressing the speaker's interest. Compare *Oedipus at Colonus* 81: "Has the stranger gone from us?" <note>original: "ἦ βέβηκεν ἡμὶν ὁ ξένος;"</note>—**<term>tois kuriois</term>** <gloss>to those with authority</gloss>, that is, Ajax himself, who is the *<term>kurios</term>* <gloss>principal person</gloss> in this matter, as the one most nearly concerned in it. For the poetic plural, compare Aeschylus, *Libation Bearers* 688, where Orestes says to Clytemnestra: "but whether I happen to be speaking to those with authority and concern in the matter, I do not know." <note>original: "εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω | τοῖς κυρίοισι καὶ προσήκουσιν λέγων | οὐκ οἶδα."</note>

**735 f.** **<term>neas boulas</term>** <gloss>new counsels</gloss>: his new 'counsels,' in respect of his supposed resolve to propitiate gods and men. **<term>neoisin.. tropois</term>** <gloss>to new ways</gloss>: the new 'dispositions,' the character of greater gentleness and docility which that resolve implies. **<term>enkatazeuxas</term>** <gloss>having yoked</gloss>: he has 'harnessed' the new resolve, as it were, to the new character, bringing it under the yoke of his chastened will. The word conveys more than the idea of 'adapting,' as in Pindar's "to yoke a song of praise to victorious deeds" <note>original: "ἔργμασιν νικαφόροις ἐγκώμιον ζεῦξαι μέλος"</note> (*Nemean Odes* 1. 7). It further implies self-conquest.

<summary>Jebb's English rendering of Ajax lines 727 to 736 describes how the Greek army threatened Teucer with stoning and drawn swords until the elders calmed them, and the Chorus reports that Ajax has gone out with a "new purpose." The textual notes and commentary discuss manuscript errors in L, the Homeric model for the sword-drawing scene, and grammatical points such as the partitive genitive, the ethic dative, and the force of the verb "yoked."</summary>

20b. ***Theology of Arithmetic*, p. 7 Ast.** And indeed Euripides, having been a student of Anaxagoras, mentions the earth thus: "The wise among mortals consider it <term>Hestia</term> <gloss>the Hearth</gloss>." Compare Euripides, fragment 944: "And Earth, mother: the wise among mortals call you Hestia, seated in the upper air."

21. **Gellius 15.20.** *Alexander Aetolus composed these verses about Euripides* <note>Meineke, *Analecta Alexandrina* 247</note>:

> The pupil of noble Anaxagoras seems to me harsh to speak with,
> a hater of laughter, who never learned to jest, not even over wine;
> but whatever he wrote, that was made of honey and of Sirens.

**Aelian, *Varied History* 8.13.** They say that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was never once seen laughing, nor even smiling at all.

22. **Athenaeus 5.220b.** His *Callias* <note>Aeschines the Socratic, fragment 16 Krauss</note> contains the quarrel of Callias with his father and the mockery of the sophists Prodicus and Anaxagoras <note>the editor queries this name</note>. For he says that Prodicus turned out Theramenes as his pupil, while the other <note>namely Anaxagoras</note> turned out Philoxenus son of Eryxis and Ariphrades, brother of Arignotus the lyre-singer. He wished to expose the teaching of the instructors through the wickedness of the men named and their greed for base pleasures.

23. **Alcidamas, quoted in Aristotle, *Rhetoric* 2.23, 1398b15.** And the people of Lampsacus buried Anaxagoras, though he was a foreigner, and they honor him even now.

24. **Aelian, *Varied History* 8.19** <note>following the epigram cited on p. 377, line 12</note>. And an altar stands for him, inscribed by some "To Mind" <note>original: "Nou"</note> and by others "To Truth" <note>original: "Aletheias"</note>.

25. **Diogenes Laertius 2.46** <note>compare p. 32, line 37, and p. 44, line 27</note>. As Aristotle says in the third book *On Poetics* <note>fragment 75</note>, Sosibius was a rival of Anaxagoras.

26. **Diogenes Laertius 10.12.** Of the ancients he <note>Epicurus; *Epicurea* p. 365, 16 Usener, compare his index p. 400</note> most approved of Anaxagoras, says Diocles, although he contradicted him on some points, and of Archelaus, the teacher of Socrates.

27. Coins of Clazomenae <note>legend: "of the Clazomenians"</note> probably show copies of statues set up there. The first type <note>around 100 BC</note> shows Anaxagoras seated facing left on a column drum, his right hand raised in teaching, his left on his knee. The second type <note>Imperial period</note> shows him standing facing right, upper body nude, his left foot set on a <term>cippus</term> <gloss>a low stone pillar</gloss>; his outstretched right hand holds the globe, and his left rests on his hip. Compare Poole, *Catalogue of Greek Coins of Ionia*, nos. 101 and 125, plate 7, nos. 4 and 9. Type 1 appears as the vignette in volume 2, part 2, 2nd edition, p. iii.

<summary>This page gathers ancient testimony on Anaxagoras's reputation and legacy: Euripides as his pupil, his famous gravity and refusal to laugh, his burial and altar to Mind and Truth at Lampsacus, Epicurus's regard for him, and coins of Clazomenae bearing his image. It then opens a section of his sayings, including his view that contemplation is the goal of life.</summary>

These spirits do nothing until they are united with the bodies, so that the bodies can hold them, since they are fugitive. So the spirits needed the bodies of necessity, and the adepts refined the bodies so that they would match the spirits through likeness. Then total mixture is achieved, and this happens only through putrefaction, dissolution and reduction, and settling; then mixture and washing; then total mixture. And this happens only through putrefaction.

Know that you dissolve these minerals with the moistures, which are the spirits, so that they become one water, like spirits within spirits. They have become equal, because the bodies have become spirits, running water within the water by which they were dissolved. When the bodies became spirits like the spirits that worked them, this soul, by which I mean the bodies, became subtle through the subtle, moist spirit, as subtle as the spirit that worked it. Then it distilled out of its vessel, being equal in subtlety. This is the balance of spirit with soul and soul with spirit: I mean that they became equal in subtlety, not in the balance of the Art. This is the <unclear>secret</unclear> explanation of the <unclear>crystallized secret</unclear> water, which distills from its vessel by that equality, unknown to the disciples and the learned. If the soul were dense, it would not distill from its vessel.

The aim of distillation is <unclear>that what is spoiled</unclear> does not return. It dissolves the earth, for unless the earth is dissolved many times, until every subtle part following it has left it, God would bring forth no crop from it. The spoiled never becomes sound again; but the sound may become spoiled, as wine turns to vinegar, and it is impossible for vinegar to become wine. We say that unless the body is loosened, it does not dissolve, and the husk is not told apart from the kernel.

The sages agree on the final imbibitions: nine, three at one time and six in six batches. But the imbibition is done three times, that is, in three batches. The portion of water is divided into three parts. With each of the three, the matter is buried for a week, taken up and fixed for a week, and fixed in its vessel. We go back to imbibing until it reaches its limit in redness: that is worldly wealth and bliss. Then cast it on any body.

Know that if you introduce the water onto the <term>iklīl</term> <gloss>the Crown, a name for the perfected part of the elixir</gloss> all at once, it shrinks from it and does not accept it quickly. Introduce it little by little, by the known measure. The weight for the Crown is a third of a third of the nine parts, and each imbibition takes seven days, until

<summary>The page explains how bodies are dissolved into spirits until both are equal in subtlety and distill together, which the author calls the balance of spirit and soul. It compares irreversible spoiling to wine turning into vinegar, and sets out a schedule of nine imbibitions in three batches to bring the "Crown" to redness.</summary>

The calcination of lead, from what Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, God have mercy on him, tested and chose. It is one of the rarities.
As for the calcination of lead, I will set out the utmost there is to it. Take <term>qalʿī</term> <gloss>tin</gloss> and amalgamate it
<margin>from here it runs <unclear>unchanged</unclear></margin>
with an equal amount of mercury. Then grind it with water and wash it free of the salt, doing this well while grinding it. Then pour off the water and grind it thoroughly with sublimed arsenic until it all turns black and becomes like black mud. After that, put it in a small pot, coated with clay and securely sealed, and roast it moderately.
<margin>nf. nfs. <note>abbreviation of nāfikh nafsihi, the self-blowing furnace</note></margin>
Then put the pot in a <term>nāfikh nafsihi</term> <gloss>a self-blowing furnace, one that draws its own draught</gloss> until the pot glows like a live coal. Then leave it for an hour and take it out: you will find it a body that grinds like mercury in its whiteness. When you see it so, grind it with sal ammoniac water until it rusts all of it. Then remove the water from it and wash it well, then roast it gently for a little while and sublime it well until it whitens, and bring it into your works. It is the utmost of the noble and precious sciences. Work with it and you will attain your joy, if God alone wills.
<margin>Rusting</margin>

<margin>Rusting</margin>

# The Book of the Command

->It is the sixty-eighth treatise of the Seventy<-

->In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful<-

Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings upon our master Muhammad the Prophet, and his family and companions, the good and pure. Before this book of ours, sixty-seven books on all the arts have gone before. In this book of mine I have set out the explanation of copper alone. We say, and success comes from God, that copper is inwardly lead. Converting it into silver is nearer than converting it into lead, because reaching the sides is nearer than reaching the inner parts. Silver lies in the sides of copper, so it is nearer; lead lies in its interior, so it is farther.

<summary>The Book of Mars and the Sun ends with a principle of testing: a small sample stands for the whole batch. The sixty-eighth treatise then opens on copper, explaining that silver lies on its "sides" and lead in its interior, so copper is more easily turned into silver.</summary>

In any case, the qualities that make someone an outstanding scholar and academic teacher are not the ones that make them a leader in the sphere of practical orientation to life or, more specifically, in politics. It is pure coincidence if someone happens to possess this quality as well, and it is very questionable when everyone who stands on the lecture platform feels challenged to lay claim to it. It is even more questionable when each academic teacher is left free to act the part of a leader in the lecture hall. For those who believe themselves most suited to it are often least suited, and above all: whether they are or not, the situation on the lecture platform provides absolutely no opportunity to prove it. The professor who feels called to be a counselor to the youth and enjoys their trust should stand his ground with them in personal, face-to-face interaction. And if he feels called to intervene in the struggles between worldviews and partisan opinions, he should do so out in the marketplace of life: in the press, in public meetings, in associations, wherever he wishes. But it is somewhat too comfortable to display one's courage of conviction in a place where those present, who may hold different views, are condemned to silence.

The tears of a lackey, the distribution of my wardrobe goods <note>original: "deferre"</note>, the touch of a familiar hand, a commonplace consolation, disheartens and softens me. Thus the laments of fables disturb our souls: and the sorrows of Dido and Ariadne move even those who do not believe them at all in Virgil and Catullus. It is an example of an obstinate and hard nature to feel no emotion at them, as they tell as a miracle of Polemon; but neither did he even pale at the bite of a rabid dog that tore away the calf of his leg. And no wisdom reaches so far as to conceive the cause of a sadness so lively and complete by judgment alone, that it does not suffer an increase by presence, when eyes and ears take their part in it: parts that can be stirred only by empty accidents. Is it reasonable that the arts themselves make use of and profit from our natural weakness and stupidity? The Orator, says Rhetoric, in this farce of his pleading, will be moved by the sound of his voice and by his feigned agitation, and will let himself be duped by the passion he represents. He will imprint upon himself a true and essential grief, by means of this buffoonery that he acts out, to transmit it to the judges, whom it touches even less: as do those persons whom they hire at funerals to assist in the mourning ceremony, who sell their tears and their sadness by weight and measure. For even though they stir themselves in a borrowed form, nevertheless, in habituating and arranging their countenance, it is certain that they are often carried away completely and take into themselves a genuine melancholy. I went among several other of his friends to escort the body of Monsieur de Grammont to Soissons from the siege of La Fère, where he was killed. I observed that wherever we passed, we filled with lamentation and tears the people whom we met, merely by the display of our funeral convoy's equipage: for not even the name of the deceased was known there. D'autre part, il ne semble pas que détermination signifie ici nécessité, puisque le sens commun croit au libre arbitre. Ainsi naît le déterminisme associationiste, hypothèse à l'appui de laquelle on invoquera le témoignage de la conscience, mais qui ne peut encore prétendre à une rigueur scientifique. Il semble naturel que ce déterminisme en quelque sorte approximatif, ce déterminisme de la qualité, cherche à s'étayer du même mécanisme qui soutient les phénomènes de la nature : celui-ci prêterait à celui-là son caractère géométrique, et l'opération profiterait tout ensemble au déterminisme psychologique, qui en sortirait plus rigoureux, et au mécanisme physique, qui deviendrait universel. Une circonstance heureuse favorise ce rapprochement. Les faits psychologiques les plus simples, en effet, viennent se poser d'eux-mêmes sur des phénomènes physiques bien définis, et la plupart des sensations paraissent liées à certains mouvements moléculaires. Ce commencement de preuve expérimentale suffit amplement à celui qui, pour des raisons d'ordre psychologique, a déjà admis la détermination nécessaire de nos états de conscience par les circonstances où ils se produisent. Consciousness indeed informs us that most of our actions are explained by motives. On the other hand, determination does not seem to mean necessity here, since common sense believes in free will. But the determinist, misled by a conception of duration and causality that we will criticize in detail a little further on, holds the determination of facts of consciousness by one another to be absolute. Thus arises associationist determinism, a hypothesis in support of which the testimony of consciousness will be invoked, but which cannot yet claim scientific rigor. It seems natural that this somewhat approximate determinism, this determinism of quality, should seek to support itself with the same mechanism that sustains the phenomena of nature: the latter would lend the former its geometric character, and the operation would benefit both psychological determinism, which would emerge more rigorous from it, and physical mechanism, which would become universal. A fortunate circumstance favors this rapprochement. The simplest psychological facts, in effect, naturally settle upon well-defined physical phenomena, and most sensations seem linked to certain molecular movements. This beginning of experimental proof is amply sufficient for anyone who, for reasons of a psychological nature, has already admitted the necessary determination of our states of consciousness by the circumstances in which they occur. From then on he no longer hesitates to consider the play being performed on the stage of consciousness as a translation, always literal and slavish, of some of the scenes executed by the molecules and atoms of organized matter. But for those who would not believe it without such authorities, let them rub their mouths thoroughly with a couple of chilies and see if they find them cooling. Thus, when certain teachers among these great healers <note>The original term *ensalmaderas* refers to women who healed through a mix of folk medicine and chanted prayers or "charms."</note> or herbalists say that the chili is "cool," and other times that it is "moist," instead of giving them credit, we shall laugh at their folly. For in what they say, they make neither head nor tail <note>original: "no atan ni desatan," an idiom meaning their words lack logic or impact.</note>; because if credit is to be given to the reasoning and judgment of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician in the Western tradition; his theories on the four "humors" dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, the chili is of greater heat than black pepper. And so we see that it scorches the vitals and wounds the intestines, and even tends to cause bloody stools <note>original: "camaras de sangre," a historical term for dysentery or severe intestinal inflammation.</note> and inflammations of the liver, doing no less than a most burning poison. Supposing then that the chili is so extremely hot, I say secondly: that if this chili is toasted, it loses much of its heat, and the same happens with pepper and every sharp and biting <term>mordicative</term> <note>something that causes a stinging or biting sensation on the skin or tongue</note> thing. The cause of this is now sought: because if one looks closely, it should rather have gained heat from the fire; for even Galen, speaking of salt and other things brought near the fire, says himself that they gain greater heat from the fire.

The response to this is to say plainly that the chili, the pepper, and everything that bites is very "hot," and likewise loses that heat with fire. The cause is that such heat was not fixed and deposited throughout the entire object, but rather in certain subtle and very delicate parts. Since the fire wasted and consumed these, the toasted item remained without its heat. I will give an example: the onion and the garlic, before they were cooked, were sharp and gave much heat; after being cooked, they neither bite nor provide heat. The cause is that the heat of the fire consumed those most subtle parts which were what gave heat to the onion. Thus, with these lost and wasted, the onion lacks them and remains "cool." This same thing happens to the chili with fire, being (as I have said) composed of most subtle and very hot parts. However, a "cold" thing, or one composed of thick <note>In Galenic science, "thick" or "gross" parts refer to the dense, earthy matter of a substance, as opposed to its "subtle" or volatile essences.</note> parts, will not experience this; for it lacks the hot and subtle parts for the fire to waste, but rather the fire will thin the thick parts it does have and leave heat within them.

The second question is asked: what is the cause by which, without being a purge <note>A "purge" refers to a formal medicinal laxative meant to expel specific humors from the body.</note>—as it truly is not—the chili tends to be purgative? two Spaniards delayed a bit longer, because they traveled about one hundred and fifty leagues in another direction until they reached the sea, where they likewise took possession in the name of Their Majesties <note>King Charles I of Spain (Emperor Charles V) and his mother, Queen Joanna.</note>. They brought back a long report of the coast they saw, and some natives from those southern coasts also came in their company. The general <note>Hernando Cortés</note> received both the Spaniards and the natives graciously and informed them of the greatness and power of Their Majesties; he gave them some jewelry, with which they departed very content and astonished to see the horses, weapons, artillery, and the manner of the Spaniards.

At the time when the Indians defeated and drove Hernando Cortés and the Spaniards out of Temistitan <note>Tenochtitlán, the Aztec capital</note>, all the provinces subject to that great city rebelled. As it appears from the preceding chapters, all or most of that land was reconquered and subjugated by the industry, courage, and good diligence of the general—sometimes without shedding blood, and also with punishment and the sword where it was necessary to use arms. Because certain provinces, which are ten, fifteen, or thirty leagues from this North Sea of ours <note>The Atlantic/Gulf of Mexico</note>, had been in rebellion since the city had risen up, and their natives had treacherously and under a false sense of security killed more than one hundred Spaniards at various times, their punishment had been deferred until the conclusion of the war and the siege of the city; for before then, there was no possibility or means to attend to it. Thus, as soon as the general had dispatched the aforementioned messengers to the South Sea <note>The Pacific Ocean</note>, he immediately arranged to send the Chief Constable <term>alguaçil mayor</term> <note>a high-ranking officer responsible for justice and military discipline</note> Gonzalo de Sandoval with thirty-five horsemen and two hundred Spaniards, along with some allied people and several lords and natives of Temistitan to those provinces. This was so they might better understand, as eyewitnesses, what had been done and punished, for two reasons: the first,

<column-break/>

so that those lands might be reduced to the obedience of Their Majesties, and if it were necessary and they were not obedient, a signal punishment should be carried out against them with rigor, and they should be given a penance equal to their deserts. The other reason was because the greatest danger among men of war is idleness and the neglect of arms and their exercise. For besides putting the state and authority of the prince in jeopardy and necessity, the soldiers and men of war become useless; because, as Titus Livius <note>Livy (59 BC – AD 17), the Roman historian. The reference is likely to Book XXIII of his *History of Rome* regarding the softening of Hannibal's troops in Capua.</note> says, sleep, wine, feasts, harlots, and continuous idleness consume the bodies and weaken the spirits day by day. And so it happened to the great Hannibal, the Carthaginian, and his army, for remaining idle in the camps and boundaries of Capua and its estates.

This general of ours, Hernando Cortés, not falling into such an error or neglect, nor letting time pass without producing some fruit, sent Captain Sandoval to those provinces, whose names are Tatactetelco, Tuxtebeque <note>Tuxtepec</note>, Guatusco, and Aulicaba <note>Orizaba</note>; he gave him the instructions and order he was to follow in that expedition and war to which he sent him.

<term>Responsos breues</term> llamamos alos que se canta̅ en las horas despues dela capitula. Lo que digo de los breues responsos se entiende en lo romano. Acerca del cognoscimiento delas <term>antiphonas</term> reglas co̅munes y buenas se ponen en las artes de canto, conuiene a saber primero <term>re la</term>, segundo <term>re fa</term>, tercero <term>mi fa</term>, quarto <term>mi la</term>, quinto <term>fa fa</term>, sexto <term>fa la</term>, septimo <term>vt sol</term>, y octauo <term>vt fa</term>: pero para mayor breuedad y certidumbre digo. Si la <term>sequencia</term>, o <term>seculoru̅ amen</term> comiença arriba del final tres, o quatro puntos, sera <term>discipulo</term>: y si fueren cinco o seys sera <term>maestro</term>. Siempre la <term>sequencia</term> del maestro comiença por preeminencia mas alta que la del discipulo. Tambien se pueden cognoscer las dichas antiphonas en el principio subiendo del signo de su final hasta el signo donde comiença la sequēcia. Pues si al principio dixere <term>re la</term> gradatim o de salto, sera primero: si <term>re fa</term>, sera segundo: y assi de todos los otros modos co̅forme ala regla superior. De forma, que la regla que sirue para el final del antiphona, y principio dela sequēcia: aprouecha para el principio dela dicha antiphona. Y si alguna vez otra cosa hallardes: entended ser yerro de pu̅tate, o falta del componedor: porque la regla es infalible. El perfecto cognoscimiento de los otros modos es el siguiente. Vn modo, tiene de arte para subir encima de su final cinco puntos: que es vn <term>diapente</term>. De forma, que para ser vn modo perfecto: ocho puntos (que son vn <term>diapaßon</term>) ha de tener. <meta>This page continues the technical instruction on identifying musical modes in Gregorian chant, specifically focusing on the distinction between "Master" (authentic) and "Disciple" (plagal) modes through their range and clef usage.</meta>

# Book Three

From this I infer: that for the <term>introit</term> <note>the opening chant of the Mass</note>, the <term>responsory</term>, and the <term>short responsory</term> <note>a brief chant used in the Divine Office</note>—because they contain verses with a faster pace or repetition (though the verse must be examined for how much it rises or falls as part of the mode)—you should not look at the final note of the verse, but rather where you stop singing, which is the last note before the verse begins. Count five notes up from the final note; if the melody rises further above those five than it descends below its final note, it will be a <term>master</term> <note>original: "maestro"; refers to an authentic mode</note>. And if it descends below its final note more than it rises above the aforementioned five notes, it will be a <term>disciple</term> <note>original: "discipulo"; refers to a plagal mode</note>. If they are equal (rising as many notes above the five as it descends below the final), it shall be a <term>master</term>, a status granted as an honor—unless the clef or a particular passage indicates it belongs to the disciples, in which case it will not be a master. You will find this rule explained in the following four examples.

---

->This is a "Master" that exceeds the range.<-

->This is a "Disciple" that exceeds the range.<-

->This is an "Equal Master."<-

->This is a "Disciple" because of the clef.<-

---

Although this knowledge is imperfect and general, it is easy to learn. For every chant that ends in <term>E-la-mi</term> <note>the note E</note> or in <term>F-fa-ut</term> <note>the note F</note>, look at the clef it carries, and you will understand by this alone which mode it is. If it is the <term>F-fa-ut</term> clef <note>F-clef</note>, such a mode will be a <term>disciple</term>; and if it is the <term>C-sol-fa-ut</term> clef <note>C-clef</note>, we shall say that mode is a <term>master</term>. Every <term>tract</term> <note>a solo chant used in the Mass during penitential seasons</note> in the Roman rite belongs to either the second or eighth mode. If such a chant ends in <term>D-sol-re</term> <note>the note D</note>, it will be of the second tone; and if it ends in <term>G-sol-re-ut</term> <note>the note G</note>, it will be the eighth mode. Every <term>short responsory</term>, whether it has an "Alleluia" or is sung without it, belongs to the sixth mode—except for *Into your hands, O Lord* <note>original: "In manus tuas domine"</note> without the "Alleluia" sung at Compline, those for the Lord's Advent at all the Hours, and the responsory for Terce on Sundays throughout the year (which begins *Incline my heart, O God* <note>original: "Inclina cor meu̅ deus"</note>), all of which belong to the fourth mode.

<column-break/>

We call <term>short responsories</term> those sung during the Hours after the Little Chapter <note>a short scripture reading</note>. What I say regarding short responsories pertains to the Roman rite. Concerning the recognition of <term>antiphons</term> <note>short chants sung before and after a psalm</note>, common and useful rules are set down in the arts of singing; specifically: first mode is *re-la*, second is *re-fa*, third is *mi-fa*, fourth is *mi-la*, fifth is *fa-fa*, sixth is *fa-la*, seventh is *ut-sol*, and eighth is *ut-fa*. But for greater brevity and certainty, I say: If the <term>sequence</term> <note>original: "sequencia"; here referring to the "differentia" or the melodic ending of the psalm tone</note> or the *World without end, Amen* <note>original: "seculoru̅ amen"; the concluding phrase of the Gloria Patri</note> begins three or four notes above the final note, it will be a <term>disciple</term>; and if it is five or six notes, it will be a <term>master</term>. The <term>sequence</term> of a master mode always begins, by right of its preeminence, higher than that of a disciple. One can also recognize these antiphons at the beginning by the interval from the final note up to the note where the sequence begins. If at the start it says *re-la* step-by-step or by a leap, it will be the first mode; if *re-fa*, it will be the second; and so on for all other modes according to the rule above. In this way, the rule that serves for the end of the antiphon and the beginning of the sequence also applies to the beginning of the said antiphon. If you ever find otherwise, understand it to be an error of the scribe or a fault of the composer, because the rule is infallible.

The perfect knowledge of the other modes is as follows. By rule, a mode has the capacity to rise five notes above its final, which is a <term>diapente</term> <note>the interval of a fifth</note>. To be a <term>master</term>, it will add four notes—a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>the interval of a fourth</note>—above that fifth. To be a <term>disciple</term>, it will carry the <term>diatessaron</term> below its final note. Any mode lacking any of the eight points mentioned above shall be called <term>imperfect</term>. Thus, for a mode to be perfect, it must have eight points, which constitute a <term>diapason</term> <note>the interval of an octave</note>. I say that five points and four points make eight because the one note that is the end of the <term>diapente</term> is counted twice, as it is also the beginning of the <term>diatessaron</term>. All modes, both masters and disciples, have two notes of "license" <note>allowable notes outside the strict modal range</note> to make the final cadences of the <term>diapason</term>. We might wonder about this, because it is commonly said among musicians that all modes carry these two notes of license. Why are these two notes called "license" rather than part of the eight notes all modes carry? Or if the eight are by rule, why are the two not also by rule? There is a difference between being "by art" <note>governed by formal rules</note> and being "by license." The Latins took the art of music from the Greeks, who gave the modes only one <term>diapason</term>, which is eight notes.

<summary>This page provides practical and theoretical rules for distinguishing between authentic (master) and plagal (disciple) modes based on range, clefs, and specific melodic intervals. It defines the mathematical structure of the octave as a combination of a fifth and a fourth and explains the concept of musical 'license' regarding range.</summary>

<keywords>musical modes, authentic vs plagal, plainchant theory, solmization, diapason, diapente, diatessaron, liturgical chant, short responsory, antiphons</keywords>

### of the Kingdom of Chile.

tain throughout the entire country, by means of their natural vehicles, the air and the water, are likely the cause of the constant fertility that learned observers admire there. Even the internal heat, originating from the many minerals capable of maintaining it—with which all that land is impregnated—may likewise contribute to this productive power. With these natural aids, the soil can perform very well without the external use of fertilizers <note>original: "abonos".</note>. 

This is the belief of farmers seasoned by experience, who judge the adoption of such methods as harmful, or at least superfluous for their fields. As proof, they cite the unalterable fecundity of the lands surrounding the Capital <note>Santiago de Chile, the administrative center of the colony.</note>. These fields were sown annually by the ancient Indians <note>Molina refers here to the indigenous Picunche people of the central valley.</note>, who were numerous in that region, and have since been cultivated by the Spaniards for a period of 239 years. Without the reinforcement or aid of fertilizers or artificial manures <note>original: "engrasos artificiales"; the author suggests that the natural mineral composition of the earth is superior to traditional animal waste.</note>, these lands have not yet shown the slightest sign of exhaustion or decline, neither in the quantity nor the quality of their harvest. It is perhaps because of this lack of manure that Chilean soil is not infested with the worms that destroy budding plants; such pests likely multiply much more than they should through the fermentation and putrefaction of dung.

translation:
# BIOLYCHNIVM.

From this foundation, therefore, has emerged the preparation of this Lamp or light, which, once ignited, burns continuously as long as the man from whose blood it is prepared draws vital breath <note>original: "vitalem ducit Spiritum", the Latin idiom for "is alive, breathes"</note>; and at the same hour, moment, or point that he breathes his last, it is extinguished together with him. Know furthermore: if the flame is bright, elevated, tranquil, and motionless, that man feels nothing that is heavy or burdensome to body or mind. But if it is otherwise, and the rising flame scintillates in various ways, or is lower, or cloudy and sluggish, let it be to you an indication of anxiety, sadness, and other Pathemata <note>passions or affections of the soul</note>. For, perpetually from the innate astral influences of the Microcosm and natural inclinations (since both that blood is nourished from the blood of the man himself, and his body from the substance of this very blood, from which the blood was, as it were, borrowed to prepare the Lamp), that flame shines out and shows itself according to the state and habit of that man, whether prosperous or adverse.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual hierarchy, transitioning from the comparison between angels and humans to a detailed analysis of the tripartite soul (Nephesh, Ruach, and Neshamah) and their origins within the Sephiroth, the divine emanations of Kabbalistic thought.</meta>

->### A Treatise on the Soul,<-

three parts, which are <term>Nephesh</term> <note>The lowest of the three parts of the soul.</note>, <term>Ruach</term> <note>The middle soul, associated with the spirit and emotions.</note>, and <term>Neshamah</term> <note>The highest soul, associated with the intellect and divine spark.</note>. The Nephesh is the vehicle of the Ruach, just as the Ruach is the vehicle of the Neshamah. Moreover, the emanation of all three is from the higher <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>, which are the roots of all roots. They differ, however, in their source of emanation; for the Neshamah emanates from <term>Binah</term> <note>Understanding; the third Sephirah.</note>, as indicated in <margin>Job 32:8.</margin> *“And the breath <note>original: "Neschamah"</note> of the Almighty <note>original: "Schadai"</note> gives them understanding.”* The Ruach, however, emanates from <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>Beauty or Compassion; the sixth Sephirah.</note>; and just as Tiphereth is the throne and dwelling place of Binah, so the Ruach is the throne and dwelling place of the Neshamah. But the Nephesh emanates from <term>Malchuth</term> <note>Kingdom; the tenth and lowest Sephirah, associated with the physical realm.</note>, and thus the Nephesh is the throne and dwelling place of the Ruach, just as Malchuth is the throne and dwelling place of Tiphereth.

Rabbi <term>Shimon bar Yochai</term> <note>original: "Schimeon Jochā"; the traditional author of the Zohar.</note> (may his memory be a blessing) explains their emanation in the section *Vayechi* in the <term>Zohar</term> <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism.</note>, folio 113, column d, with these words: "Learn, all things consist of steps established one above the other: Nephesh, Ruach, Neshamah, one level higher than the next. The Nephesh is first, which is the lowest level, as stated elsewhere; then the Ruach, which rests upon the Nephesh and has the Neshamah standing above it as the highest level of all, as has been established. This Nephesh is the Nephesh of David (concerning which see 2 Samuel 5:8, regarding Malchuth), to which it is appointed to receive Nephesh from that stream which flows and goes out. The Ruach is established over it, and the Nephesh cannot endure except through the Ruach, that spirit which is placed between Fire and Water (namely Tiphereth, which stands between <term>Gevurah</term> <note>original: "Gebhurah"; Strength/Severity, associated with Fire.</note> and <term>Gedulah</term> <note>Greatness/Mercy, associated with Water.</note>). And by this Ruach, the Nephesh is nourished. The Ruach itself endures through the state of another higher level, which is the Neshamah, from which both the Nephesh and Ruach are sustained. Thus, when the Ruach has participated, the Nephesh then participates, and all are one, and they cling to each other: the Nephesh to the Ruach, and the Ruach to the Neshamah, and all are one." Thus he spoke. The meaning of which is that the Neshamah is Binah, the Ruach is Tiphereth, and the Nephesh is Malchuth. And thus it is explained in the <term>Tikkunim</term> <note>The Tikkunei Zohar, an appendix to the Zohar focusing on the first word of Genesis.</note> with these words: <margin>Proverbs 20:27.</margin> *"The lamp of the Lord is the Neshamah of man."* The word *Ner* [Lamp] denotes the Nephesh...

# OF MUSIC.
### BY RENÉ DESCARTES.

->Its object is Sound.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' featuring intricate scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Its end is to please us and to stir various feelings within us. A song can be at once sad and delightful, and there is no wonder in such contraries: for elegists and tragedians please us all the more, the greater the grief they awaken.

The means to this end are the two chief properties of sound: its differences in duration, or time, and its differences in intensity — that is, in pitch, whether high or low. (The quality of the sound itself — from what body, and in what manner, it issues more pleasingly — is the business of the physicists.)

This alone seems to make the human voice the most pleasing sound of all: that it is, of all things, the most attuned to our own spirits. And so, perhaps, a friend's voice pleases us more than an enemy's, through a sympathy or antipathy of our feelings — on the very principle by which, they say, a sheepskin stretched over one drum falls silent when struck, while a wolfskin over another drum resonates.

->Preliminary remarks.<-
