<meta>continues from previous page</meta>is valid cognition. Thus, when a continuous sequence of cognitions of fire and other phenomena arises, an awareness whose nature is the cessation of the suffering of hunger arises. Because that which is other than valid cognition is non-valid, when that possessing such a definition is valid cognition, any other case where a sequence of cognitions of fire and so forth does not function in this manner is the reverse, non-valid cognition. Therefore, this constitutes the common definition of conventional direct perception and non-direct perception.

If one asks, "Moreover, for what purpose is this formulated?" it is stated, "Even though it is erroneous..."

Even what is produced by error becomes an auxiliary factor in certain instances. For example, regarding a particular woman with the recognition of her as one's mother serves as an auxiliary factor for pacifying attachment. Similarly, although this presentation of valid cognition and its counterfeit appearance is without an external referent <term>anālambana</term> <gloss>lacking an objective basis</gloss>, it serves as a necessary auxiliary factor for establishing what is valid cognition and what is non-valid cognition. Whatever pacification of passion is naturally established toward a mother is likewise accomplished toward another woman simply through forming such a conviction. In the same way, even though it is not valid cognition, positing it in that manner becomes an auxiliary factor produced by valid cognition, because in one case the latent impression <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>habitual mental imprint</gloss> is stable, while in the other it is not.

When proponents of Mind-Only <term>Vijñaptimātra</term> <gloss>Cognizance-Only school</gloss> examine the nature of conventional valid and non-valid cognition, they rely solely on whether latent impressions are stable or unstable as their criterion. The establishment of entities such as mere self-cognizance and selflessness is accomplished through inferential valid cognition directed toward entities, whereas the subject of inquiry <term>dharmin</term> <gloss>the bearer of attributes</gloss> is established through the direct perception of reflexive awareness <term>svasaṃvedana</term> <gloss>self-awareness</gloss>.

To demonstrate that, although apprehending a mirage as water is equally mistaken, it is nonetheless distinct, it is said, "a mirage and..."

If a mirage is excluded from water, then water is excluded from what is other than water. Therefore, apprehending both a mirage and water as water arises in relation to entities distinct from water, and thus it arises from distinct entities. For that very reason

<summary>This text articulates the Vijñaptimātra criteria for conventional valid cognition, explaining that the distinction between valid cognition and error relies on the stability of latent impressions rather than external objects. It further examines how reflexive awareness and inferential cognition establish subjects such as selflessness and distinguish errors like mistaking a mirage for water.</summary>
<keywords>pramāṇa, valid cognition, Vijñaptimātra, vāsanā, latent imprints, svasaṃvedana, reflexive awareness, dharmin, inference, perception, mirage, Buddhist epistemology</keywords>

When you secure this <term>do-ban</term> <gloss>base plate</gloss> and attach the lid to the front of the <term>maejita</term> <gloss>front torso plate</gloss>, it should align with the hole in the doll's <term>munagi</term> <gloss>chest</gloss>. At that moment, the <term>suigin</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss> located at the <term>koshi</term> <gloss>waist</gloss> flows through the internal <term>michi</term> <gloss>passage hole</gloss>. Because the mercury passes through this hole into the <term>tsutsu</term> <gloss>cylinder</gloss>, adjusting the size of the hole is difficult. If it is too large, the liquid will exit too quickly. If the size is just right, the mercury will fall steadily, drop by drop. Generally, the <term>kiadi</term> <gloss>flow rate</gloss> should be slightly less than 1 <term>bu</term> <gloss>approx. 3 mm</gloss>.

<note>A diagram depicts a bell-shaped component with a textured bottom half, representing a weight or a filter used inside the torso mechanism.</note>

Next, take the inside of the lid and place it face down upon the <term>mune</term> <gloss>chest</gloss>. Once aligned, it will fit inside the cylinder. The mercury inside will then flow forward again through the small hole in the chest. For a doll that falls forward from the chest, this allows it to settle evenly from the <term>koshishita</term> <gloss>lower waist</gloss> toward the back.

<note>original: "Sessuki" — has the double meaning of a meal and the end of the year.</note>
<note>original: "Nanatsu-oki" — waking up at 4:00 AM.</note>
<note>original: "Shibe" — a scrap of umbrella paper used as medicine.</note>
<note>original: "Torio-kuda-ya" — a pun on the shop name "Okudaya" and "taking and putting away."</note>

Rising from the ground starts with waking at four in the morning. Never lend money without collateral. Not buying what you want is a virtue. It is a loss not to work by the light of the moon. Poverty cannot catch up to those who work. Even if you split a mustard seed into a thousand pieces to burn as wood, you must never throw away the ash. There is nothing that should be discarded. Use the soot from the pot to draw fine eyebrows. A scrap of umbrella paper is a wonderful medicine for numbness. A dry well is a storage place for ladders. Even a rat's tail can be a sheath for an awl. Let the umbrellas dry. Never lend your dried bonito to others. For the pestle, the mortar, the whetstone, the millstone, and the apothecary's mortar—though it is not visible to the eye, there is no case where they do not return diminished every time they are lent. Aside from such things, rely on charm and socializing, but for savings, reading, and the abacus, there is no limit if you look upward. Take those below you as your model. If you follow these rules, even dust will pile up to form a mountain. There is no doubt in these maxims of the wealthy. The Bell of Incessant Hell is but a name; listen to this tale of how fortune and virtue flourish naturally.

Shirozaemon laughs, "I cannot even answer such a speech. If the whole world lived like that, our business at the Okudaya would have to close up and put everything away!" The only thing separating the rooms is a single paper screen. The commotion on the other side reaches Kojorō's ears. "I shall ransom five or six high-ranking ladies! I will give them this, that, and the other!" Gold, silver, and treasures are treated like dust. "Even when I saw the poor lives of my father and mother, I never dreamed of wanting money I could not have. But today, of all days, I am envious of those being ransomed. I have come to want money. It is not right to be jealous of those with good fortune, but what kind of man is he? I want to see his face." She peeks through a hole in the screen. "Oh! That is the man I know. In case of emergency..."

that it was that in the said town of San Martin, among the people who of their lineage and line had notorious [reputation], they were had and held and recognized as men who were well-known noblemen of blood, and such was thereof the public voice and fame and common opinion without having seen or heard the contrary, rather from very old and ancient men, neighbors of the said town of the age he had said, he heard them say many times that Christobal Fernandez de la Canal and Pero Fernandez de la Canal his father, and Pero Fernandez de la Canal the elder, according to how all were grandfather and great-grandfather and great-great-grandfather of the one who is litigating, whom they had much known, and all of them, at least Christobal Fernandez de la Canal and Pero Fernandez de la Canal his father, and some of them knew Pero Fernandez de la Canal the elder, their grandfather, said that the aforementioned were men who were noblemen of blood, and that said Pero Fernandez de la Canal the elder was a native of the mountain and descendant of the House of La Canal, and that for such they had held him, and seen that they had always been had and recognized in their times in the said town of San Martin, and such had always been the public voice and fame and common opinion, and he had never seen nor heard anything to the contrary, and that he had not known and did not know by the direct male line any commoners, nor relatives who were commoners, nor descendants of commoners, but rather he had known and knew them as noblemen of blood.

sino la comida, y dimos todo lo otro a los cristianos para que entre sí la repartiesen; y después de esto pasamos muchas y grandes pendencias con ellos, porque no querían hacer los indios que traíamos esclavos, y con este enojo, al partir dejamos muchos arcos turquescos, que traíamos, y muchos zurrones y flechas, y entre ellas las cinco de las esmeraldas, que no se nos acordó de ellas; y ansí, las perdimos. Dimos a los cristianos muchas mantas de vaca y otras cosas que traíamos; vímonos con los indios en mucho trabajo porque se volviesen a sus casas y se asegurasen y sembrasen su maíz. Ellos no querían sino ir con nosotros hasta dejarnos, como acostumbraban, con otros indios; porque si se volviesen sin hacer esto temían que se morirían; que para ir con nosotrosno temían a los cristianos ni a sus lanzas. A los cristianos les pasaba deesto, y hacían que su lengua les dijese que nosotros éramos de ellos mismos, y nos habíamos perdidomuchos tiempos había, y que éramos gente de poca suerte y valor, y que ellos eran los señores de aquella tierra, a quien habían de obedecer y servir. Mas todo esto los indios tenían en muy poco o en nada de lo que les decían; anntes, unos con otros sí platicaban, diciendo que los cristianos mentían porque nosotros veníamos de donde salía el sol, y ellos donde se pone; y que nosotros sanábamos los enfermos, y ellos mataban los que estaban sanos; y que nosotros veníamos desnudos y descalzos, y ellos vestidos y en caballos con lanzas; y que nosotros no teníamos cobdicia de ninguna cosa, antes todo cuanto nos daban torntábamos luego a dar, y con nada nos quedábamos y los otros no tenían otro fin sino robar todo cuanto hallaban, y nunca daban nada nadie; y de esta manera relataban todas nuestras cosas y las encarescían, por el contrario, de los otros; y así les respondieron a la lengua de los cristianos, y lo mismo hicieron saber a los otros por una lengua que ellos había, con quien entendíamos, y aquellos que la usan llamamos propriamente primahaitu, que es como decir vascongados, la cual, más de cuatrocientas leguas de las que anduvimos, hallamos usada entre ellos, sin haber otra por todas aquellas tierras. Finalmente, nunca pudo acabar con los indicios creer que éramos de los otros cristianos, y con mucho trabajo e importunación les hecimos volvera su casa, y les mandamos que se asegurasen, y asentasen sus pueblos, y sembrasen y labrasen la tierra, que, de estar despoblada, estaba ya muy llenade montes; la cual sin dubda es la mejor de cuantas en estas Indias hay, y más fértil y abundosa de mantenimientos, y siembran tres veces en el año. Tienen muchas frutas y muy hermosos ríos, y otras muchas aguas muy buenas. Hay muestras grandes y señales de minas de oro y plata; la gente de ella es muy bien acondicionada; sirven a los cristianos (los que son amigos) de muy buena voluntad. Son muy dispuestos, mucho más que los de Méjico, y, finalmente, estierra que ninguna cosa le falta para ser muy buena. Despedidos los indios, nos dijeron que harían lo que mandábamos, y asentarían sus pueblos si los cristianos los dejaban; y yo así lo digo y afirmo pormuy cierto, que si no lo hicieren será por culpa de los cristianos. Después que hobimos enviado a los indios en paz, y degraciadoles el trabajo que con nosotros habían pasado, los cristianos nos enviaron, debajo de cautela, a un Cebreros, alcalde, y con él otros dos, los cuales nos llevaron por los montes y despoblados, por apartarnos de la conversación de los indios, y porque no viésemos ni entendiésemos lo que de hecho hicieron; donde paresce cuánto se engañan los pensamientos de los hombres, que nosotros andabamosa les buscar libertad, y cuando pensábamos que la teníamos, sucedió tal al contrario, porque tenían acordado de ir a dar en los indios que enviábamos asegurados y de paz; y ansí como lo pensaron, lo hicieron; lleváronnos por aquellos montes dos días, sin agua, perdidos y sin camino, y todos pensamos perecer de sed, y de ella se nos ahogaron siete hombres, y muchos amigos que los cristianos traían consigo no pudieron llegar hasta otro día a mediodíaadonde aquella noche hallamos con ellos veinte y cinco leguas, poco más o menos, y al fin de ellas llegamos a un pueblo de indios de paz, y el alcalde que nos llevaba nos dejó allí, y él pasó adelante otras tres leguas, a un pueblo que se llamaba Culiazan, adonde estaba Melchor Díaz, alcalde mayor y capitán de aquella provincia.

### CAPITULO XXXV

*De cómo el alcalde mayor nos recibió bien la noche que llegamos*

Como el alcalde mayor fue avisado de nuestra salida y venida, luego aquella noche partió, y vino adonde nosotros estábamos, y lloró mucho con nosotros, dando loores a Dios nuestro Señor por haber usado de tanta misericordia con nosotros; y nos habló y trato muy bien; y de parte del gobernador Nuño de Guzman y suya nos ofreció todo lo que tenía y podía; y mostró mucho sentimiento de la mala acogida y tratamiento que en Alcaraz y los otros habíamos hallado, y tuvimos por cierto que si el se hallara allí, se excusara lo que con nosotros y con los indios se hizo; y pasada aquella noche, otro día nos partimos, y el alcalde mayor nos rogó mucho que nos detuviésemos allí, y que en esto haríamos muy gran servicio a Dios y a Vuestra Majestad, porque la tierra estaba despoblada, sin labrarse, y toda muy destruida, y los indios andaban es-

<meta>continues from previous page: ...himself, knowing how long we had been in that land and the dangers and hardships we had endured. That night we gave thanks to God our Lord for bringing us out of our captivity,</meta> except for the food, and we gave everything else to the Christians so they could divide it among themselves. After this, we had many great disputes with them because they did not want to set free the Indians we were bringing as slaves. Because of this anger, upon departing, we left behind many Turkish-style bows that we were carrying, as well as many pouches and arrows. Among them were the five emeralds, which we completely forgot about, and thus we lost them. We gave the Christians many cow hides <note>likely bison hides</note> and other things we were carrying. We saw ourselves in great difficulty with the Indians to get them to return to their homes, reassure themselves, and plant their corn. They did not want anything but to go with us until they could leave us, as they were accustomed, with other Indians; for if they returned without doing this, they feared they would die. To go with us, they did not fear the Christians or their lances.

The Christians cared little about this and made their <term>lengua</term> <gloss>interpreter</gloss> tell them that we were of their own kind, that we had been lost a long time ago, that we were people of little luck and value, and that they were the lords of that land whom they had to obey and serve. But the Indians valued all of this very little or not at all. Instead, they spoke among themselves, saying that the Christians were lying because we came from where the sun rises and they from where it sets; that we healed the sick and they killed those who were healthy; that we came naked and barefoot, and they were clothed and on horses with lances; that we felt no greed for anything, but rather gave away everything we were given, never keeping anything for ourselves, while the others had no goal other than to steal everything they found and never gave anything to anyone. In this way, they recounted all our deeds and praised them, in contrast to the others. 

They responded this way to the Christians' interpreter, and they made the same known to others through an interpreter they had, whom we could understand. Those who use that language we call properly <term>primahaitu</term> <gloss>a term Cabeza de Vaca uses to describe a widely understood common language, comparing it to Basque</gloss>, which is like saying "Basque speakers." We found it used among them for more than four hundred leagues of what we traveled, without finding any other throughout those lands. Finally, we could never convince the Indians to believe that we were of the other Christians, and with much labor and insistence, we made them return to their homes. We ordered them to be reassured, settle their villages, and plant and till the land, which, due to being depopulated, was already very full of thickets. It is without a doubt the best of all that there are in these Indies, the most fertile and abundant in provisions, and they plant three times a year. They have many fruits and very beautiful rivers, and many other very good waters. There are great signs and traces of gold and silver mines. The people of it are very well-disposed; they serve the Christians (those who are friends) with very good will. They are very capable, much more so than those of Mexico, and, finally, it is a land that lacks nothing to be very good. 

Once the Indians had left, they told us they would do what we ordered and would settle their villages if the Christians let them. I say and affirm this as very certain: if they do not do so, it will be the fault of the Christians. After we had sent the Indians away in peace and thanked them for the effort they had undergone with us, the Christians sent us, under guard, to a certain Cebreros, an <term>alcalde</term> <gloss>magistrate/mayor</gloss>, and with him two others. They took us through the mountains and uninhabited lands to distance us from the company of the Indians, and so that we would not see or understand what they actually did. It appears here how deceived the thoughts of men are: we were walking to seek their freedom, and when we thought we had obtained it, the exact opposite happened, because they had planned to go and attack the Indians whom we had sent back reassured and in peace. And just as they planned it, they did it. They led us through those mountains for two days without water, lost and without a path, and we all thought we would perish from thirst. Seven men died from it, and many friends the Christians were bringing with them could not arrive until the next day at midday where we had been with them that night, twenty-five leagues, more or less. At the end of that, we arrived at a town of peaceful Indians, and the magistrate who was leading us left us there, and he went on three leagues further to a town called Culiazan, where Melchor Díaz, the <term>alcalde mayor</term> <gloss>chief magistrate</gloss> and captain of that province, was.

### CAPITULO XXXV

*Of how the chief magistrate received us well the night we arrived*

As the chief magistrate was informed of our departure and arrival, he left that same night and came to where we were. He wept a great deal with us, giving praise to God our Lord for having used so much mercy with us. He spoke to us and treated us very well; and on behalf of Governor Nuño de Guzman and himself, he offered us everything he had and could. He showed great regret for the bad reception and treatment we had encountered in Alcaraz and the others, and we held it for certain that if he had been there, what was done to us and to the Indians would have been avoided. Once that night had passed, the next day we departed, and the chief magistrate begged us a great deal to stay there, and that in doing so we would do a great service to God and to Your Majesty, because the land was depopulated, not being farmed, and all very destroyed, and the Indians were wandering...

<summary>Cabeza de Vaca describes his struggle to protect the indigenous people from the deceitful treatment of fellow Christians, noting the contrast between his group’s peaceful conduct and the Spanish soldiers' greed. Despite his efforts, he is placed under guard by officials, only to be later received with kindness by the chief magistrate, Melchor Díaz.</summary>

De aquel corredorcillo y de otras partes de la ciudad se ve una punta de sierra nevada en forma de pirámide; tan alta, que, con estar veinte y cinco leguas de ella y haber otras sierras en medio, se descubre mucha altura de aquella punta; no se ven peñas ni riscos, sino nieve pura y perpetua, sin menguar jamás. Llásmanle Uillcanuta: quiere decir cosa sagrada o maravillosa más que las comunes, porque este nombre Uillca nunca lo dieron sino a cosas dignas de admiración; y cierto, aquella pirámide lo es, sobre todo encarecimiento que de ella se pueda hacer. Remítame a los que la han visto o la vieren.

Al poniente de las casas de mi padre estaban las de Vasco de Guevara, conquistador de los segundos, que después fueron de la Coya Doña Beatriz, hija de Huayna Cápac. Al mediodía de las de Tomás Vázquez estaban las de Don Antonio Pereira, hijo de Lope Martín, portugués. Luego se seguían las casas de Pedro Alonso Carrasco, conquistador de los primeros. Al mediodía de las casas de Pedro Alonso de Carrasco había otras de poco momento, y eran las últimas de aquel barrio, el cual se iba poblando por los años de mil y quinientos y cincuenta y siete y ocho.

Volviendo a las faldas del cerro Carmenca, decimos que al poniente de las casas de Diego de Silva están las que fueron de Francisco de Villafuerte, conquistador de los primeros y uno de los trece compañeros de Don Francisco Pizarro. They call it <term>Uillcanuta</term>: it means sacred or marvelous thing more than the common ones, because this name <term>Uillca</term> they never gave except to things worthy of admiration; and certainly, that pyramid is so, above any praise that can be made of it. IV. Otra conſonancia diverſa, puede admitir el verſo, porque en rigor no dize, no ay mejor coſa que comer, &c. mas al contrario, אין טוב באדם שיאכל *No bueno enel hombre, que coma y beva, y que vea ſu alma el bien en ſu trabajo.* Y conforme a eſto, comenta R. Semuel Iom tob. No ay tanto bien, o tanta felicidad enel hombre terreſtre, y ſugeto a mil calamidades, que coma y beua, ideſt, q́ goze deſte mundo, y juntamente ſu alma, del otro; pues como dizen los antiguos, לא כל אדם זוכה לשתי שלחנות (*Ni todos los hombres merecen gozar de dos meſas.*) Mas ſi alguna vez ſe halla algun hombre tan felice, ſe puede dezir por el, que fue particularmente protegido de la mano del Señor: y dá para eſto vna razon diziendo, que quien puede comer, y apreſurarſe en gozar los bienes deſte mundo, mas que yo? y con todo no por eſſo, pierdo las eſperanças de gozar el futuro de las almas.

V. R Baruch Jazia deſta ſuerte expone. No es bueno ni juſto que el hombre coma y beua, y ſe dé a entender, que por eſta via gozandoſe de ſus trabajos, podra felicitar ſu alma: porque גם זו *tambien eſta a ſaber el alma, veo yo que es de la mano de Dios,* divina y eſpiritual, y que aſſi no ſe felicita con los bienes terreſtres y materiales, mas con lo que es de ſu natural celeſte. Y dá para eſto la ſiguiente razon, quien ay que coma, y pienſe del dia del juizio, ſino yo? o el que es mortal como yo? Y pues eſto es aſſi, no puede aver enel

<meta>catchword: enel</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>EN EL ECCLESIASTE.</header>

enel hombre que come y beue como los otros animales brutos, eſte ſentimiento y cuydado del caſtigo futuro, a no ſer en quanto el alma eſpiritual differente dellos.

VI. Tambien puede eſte verſo admitir otro ſentido: es a ſaber, que ningun bien terreſtre o eſpiritual deue el hombre atribuyr a ſu induſtria y meritos, mas a la divina providencia. No ay bien enel hombre (dize,) ni conſiſte en comer y beuer en eſte mundo, y gozar deſpues ſu alma el fruto de ſus trabajos, todo viene de la mano de Dios. Porque como dize en otro lugar, a los mas entendidos y diligentes, falta muchas vezes el pan, y la ſalvacion depende no ſolamente del hombre, mas principalmente del auxilio y favor divino. Y en prueva deſto ſigue, que quien pudiera comer, eſto es, gozar deſte mundo, y juntamente ſentir y atender a la expeculacion y ciencia, mas que yo? Ninguno: mas eſto en mi, fue dadiva celeſte, y nada adqueri por proprio valor, ni meritos.

VII. O de otro modo, no conſiſte el bien del hombre, en comer y beuer, y moſtrar que ſu alma ſe felicita con ſus trabajos y riquezas: porque la felicidad no conſiſte en eſtas coſas mundanas, que la tierra produze, mas en las divinas, que ſolamente proceden de la mano del Señor.

En eſta conformidad ſe pueden tambien explicar los otros verſos, donde el ſabio parece que loa el comer, y beuer. Y aſſi enel cap. 3. 14. *Yo ſé que no ay mejor coſa en ellas, que ſalvo alegrarſe, y hazer bien en ſu vida. Y tambien todo el hombre que come y beue, y ve bien de ſu trabajo, dadiva del Dios es,* por eſta comida, ſe hade entender, la eſpiritual de la contemplacion de la Ley. O tratando en los verſos precedentes de la vanidad de las riquezas, dize, que el que con tanto cuydado las grangea, no ſaca dellas mas utilidad que comer y beuer, y hazer en ſu vida lo bueno en los ojos del Señor, o limoſnas por ſu alma. Y que el que eſto alcançáre, ſe puede

This is the natural condition of impious and extremely greedy men. Or he may be saying, take my example: who ate or lived more sumptuously and magnificently than I lived, or [was] more hurried and ready for work? And yet I did not condemn myself for that reason.

IV. The verse can admit another different consonance, because in rigor it does not say "there is no better thing than to eat, etc.," but on the contrary: <term>אין טוב באדם שיאכל</term> <gloss>"There is no good in man that he should eat and drink, and that his soul should see the good in his labor."</gloss> And according to this, R. Samuel Yom Tob comments: There is not so much good, or so much happiness in the terrestrial man, who is subject to a thousand calamities, in eating and drinking—that is, in enjoying this world—and together with his soul, the other; for as the ancients say, <term>לא כל אדם זוכה לשתי שלחנות</term> <gloss>"Not all men deserve to enjoy two tables."</gloss> But if some man is sometimes found to be so happy, it can be said of him that he was particularly protected by the hand of the Lord. He gives a reason for this, saying: Who can eat and hasten to enjoy the goods of this world more than I? And yet, for that, I do not lose the hopes of enjoying the future of souls.

V. R. Baruch Jazia explains it in this way: It is not good or just that man should eat and drink and give himself to understand that by this way, enjoying his labors, he will be able to make his soul happy; because <term>גם זו</term> <gloss>"also this, to know the soul,"</gloss> I see that it is from the hand of God, divine and spiritual, and that thus it is not made happy with terrestrial and material goods, but with what is of its celestial nature. He gives the following reason for this: Who is there that eats and thinks of the day of judgment but I? Or he who is mortal like me? And since this is so, there cannot be in

<column-break/>

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>ON ECCLESIASTES.</header>

the man who eats and drinks like other brute animals this sentiment and care for future punishment, unless it is in the spiritual soul that is different from them.

VI. This verse can also admit another meaning: that is to say, that man should not attribute any terrestrial or spiritual good to his industry and merits, but to divine providence. There is no good in man (he says), nor does it consist in eating and drinking in this world, and his soul later enjoying the fruit of his labors; everything comes from the hand of God. Because as he says in another place, the most understanding and diligent often lack bread, and salvation depends not only on man, but mainly on divine help and favor. And in proof of this, he continues that who could eat—that is, enjoy this world—and at the same time feel and attend to speculation and science, more than I? None. But this, in me, was a celestial gift, and I acquired nothing by my own value or merits.

VII. Or in another way: the good of man does not consist in eating and drinking, and showing that his soul is made happy by his labors and riches, because happiness does not consist in these mundane things that the earth produces, but in the divine ones, which proceed only from the hand of the Lord.

In this conformity, the other verses where the wise man seems to praise eating and drinking can also be explained. And thus in chap. 3:14: *I know that there is nothing better in them, than to rejoice, and to do good in his life. And also every man that eats and drinks, and sees good of all his labor, it is the gift of God.* By this food, one must understand the spiritual food of the contemplation of the Law. Or, dealing in the preceding verses with the vanity of riches, he says that he who gathers them with such care does not derive from them more utility than to eat and drink, and to do what is good in the eyes of the Lord in his life, or alms for his soul. And this is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death. He said: The Lord came from Sinai and dawned upon them from Seir; He shone forth from Mount Paran, and He came from among ten thousands of holy ones; at His right hand was a fiery law for them. Indeed, He loves the peoples; all His holy ones are in Your hand, and they followed at Your feet, receiving Your words. Moses commanded us a law <term>Torah</term> <gloss>teaching or instruction</gloss>, an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob. And He was King in Jeshurun <note>a poetic name for Israel</note>, when the heads of the people were gathered, the tribes of Israel together.

Let Reuben live and not die, and let his men be few in number. And this for Judah; and he said: Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people; let his hands be sufficient for him, and be a help against his adversaries.

And of Levi he said: Your <term>Thummim</term> and Your <term>Urim</term> <gloss>sacred lots used for divination by the High Priest</gloss> belong to Your pious man, whom You tested at Massah, and with whom You strived at the waters of Meribah; who said of his father and mother, "I have not seen them," and he did not acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they observed Your word and kept Your covenant. They shall teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel; they shall put incense before You and whole burnt offerings upon Your altar. Bless, Lord, his substance, and accept the work of his hands; strike the loins of those who rise against him and of those who hate him, so that they rise no more.

Of Benjamin he said: The beloved of the Lord shall dwell in safety by Him; He covers him all the day long, and He dwells between his shoulders.

And of Joseph he said: Blessed of the Lord be his land, with the precious things of heaven, with the dew, and with the deep that couches beneath; with the precious fruits of the sun, and with the precious yield of the months; with the finest produce of the ancient mountains, and with the precious things of the everlasting hills; with the precious things of the earth and its fullness, and the favor of Him who dwelt in the bush. Let these come upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the head of him who was prince among his brothers. His firstborn bull is his glory, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth; these are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and these are the thousands of Manasseh.

And of Zebulun he said: Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents. They shall call peoples to the mountain; there they shall offer righteous sacrifices; for they shall suck the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand.

And of Gad he said: Blessed is He who enlarges Gad; he dwells like a lioness, and tears the arm, even the crown of the head. He chose the first part for himself, for there the commander's portion was reserved; and he came with the heads of the people; he executed the justice of the Lord and His ordinances with Israel.

And of Dan he said: Dan is a lion's whelp that leaps from Bashan.

And of Naphtali he said: O Naphtali, satisfied with favor, and full of the blessing of the Lord, possess the sea and the south.

And of Asher he said: Blessed be Asher above sons; let him be favored by his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil. Your bolts shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be.

There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to help you, and in His majesty through the skies. The eternal God is a dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms; He drove out the enemy before you and said, "Destroy!" So Israel dwells in safety, the fountain of Jacob alone, in a land of grain and wine; His heavens also drop down dew. Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the Lord, the shield of your help, and the sword of your majesty! Your enemies shall cringe before you, and you shall tread upon their high places.

<column-break/>

Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the Lord showed him all the land: Gilead as far as Dan, all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the Western Sea, the Negeb, and the Plain—that is, the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees—as far as Zoar. And the Lord said to him, "This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying, 'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there."

So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord. And He buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows the place of his burial to this day. Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died; his eye was not undimmed, and his vigor had not abated. And the people of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days; then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were ended.

And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him; so the people of Israel obeyed him and did as the Lord had commanded Moses. And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the Lord sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land, and for all the mighty power and all the great terror that Moses performed in the sight of all Israel.

Completed on this Yom Kippur <gloss>Day of Atonement</gloss>, I stood and read to all Israel in my day.
The humble author <note>literally "the small author"</note> erased my perfection <note>or "innocence"</note> to their place <unclear>Amen</unclear>.

סלמותם בה יצעו החותות עד ענר מי טיפעל דבורו ויעשה רוסס בגרמי' ביהיס' טמט
בגבעון רוס וכתי' ודיום וגו' ובחכמי מפי' מהיו פועלי' בהבטת עיניהם כמ"ט נתן עיניו
בו ונעשה גל של עצמות וחין להפלס מזה טחס ימנח בטבע בעלי חיים מה ממית
בניכוי עינו למה סיתחיך בחייר מנוג חרסיתו כם מימכלו עיני חחד קרוט יזיקו
לרעים וייטיבו לטובי' טכח לוחן הרלח' והקו היכוכי היוכ' ממנו כלכל מכפס המקלת
ולהיות מחט החכמה נכרכת מחוס היעין ומבטי רחותה הס כחכיס ביד גבור וכמ"ש
רז"ל מקרב לרם בן יהודה בן גרים ורבים כחלה וכן חס ימנח דבור חכוני
גטמיי יקדר פעולה לו מעטס וכמ"ס חליו כל טכן טרחני טימנח דבור טכלי רוחני
יקדר פעולות כוללות ומעטיס ומזה הענין והמין ברבר יי' טמיס כעמו וכן בכביחיס
וחקמעה קרום לח מדרבר ודבר יי' חל מפה רומ"יי דבור בי וזה הדבור כמטך כפי מעלת
המדבר וקורבתו לבותו וכן לחמר החכם הנמ' בספר חור הטכל וז"ל כן הדבור החלהי
הבט לכל מי מרבר לחקו חו מרבר עור לו ודבר לעתיר לח ענין לל ם' והסתתק עמס
בסס דבור מפני מהדבור מורה על ההנהגה מתרגום ונקב ודבר ונדרל מהס תכלית
ההבדל בעבס ובענין זולתי סס הכהנה ומה סיורס עליו מתוק סס היות זה הדבור
כמלח להסלוס בו חפץ וכוונה ורונה וזה נס כן בדמותו ע"כל והבן זה מחר
מהוח כינך מפת יקום בעניינים החלקיים זסו דעתי' בענין הזה והוא מקום לכל לפי
דעת

<header>Chapter Four of the Fifth Treatise</header>

<note>A decorative printer's ornament appears at the beginning of the chapter.</note>

...to do evil to him for good, according to the thought and intention they have at the time of their contemplation and their desire to influence that matter with good or evil. With this, the cause of the matter of amulets and incantations will be clarified, and the benefit drawn from them according to the mentioning of a thing without contemplation. It acts like the specific magic in a specific Kabbalah from it, the content of a seal of a property <note>term: "segulah"</note> and its cause. This is not understood. 

From this matter, as it is said in the words of our Sages in tractate *Shabbat*, in the chapter "Those who whisper" <note>term: "Lachashin"</note>. Three of wisdom are hinted at here. They act in matters of the selection of the Sages. For their mouth is the body, and this is the cause of the property of the seal of the incantations. Because the incantation placed in their mouth was useful, as it is said: "Life is in the hand of the tongue." Assistance will not be supported by the seal of the incantation written by those who whisper, but by the seal of the incantations of others according to the degree of their perfection with them, of blessed memory. The absence of the seal of the property from the seal of the Sages is because it moved from their mouths. They say "from the mouth of those who whisper," as it was noted what acquired a certain property. When it is moved from its place, its property is lost. 

Therefore, any matter that was once a source of properties for medicines for the doctors of their time, they established a seal and wrote it in a book. In our time, their property is absent because of the transfer of the seal from place to place. There is no doubt that the place has a great impression on the acquisition of the property or the form for a matter. As mentioned in the fourth book of the *Sefer Ha-Kilyot* <gloss>Book of Kidneys</gloss>. If so, the action of the names and the amulets is in the Kabbalah. It is possible that the seal of the property is absent when transferring things from mouth to mouth. 

As the Sages said: "For the correction of those who whisper, they do not act by themselves but only for the seal from the absolute mouth." Behold, the whisper before eating kills the scorpion, etc. It is said that the whisper depends on the person <note>term: "chomet"</note> according to his level and his place in wisdom. His words will act on things that stand outside, as explained regarding the prophets. According to their perfection in it, they produced signs. Until there was one whose speech acts and makes an impression on the celestial bodies, as the sun stood in Gibeon, and it is written: "And the sun stood still," etc. Among the Sages of Egypt, they would act by the gaze of their eyes, as it is said: "He cast his eyes upon him and he became a heap of bones." 

One should not wonder at this, for it is found in the nature of animals that one kills by the sight of its eye. Why should it be unique to the nature of a person's temperament? So too if the eyes of a holy one are focused, they will harm the wicked and do good for the righteous. It is within the power of the sight and the line of sight that goes out from it to everything that receives the influence. Since the essence of wisdom is recognized by the depth of contemplation and the gaze of its vision, they are like arrows in the hand of a warrior. 

As our Sages said regarding the approach of the person, the son of Judah, the son of Gerim, and many like these. So if a physical human speech is found to have a small action, how much more so for a spiritual person. If a spiritual intellectual speech is found, it will produce comprehensive actions and deeds. From this matter and kind is the "by the word of the Lord the heavens were made." So too with the prophets and the amulet. Before he speaks, the word of the Lord is on his mouth. This speech is according to the level of the speaker and his closeness to his Creator. So too says the wise man mentioned in the book *Or Ha-Sekhel* <gloss>Light of the Intellect</gloss>: "Thus the Divine speech looks to everyone who speaks it, or speaks to him, and will speak in the future." 

This is the concept of "and he was silenced with the name of speech," because speech indicates leadership, from the translation "and he shall lead" <note>term: "ve-dibber"</note>. There is an ultimate distinction between them in essence and matter, except for the name of the intention and what it indicates. The strength of the name being this speech is filled with the completion of desire, intention, and will. This is also in its image. Understand this well from the truth. Behold, you are a source of rising in particular matters. This is my opinion on this matter. It is a place for everyone according to their knowledge.

היו חמשה פתחים זה לפנים מזה וכו'. ברייתא זו לענין טומאה נשנית וכדתנן בפ' י"ג דאהלות העושה מאור בתחלה שיעורו מלא עול משפט מקדח לענין להביא ולהוציא את הטומאה וכדמפרש חסר לפנינו גריס שס פ"ג ד' י"ד פתח שעשהו למאור שיעורו מלא מקדח הגופו נר מצוה למאור (שבזמנו להאור שכנגדו כגון שבבית שיש בנין ואין כאן מאור הלכך היו בונין כמו חלונות קטנים ושיעורו כפומא דנפא) שיעורו כפומא דנפא שפי' חלונות זו לפנים מזו סתומות שעשוי למאור שיעורו מלא מקדח. וס"ל הני ככונה כדמוכח דלקמן: ולא מסייעא למאן דאמר חמרין בנין. הברייתא זו סיוע למאן דאמרי הבתים חזיין להיות פתוחה להוסיף לאור לה נעשית אלא להכניס את האורה ומכאן שאין לה חזקה אינה מביאה את הטומאה:

### הלכה יא מתני' *אין עושין חלל תחת רשות הרבים בורות שיחין ומערות ר"א מתיר כדי שתהא עגלה מהלכת וטעונה אבנים *אין מוציאין זיזין וכצטצראות לרשות הרבים אלא אם רצה כונס לתוך שלו *ומוציא *לקח חצר ובה זיזין וכצטצראות הרי זו בחזקתה: גמ' נפלו ומבקש לבנותן רבי יוחנן אמר *ויותר ריש לקיש אמר לא ויותר מתניתין מסייעה לדין ומתניתין מסייעה לדין מתניתין מסייעה לרבי יוחנן *מי שהיתה יד דרך הרבים עוברת בתוך שדהו ונטלה ונתן להן מן הצד מה שנתן נתן ושלו לא הגיע מהני' מסייעה לריש לקיש *לקח חצר ובה זיזין וכצטצראות ונפלו בונה אותן בחזקתן:

->הדרן עלך פרק חזקת הבתים<-

### הלכה א מתני' המוכר את הבית לא מכר את היציע אע"פ שהיא פתוחה לתוכו ולא את החדר שלפנים ממנו ולא את הגג בזמן שיש לו מעקה גבוה עשרה טפחים רבי יהודה אומר אם יש לו צורת פתח אע"פ שאינו גבוה עשרה טפחים אינו מכור: גמ' רבי נחום בשם רבי חייה בר בא והוא שיהא בה ארבע על ארבע על רום עשרה ובלבד במקורה ובמגופף. אמר לון רבי זירא כל הדין פירושא הפרש לכון ר' חייה בר אבא ולא את הגג בזמן שיש לו מעקה גבוה עשרה טפחים. סוף דבר מעקה היו אחורי בתים מקיפין אותו היו שם עמודים וכלוסניות על גביהן. נישמעינה מהדא ר' יהודה אומר אם יש לו צורת פתח אף על פי שאינו גבוה עשרה טפחים אינו מכור. אמרין והוא שיש שם מעקה גבוה עשרה טפחים:

->הלכה<-

מקלקין ופוחת מלמטה שלח פדתו: זיזין. בליטות קטנים: וכלילכלאות. קורות גדולות סמך יכסו בהן בני רשות הרבים לח"כ היו למעלה מגמל וביסו וסולו שלח יחפיר הדרך על בני ר"ה: כונס לתוך שלו. סמכיס בקרקע שלו כשיעור הולכת הזיזין ומוציא: הרי זו בחזקתה. דטוענין ללוקח ואמרינן סמס לו המוכר לו כנס לתוך שלו: גמ' נפלו. זיזין וכנטכלאות ומבקש לבנותן להוציאן לר"ה כבתחלה ולכקח חלל ובה זיזין וגו' ומוכספת קלי: ויותר. לבני ר"ה ולינו יכול להוציא: מי שהיתה דרך הרבים וכו'. מתני'. מסני' סיס לקמן בפ"ו מסוס דמילר ססחיזיק בו כניס ססור לקלקלו וס"ל כרבי יוחנן כמו ססחיזיק בו כניס סול: מתניתי'. תוספתא בפ"ב מסייעה לר"ל דקתני כסדיס נפלו בונה אותן במקומן:

->הדרן עלך חזקת הבתים<-

### הלכה א מתני' המוכר את הבית. סולט. כגון חלר סעוסין סביבות כתלי הבית מחוץ כמין סכוי עוסין כמקדס לסכין וסוליט התחתונה ויס סעוסין לותס כעובי הכתל ולע"פ ספתוס לבית ותסמיסו כתוכו לפ"ס לינו מכור וסול דקוי ד' אמות כדחמר בגמרל: ולס לס ססדר סלפניס. מן סס סבית ולפ"ס ססול פתוס לבית וסמיסו עליו וקמ"ל כסדר דלע"פ דמנזר לו מלוים החיכוניס סל סבית לס למרינן דססדר ככלל סבית סול מלסד כסר מלר ספלוני חלס למרינן מלוים סלסון לו סמכרי סבית החיכוניס ניכרס סס כזמן סיס לו מעקה גבוס עשרה טפחים. סוי מקוס ססון כפני עלמו ולס כטל לגבי סבית: לס יס לו לורת הפתח. ולינו סלכס כרבי יהודה: גמ' וסול סיס כס לרכע. לרכע למות וסוליט קמי דכפחות מד' למות לס ססיס וכטל לגבי בית: כל סדין פירוסל ספרס לכון ל'. סיינו מס דקתני ר' יסודס וכו' עלס על ססלריך דוקל ל' על ד' ומקורה ומגופף ועל רוס עשרה: ולס לס סגג וכו' סוף דבר מעקה. כעין סיס לס סוף דבר סול כלומר לי נימל דוקל מעקה קסס סס"ק ולס סיו לסורי כתיס מקיפין לותו וסיו סס עמודים ע"ג סכתי' וכלוסניות על גביסן מסו לו סיו כמקנס לו לס: ניסמעינס מן סדל. לכ' יסודס דלמר לס יס לו לורת הפתח וכו' ועמודים וכלוסניות על גביסן ככורת הפתח סוו ור' יסודס סול דס"ל ללורת הפתח מסני: למרין. סיומל דמילתל סיס כלומר ס"מ דסמניס כ' יסודס לסכניס ולסוכין וסול סס מעקה גבוס עשרה טפחים לכל מילתל לססריס לס מסני ועלס קלמר ר' יסודס דלס יס לו לורת הפתח כמי מסני:

->הלכה<-

---

->מראה הפנים<-

היו חמשה פתחים וכו'. כככר סכסתי כתוספתס דלסלות כפ"ס. וסרמכ"ן ז"ל סניס דסכס דפליגי סתס כר' י"ל כענין לס כנס לסחזיר כסליס למקומן לפסק סרמכ"ס ז"ל לפסוקי ספסטס ולס זכר ללוס מסתוספתל. ולפסר דדוקל וספרס ספי' דסכל דקוס כפ"י מס' סכניס ס"ד כו' וסיינו דלס כסני סכני נענין לס כפלו כנין לו כפלו סכותל כנגד זס ססיו לותס וססמיסס כס סלור ללון וכסלס וססדר כיוס כולן כמסס מקדס סזול וכונס לותי כמקומן ומוכס לדתנן כתוספתל וללו מלו סססמיסו כו כניס סול: חכל לס מסמע סכי מסתוספתל. ומכל מקוס סול ז"ל דסק סמני' כמולס סתס סלוקי פתחיס ללו וכו' וסס סיינו דוקל ססיו עשויין ללור עכ"ל סס:

### סליק פירקא בסיעתא דשמיא

סליק פירקא בסיעתא דשמיא כדכתב כפ"ו מכסיס סלכ' ז' וסלס סס פתחס ללורס לפי' פחות מכמ"ק וכו' ולח"כ פרק ד המוכר לס סבית. סולט. מס דפירסתי כפניס סס דכרי סר"י ז"ל וסרמכ"ס ז"ל כפ"י מס' סכניס סלכ' י"ס: וסיינו סלס ססדר סול דככלל סבית לענין סכירות לכל כסכילס ססדר סול כפני עלמו כדמפרס כגמרל: ודעת סרמכ"ס ז"ל סכתב וסול ססי' עליו מעקה חלס סלס סול ססדר סססדר סכית ומגופף לדעתו דלס סיס כתוך סוכי סל כיתל ככלל סבית סול ולפעמיס לסמס. וזסו דכדכרי סתוספתל ססכלתי. וכפ"י דלכ"כ סס כתב סס"מ כדין סלולס סול דסדר מכפל ליס זיזין וסול קטנס כמין סכיכות סכותליס סכתוכו פ"ד מכלכות וסלכס פירסתי כסמנו סס וכו' לכינו סלסון לכן ז"ל. וכפי' סס"ל יוסף סלוי ז"ל חכר כית סכסילס סלכס ט' וסכי פי' לכקמל חללס קלמר כב יוסף ססס כריס פרקין וקלמר לפני לס מלסתי מזו: מתניתי' מסייעה לריס לקיס. דכדכרי סתוספתל סך פסק סס סתס לכל לפסס מוככיל וסילס סל"י ז"ל ע"פ סגמ' גבי סנית וסיינו פותסו לתוך ססל סתס כדכרי סתוספתל ססכלתי. וכפ"י סס"ל יוסף סלוי ז"ל חכר כית וכו' סס"מ ק"ו ז"ל סס: דלקמן חלל מכריות לסריס ומסו לס. ויס לומר דמכסי' מתני' ל"ק דלס מוקמי מלד כס סדין פירוסל וכו'. כסמיס וסכי מסמע סתס דלס קסיד מר זוטרל חלל סיסל כרכיס דלס כססחיזיק כסלס דכר ממס ססיס כגון כסס כמתני' וכן כדי' דמתני' כרחכו לרכע למות וכ"ס סרמכ"ס ז"ל סס וסרסכ"ס ז"ל פירס סרכע על לרכע:

->עמודי ירושלים חנינא<-

**If there were five openings, one inside the other...** This Baraita was taught regarding the laws of ritual impurity. As we learned in Chapter 13 of Ohalot: one who makes a light-hole <note>aperture</note> initially, its size is the full measure of a drill's bit to bring in or take out ritual impurity. As explained before us, the version there in Chapter 14 is: a door made for light, its size is a drill's bit; for a lamp <note>meant for its own time, for the light opposite it, such as in a house where there is construction and no light, they would build small windows</note>, its size is the "mouth of a bellows" <note>original: "fuma de-napa"</note>. This explains windows one inside the other that are closed and made for light. It seems these are intentional, as proven later. **And it does not support the one who says "they are for building."** This Baraita supports those who say houses are meant to be open to add light, rather than being built merely to bring in the light. From this, it has no presumption of right and does not bring ritual impurity.

### Law 11 - Mishnah
**One may not make a hollow space <note>cavity or cellar</note> under the public domain — neither pits, nor trenches, nor caves. Rabbi Eliezer permits it, provided that a wagon can travel over it while loaded with stones.**
**One may not extend architectural projections <term>zizin</term> or balconies <term>kitztzaraot</term> into the public domain, unless the builder recedes his wall into his own property and then extends them.**
**If one purchased a courtyard that already had projections or balconies, it remains in its established presumption of right.**

**Gemara:** If they fell and one seeks to rebuild them: Rabbi Yochanan says, it is permitted. Resh Lakish says, it is not permitted. Our Mishnah supports this one, and our Mishnah supports that one. Our Mishnah supports Rabbi Yochanan: **If a public path passed through his field and he took it and gave them a path on the side, what he gave is given, but his own does not return to him.** The Mishnah supports Resh Lakish: **If one purchased a courtyard with projections and balconies and they fell, he may rebuild them in their presumed location.**

->May we return to you, "Presumption of Houses" Chapter!<-

### Law 1 - Mishnah
**One who sells a house has not sold the annex <term>yatzia</term>, even if it is open into the house. Nor has he sold the inner room, nor the roof, provided it has a parapet ten handbreadths high. Rabbi Yehuda says: If it has the form of a doorway <term>tzurat ha-petach</term>, even if it is not ten handbreadths high, it is not sold.**

**Gemara:** Rabbi Nachum in the name of Rabbi Hiyya bar Ba: This applies only when it is four by four cubits, ten handbreadths high, and provided it is roofed and enclosed. Rabbi Zera said to them: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba explained all of this distinction to you. **"Nor the roof when it has a parapet ten handbreadths high."** Ultimately, a parapet was a fence behind the houses surrounding it. There were pillars and beams upon them. Let us learn from this: Rabbi Yehuda says if it has the form of a doorway, even if not ten high, it is not sold. They said: This applies only if there is a parapet ten handbreadths high.

->Law<-

**Disturbing and diminishing from below...** <term>Zizin</term> are small projections. <term>Kitztzaraot</term> are large beams. The concern was that they would cover those in the public domain, therefore they had to be higher than a camel and its rider so they would not impede the path. **Recedes into his own property.** He moves his ground back by the measure of the projection's length. **Remains in its established presumption.** We argue on behalf of the buyer that perhaps the seller had receded his wall into his own property. **Gemara: If they fell.** The projections and balconies, and he wants to rebuild them in the public domain as before. **It is permitted.** For the public, and he cannot extend them. **One who had a public path...** This Mishnah appears later in Chapter 6. Since the public has established a right to it, it is forbidden to ruin it. This follows Rabbi Yochanan, that since the public has established a right, it is theirs. **Our Mishnah.** The Tosefta in Chapter 2 supports Resh Lakish, which explicitly teaches: if they fell, he may rebuild them in their place.

->May we return to you, "Presumption of Houses"<-

### Law 1 - Mishnah
**One who sells a house.** This refers to a <term>sullet</term> <gloss>a type of side-structure</gloss>, such as a gallery built around the walls of the house from the outside, like the structures in the Temple. Even though it is open to the house and its use is within it, it is not sold. This is only if it is four cubits, as said in the Gemara. **Nor the inner room.** Even though it opens to the house and is used by it, it teaches us that even if he refers to the "outer rooms of the house," we do not say the inner room is included in the "so-and-so's house." Rather, the outer rooms are recognizable as the house. **When it has a parapet ten handbreadths high.** It is considered a significant place in its own right and is not nullified relative to the house. **If it has the form of a doorway.** The law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda. **Gemara: Provided it is four.** Four cubits. For less than four cubits, it is not significant and is nullified relative to the house. **All of this distinction...** That is, what Rabbi Yehuda taught, requiring 4x4, roofed, enclosed, and ten high. **Ultimately a parapet.** Like a fence. That is, if we say specifically a parapet is required, what if there were pillars and beams? Would they be considered a roofed area or not? **Let us learn from this.** Rabbi Yehuda says the form of a doorway is sufficient. Pillars and beams are like the form of a doorway.

---

->The Face of the Image<- <note>Pnei Moshe commentary</note>

**If there were five openings...** As I already wrote regarding the Tosefta of Ohalot. Nachmanides noted that they argue there regarding whether one can return projections to their place. Maimonides ruled on the simple meaning. It is possible the distinction is that this refers to a wall facing another, where the use was for light, and if it fell, he may rebuild it in its place. This is proven from the Tosefta.

### The Chapter is finished with the help of Heaven

The chapter is finished with the help of Heaven. As written in Chapter 6 of the Laws of Neighbors, Law 7. And if he made an opening for light, even less than a drill's measure... And then Chapter 4: One who sells a house. <term>Yatzia</term>. What I explained is according to the words of the Riaz and Maimonides in Chapter 10 of Neighbors. The inner room is included in the house regarding rentals, but in a sale, it is a separate entity. Maimonides' view is that a parapet makes it a distinct house.

<summary>This page concludes the third chapter of Bava Batra, focusing on public domain encroachments, and begins the fourth chapter, which defines what architectural features are included in the legal sale of a "house." It establishes that significant annexes, inner rooms, and roofs with high parapets are legally distinct from the main house in sales contracts.</summary>

# The Book of "These are the Words"
<note>original: *Sefer Elleh ha-Devarim*, the Hebrew title for Deuteronomy, taken from its opening words</note>

**Right Column**

...from the midst of a nation, by trials, by signs, and by wonders,
and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by an outstretched arm,
and by great terrors, according to all that
the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes.
You were shown, so that you might know that the LORD is
God; there is no other besides Him. From
the heavens, He made you hear His voice to discipline you,
and upon the earth, He showed you His great fire,
and His words you heard from the midst of the fire.
And because He loved your ancestors, He chose
their offspring after them, and He brought you out with His presence, by His 
great power, from Egypt; to drive out nations greater
and mightier than you from before you, to bring you in, to give
you their land as an inheritance, as it is this day.
And you shall know today, and lay it to your heart, that
the LORD is God in the heavens above
and upon the earth below; there is no other.
And you shall keep His statutes and His commandments which
I command you today, so that it may go well with you
and with your children after you, and so that you may prolong your days
upon the land which the LORD your God is giving
to you for all time. <note>The Hebrew letter "פ" (Pe) marks a *Petuchah*, a major paragraph break in the scroll</note>
Then Moses set apart three cities across
the Jordan, toward the sunrise <note>meaning to the East</note>: so that there might flee
there a manslayer who kills his neighbor without
intent, not having hated him in time
past; he shall flee to one of these
cities and live: Bezer in the wilderness on the
tableland for the Reubenites; Ramoth
in Gilead for the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan

<column-break/>

**Left Column**

to the Manassites: <note>This completes the list of cities of refuge from the previous column</note> And this is the Torah <note>instruction or law</note> which

Moses spoke to the children of Israel when they went out
from Egypt: across the Jordan, in the valley opposite

who lived in Heshbon, whom
Moses and the children of Israel defeated when they went out from Egypt.
And they took possession of his land and the land of Og,
king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites who
were across the Jordan toward the sunrise: from Aroer,
which is on the edge of the Arnon Brook, even to Mount
Sion—that is, Hermon—and all the Arabah <note>the plain or valley</note> across
the Jordan eastward, as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under
the slopes of Pisgah.
<note>פ - Paragraph break</note>
And Moses called to
all Israel and said to them: "Hear,
O Israel, the statutes and the ordinances
which I speak in your ears today;
you shall learn them and be careful to do them.
The LORD our God made a covenant
at Horeb <note>the mountain where the Law was given, also called Sinai</note>. Not with our ancestors did
the LORD make this covenant, but with us—
we who are here today, all of us alive.
Face to face the LORD spoke with you on the mountain
from the midst of the fire. I stood between the LORD
and you at that time to tell you the
word of the LORD, for you were afraid because of the fire and
did not go up the mountain, saying:

who...'"

(Left Column)
<margin>Afumiya</margin>
<margin>Afumiya</margin>
<margin>A child of man</margin>
By writing the name called Afumiya today, one sees the seeds of gossip in this fleeting world. The talk of the people in the village, criticizing the young woman of the house <note>original: "里の小かゝ" (sato no kokaka), referring to the daughter or young mistress of the establishment</note> (Baifu of Afumiya), became a struggle. Even the sliding doors at the gate were locked, yet because she would not mingle with those who entered, the depth of the world's malice made her heart bitter. Since she would not refuse them, she became the subject of gossip. A volume titled "Waking from Sleep" <note>original: "寝覚" (Nezame)</note> was circulated, focusing on the rumors surrounding Afumiya. This focus on Afumiya turned to profit, making her famous in the world.

<column-break/>

(Right Column)
<margin>Afumiya</margin>
<margin>Afumiya</margin>
Writing the entrance of the servant girl, with no words to speak, discarding the door behind her, calling it the Age of the Gods <note>original: "神代" (kamiyo), an idiom implying something archaic or long-distant</note>. She was urged to take this letter to Afumiya. Without a suspicious heart, the daughter of Afumiya, the girl of the west, was treated with respect. Remembering the modesty of her words, her mother wrote a letter <note>original: "玉章" (tamazusa), a literary term for a letter</note>. Afumiya took this hidden note to be a matter concerning her family home. She masked the affair, claiming it was nothing but an innocent matter concerning the name Afumiya itself. To speak of it beyond that is sorrowful. The talk of the world, speaking of the mouth of Afumiya, what shall we call it? Until now, it was a thing of the past, a matter regarding the parents of Afumiya.

<summary>This page describes the rise of gossip surrounding a young woman named Afumiya, whose refusal to engage with suitors leads to rumors that ironically increase her fame, culminating in the exchange of a letter that she misinterprets as a simple family matter.</summary>

Lord Nabeshima Heizaemon-no-jō Kiyohisa resided in Honjō Village. Before the local festival, he and his wife would come out every night carrying poles, spending the entire night poking at the moat. Because people would drain the moat and catch carp for the festival, he did this to make the fish flee. Beyond that, his compassion regarding public works was boundless. In his daily life, he was a devout believer in the Hikosan faith, and every year at the year’s end, he would seclude himself in prayer. Once, while he was at the Upper Shrine, heavy snow fell and the path became unclear; he fell off a cliff and dropped into a valley. When they searched for him in that area, they found the <term>Amida Sanzon</term> <gloss>The Trinity of Amida Buddha</gloss> that he had been holding. He brought them back and made them the principal objects of worship for the Tokuzen Hikosan shrine. It is said that the original deity of Hikosan is the Amida Trinity. It is a mysterious event. It appears that the prosperity of his house is due to that merit. This is the rumor among the old folks.

The image of the Tokuzen Gongen deity is said to be the same as the principal image of the Zōryū-bō of Hikosan. It is said that when it was lost in a fire, the original image was sunk into a well, and because of that, the mountain was safe. I heard this story from the abbot some years ago. (The sacred body of Tokuzen Gongen is viewed during each succession.)

When Nabeshima Monda-dono was young, he was taken in as an adopted son by Lord Naoshige. However, upon the birth of Lord Katsushige, the fief at the former site of Yokotake was given to Monda-dono.

Do you think the spears of the Nabeshima clan are weak? I shall show you my proof before everyone tomorrow. This is quite different from your criticisms from behind the walls. and then returned home.

According to one account, the messenger mentioned above was Naritomi Hyōgo, though some also say it was Kuboshiro Kuboshi.

Regarding the instruction that descendants should not study military tactics: When one faces the battlefield, the power of discernment emerges, and it is something that cannot be stopped by any means. If you are governed by analytical thinking, you will be unable to break through enemy lines. A lack of calculation is essential when standing before the jaws of a tiger. If you have been listening to theories of military tactics, you will be filled with doubts, and you will never reach a resolution. It is said that he commanded his descendants not to study the practice of military tactics.

A certain general once said that for samurai other than the troop commanders, when testing armor, one should only test the front. Furthermore, he noted that the cords of the armor do not require special care, but the helmet must be inspected thoroughly. It is something one carries toward the enemy camp, after all, when taking a head.

Those who appear calm at the moment of death are suspicious. There are many such examples. It is understood that if a man who habitually talks a great deal becomes flustered at the moment of his death, he is not a true warrior.

When the Taikō Toyotomi Hideyoshi was a man of low standing, his companions left him behind. However, after he became the ruler of Japan, he spent every night writing out the administration of the realm and the allocation of stipends for his retainers.

In the <term>Enzan Hōgo</term> <gloss>Dharma words from Salt Mountain</gloss>, it is written: From a young age, a single doubt arose within me. If I were to inquire, "Who is the one who answers when I ask who it is that has achieved this personhood?" From the moment that singular doubt began, it grew deeper as the years passed. When I decided to enter the priesthood, a great vow arose. If I am to become a monk, I shall not seek the Way for my own sake alone. I shall attain the great law of the Buddhas, save all sentient beings, and only then seek complete enlightenment. Furthermore, until this doubt is resolved, I shall not study Buddhist teachings, nor shall I learn the etiquette of the clergy. If I must mingle with people, I shall place myself only among the wise teachers or in the mountains. After becoming a monk, as my doubt grew deeper, this vow also intensified. In the interval between the previous Buddha who has already attained nirvana and the future Buddha who has yet to appear in this world, at a time when the Buddhist law is fading, I wish to manifest a great path that will be an obstacle-free guide for the beings of this Buddha-less world. Even if I were to fall into the Avīchi hell <note>the lowest, most painful level of hell</note> because of the sin of this attachment, if I could only take the place of the suffering of sentient beings, I would never retreat.

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of action over theory in battle, the character of a true warrior, and includes a philosophical reflection on the vow of a monk to delay personal enlightenment to serve others.</summary>

# ON THE STEREOMETRIC LINES AND FIRSTLY

---

The present **Stereometric lines** <note>A specialized scale on the instrument where divisions are proportional to the cube roots of numbers, used for calculating volumes and scaling three-dimensional objects</note> are so named because their division is according to the proportion of solid bodies, up to 148. From these we will derive many uses, the first of which shall be the one already proposed: namely, how—given one side of any solid body—one can find the side of another which has a given proportion to it. 

For example, let line **A** be the diameter, for instance <note>original: "v.g.", an abbreviation for the Latin *verbi gratia*</note>, of a sphere—or a "ball," to use more common speech—or perhaps the side of a cube or other solid. Let it be proposed to us that we must find the diameter or side of another [solid] that has the same proportion to the first as 20 has to 36. Take line **A** with the compasses <note>referring to a pair of dividers used to transfer distances</note> and, opening the instrument, apply this measurement transversally to point 36 of the **Stereometric lines**. Once this is done, immediately take the interval between the points 20 and 20, which

will result in line **B**, the diameter or side of the solid [corresponding] to the other (whose side was **A**) in the given proportion of 20 to 36.

# ¶ Part Three: in which twelve stimuli will be enumerated, by which every hardened and unrefined person may be encouraged and led to easily weep for the cruel death and bitter passion of our most pious Redeemer

In the center, Jesus is tied to a pillar, his body slightly turned and head bowed. He is surrounded by four muscular men in dynamic poses, who are scourging him with bundles of rods or whips. Jesus is shown with a halo and wearing only a loincloth. The setting appears to be an interior with a window frame visible in the background.</image-desc>

The proud mind of the human creature does not deign to have compassion for its Lord dying on the cross. The hardened soul thinks, in its self-importance <note>original: "gravita," referring to a sense of worldly dignity or seriousness</note>, that it is not fitting to weep and lament in such a case. And you shall describe how these nerves are distributed through the muscles of the neck and the shoulders, and how they provide sensation and motion to the arms and the hands. --- the senses original: "sensi"; referring to the physiological transmission of sensory data to the brain. The spinal cord is the source of the nerves which give voluntary motion to the limbs. Note how the marrow original: "midolla"; the spinal cord is protected within the hardness of the bone, for it is the most vital part of the body after the brain. --- of the ligaments original: "legamenti"; the connective tissues holding the joints together. The vertebrae of the neck are seven, and they are bound together by strong ligaments and cartilage original: "cartilagine". Without these, the weight of the head would cause the spine to collapse upon itself like a chain. --- the center of gravity original: "centro della gravità"; a core concept in Leonardo's mechanical studies of the body. When the neck bends, the vertebrae on the side of the contraction are compressed, while those on the opposite side are stretched. This is why the marrow must be flexible and situated exactly in the center of the vertebral column. ## Ermenia.

Ermenia per se medesimo, cioè in Lajazzo d' Erminia, ove si fa il forzo della mercatanzia, perché ene alla marina, e ivi dimorano del continovo i risedenti mercatanti.
Pepe, e gengiovo, e zucchero, e cannella, e incenso, e verzino, e lacca, e cotone, e tutte spiezerie grosse, e ferro, e rame, e stagno, tutte si vendono in Erminia a ruotoli d' occhia 15 per uno ruotolo, e di ruotoli 33 per uno Catars d' Erminia.
Sete, e tutte spezie sottile vi si vendono a occhia di occhie 12 per uno ruotolo, e chiamasi occhia della piazza.
Oro si vende a pesi, che gli 50 pesi fanno 1 mars d' Erminia.
Argento si vende a mars, ch' è 50 pesi.
Pelle si vendono a peso del marchio, e dassi 40 de' detti pesi per una ara grande di pelle.
Tele line, e canovacci si vendono a centinajo di canne, e a pregio di tanti Bisanti, e den. 10 taccolini per bisante.
Sapone, e lana, e ciambellotti si vendono a ruotoli d' occhie 15 per uno ruotolo.
Biado si vende all' Ajazzo in Erminia a moggio, & a marzapanni, cioè in grosso, e a moggio a minuto a marzapanni, e gli 10 marzapanni fanno 1 moggio.
Seta chermisi si vende a occhia ch' è pesi 110 di diremo.
Zafferano si vende a occhia ch' è pesi 112 di diremo.
Olio si vende a botte tale come ella ene.
Il bisante di Romania si conta 10 taccolini d' argento, e il taccolino vale den. 10 d' Erminia, e il denaro vale 4 folleri.

*Quello, che la Zecca d' Erminia da dello mars dell' argento a chi il mette nella detta Zecca.*

Di Sardescho - - - - - - - - - - - taccolini 114 denari 1.
Di piatte della bolla di Vinegia taccolini 113 e denari 1.
A lega di Tornesi grossi taccolini 111.
A lega di Gigliati taccolini 110. e denari 5.
Di bracciali, cioè Buenmini taccolini 109. e denari 2.

<meta>This page moves from the description of trade in Setalia (modern Antalya) to Armenia—specifically the port of Lajazzo (modern Yumurtalık), which was the primary gateway for trade between Europe and the Mongol Empire's Silk Road in the 13th and 14th centuries.</meta>

CHAPTER XI.

## Armenia.

Armenia itself—that is, in Lajazzo <note>modern Ayas or Yumurtalık, Turkey; a major port of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia</note>—is where the bulk of the merchandise is traded, because it is on the coast and merchant residents live there continually.

Pepper, ginger, sugar, cinnamon, incense, brazilwood <note>original: "verzino," a wood used to produce red dye</note>, lacquer, cotton, and all bulk spices, as well as iron, copper, and tin, are all sold in Armenia by the *ruotolo* <note>a standard Mediterranean unit of weight, the rotolo</note> of 15 *occhia* <note>the okka, a common unit of weight in the Eastern Mediterranean, roughly 1.2 kg</note> per *ruotolo*, and 33 *ruotoli* make one *Catars* <note>a cantaro or hundredweight</note> of Armenia.

Silk and all fine spices are sold there by the *occhia* at a rate of 12 *occhia* per *ruotolo*, and this is called the "market *occhia*."

Gold is sold by weight, where 50 *pesi* <term>pesi: literally "weights"</term> make 1 *mars* <note>a mark, a unit of weight for precious metals</note> of Armenia.

Silver is sold by the *mars*, which is 50 *pesi*.

Hides are sold by the weight of the mark, and 40 of these weights are given for one large *ara* <note>a specific measurement or bundle size</note> of hide.

Linen cloths and canvases are sold by the hundred *canne* <term>canna</term> <note>a "cane" or rod, a linear measure of roughly 2 meters</note>, at the price of a certain number of Bezants <note>original: "Bisanti," a gold or silver coin used throughout the Levant</note>, with 10 *taccolini* <note>likely the Armenian takvorin, a silver coin</note> per Bezant.

Soap, wool, and camlets <note>original: "ciambellotti," a cloth made from camel or goat hair</note> are sold by the *ruotolo* of 15 *occhia*.

Grain is sold at Lajazzo in Armenia by the *moggio* <note>a dry measure for grain</note> and by the *marzapanni*; that is, in bulk by the *moggio* and in smaller amounts by the *marzapanni*, and 10 *marzapanni* make 1 *moggio*.

Crimson silk is sold by the *occhia*, which weighs 110 *diremo* <note>the dirhem, a small unit of weight used for high-value goods</note>.

Saffron is sold by the *occhia*, which weighs 112 *diremo*.

Oil is sold by the barrel, just as it is.

The Bezant of Romania <note>referring to the Latin Empire or Byzantine territories</note> is counted as 10 silver *taccolini*, and the *taccolino* is worth 10 Armenian *denari* <note>pennies</note>, and the *denaro* is worth 4 *folleri* <note>small copper coins</note>.

->*What the Armenian Mint gives for a mark of silver to whoever brings it to the said Mint:*<-

Of Sardinian silver - - - - - - - - - - - 114 *taccolini*, 1 *denaro*.
Of Venetian bullion plates <note>original: "piatte della bolla di Vinegia"</note> - 113 *taccolini* and 1 *denaro*.
At the alloy of the *Gros tournois* <note>original: "Tornesi grossi," a silver coin of France</note> - 111 *taccolini*.
At the alloy of the *Gigliati* <note>original: "Gigliati," silver coins of Naples/Provence featuring lilies</note> - 110 *taccolini* and 5 *denari*.
Of bracelets, that is, *Buenmini* <note>likely referring to Bohemian groschen or a specific form of imported bullion</note> - 109 *taccolini* and 2 *denari*.

A most humble physician, with devotion, sends the present writing <unclear>...</unclear>
Having conceived the intent to obey according to my own judgment, both to satisfy your petition and to pay my debt <note>The "debt" likely refers to the social obligation a client owes a patron</note>, and so that it may be for your preservation and the increase of your knowledge <term>science<note>original: "siencia"; in this period, science referred to organized knowledge or a formal branch of learning</note></term>.
I shall write for your Holiness a treatise on poisons, which is useful even if brief. First, I will set down the division of this treatise, because each division is better understood through its individual parts. Secondly, I will divide each member of the aforementioned divisions down to the final individual parts, because in this way the knowledge of each thing is acquired by descending from the most general things down to the most specific. Third, I will set down the manner according to which poison kills and causes harm <term>harm<note>original: "nocumento"; a formal medical term for injury or damage to the body</note></term>, giving it in the manner of a medicine to the human body; for in this way, one finds the knowledge of how to cure the harm <insert>itself through medicine</insert>.

<meta>The text continues the alchemical poem from the previous page, shifting from the metaphor of a garden to the metaphor of "The Sword" and the "Afterlife Creation." It maintains the theme of transformation through nature-based allegories.</meta>

->A SYMBOL<-

### THE SWORD

<note>original: "al-sayf"</note>
You see it like rose-colored amber in its hue,
and it turns white like camphor if transparency touches it.
<note>In alchemy, amber often represents the "Red Work" (rubedo) and camphor represents the "White Work" (albedo).</note>

And when the sun kindles the fire of its rays upon it,
it continues to elevate what it discharges and reveals.
<note>This describes the process of sublimation or distillation using solar heat.</note>

<margin>The level ground of the earth</margin>
<gloss>meaning the rain</gloss> <gloss>poured</gloss> <gloss>meaning from the clouds</gloss> <gloss>the plural of "hadba," which is the mountain</gloss>
The flooding rain pierced the plateaus through the dripping,
turning them into level, empty plains.

<margin>With the deterrent within it, it does not need that</margin>

### THE SWORD

<margin>in it</margin>
<gloss>Gemini is a fruit</gloss>
<note>The term "Gemini" (al-Jawza') here likely refers to an alchemical ingredient or a specific astrological timing for the experiment.</note>
And Gemini rained stars into it,
and the shaking revealed what the sinking had hidden.

There, an afterlife creation returned
for its bodies, in which they find familiarity with their spirits.
<note>Alchemists often described the "reanimation" of dead matter as a spiritual resurrection.</note>

<margin>Address</margin>
They revolve as if time loves their newness,
so it has no transgression against them nor any diversion.

That is a resurrection without gathering or spreading,
as if the eternal exiles were a slow march within it.
<note>original: "nufaah." This refers to discarded or purged materials that are "reborn" in the alchemical process.</note>

If you are one who seeks to decipher our symbol,
do so with diligence, and do not let the description lead your intellect astray.

Do not let the eggs distract you from all our peels,
our oils, the hair, the blood, and the skull.

<gloss>The hoof</gloss>
Nor the bone, the biles, the urine, and the filth,
nor the feathers, the furs, the dung, and the hoof.
<note>This list refers to the "Animal Stone" path of alchemy, where practitioners sought the elixir within organic waste and biological materials.</note>

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "nor striking."</meta>

<summary>This page uses the metaphor of "The Sword" and "Resurrection" to describe the refinement of matter. The author warns the reader to look past literal descriptions of organic materials like hair and blood to find the true alchemical secret.</summary>

<keywords>The Sword, Amber, Camphor, Gemini, Afterlife Creation, Resurrection, Animal Stone, Organic Alchemy</keywords>

الملك وقال لحكماء بابل اي رجل يقرأُ هذه الكتابة ويبين لي تفسيرها فانهُ
يلبسُ الارجوان وقلادة من ذهب في عنقهِ ويتسلط ثالثاً في المملكة
٨ * ثم دخل كل حكماءِ الملك فلم يستطيعوا ان يقرأوا الكتابة ولا ان
٩ يعرفوا الملك بتفسيرها * ففزع الملك بيلشاصر جداً وتغيرت فيهِ هيئتُهُ
١٠ واضطرب عظماؤُهُ * اما الملكة فلسبب كلام الملك وعظمائهِ دخلت
بيت الوليمة فاجابت الملكة وقالت ايها الملك عِش الى الابد .
١١ لا تفزعك افكارك ولا تتغير هيئتُك * يوجد في مملكتك رجل فيهِ روح
الآلهة القدوسين وفي ايام ابيك وُجِدَت فيهِ نيرة وفطنة وحكمة كحكمة الآلهة
والملك نبوخذنصر ابوك جعلهُ كبير المجوس والسحرة والكلدانيين والمنجمين .
١٢ ابوك الملك * من حيث ان روحاً فاضلة ومعرفة وفطنة وتعبير الاحلام وتبيين
الغاز وحل عقد وُجِدَت في دانيال هذا الذي سماهُ الملك بلطشاصر .

->فليدع الآن دانيال فيبين التفسير<-

١٣ حينئذٍ أُدخل دانيال الى قدام الملك . فاجاب الملك وقال لدانيال
أنت هو دانيال من بني سبي يهوذا الذي جلبهُ ابي الملك من يهوذا
١٤ * قد سمعت عنك ان فيك روح الآلهة وان فيك نيرة وفطنة وحكمة
١٥ فاضلة * والآن أُدخل قدامي الحكماء والسحرة ليقرأوا هذه الكتابة ويعرفوني
١٦ بتفسيرها فلم يستطيعوا ان يبينوا تفسير الكلام * وانا قد سمعت عنك
انك تستطيع ان تفسر تفسيراً وتحل عقداً . فان استطعت الآن ان تقرأ
الكتابة وتعرفني بتفسيرها فتلبس الارجوان وقلادة من ذهب في عنقك
وتتسلط ثالثاً في المملكة
١٧ فاجاب دانيال وقال قدام الملك . لتكن عطاياك لنفسك وهَبْ
١٨ هباتك لغيري . لكني اقرأ الكتابة للملك واعرفهُ بالتفسير * انت ايها
الملك فالله العلي اعطى اباك نبوخذنصر ملكوتاً وعظمةً وجلالاً وبهاءً
١٩ * وللعظمة التي اعطاهُ اياها كانت ترتعد وتفزع قدامهُ جميع الشعوب والامم
