Op nieuw te groeten, als de Winter is geweken,
Spreek, spreek oud *Merestyn*, want ’t is aan u gebleken,
Dat *Haringkarspel* u verlaat, en weder vind
Als Astra's friffe geur Boreas koude bind,
En sluit den winter Vorst, en doet de dagen groeijen,
Om Flora en Pomoon’ haar gaven te doen bloeijen.
Oud *Merestyn*, wel eer den *Wyckerschans* genoemd,
Uw *Haringkarspel* maakt uw naam alom beroemd,
En geeft u meerder glans dan al uw sier'lykheden.
Vaar wel oud *Merestyn*! ik moet weêr verder treden,
Daar ’t ad’lyk *Adrichem* my op zyn schoonheid nood.
ô Loff’lyk Landgeſigt! uw glorie is te groot
Voor myn geringen Zang om u uw roem te geven :
De aloudheid heeft u eêr met Arkums naam beſchreven,
Toen gy u ſpiegelde in de blanke Zwane-meer,
Die nu is opgedroogd, om met haar groente u weêr
Een nieuwen welluſt, voor haar water, te vertoonen,
’t Schynt dat al het ſieraad u wil gelyk bekroonen,
Daar ge aan Sint Aagte-dyk uw trotſe gevel-praal
En toren ſteekt om hoog, bevryd voor ’t oorlogs ſtaal
Der kleine Friezen, ’t geen gy eertyds moeſt gevoelen,
Toen de oorlog, om zyn moed op uw Kaſteel te koelen,
Het heeft ten gronde toe verwoeſt, vernield, geſloopt,
En ’t vorige ſieraad in puin op een gehoopt,
Waar uit Heer vander Burg u weder heeft herboren,
En in een beet’ren ſtaat geſteld als ooit te voren,
Gelyk we, ô *Adrichem*! nu zien in uwen ſtand,
En langs uw bréde Laan, ten wederzyds beplant
Met hoge bomen, uw ſieraad van verre ontdekken.
ô Schoon gezigt! gy kunt myn hart tot vreugt verwekken,
Te meêr, wanneer ik denk wie hier vaak ruſt geniet,
De wakk’re *Trip*, die ’t Y en d' Amſtel naar ’t gebied
Van Themis wetten, en haar vierſchaar ſtaig doet horen,
Heeft dit oud ad’lyk Huis tot zyn vermaak verkoren.
Wat heil, ô *Adrichem*! geniet gy door uw Heer,
Wanneer hy zyne zorg legt op uw grond ter neêr,
Om onbekommerd daar een weinig ruſt te vinden?
Waar aan hy zig door ’t ampt van Schepen voeld verbinden,
Om ’t kwaad te ſluitten door den ſchnit van ’t wettig zwaard.
Al is ons Amſterdam by het Heel-Al vermaard,
Door magt en koopmanſchap, door duizende van ſchepen,
Die ’t eelſt van ’t ooſte en ’t weſte op onzen Yſtroom ſlépen,
Nog hoeft het gróter roem, wyl ’t regt met wys beleid
Daar ſteeds gehandhaafd word, om met omzigtigheid
Het kwaad te ſtraffen, en het goede te belónen,
ô Ed’le *Trip*! die lof moet u het eerſt bekroonen,
Waar aan gy ſteeds uw zorg, en vlyt en tyd beſteed,
Als ge op ons Kapitool ter marm’re Vierſchaar treed,
Om met Aſtrea's ſchaal het wettig regt te wégen,
De hemel geef aan u zyn heil en gunſt en zegen !
En houd uw *Adrichem* met u gelyk in ſtaat!
Terwyl myn Zangeres dit land gezigt verlaat,
Om ’t heff’lyk *Merestyn* by ’t lomm’rend groen te aanſchouwen.
Heeft een der Goden dit ſieraad der landgebouwen
Tot zyn vermaak geſtigt? ô Ja! ik tyffel niet,
Of Faunus voerd alhier het opperſte gebied,
Wyl hem de zorg voor ’t Land door ’t noodlot is gegéven.
ô Faunus! ’k nader dan uw groene wandel-dréven,

<column-break/>

Dog met de eerbiedigheid, die aan uw grootheid voegd.
Myn Zangeres zal blyde, en dubbel vergenoegd,
Zo ge u verwaardigd om haar lágen Zang te horen,
Van hier vertrekken, want niets kan meêr haar bekóren,
Dan dat zy overal uw lof en glorie meld,
En Faunus groten naam in háre Zangen *spelt*.
Maar Echo wat wilt gy aan my te kennen géven?
Waarom den Naam van *Spelt* my weder toe gedréven?
Wat kan, wat zal ik uit dit enkel woord verſtaan?
Spreek Echo! ſpreek nu voort! Maar ach! wat gaat my aan,
Dat ik de ſpraak u verg, die lang al is verdwénen,
Van dat Narciſſus u deed om zyn weêrmin wénen,
Zyt gy in lugt vergaan, en houd dén nagalm maar,
Hoe worde ik dan het woord van *Spelt* door u gewaar?
Hoe vinde ik dit geheim, of wat het aan wil tónen?
Ben ik bedrogen? hoe! zou Faunus hier niet wónen?
ô Neen! want *Merestyn* behoord Heer *vander Spelt*.
ô Echo! gy hebt my de waarheid voor geſteld,
Dog als de Sphinx voorheen deed zyne raadzels hóren.
ô Lugtig *Merestyn*! gy kunt het oog bekóren
Door uw volmaakten ſtand, en net beplante laan;
Hoe ver kan ’t wélig oog hier veilig weiden gaan,
Om in de ſchaduwe der hoog getopte bomen,
Al ’t land- en hofvermaak op één tyd te bekómen:
Uw net vierkant gebouw heeft myne tyffeling
Veroorzaakt, daar ik eerſt uw ſchoon gezigt ontfing,
’t Geen my beſluitten deed, dat ééne van de Goden
Voor uw vermaak de zaal was van Jupyn ontvloden,
Om lier in eenzaamheid te vinden zynen luſt,
Maar neen, Heer *vander Spelt* vind hier zyn vreugde en ruſt,
Wanneer de bloeityd boom, en kruid, en bloem doet bloeijen.
ô *Merestyn*! gy moet altoos in aanzien groeijen,
Op dat uw luister dag op dag nog meêr vergroot,
Vaar wel! wyl *Heemskerk* my op zyne ſchoonheid nood,
Des trede ik voort om my daar verder te vermáken.
Aloud en ſierlyk Dorp! gy doet myn yver blaken,
Als ik u net gebouw van Kerk en Toren zie,
Myn aandagt word verrukt en opgenomen, wie
Verwonderd zig ook niet, die u, na zo veel járen,
In zulk een ſtand aanſchouwd? behoed voor de geváren
Der binnenlandſe twiſt, wier bloedige oorlogsgloed
Zo véle Stéden heeft in dollen overmoed
Verwoeſt, vernield, en in een painhoop doen veränd’ren,
Wie teld de Dorpen en Kaſteelen by elkand'ren,
Die zy heeft neêr geſtort! toen ’t woedend oorlogszwaard
Der Hoekſe en Cabelauſe alom de vrugtb’re aard
Met bloed bemorſte van rampzalige onderdânen,
’t Geen wees en weduw vaak deed ſmelten in haar trânen.
Gelukkig *Heemskerk*! dat nog tot zyt behoed,
Gelyk de ſtand vertoond, waar in men u begroet,
Om met myn Zangereſſe ook uwen lof te zingen.
De Twéde Willem kon der Friezen magt hier dwingen,
Door ’t opgebouwd Kaſteel, tot uwe veiligheid,
Zo keerd men een vyand af door wysheid en beleid,
Om de onderdânen voor zyn woede te bewáren,
De weêrſtand doet alleen zyn wreev'len moed bedáren,
Daar hy het alles dreigd met vuur en ſtaal en koord.
Onmenſch'lyke oorlog wat hebt gy al volk vermoord,
En veld en land verwoeſt, en derelyk geſchonden,
Want alle gruuw’len zyn met u te zaam’ verbonden:
Hier word de Landman uit zyn hut en ſtal gejaagd,
Daar word het kind ontzield, gints ſchend me een kuiſſe Maagd,

<meta>catchword: En</meta>

---

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

En zet het huis en hof door de oorlogstoorts in kolen :
De kwynende oudheid ziet men langs de landen dólen,
Geplonderd en verjaagd, van eigendom ontbloot,
De zuigeling word in zyn moeders arm gedood.
Maar hoe! wat noopt my om die gruuw’len af te málen?
Uw oudheid, *Heemskerk*, deed my van het ſpoor verdwälen,
Dies kére ik op op nieuw weêr tot uw landſieraad.
Hoe vrolyk ſtreeld gy ’t oog, wanneer het ſpélen gaat
Langs dézen rycweg, dien de bomen ſchaduw’ géven,
Men laat Tiberius in zynen welluſt léven
Op ’t dart’le Caprea, ik kieze uw needrigheid,
Waar by de deugd zig voegd, die ſchóner glans verſpreid
Dan ooit een weeld’rig hof kan aan het oog vertónen,
Vaar wel, *Marquette* moet in ’t end myn zang bekrónen
Met zyn alom beroemd en overoud geſtigt,
’t Geen Koning Willem Hollands Graaf heeft opgerigt,
Gelyk myn Dignit-inf ſtraks by *Heemskerk* heeft gezongen,
Waar door de wilde Fries getemd wierd en bedwongen
In zyn baldadigheid: wy zien nog ’t overſchot
Der ſterkte in ’t oud Rondeel, ſchoon dat het ad’lyk ſlot
Verdelgt is en verwoeſt door vinnige oorlogs vlágen;
De Kenn'merlander ſcheen dus zelfs zyn hart te knágen,
Om Heemſteê, Brederode, en Aſſendelft hun val
Te ſmóren onder ’t puin van deez’ geſloopten wal.
ô Blinde weêrwraak! wat kunt gy al gruuw’len géven!
*Marquette* voelde ’t leed ’t geen Haarlem had bedréven,
Dat ad’lyk ſlot bezuurde u felle woede en haat:
Men oordeel van zyn ſterkte en vaſt gebouwden ſtaat,
Toen hertog Albrecht met zyn t’zaam gerukte knegten,
Hier moeſt elf wéken tyd het ad’lyk ſlot bevegtên.
Eêr heer van Heemſkerk zig boog voor zyne oorlogs magt,
Maar Haarlem! ſchoon gy hebt dit huis ten val gebragt,
Wat hebt gy tog verrigt, dan om ’t met nieuwen luiſter,
Uit ’t omgewroete puin, en uit het ak’lig Juiſter
Zyn trotſſen gevel te doen heffen naar om hoog?
Gy hebt het wit geenzints getroffen, ſchoon de boog
Van uwe rázerny op ’t hevigt waar geſpannen,
Om alles door geweld en woede te overmannen:
Maar ſterk en oud Rondeel, is ’t waarheid, ’t geen men zegt,
Stong in uw middelrond een Toren opgeregt,
Die aan de zélui kon tot eene baak verſtrekken,
Om ’s nagts, door ’t brandend ligt, hun regten ſtreeck te ontdekken?
Maar hoe! gy antwoord niet, en voed myn twyffeling,
’k Laat die onzeek're zaak dan zo ik die ontfing,
Om d'oorſprong van uw Naam, *Marquette*, naar te ſpóren:
Het huis te *Heemskerk* heeft men u genoemd te vóren,
Of anderſints het huis te *Zevenbergen*, maar
Toen ’t oud en ridderlyk geſlagt van Heemſkerk waar
Het lévens ligt ontroofd, vervierd gy aan Vianen,
Van die aan Arenberg, om dus het ſpoor te bânen
Waar door heer de Hartaln u heeft voor geld gekogt,
En u den nieuwen naam *Marquette* toe gebragt,
Naar ’t dorp *Marquette*, in ’t land van Vlaanderen gelégen.
Dus hebt gy ménigmaal een and’ren heer gekrégen,
Eêr *Rendorp* u heeft tot zyn eigendom gemaakt,
*Marquette* hoe veel zoet en zuur hebt gy geſmaakt,

<column-break/>

Van uwen opbouw, nu vyf eeuwen haaſt geléden?
Wat heeft men ménigmaal rondom uw grond geſtrédên?
Dat gras, en bloem en kruid ſcheen enkel bloed te zyn;
Maar na die ſtormen kreegt ge een lieven zonnenſchyn
Van eendragt en vermaak, gelyk we u nu aanſchouwen,
Daar gy het oog kunt in verwond'ring bezig houwen.
Als men uw Voorpoort langs de Heinigen ontmoet,
By ’t ſchaduwend geboomt, ’t geen Febus held'ren gloed
Een weinig mátigd, om hier meêr vermaak te vinden.
*Marquette* ’k zou me altoos aan uw gezigt verbindên,
Tenzv my de Amſtel-ſtad weêr dwong te rug te gaan,
Dewyl myn zangeres haar wand’ling heeft voldaan.
Lang moet ge, ô ad’lyk huis! uw Torentje verheffen!
Nooit moet u tegenſpoed, of ramp, of onheil treffen!
Maar ſtreke tot *Rendorps* vreugde, als hy de buiten lugt
Komt zoeken op uw grond, om daar de zoete vrugt
Der lieff'lyke eenzaamheid met vrolykheid te ontvangen,
Zo ſtrekt uw beider Naam het ſlot van myne zangen.
ô Kenn'merland wat zyt gy aan ’t geval verpligt,
Daar zo veel landſieraad is op uw grond geſtigt
Van Dorpen, Sloten, en beroemde Hérenhoven;
Het ſchvnt ge Italiën zyn luiſter wilt beróven
Met uwe uitmuntende ſierâden, ſchoon- en pragt,
Natuur heeft, zo het ſchynt, hier alleſt-zaam gebragt
Waf haar vermogen ooit een landſtreeck heeft gegevên,
Zy heeft ’t beleid en kunſt ook herwaards aangedréven,
Om zig te páren met haar toegenégenheid,
Die zo veel wond’ren heeft op uwen grond verſpreid.
Herulers koft ge u nu eens uit graf verheffen,
Met wat verwondering zou Kenn’merland u treffen?
Uwe oude woonſteê zou voor u onkenny'lyk zyn,
De digte boſſchen, die den held’ren zonnenſchyn
Wel eer beletten om het aardryk te genâken,
Zyn nu geheel verſtrooid, verwoeſt, om plaats máken
Voor Huizen, Tuinen, en voor Dorpen groots van ſtand,
Toen de Arendſlandaard wierd op uwen grond geplant
Door Romens legermagt, toen laagt gy haaſt begrâven
In diepe onwétênheid, men wiſt van land, nog haven,
Men kende ſtreeck nog weg, maar wel een woesten grond,
En náre boſſen, daar ge u zelven onderwond
De Goden van dit land met ’t offer te veréren,
Zo weet natuur en tyd het alles om te kéren.
Vaar wel dan Kenn'merland! vergroot van dag tot dag
In ſchoonheid en ſieraad! wyl ik met diep ontzag
Van uwe gronden ga, om elders weêr te vinden
’t Geen ik in u verlaat, ſchoon gy my ſchynt te binden
Aan ’t geen ik heb gezien, en in myn weg ontmoet.
De hemel géve aan u zyn heil en overvloed,
Om uwe Héren, en bewoonders te behágen!
Myn Digt-nimf moet zig naar de Tekenkunſt gedrágen
Daar zy haar bénen leid daar volgt zy op het ſpoor.
Wel aan, Terpſichoré! ga dan vryhartig voor,
Ik zal myn zangeres ſteeds aan uwe Etsnaald páren,
Geen Eendragt kan meêr vreugde, of gróter welluſt báren,
Dan daar de Tekenkunſt paard met de Poëzy,
Die beide hunnen troon beveſtigen aan ’t Y.
Hier zwygt myn zangſter om den adem te herhalen,
Tot dat zy ’t landvermaak op nieuw weêr af komt málen,
En met een nieuwen luſt een nieuwe reis begint,
Wyl zy van Kenn’merland zig thans voldaan bevind.

translation:
<meta>Continuity: Following the previous account of the estates of Meervliet and Velzen, the poetic journey continues through the landscapes and country houses of Merestyn, Haringkarspel, Adrichem, Heemskerk, and finally, Marquette.</meta>

To greet you anew, now that the Winter has departed,
Speak, speak old *Merestyn*, for it has become evident to you,
That *Haringkarspel* leaves you, and finds again,
As the fresh scent of Astraea binds Boreas's cold,
And locks up the winter frost, and causes the days to grow,
To make Flora and Pomona <note>Goddesses of flowers and fruit, respectively.</note> bloom with their gifts.
Old *Merestyn*, formerly called the *Wyckerschans* <note>Literal meaning: "Wijk rampart/defense work."</note>,
Your *Haringkarspel* makes your name famous everywhere,
And gives you more luster than all your gracefulness.
Farewell old *Merestyn*! I must tread further again,
Where noble *Adrichem* invites me with its beauty.
Oh praiseworthy landscape! Your glory is too great
For my meager song to give you your due fame:
Antiquity once described you with the name of *Arkum*,
When you mirrored yourself in the bright Swan-lake,
Which has now dried up, in order to show you a new
Delight in its greenery, in place of its water.
It seems that all the ornament wishes to crown you alike,
Where you thrust your proud gable-splendor and tower
High at Sint Aagte-dyk, freed from the war-steel
Of the small Frisians, which you once had to feel,
When the war, to cool its courage on your Castle,
Destroyed, ruined, and demolished it to the ground,
And heaped the former ornament in ruins together,
From which Lord vander Burg has reborn you again,
And placed you in a better state than ever before,
Just as we, oh *Adrichem*! now see in your condition,
And discover your ornament from afar along your broad Lane,
Planted on both sides with high trees.
Oh beautiful sight! You can awaken my heart to joy,
The more so, when I think of who often enjoys rest here,
The alert *Trip* <note>A prominent Amsterdam patrician family known for their wealth and political involvement.</note>, who hears the *Y* and the *Amstel*
Being brought to the jurisdiction of Themis's laws <note>Themis is the Greek goddess of divine law and order.</note> and her tribunal,
Has chosen this old noble House for his pleasure.
What salvation, oh *Adrichem*! do you enjoy through your Lord,
When he lays his care down upon your ground,
To find a little rest there, unconcerned?
To which he feels himself bound by the office of Alderman,
To close off evil through the cut of the lawful sword.
Even though our Amsterdam is renowned throughout the Universe,
By power and commerce, by thousands of ships,
Which carry the finest of the East and the West on our Y-stream,
It still needs greater fame, since justice with wise policy
Is constantly maintained there, in order to punish
Evil with caution, and to reward the good.
Oh noble *Trip*! That praise must crown you first,
To which you constantly devote your care, and diligence, and time,
When you step onto our Capitol at the marble Tribunal,
To weigh lawful justice with Astraea's scales <note>Astraea is the goddess of justice.</note>,
May heaven give you its salvation and favor and blessing!
And keep your *Adrichem* in the same state with you!
While my Songstress leaves this landscape,
To behold the stately *Merestyn* by the shading green.
Has one of the Gods founded this ornament of country buildings
For his pleasure? Oh Yes! I do not doubt,
Whether Faunus <note>Roman god of the forest, plains, and fields.</note> holds supreme rule here,
Since the care for the Land has been given to him by fate.
Oh Faunus! I then approach your green walking-paths,

<column-break/>

But with the reverence that befits your greatness.
My Songstress shall, joyous and doubly satisfied,
If you deign to hear her lowly Song,
Depart from here, for nothing can charm her more,
Than to proclaim your praise and glory everywhere,
And *spell* <note>In Dutch, "spelt" can mean "spells out" or "articulates." The text plays on the surname "Vander Spelt."</note> Faunus's great name in her Songs.
But Echo, what do you wish to make known to me?
Why have you driven the Name of *Spelt* to me again?
What can, what shall I understand from this single word?
Speak Echo! Speak on now! But alas! What ails me,
That I ask of you the speech that has long since vanished,
From the time that Narcissus made you weep for his unrequited love?
Have you vanished into air, and do you keep only the reverberation,
How then do I become aware of the word *Spelt* through you?
How do I find this secret, or what it wishes to show?
Am I deceived? How! Would Faunus not live here?
Oh No! For *Merestyn* belongs to Lord *vander Spelt*.
Oh Echo! You have presented the truth to me,
Though like the Sphinx formerly let his riddles be heard.
Oh airy *Merestyn*! You can charm the eye
Through your perfect state, and neatly planted lane;
How far can the lush eye safely pasture here,
To obtain all the land- and court-pleasures at once,
In the shadow of the high-topped trees:
Your neat square building caused my doubting,
When I first received your beautiful sight,
Which made me conclude that one of the Gods
Had fled the hall of Jove <note>Jupiter.</note> for your pleasure,
To find his delight here in solitude,
But no, Lord *vander Spelt* finds his joy and rest here,
When the flowering season makes tree, and herb, and flower bloom.
Oh *Merestyn*! You must always grow in esteem,
So that your luster increases even more day by day,
Farewell! Since *Heemskerk* invites me with its beauty,
Therefore I step forward to amuse myself there further.
Old and graceful Village! You make my zeal blaze,
When I see your neat building of Church and Tower,
My attention is enraptured and absorbed, who
Does not also marvel, who beholds you, after so many years,
In such a state? Preserved from the dangers
Of domestic discord, whose bloody war-glow
Has destroyed, ruined, and turned so many Cities
Into a heap of ruins in mad arrogance,
Who counts the Villages and Castles together,
That she has cast down! When the raging war-sword
Of the Hook and Cod factions everywhere sullied the fertile earth
With the blood of miserable subjects,
Which often made orphans and widows melt in their tears.
Happy *Heemskerk*! That you are still preserved,
As the state shows, in which one greets you,
To sing your praise also with my Songstress.
The Second William <note>William II, Count of Holland.</note> could force the power of the Frisians here,
Through the built-up Castle, for your safety,
Thus one turns away an enemy through wisdom and policy,
To save the subjects from his rage,
Resistance alone makes his vengeful courage subside,
When he threatens everything with fire and steel and cord.
Inhuman war, what people you have murdered,
And ruined field and land, and ravaged them,
For all horrors are bound together with you:
Here the Farmer is chased from his hut and stable,
There the child is un-souled, yonder one violates a chaste Virgin,

<meta>catchword: En</meta>

---

And sets house and home ablaze with the war-torch:
One sees the withering old age wandering along the lands,
Plundered and chased, stripped of property,
The infant is killed in its mother’s arms.
But how! What urges me to paint those horrors?
Your antiquity, *Heemskerk*, made me wander from the path,
Thus I turn again anew to your land-ornament.
How joyfully you stroke the eye, when one goes playing
Along this road, which the trees give shadow,
Let Tiberius live in his lust
On the wanton Caprea, I choose your humility,
Where virtue joins itself, which spreads a more beautiful luster
Than any luxurious court can show to the eye,
Farewell, *Marquette* must in the end crown my song
With its widely famous and ancient foundation,
Which King Willem, Count of Holland, has erected,
Just as my Muse just sang by *Heemskerk*,
Whereby the wild Frisian was tamed and subdued
In his wantonness: We still see the remnant
Of the strength in the old Roundel, although the noble castle
Is destroyed and ruined by stinging war-flags;
The Kennemerlander thus seemed to gnaw even his own heart,
To smother Heemstede, Brederode, and Assendelft in their fall
Under the rubble of this demolished rampart.
Oh blind revenge! What horrors can you provide!
*Marquette* felt the suffering that Haarlem had committed,
That noble castle suffered for your fierce rage and hatred:
One judges its strength and firmly built state,
When Duke Albrecht with his gathered servants,
Had to besiege the noble castle here for eleven weeks,
Before the Lord of Heemskerk bowed to his war-power,
But Haarlem! Although you brought this house to a fall,
What did you accomplish, other than to have its proud gable
Lift itself high again with new luster,
Out of the overturned rubble, and out of the dreadful... <note>The text "Juiſter" appears to be an archaic or corrupted term for gloom or sorrow.</note>
You have not hit the mark at all, although the bow
Of your fury was drawn to the most intense degree,
To overcome everything by violence and rage:
But strong and old Roundel, is it truth, what they say,
Stood in your center-round a Tower erected,
Which could serve as a beacon to the sailors,
To discover their right course at night, through the burning light?
But how! You do not answer, and feed my doubting,
I leave that uncertain matter then as I received it,
To trace the origin of your Name, *Marquette*:
The house at *Heemskerk* you were called before,
Or otherwise the house at *Zevenbergen*, but
When the old and knightly lineage of Heemskerk was
Deprived of the light of life, you passed to Vianen,
From there to Arenberg, to thus clear the path
Through which Lord de Hartaln bought you for money,
And brought the new name *Marquette* to you,
According to the village *Marquette*, situated in the land of Flanders.
Thus you have many times received a different lord,
Before *Rendorp* made you his property,
*Marquette*, how much sweet and sour have you tasted,

<column-break/>

Since your construction, now almost five centuries ago?
What has one many times fought for around your ground?
That grass, and flower, and herb seemed to be only blood;
But after those storms you received a lovely sunshine
Of concord and pleasure, just as we see you now,
Where you can keep the eye busy in wonder.
When one meets your Foregate along the Heinigen,
By the shadowing trees, which moderate Phoebus's <note>The sun's.</note> bright glow
A little, in order to find more pleasure here.
*Marquette* I would always bind myself to your sight,
Unless the Amstel-city forced me to go back,
Since my songstress has completed her wandering.
Long must you, oh noble house! lift your small Tower!
Never must adversity, or disaster, or misfortune meet you!
But stretch to *Rendorp's* joy, when he comes to seek
The outside air on your ground, to receive there the sweet fruit
Of lovely solitude with cheerfulness,
Thus your both Names stretch the end of my songs.
Oh Kennemerland what are you obligated to the event,
Where so many land-ornaments have been founded on your ground
Of Villages, Castles, and famous Noble-courts;
It seems you wish to rob Italy of its luster
With your excellent ornaments, beauty, and splendor,
Nature has, it seems, brought everything here
That her power has ever given to a region,
She has also driven the policy and art hitherward,
To pair itself with her affection,
Which has spread so many wonders upon your ground.
If you could now lift yourself once from the grave,
With what wonder would Kennemerland strike you?
Your old dwelling-place would be unrecognizable to you,
The dense forests, which formerly prevented the bright sunshine
From approaching the earth,
Are now entirely scattered, destroyed, to make room
For Houses, Gardens, and for Villages of great state,
When the Eagle-standard was planted on your ground
By Rome's military force, then you lay almost buried
In deep ignorance, one knew of neither land nor harbor,
One knew neither region nor path, but a wild ground,
And gloomy forests, where you undertook yourself
To honor the Gods of this land with the sacrifice,
Thus nature and time know how to turn everything.
Farewell then Kennemerland! Grow from day to day
In beauty and ornament! While I go with deep awe
From your grounds, to find elsewhere again
What I leave in you, although you seem to bind me
To what I have seen, and met on my way.
May heaven give you its salvation and abundance,
To please your Lords, and inhabitants!
My Poem-nymph must conduct herself toward the Art of Drawing
Where she leads her legs, there she follows on the trail.
Well then, Terpsichore! <note>The muse of dance and chorus.</note> Go then freely ahead,
I shall constantly pair my songstress to your Etching-needle,
No Concord can bear more joy, or greater delight,
Than where the Art of Drawing pairs with Poetry,
Which both confirm their throne at the Y.
Here my songstress is silent to catch her breath,
Until she comes to paint the land-pleasure again anew,
And with a new lust begins a new journey,
Since she finds herself satisfied with Kennemerland for now.

-> G. TYSENS. <-

### Concerning the ninth house and the questions it contains.
### CHAPTER 9.

<margin>1</margin>
<meta>A decorative initial letter L is adorned with patterns of flowers and leaves.</meta>
The ninth house, called the cadent of the western angle, or otherwise the house of God, naturally contains the questions and inquiries that can be proposed regarding the property of a temple or church, a chapel, a monastery, and a hermitage.

<margin>2</margin>
Also concerning the affairs of priests, monks, nuns, devout persons, and hermits. Regarding divine service, such as matins, prime, terce, and other <term>canonical hours</term> <note>Fixed times of day set aside for prayer and devotion in the Christian tradition.</note>, and concerning the mass and prayer.

<margin>3</margin>
Furthermore, those questions that one can raise about the clothing and vestments of a priest, a preacher, or a student, and about his study, school, companions, and books.

<margin>4</margin>
Also to know if someone seeking to become a priest will receive his <term>orders</term> <note>The formal religious initiation or promotion into the priesthood.</note> or not.

<margin>5</margin>

<margin>6</margin>
What status a student will have after returning from his studies: whether he will be a doctor in some faculty, a judge in some seat, a counselor, or a president in the high courts.

<margin>7</margin>
Whether the thing to which a man aspires will come to fruition.

§. 34. Lorsque l'homme est parfaitement satisfait de l'estat où il est, ou lorsqu'il est absolument libre de toute inquietude, quelle volonté luy peut il rester que le continuer dans cet estat? Il vaut mieux, dit St. Paul (1 Cor. VII. 9.), se marier que bruler. Tant il est vray que le sentiment present d'une petite brulure a plus de pouvoir sur nous que les attraits de plus grands plaisirs considerés en eloignement.

§. 35. Il est vray que c'est une maxime si fort établie, que c'est le bien et le plus grand bien qui determine la volonté, que je ne suis nullement surpris d'avoir supposé cela comme indubitable. Cependant après une exacte recherche, je me sens forcé de conclure, que le bien et le plus grand bien, quoyque jugé et reconnu tel, ne determine point la volonté; à moins que venans à le desirer d'une manière proportionée à son excellence, ce desir nous rende inquiets de ce que nous en sommes privés. Posons qu'un homme soit convaincu de l'utilité de la vertu, jusqu'à voir qu'elle est necessaire à qui se propose quelque chose de grand dans ce monde, ou espere d'estre heureux dans l'autre: cependant jusqu'à ce que cet homme se sente affamé et alteré de la justice, sa volonté ne sera jamais determinée à aucune action qui le porte à la recherche de cet excellent bien, et quelque autre inquietude venant à la traverse entrainera sa volonté à d'autres choses. one can consider and contemplate an absent good without pain; but in proportion as there is desire anywhere, there is just as much uneasiness [*inquietude*].

§. 32. Who is there who has not felt in desire what the wise man says of hope (Proverb. XIII. 12.), that being deferred it makes the heart sick? Rachel cries (Genes. XXX. 1.): give me children, or else I die.

§. 34. When a man is perfectly satisfied with the state in which he is, or when he is absolutely free from all uneasiness, what will can remain to him but to continue in this state? Thus the wise Author of our being has placed in men the discomfort of hunger and thirst, and other natural desires, in order to excite and determine their wills toward their own preservation and the continuation of their species. It is better, says St. Paul (1 Cor. VII. 9.), to marry than to burn. So true is it that the present feeling of a small burning has more power over us than the attractions of greater pleasures considered at a distance.

§. 35. It is true that this is a maxim so firmly established—that it is the good and the greatest good which determines the will—that I am in no way surprised at having assumed it as indubitable. However, after a careful search, I feel forced to conclude that the good and the greatest good, though judged and recognized as such, does not determine the will at all; unless, coming to desire it in a manner proportioned to its excellence, this desire makes us uneasy because we are deprived of it. Let us suppose that a man is convinced of the utility of virtue, to the point of seeing that it is necessary for whoever proposes something great in this world, or hopes to be happy in the other: nevertheless, until this man feels hungering and thirsting for righteousness, his will will never be determined toward any action that leads him to the pursuit of this excellent good, and some other uneasiness coming across his path will draw his will toward other things. On the other hand, let us suppose that a man addicted to wine considers that, leading the life he leads, he is ruining his health and dissipating his wealth, that he is going to dishonor himself in the world, bring diseases upon himself, and finally fall into indigence even to the point of no longer having the means to satisfy this passion for drinking which so strongly possesses him. However, the returns of uneasiness he feels at being absent from his companions in debauchery draw him to the tavern at the hours he is accustomed to go there, although he then has before his eyes the loss of his health and his wealth, and perhaps even that of the happiness of the next life: a happiness which he cannot regard as an inconsiderable good in

Since the ounce weighs eight drachmas, and our *écu* <note>The *écu* was a large silver coin used in France; the "écu of six francs" mentioned here was a standard high-value currency in the 18th century.</note> of six francs weighs nearly an ounce, there would be nearly eight drachmas to one of our *écus*.

I do not know if, under the successors of Marcus Aurelius, they continued to pay these salaries to the Professors of Athens, and I see little likelihood of it once the Empire was overwhelmed by disasters. There is even less reason to believe it under the Christian Emperors, who nearly all possessed great zeal for the destruction of Idolatry, and who well knew that the Philosophers, especially the Platonists, desired nothing so much as to prevent its ruin. We see, nevertheless, that under Theodosius the Younger <note>Theodosius II (reigned 402–450 AD), the Eastern Roman Emperor famous for the Theodosian Code and for overseeing the transition from pagan to Christian legal structures.</note>, the Professors of the Platonic School teaching in Athens were permitted to leave their property to that School upon their death. SIMPL. And this too I understand perfectly.

SALV. Now know, Signor Simplicio, that astronomers and mathematicians have found infallible rules by way of geometry and arithmetic to be able, thanks to the quantity of these angles B and C and their differences, joining to them the knowledge of the distance of the two places A and E, to find the distance of sublime things to a palm's breadth, provided, however, that said distance and said angles are taken correctly.

SIMPL. Such that, if the rules depending on geometry and arithmetic are just, all the fallacies and errors that might be met in wishing to investigate such altitudes of new stars, or comets, or other things, must depend on the distance AE and the angles B and C not being well measured. And thus all those diversities that are seen in these 12 investigations depend not on defects of the rules of the calculations, but on errors committed in investigating such angles and such distances by means of instrumental observations.

SALV. That is so, nor does any difficulty arise from this. Now you must attentively note how, in removing the star from B to C, whence the angle becomes always more acute, the ray EBG continues to move away from the ray ABD on the side below the angle, as shown by the line ECF, whose lower part EC is more remote from the part AC than EB is. But it can never happen that, for any immense removal, the lines AD and EF totally disjoin, since they must finally go to join at the star. And one could only say that they separate and reduce themselves to being parallel when the removal is infinite, which case cannot occur. O Sun, O thing alone and singular,
that measures the time for us in this way,
that gladdens the earth and the air and the sea
when they see again Thy joyful face!

through Thy rays in such a round body,
Thy virtue produces everything,
descending down through Thy clear light.

### Similitude

More perfect than any other figure
is the spherical figure, which
has no principle or end to its measure.
This is an eternal similitude.
Its pure light cannot be stained
by any corruptible and mortal thing;
to all things it gives generation,
beginning and end, and various condition.

Now let no one marvel
how there is one God in three persons,
distinct and each one singular,
not mixed but with perfect union.
You see the Sun, and of the solar body

you know that the one is not that which the other is,
and one is not after nor before the other.

that mirror generates the splendor,

proceeds the heat,
and there will never be nor was there

immediately He does His works.
Just as it appears in the East,
you see it rise, its heat is felt.

Let us come to the tenth century. Only two codices of this century shall be mentioned by us: the DCLXXI, which, besides the XL Homilies of Saint Gregory, much at variance with the edition of the famous Maurist Fathers, has a calendar at the beginning, though missing three months; and the DCCXX, in which Saint Augustine's book *de quantitate animae* <gloss>on the quantity of the soul</gloss> is transcribed. In the ninth century, the lives of the saints are copied, which are described in the MXXV Codex, quite beautiful and ornate. This codex would deserve to be seen by the Bollandist Fathers.

But the Pope having died during this concession, and Clement VI having been elected, the Emperor, seeing with what liberality the Pontiff had donated the lands of the empire, so as not to be less liberal with the things of others than the Pope had been, donated to all those who were tyrants in the lands of the Church their own lands [A.D. 1345], so that they might possess them with imperial authority. Through this, Galeotto Malatesti and his brothers became lords of Rimini, Pesaro, and Fano; Antonio da Montefeltro of the March and Urbino; Gentile da Varano of Camerino; Guido da Polenta of Ravenna; Sinibaldo Ordelaffi of Forlì and Cesena; Giovanni Manfredi of Faenza; Lodovico Alidosi of Imola;<note>original: "Qui principia l' epoca in cui prevale in Italia il principato." <gloss>Here begins the era in which the principality prevails in Italy.</gloss></note> and besides these, in many other lands, many others, so that of all the lands of the Church, few remained without a prince. This thing kept the Church weak until Alexander VI, who in our times, with the ruin of their descendants, restored its authority to it. The Emperor was at Trento when he made this concession, and he made it known that he wanted to pass into Italy, from which many wars followed in Lombardy, through which the Viscontis took possession of Parma. At this time, Robert, King of Naples, died, and there remained only two granddaughters born of his son Charles, who had died some time before. He left it that the eldest, named Giovanna, should be heir to the kingdom, and that she should take as her husband Andrea, son of the King of Hungary, his grandson.<note>original: "Regnava in que' tempi in Ungheria un altro ramo d' Angiò." <gloss>Another branch of Anjou reigned in Hungary in those times.</gloss></note> Andrea did not stay with her long, as he was killed by her, and she married another cousin of hers, the Prince of Taranto, named Lodovico. But Lodovico, King of Hungary and brother of Andrea, to avenge his death, came with men into Italy and drove Queen Giovanna and her husband out of the kingdom [A.D. 1348].

XXXI. — At this time a memorable thing happened in Rome: one Niccolò di Lorenzo,<note>original: "Cola di Rienzo, che abbattè il reggimento soffocatore di libertà, ordinato in Roma dai pontefici." <gloss>Cola di Rienzo, who struck down the liberty-suffocating government ordered in Rome by the pontiffs.</gloss></note> chancellor in the Campidoglio, drove out the senators of Rome and made himself, under the title of Tribune, head of the Roman republic [A.D. 1347]. He restored it to its ancient form with such a reputation for justice and virtue that not only the nearby lands, but all of Italy sent him ambassadors, such that the ancient provinces, seeing how Rome was reborn, lifted their heads, and some moved by fear, some by hope, honored him. But Niccolò, despite such a reputation, abandoned himself in his beginnings; because, invited under such a weight, without being driven out by anyone,<note>original: "Aggiungi che fu osteggiato dai nobili e abbandonato dal popolo, cui era divenuto increscioso, dicesi per il suo vano sfarzo, e perchè il buono stato da lui predicato non corrispose poi alle aspettazioni al solito esorbitanti." <gloss>Add that he was opposed by the nobles and abandoned by the people, to whom he had become tiresome, it is said because of his vain ostentation, and because the good state he preached did not then correspond to the usually exorbitant expectations.</gloss></note> he secretly fled and went to find Charles, King of Bohemia, who by order of the Pope, in contempt of Louis of Bavaria, had been elected Emperor.<note>original: "Carlo IV." <gloss>Charles IV.</gloss></note> This man, to gratify the Pontiff, sent him Niccolò as a prisoner.

# Collected Illustrations of the Three Realms, Volume 7: Geography

Page 43

At Cuiwei Temple, there is a well in the temple courtyard. This is where the Master <term>Ma Yi</term> <gloss>Master Hemp-Clad</gloss> once placed his <term>zhuxi</term> <gloss>a monk's staff, placed upright to signal residence</gloss>. One peak stands uniquely and prominently, rising in the southeast corner; this is called Cuiwei Peak. Seventy miles further, one reaches the summit, which is twice as wide as an ordinary mountain top. Looking around, the mountain ranges and villages for hundreds of miles can be counted one by one. Ten miles north of the village is the Xianyuan Guan <gloss>Temple of the Immortal Source</gloss>, surrounded by dense forests and hills. 

Crossing Xingling Ridge to the south, one sees many peaks and layers of ridges, all offering wonder and beauty in a single glance. From Hengling, one climbs a small hill; on the left side of the path, the bamboo and cedar forests are dark and gloomy, and there is a pool called the White Dragon Pool. The massive stones in the stream are astonishing, surging and crashing, and the depth is unfathomable. It is said that the Yellow Emperor, along with Fuqiu and Rongcheng, ascended to heaven from this mountain; thus, it is named Mount Huangshan <gloss>Yellow Mountain</gloss>.

# Imperial Collection of Four Treasuries, Volume 5
The numbers of the combined calculation, which correspond to the changes of the ten thousand things, all originate from the foundation of four. Because one diligently guards these four, one obtains the numbers of the four initial Heaven and Earth states through the symbols of the four energies and the four centers, thus residing in the correct middle position of the four directions. In this way, one can summarize the origins of all things and encompass the fundamentals of the numbers. All other numbers in the <term>Yi</term> change according to events and do not maintain a constant measure, but the four of the four-fold path is never altered. This is the reason why.

Four emerges from two, and two emerges from one. The division of two into one to act as the substance all permeates through; this is detailed in the section on numbers.

### 4. The Five Elements are not yet the "Five Materials," so they can be Symbolized
Kong Yingda's commentary on the classic mostly maintains the views of earlier scholars. Therefore, although he points to seven, eight, nine, and six as the four, and believes that the division of the four acts as the substance <note>referring to the core structure of the divination process</note>—all of which permeates through, detailed in the section on numbers—his so-called "four" still points to water, fire, wood, and metal, so it also does not depart from the four elements.

# Thousand-Gold-Hammer
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in Jiangnan, two to three feet tall. Treats poison from snake or insect bites; apply to sores to grow muscle and stop pain.</gloss>

# Tu-Luo-Cao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in Lingnan mountain valleys. Leaves are fine and long. Sweet, warm, non-toxic. Treats cold abdominal qi, pain, and abdominal masses. Can also be pounded into juice and taken warm.</gloss>

# Yi-Dai-Cao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in the mountain valleys of Guizhou like An-mountain. Leaves are round, two to three feet high. Harvest in the second month. Sweet taste, warm, non-toxic. Treats blood-qi fatigue and lower back and knee weakness. Treats wind-related looseness, emaciation, lack of color, and weak yang. No seeds. Women with old blood-stasis soak it in wine to drink. It expels disease extremely quickly, hence the name Yi-Dai [Wait-and-See].</gloss>

# Yaowang-Cao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Bitter, green with juice. Sweet taste, neutral, non-toxic. Resolves all poisons, stops nosebleeds and vomiting blood, and relieves restlessness.</gloss>

# Jinzi-Root
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows on Siming Mountain. More than a foot tall. Leaves are round, thick, and lustrous; they do not wither in winter. Root as thick as a finger. Also called Genzi. Bitter taste, warm, non-toxic. Treats knotted masses in the chest and abdomen, long-term stagnation, and pain beneath the navel. Also treats ghost-qi, shooting pain, cholera, gu-poison, and sudden bloody stools. Grind and take with wine.</gloss>

# Lu-Yao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in the Hu states. Resembles thatch, yellow-red color. Salty taste, warm, non-toxic. Treats internal damage and blood stasis, stops pain, cures the five internal organs, removes evil-qi, and supplements deficiency. For postpartum blood conditions, boil in water and take. Also pound and apply to injured areas. Shizhen says: The "Waitai Mi" secret method for treating internal horse-kick injuries: take one liang of Lu-yao powder, mix with a cup of cow's milk and take.</gloss>

<column-break/>

# Wu-Feng-Yao-Yao-Cao <gloss>Windless-Shaking-Grass</gloss>
<gloss>Shiyi says: Grows in the Da-Qin [Roman] Empire and Lingnan. Harvest on the fifth day of the fifth month in the various mountain wilds. It is often found there. The head is like a pellet; the tail is like a bird's tail. Two leaves open and close; it moves by itself. It is said that its name is Wu-Feng-Yao-Yao-Cao, but the object is different. Duan Chengshi’s "Yang Za Yan" says Yazhou produces a Dancing Grass; it has three leaves, like Jue-ming; one leaf is at the tip of the stem, two leaves reside halfway up the stem opposite each other. When people approach it, sing, or clap hands, it shakes like dancing. According to this, it is the Tang "Beauty Grass," and is of the same type as the Wu-Feng-Yao-Yao. Also according to the "Classic of Mountains and Seas": On Mount Guyao, the Emperor’s daughter died, and her horse transformed into a plant; its leaves overlap, flowers are yellow like rabbit silk (dodder); wearing it makes others love you. Guo Pu’s annotation says it is also called "Wild-Husband Grass." This statement is similar to Chen Cangqi’s remark about wearing it to encourage love. It is one and the same.</gloss>

# Tang Hai-Yao Bencao <gloss>Tang Maritime Herbal</gloss>
One type.

# Yi-Nan-Cao <gloss>Male-Wishing Grass</gloss>
<gloss>Tao says: Grows in the mountain valleys of Guangnan. Has pods about two feet long, with thin leaves like paper, the size of cicada wings. Treats evil spirits in small boys and girls. Put it in a red silk bag and wear it on the arm to ward off evil. This grass grows in the South, hence the name. It is different from the Yi-Nan of the Daylily.</gloss>

# Song Kaibao Bencao
One type.

**Left Column**

Zilu said: "I wish to share my carriages, horses, and light fur robes with my friends, and if they are worn out, I would feel no regret."
<margin>"Clothes" <note>pronounced in the departing tone</note>.</margin>
Yanyuan said: "I wish not to boast of my goodness, and not to impose my toils on others."
<margin>To boast means to brag; goodness refers to ability. To impose means to exaggerate [one's own state]. Toil refers to having merits. What [he] desires is thus not to boast. Or, it is said that toil means laborious tasks; laboring at tasks and not imposing them on others is also something [he] does not wish to do.</margin>
Zilu said: "I wish to hear your intent." The Master said: "To bring peace and comfort to the aged."

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

<margin>Therefore, one must be cautious in how one judges people by trivial matters.</margin>
○ The Master said: "Ingratiating words and an ingratiating countenance are rarely associated with true virtue." Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of this, and Qiu <note>Confucius refers to himself by his personal name</note> is also ashamed of it. Concealing one's resentment while befriending that person, Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of this, and Qiu is also ashamed of it.
<margin>Ingratiating means excessive. Master Cheng said: "Zuo Qiuming was a famous man of old." Master Xie said: "These two things are more shameful than peeping through a hole in the wall." That Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of it and that I, Qiu, am also ashamed of it, shows what one should cultivate. The Master speaks of himself, that he is also ashamed of it, because by linking his own name with [Qiu-ming's], he deeply warns the student to observe this and establish one's heart.</margin>
○ Yanyuan and Jilu were in attendance. The Master said: "Why do you not each speak of your intent?"
<margin>Why do you not.</margin>

<summary>This page concludes with the Master asking his disciples to express their personal aspirations, while also cautioning against deceptive behavior such as ingratiating speech and superficial displays of virtue.</summary>

Ce fut au milieu d’étreintes convulsives, de cris forcenés, de morsures frénétiques, un accouplement hideux, accouplement de chair et d’os, jouissance de brutes, rapide, dévorante mais qui ne venait que du sang.

Le sommeil arrêta enfin toutes ces fureurs.

Après cinq heures d’un calme bienfaisant, je me réveillai le premier.

Le soleil brillait déjà de tous ses feux. Les rayons perçaient joyeusement les rideaux et se jouaient en reflets dorés sur les riches tapis, les étoffes soyeuses.

Ce réveil enchanteur, coloré, poétique, après une nuit immonde, me rendait à moi-même; il me semblait que j’échappais à un cauchemar affreux, et j’avais près de moi, dans mes bras, sous ma main, un sein doucement agité, sein de lis et de roses, si jeune, si frêle et si pur, qu’à l’effleurer seulement du bout des lèvres on eut pu craindre de le flétrir. O la délicieuse créature! Fanny dans les bras du sommeil, demi-nue, sur un lit à l’orientale, réalisait tout l’idéal des plus beaux rêves. Sa tête reposait, gracieusement sur son bras arrondi; son profil se dessinait suave et pur comme un dessin de Raphaël; son corps, dans chacune de ses parties comme dans son ensemble, était d’une beauté prestigieuse.

C’était une volupté bien grande de savourer à loisir la vue de tant de charmes, et c’était pitié aussi de songer que, vierge depuis quinze printemps, une seule nuit avait suffit pour les détruire.

Fraîcheur, grâce, jeunesse, la main de l’orgie avait tout sali, tout souillé, tout plongé dans l’ordure et la fange.

Sleep finally put an end to all these furies.

After five hours of a restorative calm, I was the first to wake.

The sun was already shining with all its intensity. Its rays pierced the curtains joyfully, playing in golden reflections upon the rich carpets and the silken fabrics.

This enchanting, colorful, and poetic awakening, coming after a foul night, restored me to myself. It seemed as though I were escaping a frightful nightmare, and I had beside me, in my arms, under my hand, a gently heaving breast—a breast of lilies and roses, so young, so frail, and so pure that one might have feared to wither it by merely brushing it with the tips of one’s lips. Oh, the delicious creature! Fanny, in the arms of sleep, half-naked on an oriental bed, realized the entire ideal of the most beautiful dreams. Her head rested gracefully upon her rounded arm; her profile was drawn, sweet and pure like a sketch by <note>Raphael Sanzio, the Renaissance painter known for his depictions of purity and grace</note> Raphael; her body, in each of its parts as in its entirety, was of a prestigious beauty.

It was a great pleasure to savor at leisure the sight of so many charms, and it was also a pity to think that, having been a virgin for fifteen springs, a single night had sufficed to destroy them.

Freshness, grace, youth—the hand of the orgy had dirtied everything, soiled everything, plunged everything into filth and mire.

Le jeu est donc désavantageux, dans le cas même où la mise est égale au produit de la somme espérée par sa probabilité. **PHILOSOPHICAL ESSAY**

This rule leads to results consistent with the indications of common sense, which one can, by this means, evaluate with some exactitude. Thus, in the previous question, one finds that if Paul's fortune is two hundred francs, he should not reasonably bet more than nine francs. The same rule also leads to distributing the danger over several parts of a property one hopes for, rather than exposing it all to the same danger. It follows likewise that in the most equal game, the loss is always relatively greater than the gain; for the product of the fortune taken as unity, increased by the gain and raised to a power equal to the probability of the gain, multiplied by this unity decreased by the loss and raised to a power equal to the probability of the loss, is always less than the player's fortune before his stake. Supposing, for example, this fortune is one hundred francs, and the player risks fifty on the game of *croix et pile* <gloss>heads or tails</gloss>; his fortune after his bet, can be, by virtue of his expectation, either one hundred and fifty francs or only fifty; the probability of each of these two cases is 1/2; this fortune is therefore, by the preceding rule, equal to the square root of the product of one hundred and fifty by fifty; it is thus reduced to eighty-seven francs, that is to say that this latter sum would provide the player with the same moral advantage as the state of his fortune after his bet. The game is therefore disadvantageous, even in the case where the stake is equal to the product of the expected sum and its probability. One can judge by this the immorality of games in which the expected sum is below this product. They subsist only through the false reasoning and greed that they foster, and which, by leading the people to sacrifice their necessities to chimerical hopes whose improbability they are unable to appreciate, are the source of an infinity of evils.

à déterminer l'espèce, parce que Aristote a négligé d'en donner la description 1). Aldrovande 2) imite l'exemple de Belon, en décrivant et en figurant le hobereau sous le nom de Subbuteo, ce qui ne l'empêche pas d'énumérer dans la suite 3), comme espèce particulière, le Falco arborealis d'Albert le grand. Ray 4) fait aussi mention du Subbuteo et du Dendrofalco comme de deux espèces distinctes. Frisch 5) en donnant une bonne figure de l'adulte du hobereau, lui attribue très mal à propos les noms de Rochier, Lithofalco ou Esalon. Brisson 6) a le premier réuni au hobereau le Falco arborealis d'Albert le grand ou le Dendrofalco de Gessner, mais il emploie ce dernier nom pour désigner l'espèce. Linné 7), ayant suivi cet exemple, préfère cependant le nom de Falco subbuteo à celui de Dendrofalco, et à dater de cette époque, le hobereau figure dans tous les écrits des naturalistes, sous la dénomination latine de Falco subbuteo. Il existe, dans les différents ouvrages d'histoire naturelle, un grand nombre de figures plus ou moins bonnes du hobereau; nous nous bornons à citer celles contenues dans les ouvrages de Buffon 8), de Borkhausen 9), de Naumann 10) et de Gould 11).

Le hobereau porte en anglais le nom de «hobby.» En Allemagne, il est assez généralement connu sous celui de Baumfalke; cependant, la plupart des naturalistes allemands modernes ont cru devoir suivre l'exemple de Naumann, qui a conféré à cette espèce le nom allemand de Lerchenfalke, ce qui signifie faucon aux alouettes. Les fauconniers hollandais se servent indistinctement, pour désigner le hobereau, des noms de «boomvalk» et de «molliet»; mais ce dernier mot est évidemment corrompu de «baillet», usité du temps de Merula 12).

Le hobereau a été observé dans presque toutes les parties tempérées de l'Europe; il habite aussi la grande Bretagne 13) et la Suède méridionale 14), mais il ne se trouve, ni en Islande, ni dans le nord de la Scandinavie. Il est commun en Hollande, en France et en Allemagne; les naturalistes italiens en font mention comme d'un oiseau généralement connu dans leur pays; Küster 15) l'énumère parmi les espèces de la Sardaigne, et le comte von der Mühle 16) constate qu'en Grèce il est commun en hiver, mais qu'en été il habite de préférence la Rumélie. Les voyageurs hollandais et Mr. Smith ont recueilli des individus de cette espèce au Cap de Bonne Espérance; Pallas dit qu'elle se trouve en abondance dans toute la Russie et la Sibérie jusqu'au Kamtschatka 17), et le musée britannique 18) en possède un individu originaire de la Chine 19). En été, le hobereau habite de préférence les petits bois, où il établit son aire sur les arbres élevés et près de leur cime. Les œufs, au nombre de trois à quatre, sont d'un blanc sale, recouvert de tous côtés par des taches de forme assez diverse, plus ou moins distinctes ou lavées, et d'un brun rougeâtre. Il quitte, en hiver, les contrées froides et tempérées de l'Europe, et c'est alors qu'il fait de

<column-break/>

préférence la chasse aux alouettes qu'il a l'habitude d'accompagner lors de leurs migrations. Il se nourrit également d'autres oiseaux de petite taille, particulièrement d'hirondelles, et on le voit souvent poursuivre ou prendre toutes sortes d'insectes, soit à défaut d'autre nourriture, soit par prédilection pour ce genre de chasse, soit lorsqu'au jeune âge il n'a pas encore acquis assez de dextérité pour attraper les oiseaux qui forment sa proie favorite.

Le hobereau est le plus doux et le plus familier des oiseaux de proie d'Europe; il s'apprivoise facilement, surtout quand il a été enlevé du nid, et son éducation ainsi que son affaitage ne demandent que peu de soins. Excellent voleur, cette qualité et celles que nous venons d'énumérer le rendraient très précieux pour la chasse au vol, s'il était doué d'un caractère plus féroce et plus sanguinaire, et s'il savait se servir avec plus de dextérité de ses serres. Réduit en captivité, où il ne peut exercer ses forces comme à l'état sauvage, on ne parvient pas même à lui faire voler des alouettes qu'il sait cependant fort bien attraper, lorsqu'il se trouve en pleine liberté; aussi arrive-t-il souvent qu'au lieu de poursuivre le gibier, il s'amuse à faire la chasse aux hannetons, aux sauterelles ou à d'autres insectes qu'il rencontre dans les airs. Ne pouvant être employé avec succès que pour le vol des oiseaux sillés ou d'échappe, ce faucon n'est nullement estimé aujourd'hui, et on ne le voit jamais chez les fauconniers. Il paraît cependant que d'autres peuples en font encore usage: car Pallas 20) constate que les Calmouks se servent de cette espèce comme oiseau de chasse, et on voit par une notice publiée récemment par Mr. Drummond Hay 21), que ce petit faucon est fort en honneur chez l'Empereur de Maroc. Quoique les anciens fauconniers aient fait peu de cas du hobereau comme oiseau de chasse 22), et qu'ils n'en aient souvent fait mention qu'en passant, ce faucon n'en a pas moins acquis une certaine célébrité, parce que c'était l'oiseau choisi de préférence par la jeunesse 23), par les oiseleurs 24) et en général par des personnes, dont le rang et les moyens ne leur permettaient pas d'entretenir des fauconneries; de là probablement l'usage qui existe dans quelques provinces de la France, de donner le nom de hobereau aux petits seigneurs ou aux gentilshommes de campagne qui font de la chasse une affaire de profit plutôt que de plaisir 25).

LE FAUCON SAPHIR. — Il existe en Syrie, en Grèce, en Sardaigne et probablement aussi dans plusieurs autres parties du midi de l'Europe, un faucon ressemblant au hobereau par ses ailes qui dépassent la queue, mais qui est d'une taille plus forte, et dont le plumage offre une teinte brune, uniforme et foncée dans les adultes, plus claire dans les jeunes. Ce faucon, découvert seulement il y a quelques années et décrit par le professeur Gené 26) de Turin, comme espèce nouvelle, sous le nom de Falco Eleonorae, n'a pas été inconnu aux anciens faucon-

to determine the species, because Aristotle neglected to provide a description of it <note>1)</note>. Aldrovandi <note>2)</note> follows the example of Belon by describing and illustrating the hobby under the name <term>Subbuteo</term>, which does not prevent him from later enumerating <note>3)</note>, as a distinct species, the <term>Falco arborealis</term> of Albertus Magnus. Ray <note>4)</note> also mentions the <term>Subbuteo</term> and the <term>Dendrofalco</term> as two distinct species. Frisch <note>5)</note>, while providing a good illustration of the adult hobby, very inappropriately attributes to it the names <term>Rochier</term>, <term>Lithofalco</term>, or <term>Esalon</term>. Brisson <note>6)</note> was the first to reunite the <term>Falco arborealis</term> of Albertus Magnus (or the <term>Dendrofalco</term> of Gessner) with the hobby, but he uses the latter name to designate the species. Linnaeus <note>7)</note>, having followed this example, nevertheless prefers the name <term>Falco subbuteo</term> to that of <term>Dendrofalco</term>, and from that time, the hobby has appeared in all the writings of naturalists under the Latin designation <term>Falco subbuteo</term>. There exists, in various natural history works, a large number of more or less accurate illustrations of the hobby; we shall limit ourselves to citing those contained in the works of Buffon <note>8)</note>, Borkhausen <note>9)</note>, Naumann <note>10)</note>, and Gould <note>11)</note>.

The hobby bears the name "hobby" in English. In Germany, it is quite generally known by the name <term>Baumfalke</term> <gloss>tree falcon</gloss>; however, most modern German naturalists have thought it necessary to follow the example of Naumann, who conferred upon this species the German name <term>Lerchenfalke</term> <gloss>lark falcon</gloss>. Dutch falconers use the names "boomvalk" and "molliet" indiscriminately to designate the hobby; but the latter word is clearly a corruption of "baillet," used in the time of Merula <note>12)</note>.

The hobby has been observed in almost all the temperate parts of Europe; it also inhabits Great Britain <note>13)</note> and southern Sweden <note>14)</note>, but it is found neither in Iceland nor in northern Scandinavia. It is common in Holland, France, and Germany; Italian naturalists mention it as a bird generally known in their country; Küster <note>15)</note> enumerates it among the species of Sardinia, and Count von der Mühle <note>16)</note> notes that in Greece it is common in winter, but that in summer it prefers to inhabit Rumelia. Dutch travelers and Mr. Smith have collected individuals of this species at the Cape of Good Hope; Pallas says that it is found in abundance throughout Russia and Siberia as far as Kamchatka <note>17)</note>, and the British Museum <note>18)</note> possesses an individual originating from China <note>19)</note>. In summer, the hobby prefers to inhabit small woods, where it builds its nest on high trees, near their tops. The eggs, numbering three to four, are of a dirty white, covered on all sides with spots of rather diverse shapes, more or less distinct or washed, and of a reddish-brown color. In winter, it leaves the cold and temperate regions of Europe, and it is then that it makes 

<column-break/>

a point of hunting larks, which it has the habit of accompanying during their migrations. It also feeds on other small-sized birds, particularly swallows, and one often sees it pursuing or catching all sorts of insects, either for lack of other food, by preference for this type of hunting, or when, at a young age, it has not yet acquired enough dexterity to catch the birds that form its favorite prey.

The hobby is the gentlest and most familiar of the birds of prey of Europe; it is easily tamed, especially when taken from the nest, and its training and manning require little care. An excellent flyer, this quality and those we have just enumerated would make it very precious for falconry, if it were gifted with a more ferocious and bloodthirsty character, and if it knew how to use its talons with more dexterity. Reduced to captivity, where it cannot exercise its strength as in the wild state, one does not even succeed in making it hunt larks, which it knows how to catch very well, however, when it is in full liberty; thus it often happens that instead of pursuing game, it amuses itself by hunting cockchafers, grasshoppers, or other insects that it encounters in the air. Not being able to be used with success except for the flight of birds using a lure or by "escape" <note>a method where the hawk is flown at wild quarry without prior conditioning</note>, this falcon is not in the least esteemed today, and it is never seen among falconers. It appears, however, that other peoples still make use of it: for Pallas <note>20)</note> notes that the Kalmyks use this species as a hunting bird, and we see by a notice published recently by Mr. Drummond Hay <note>21)</note>, that this small falcon is held in high honor by the Emperor of Morocco. Although the old falconers thought little of the hobby as a hunting bird <note>22)</note>, and often only mentioned it in passing, this falcon has nonetheless acquired a certain celebrity, because it was the bird chosen by preference by youth <note>23)</note>, by bird-catchers <note>24)</note>, and in general by people whose rank and means did not allow them to maintain falconries; from this comes, probably, the usage that exists in some provinces of France to give the name <term>hobereau</term> to minor lords or country gentlemen who treat hunting as a matter of profit rather than pleasure <note>25)</note>.

THE ELEONORA'S FALCON. <note>Original: "LE FAUCON SAPHIR"</note> — There exists in Syria, Greece, Sardinia, and probably also in several other parts of southern Europe, a falcon resembling the hobby in its wings, which extend beyond the tail, but which is of a larger size, and whose plumage offers a brown, uniform, and dark tint in adults, lighter in the young. This falcon, discovered only a few years ago and described by Professor Gené <note>26)</note> of Turin as a new species under the name <term>Falco Eleonorae</term>, was not unknown to the ancient falconers.

For successive turns, the number of which is *a*, one contends that the event will happen, for which to happen there are *b* cases, but for which it does not happen there are *c* cases; his chance (setting d ⚭ b + c) to the chance of the opponent is as *ba* to *da — ba*. That is to say, as *b* multiplied by itself as many times as there are units in *a*, to the sum of *b + c* multiplied by itself as many times, minus *b* multiplied by itself.

<meta>This page continues the argument from Chapter 2. While the previous page warned against taking biblical metaphors too literally (like imagining angels as literal birds or beasts), this page explains the positive purpose of these symbols: they serve as a necessary "bridge" or "hand-holding" for the human mind to transition from the physical world to the spiritual realm.</meta>

->[OF THE] CELESTIAL HIERARCHY<-
<note>original: "οὐρανίας ἱεραρχίας." This is the running header of the book.</note>

->[c ii]<-
<note>This is a "signature mark," used by early printers to keep the pages in the correct order for binding.</note>

...deeming [our hierarchy] worthy of a **super-worldly** <note>literally "hyper-cosmic," meaning existing beyond the physical universe</note> imitation of the celestial hierarchies. By diversifying the immaterial hierarchies with material shapes and formal compositions, Scripture has handed them down to us. This was done so that, in a way proportionate to our own nature, we might be led upward from these most sacred fashioned-forms to the simple, formless elevations and likenesses. 

For it is not possible for our human mind to be extended toward that immaterial imitation and contemplation of the celestial hierarchies unless it uses the **material guidance** <note>"hylaia cheiragogia," literally "material hand-holding." A key concept in Dionysius where physical objects "lead us by the hand" to God</note> suited to it. It must consider visible beauties as icons of invisible loveliness, and sensory fragrances as imprints of the **intellectual distribution** <note>original: "noētēs diadosis" — the way God "spreads" or "distributes" his presence into the mind</note> of God. 

It must see material lights as an image of the immaterial gift of light, and the detailed sacred teachings of the priests as a reflection of the mind's own contemplative fulfillment. We should view the orderly arrangements of our ceremonies here on earth as a way to reach a harmonious and ordered habit toward divine things. Furthermore, we should see the participation in the most divine **Eucharist** <note>literally "thanksgiving," referring to the central Christian rite of communion</note> as a way of sharing in the fellowship of Jesus. In short, all those things that are given to the celestial beings in a **super-worldly** manner are handed down to us through symbols.

<margin>T</margin>herefore, for the sake of this proportionate **deification** <note>"theosis." The process of becoming "god-like" or united with God through grace</note> of ours, the benevolent **Source of Rites** <note>"Teletarchia." A title for God or Christ as the one who initiates and perfects all sacred ceremonies</note> has revealed the celestial hierarchies to us. By making our own earthly hierarchy a "fellow-minister" with them through this likeness—as far as our power allows—the Source has described the super-celestial beings through sensory images in the holy scriptures.

### VOCABULARY
*   **Celestial hierarchies**: The ordered ranks of angels in heaven.
*   **Imitation**: The process by which a lower rank tries to mirror the qualities of a higher rank.
*   **Immaterial things**: Realities that have no physical body or "matter."
*   **Intellectual distribution**: The way spiritual truths are shared or spread into the human intellect.
*   **Most divine Eucharist**: The sacrament of the Lord's Supper, viewed here as a way for humans to participate in the life of Jesus.
*   **Source of Rites**: The divine principle that establishes and governs all sacred rituals.
*   **Deification**: The ultimate goal of the soul, which is to be made like God.

<summary>Dionysius explains that material symbols—like light, fragrance, and the Eucharist—are necessary tools that "lead the human mind by the hand" toward immaterial spiritual truths. He argues that the earthly church hierarchy is a symbolic mirror of the angelic hierarchy in heaven, designed to help humans achieve deification.</summary>
<keywords>celestial hierarchy, symbols, theosis, deification, Eucharist, Jesus, contemplation, spiritual guidance, angels</keywords>

Καὶ Σάπωριν δὲ στρατηγὸν ἀπέστελλε τῇ Ἕῳ ταῦτα διαπραξόμενον, ἐπίσημον ἄνδρα μάλα διαγενόμενον. Καὶ ἀπαραβάτως ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἔθνει εἰς πέρας ὁ θεῖος οὗτος νόμος ἐγίνετο. ...condemning them, as if they were shifting into other opinions like the shifting tides of the Euripus <note>A strait in Greece known for strong, reversing currents</note>, they completely withdrew from their communion, and firmly attached themselves to the proponents of the <term>homoousios</term>, and were united.

### CHAPTER III.
**How by the law of Gratian those of Arius were driven out, and those of the <term>homoousios</term> faith were introduced into the churches; and what things happened in Antioch because of Paulinus and Meletius.**

Gratian, as has been said, dedicating the first-fruits of his reign to the King of all, God, wrote a law granting the return of the exiled bishops; and he ordered that those of Arius be driven from the sacred shrines, and the churches be given back to those standing by the faith in Nicaea. He also sent Sapor the general to the East to accomplish these things, a man who had become very distinguished. And without deviation in every nation, this divine law was brought to fulfillment. But in Antioch, there was a great deal of rivalry among the multitude, having such a cause: those who were champions of the <term>homoousios</term> faith and the apostolic dogmas were divided. For some, having been separated from the Arian madness immediately after the plot against Eustathius, were by themselves, led by Paulinus; others, having stood apart from the ungodly after the ordination of Euzoius, were guided by the most wise pastoral care of Meletius. But Paulinus, on account of his exceeding mildness, was not led into exile by Valens; Meletius, however, having previously been condemned to exile, was brought back by Julian; and again having been condemned to flight under Valens, he then returned to Antioch by the decree of Gratian. And having come, he finds Paulinus already advanced to deep old age; and immediately all who were of his portion moved every rope <note>idiom: "left no stone unturned"</note> so that Meletius might become a fellow-enthroned bishop with Paulinus. But Paulinus avoided the joint session, maintaining that the action was against the ecclesiastical canon, since Meletius had received his ordination from Arians. The multitudes, not tolerating this, enthroned Meletius in one of the shrines before the city. When this happened, much verbal strife flowed in; and from the excessive rivalry, they turned to absurd attempts; and a riot was expected from both sides of the people being angry. Then, a wonderful counsel having occurred, they came to an agreement on the following conditions: for it was agreed to bind with oaths those who were considered suitable to be bishops, or were expected to be; of whom there were five others, and Flavian himself; so that no one should come into the bishopric, nor be eager for it, nor tolerate the ordination, even if something should happen, coming upon them, as long as Paulinus and Meletius remained in life. If one of them died first, the survivor should hold the throne of the deceased; and after his subsequent death, then one of the candidates, whomsoever the...

<column-break/>

...abolishing the Nicene profession of faith, and celebrating their churches separately. But that attempt was in vain for them: for very many, having perceived their contention, because like the Euripus <note>the strait between Euboea and Boeotia</note> they shifted now here, now there, they entirely abstained from their communion, and constantly joined themselves through union to the praisers of the <term>homoousios</term> <gloss>consubstantial</gloss> faith.

### CHAPTER III.
**That by the constitution of Gratian the Arians were banished, and the professors of the <term>homoousios</term> <gloss>consubstantial</gloss> faith were placed over the churches, and what things happened at Antioch on account of Paulinus and Meletius.**

Gratian, as we have said, consecrating the first-fruits of his empire to the Emperor of all things and to God, promulgated a law by which he both restored the exiled bishops and permitted the Arians to be driven out of the sacred buildings, and those buildings to be returned to the champions of the Nicene faith. And he sent the general Sapor, a very distinguished man, to the East to put it into execution. And that divine constitution was duly brought to its legitimate end in every province. But at Antioch there was a huge contention and disagreement among the common people, for a reason of this kind: Those who defended the <term>homoousios</term> <gloss>consubstantial</gloss> faith and the Apostolic dogmas had gone into two parts: for some, immediately after the snares laid for Eustathius, abhorring the Arian madness, held their assemblies under the bishop Paulinus. Some, however, fleeing the commerce of the impious after the election of Euzoius, were pastured under the most wise shepherd Meletius. <note>Marginal number 226</note> And Paulinus, indeed, on account of his excellent kindness, had not been driven into exile by Valens. Meletius, however, when he had first been punished with exile, had been restored by Julian: and having been ordered to be deported again under Valens, relying on the edict of Gratian, he had then returned to Antioch, and had found Paulinus living in extreme old age. There, all those who were of his faction "moved every rope" <note>tried every means</note> so that Meletius might be placed on the same throne with Paulinus. Paulinus did not admit that matter, repeatedly saying that such an act was against the ecclesiastical canons, because Meletius had received consecration from Arians. But the people, not bearing it, placed Meletius on the throne of a certain suburban temple. Which being done, a great strife of words arose. And the matter, from an excessive zeal for contending, went into absurd undertakings: and with the common people on both sides being indignant, a sedition was expected. But then, a marvelous plan having been found, the matter was reduced to concord by an agreement of this kind. For it was decided that whoever were already, or might at some time be, suitable to perform the episcopal function—of whom there were five others, and Flavian was the sixth—should be bound by the sacrament of an oath that none of them would take up the bishopric, nor pant after that dignity, and even would not approve an election if by chance it were made concerning any of them, as long as Paulinus and Meletius remained in life; and that when one had died, the other who survived should succeed into his...

6. Bücheler reads ὄφρα for ἤ ῥα, making Apollo the subject of ἐχάλασσε and ἐκλήϊσε. The common reading is preferable.
8. **τόξον**: the “bow” must include the quiver, which alone, to speak properly, is hung on the back of Apollo. **πρὸς κίονα πατρὸς ἑοῖο** is briefly put for “the pillar against which stood his father’s seat.” So Arete sits κίονι κεκλιμένη, ζ 307, and Odysseus sits πρὸς κίονα μακρήν, ψ 90. In both cases the pillar is near the hearth, and appears to be the place for the master or mistress of the house. In θ 65 f. the herald puts a seat for Demodocus against a pillar, on which he hangs the lyre of the minstrel.
10. **νέκταρ**: cf. the scene of the gods drinking nectar in Δ 1 f.
11. Gemoll objects to the usual punctuation (adopted in the text), on the ground that the order should be ἔνθα δ᾽ ἔπειτα, and that in Ο 86 all the gods pledge Hera. He therefore punctuates at the end of the line, supplying a verb for δαίμονες from δεικνύμενος. But the point is that the gods remain standing until Apollo is seated; and this is best brought out by the punctuation of the text. **ἔνθα** is emphatic in this position: “then and not till then,” *tum demum*.
13 = 126.
14–18. This invocation has been suspected by many commentators, who think that it is the beginning of a hymn to Leto (or a complete hymn). According to Ilgen it may have been interpolated

<column-break/>

owing to the similarity of χαίρει δέ τε πότνια Λητώ to χαῖρε κτλ. But there is no good reason why Leto should not be honoured in a hymn addressed to her son, and the invocation is not unsuitable at this place.
14. **μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Λητοῖ**: for the formulaic order cf. *Eur. Bacch.* 565 μάκαρ ὦ Πιερία, *Ar. Nub.* 1205 μάκαρ ὦ Στρεψιάδες, *Orph. h.* iii. 12 μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Νύξ. The position of ὦ is Homeric; e.g. Δ 159, δ 26, θ 408, σ 122, υ 199, xxvi. 11. The order is not found in Attic prose. (In *Plat. Euthyd.* 271 c Stallbaum reads θαυμασία, ὦ Κρίτων for θαυμάσι᾽ ὦ Κρίτων.) For later poetry cf. *Anth. Pal.* vi. 239. 1 ἀγρονόμ᾽ ὦ Πάν.
15. It is natural to mention both the children of Leto, although the hymn is addressed to one of them. Artemis is joined with Apollo in the invocation at 165, where see note.
16 = *Orph. h.* xxxv. 5. **Ὀρτυγίῃ**: hardly the Syracusan Ortygia, as Fick (*Odyssee* p. 281) supposes, although that place was closely associated with Artemis; see *Pind. Nem.* i. 1 f., *Pyth.* ii. 7. Delos itself was anciently called Ortygia (schol. Apoll. Arg. A 419, Athen. ix. 392 D and in Alexandrian poetry e.g. *Callim. h. Ap.* 59, followed by *Verg. Aen.* iii. 124, Hesych. s.v. Ὀρτυγία, Eust. 1558), but the islands are here expressly distinguished; cf. *Anth. Pal.* vi. 273 Ἄρτεμι Δᾶλον ἔχουσα καὶ Ὀρτυγίαν ἐρόεσσαν. We may here follow Strabo (x. 5. 5), who identifies Ortygia with Rheneia. The Ortygia of o 404 is unknown. For further references see Preller-Robert i.
