Following the description of the gods' fearful reaction to Apollo's arrival in the halls of Zeus, the text now details Leto’s motherly care in disarming him and the subsequent welcoming ceremony among the Olympians.</meta>

# III TO APOLLO

She <note>Leto</note> unstrung his bow and closed his quiver,
and taking it from his strong shoulders with her hands,
she hung the bow against a pillar of his father
from a golden peg; and she led him and seated him on a throne.
<margin>10</margin> Then his father gave him nectar in a golden cup,
welcoming <note>original: "δεικνύμενος"</note> his dear son, and then the other gods
sit down there; and queenly Leto rejoices,
because she bore a bow-bearing and mighty son.
Hail, O blessed Leto, since you bore glorious children,
<margin>15</margin> Lord Apollo and Artemis the shooter of arrows,
the one in Ortygia, and the other in rocky Delos,

---

6. **truly then** <note>original: "ἤ ῥα"</note>] **until** <note>original: "ὄφρα"</note> Bücheler    7. **with her hands** [corrupt form] L    8. **hung up** [incomplete] L : **the bows indeed** Stoll : **and the bows** Schneidewin || **before** <note>original: "πρὸ"</note> EL    9. **seated** [variant spelling] M    11. **and** <note>original: "δὲ"</note> omitted in pH    12. **queenly** [incomplete] L    14. **blessed Leto** [variant case] M

---

6. Bücheler reads "until" <note>original: "ὄφρα"</note> for "truly then" <note>original: "ἤ ῥα"</note>, making Apollo the subject of the verbs "unstrung" and "closed." The common reading is preferable.
8. **the bow** <note>original: "τόξον"</note>: the “bow” must include the quiver, which alone, to speak properly, is hung on the back of Apollo. **against a pillar of his father** <note>original: "πρὸς κίονα πατρὸς ἑοῖο"</note> is briefly put for “the pillar against which stood his father’s seat.” So Arete sits "leaning against a pillar" <note>original: "κίονι κεκλιμένη"</note>, *Odyssey* 6.307, and Odysseus sits "against a tall pillar" <note>original: "πρὸς κίονα μακρήν"</note>, *Odyssey* 23.90. In both cases the pillar is near the hearth, and appears to be the place for the master or mistress of the house. In *Odyssey* 8.65 f. the herald puts a seat for Demodocus against a pillar, on which he hangs the lyre of the minstrel.
10. **nectar**: cf. the scene of the gods drinking nectar in *Iliad* 4.1 f.
11. Gemoll objects to the usual punctuation (adopted in the text), on the ground that the order should be "then and thereafter" <note>original: "ἔνθα δ᾽ ἔπειτα"</note>, and that in *Iliad* 15.86 all the gods pledge Hera. He therefore punctuates at the end of the line, supplying a verb for the **gods** <note>original: "δαίμονες"</note> from the word for **welcoming** <note>original: "δεικνύμενος"</note>. But the point is that the gods remain standing until Apollo is seated; and this is best brought out by the punctuation of the text. **then** <note>original: "ἔνθα"</note> is emphatic in this position: “then and not till then,” <note>Latin: "tum demum"</note>.
13 = 126 <note>Note: This indicates line 13 is identical to line 126 of the hymn.</note>.
14–18. This invocation has been suspected by many commentators, who think that it is the beginning of a hymn to Leto (or a complete hymn). According to Ilgen it may have been interpolated

<column-break/>

owing to the similarity of "and queenly Leto rejoices" <note>original: "χαίρει δέ τε πότνια Λητώ"</note> to "hail [blessed Leto]" <note>original: "χαῖρε κτλ."</note>. But there is no good reason why Leto should not be honoured in a hymn addressed to her son, and the invocation is not unsuitable at this place.
14. **O blessed Leto** <note>original: "μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Λητοῖ"</note>: for the formulaic order compare Euripides, *Bacchae* 565 "O blessed Pieria" <note>original: "μάκαρ ὦ Πιερία"</note>, Aristophanes, *Clouds* 1205 "O blessed Strepsiades" <note>original: "μάκαρ ὦ Στρεψιάδες"</note>, *Orphic Hymn* iii. 12 "O blessed Night" <note>original: "μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Νύξ"</note>. The position of "O" <note>original: "ὦ"</note> is Homeric; e.g. *Iliad* 4.159, *Odyssey* 4.26, 8.408, 18.122, 20.199, and Hymn 26.11. The order is not found in Attic prose. (In Plato, *Euthydemus* 271 c Stallbaum reads "wonderful one, O Crito" <note>original: "θαυμασία, ὦ Κρίτων"</note> for "O wonderful Crito" <note>original: "θαυμάσι᾽ ὦ Κρίτων"</note>.) For later poetry compare *Greek Anthology* vi. 239. 1 "O Pan of the fields" <note>original: "ἀγρονόμ᾽ ὦ Πάν"</note>.
15. It is natural to mention both the children of Leto, although the hymn is addressed to one of them. Artemis is joined with Apollo in the invocation at line 165, where see note.
16 = *Orphic Hymn* xxxv. 5. **Ortygia**: hardly the Syracusan Ortygia, as Fick (*Odyssey* p. 281) supposes, although that place was closely associated with Artemis; see Pindar, *Nemean Odes* 1.1 f., *Pythian Odes* 2.7. Delos itself was anciently called Ortygia (Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius, *Argonautica* 1.419, Athenaeus ix. 392 D and in Alexandrian poetry e.g. Callimachus, *Hymn to Apollo* 59, followed by Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.124, Hesychius under the entry "Ortygia", Eustathius 1558), but the islands are here expressly distinguished; cf. *Greek Anthology* vi. 273 "Artemis who holds Delos and lovely Ortygia." We may here follow Strabo (x. 5. 5), who identifies Ortygia with Rheneia. The Ortygia of *Odyssey* 15.404 is unknown. For further references see Preller-Robert volume i.

The commentary discusses Homeric architectural features, the formulaic language of divine invocations, and the geographic identification of Ortygia and Delos.</summary>

translation:
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, King Abgarus of Edessa has successfully negotiated his return from the Roman court. However, upon his return, he finds himself suffering from a debilitating physical ailment that local medicine cannot cure.</meta>

# [PROCOPIUS ON THE PERSIAN WARS, BOOK II, CHAPTER 12]

At any rate, being burdened by his pains and his resulting inability to move, he brought the matter before the physicians. From every land he gathered all those who were wise in such things. <margin>21</margin> But when, later on (for they <margin>5</margin> were not able to discover any cure for the affliction), he gave up on them and, falling into a state of helplessness, he lamented his current fortunes. 

At about that same time, <margin>22B208</margin> Jesus, the Son of God, was living in the body and conversing with the people in Palestine. By never committing any sin at all, and by performing impossible deeds, he clearly demonstrated <margin>10</margin> that he was truly the Son of God. For, by calling to the dead, he raised them as if from sleep <margin>23</margin>; he opened the eyes of those who had been born blind; he cleansed the white spots <note>The original Greek term is "leukas," referring to skin lesions associated in the ancient world with leprosy.</note> from the whole body and cured the lameness of feet; and he healed all those other ailments which are named "incurable" by physicians. 

<margin>15</margin> When Abgarus heard these things reported by those <margin>24</margin> frequenting Edessa from Palestine, he took courage. He wrote a letter to Jesus, begging him to depart from Judea and the ungrateful <note>The Greek "agnomonon" implies people who are both uncomprehending and unthankful.</note> people there, and to come live with him for the <margin>20</margin> remainder of his life. When Christ saw this message <margin>25</margin> delivered to him, he wrote back to Abgarus; he explicitly refused to come, but he promised him health in his letter. 

They say that he also added this: that <margin>26</margin> the city would never be capturable by barbarians. Those who <margin>25</margin> wrote the history of that time were entirely unaware of this postscript <note>original: "akroteleution"</note> to the letter, for they made no mention of it anywhere. However, the people of Edessa claim that it was found with the letter, so that indeed—

<note>Translator's note on the critical apparatus: In line 22, the scholar Scaliger suggests the reading 'refusing' (apolegon), while manuscript P has 'washing away' (apoleuon) and Dindorf suggests 'waiving' (aponeuon). In line 25, the word 'postscript' (akroteleution) is written in the margin of manuscript P, whereas 'extreme' or 'end' (akrotaton) appears in the main body of the text.</note>

<summary>King Abgar of Edessa, suffering from an incurable illness, writes to Jesus after hearing of his miracles in Palestine. Jesus sends a written reply promising Abgar health and declaring that Edessa will never fall to foreign invaders.</summary>
<keywords>Abgar V, Jesus Christ, Edessa, miracles, leprosy, Abgar Legend, letter of Jesus, Persian Wars, hagiography</keywords>

<margin>ὅτι Φιλομαθής τις ὤν</margin>
-ς. Φιλομαθής τις ὤν, καὶ τοῖς περὶ σοφίας λόγοις πάνυ ἐσπουδακώς, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκείνῳ μὲν ἐδόκουν εἶναι πάνυ σοφός, καὶ
πολλοῖς ἄλλοις φιλοσόφοις· τέλος δὲ καὶ ἐμαυτῷ· καὶ ἔπειτα ἐπειρώμην δείκνυναι αὐτῷ ὅτι οἴοιτο μὲν εἶναι σοφός, εἴη δὲ
οὔ. ἐντεῦθεν οὖν τῷ τε ἀνδρὶ τούτῳ ἀπηχθόμην καὶ πολλοῖς τῶν παρόντων· ἐμαυτῷ δὲ διαλογιζόμενος ἀπιὼν ᾤμην
ἐμαυτὸν εἶναι σοφώτερον· ὃς γὰρ οὗτος μὲν οἴεταί τι εἰδέναι οὐκ εἰδώς, ἐγὼ δὲ ὥσπερ οὖν οὐκ οἶδα, οὐδὲ οἴομαι· ἔοικα
οὖν τούτου γε σμικρῷ τινι αὐτῷ τούτῳ σοφώτερος εἶναι, ὅτι ἃ μὴ οἶδα οὐδὲ οἴομαι εἰδέναι. ἐντεῦθεν ἐπ’ ἄλλον ᾖα τῶν
ἐκείνου δοκούντων σοφωτέρων εἶναι, καὶ ταὐτὰ ταῦτα ἔδοξέ μοι, καὶ ἐνταῦθα κἀκείνῳ καὶ ἄλλοις πολλοῖς ἀπηχθόμην.
μετὰ ταῦτ’ οὖν ἐφεξῆς ᾖα, αἰσθανόμενος μὲν καὶ λυπούμενος καὶ δεδιὼς ὅτι ἀπηχθανόμην, ὅμως δὲ ἀναγκαῖον ἐδόκει
εἶναι τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ περὶ πλείστου ποιεῖσθαι· ἰτέον οὖν, σκοποῦντι τὸν χρησμὸν τί λέγει, ἐπὶ ἅπαντας τοὺς δοκοῦντάς τι
εἰδέναι. καὶ νὴ τὸν κύνα, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, δεῖ γὰρ πρὸς ὑμᾶς τἀληθῆ λέγειν, ἦ μὴν ἐγὼ ἔπαθόν τι τοιοῦτον· οἱ μὲν
μάλιστα εὐδοκιμοῦντες ἔδοξάν μοι ὀλίγου δεῖν πλεῖστοι ἐνδεεῖς εἶναι ζητοῦντι κατὰ τὸν θεόν, ἄλλοι δὲ δοκοῦντες φαυ-
λότεροι, ἐπιεικέστεροι εἶναι ἄνδρες πρὸς τὸ φρονίμως ἔχειν. δεῖ δὴ ὑμῖν τὴν ἐμὴν πλάνην ἐπιδεῖξαι ὥσπερ πόνους
τινὰς πονοῦντος, ἵνα μοι καὶ ἀνέλεγκτος ἡ μαντεία γένοιτο. μετὰ γὰρ τοὺς πολιτικοὺς ἐπὶ τοὺς ποιητὰς ᾖα τούς τε
τῶν τραγῳδιῶν καὶ τοὺς τῶν διθυράμβων καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους, ὡς ἐνταῦθα ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρῳ καταληψόμενος ἐμαυτὸν ἀμαθέ-
στερον ἐκείνων ὄντα. ἀναλαμβάνων οὖν αὐτῶν τὰ ποιήματα ἅ μοι ἐδόκει μάλιστα πεπραγματεῦσθαι αὐτοῖς, διη-
ρώτων ἂν αὐτοὺς τί λέγοιεν, ἵν’ ἅμα τι καὶ μανθάνοιμι παρ’ αὐτῶν. αἰσχύνομαι οὖν ὑμῖν εἰπεῖν, ὦ ἄνδρες, τἀληθῆ·
ὅμως δὲ ῥητέον. ὡς ἔπος γὰρ εἰπεῖν ὀλίγου πάντες οἱ παρόντες ἂν βέλτιον ἔλεγον περὶ ὧν αὐτοὶ ἐποίησαν. ἔγνων
οὖν αὖ καὶ περὶ τῶν ποιητῶν ἐν ὀλίγῳ τοῦτο, ὅτι οὐ σοφίᾳ ποιοῖεν ἃ ποιοῖεν, ἀλλὰ φύσει τινὶ καὶ ἐνθουσιάζοντες
ὥσπερ οἱ θεομάντεις καὶ οἱ χρησμῳδοί· καὶ γὰρ οὗτοι λέγουσι μὲν πολλὰ καὶ καλά, ἴσασι δὲ οὐδὲν ὧν λέγουσι.
τοιοῦτόν τί μοι ἐφάνησαν πάθος καὶ οἱ ποιηταὶ πεπονθότες, καὶ ἅμα ᾐσθόμην αὐτῶν διὰ τὴν ποίησιν οἰομένων καὶ
τἆλλα σοφωτάτων εἶναι ἀνθρώπων ἃ οὐκ ἦσαν. ἀπῇα οὖν καὶ ἐντεῦθεν τῷ αὐτῷ οἰόμενος περιγεγονέναι ᾧ καὶ
τῶν πολιτικῶν. τελευτῶν οὖν ἐπὶ τοὺς χειροτέχνας ᾖα· ἐμαυτῷ γὰρ συνῄδη οὐδὲν ἐπισταμένῳ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν,
τούτους δέ γ’ ᾔδη ὅτι εὑρήσοιμι πολλὰ καὶ καλὰ ἐπισταμένους. καὶ τούτου μὲν οὐκ ἐψεύσθην, ἀλλ’ ἠπίσταντο ἃ
ἐγὼ οὐκ ἠπιστάμην καὶ ἦσαν μου σοφώτεροι. ἀλλ’, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, ταὐτόν μοι ἔδοξαν ἔχειν ἁμάρτημα ὅπερ
καὶ οἱ ποιηταὶ καὶ οἱ ἀγαθοὶ χειροτέχναι· διὰ τὸ τὴν τέχνην καλῶς ἐξεργάζεσθαι ἕκαστος ἠξίου καὶ τἆλλα τὰ
μέγιστα σοφώτατος εἶναι, καὶ αὐτῶν αὕτη ἡ πλημμέλεια ἐκείνην τὴν σοφίαν ἀπέκρυπτεν· ὥστ’ ἐμὲ ἐμαυτὸν
ἀνερωτᾶν ὑπὲρ τοῦ χρησμοῦ πότερα δεξαίμην ἂν οὕτως ὥσπερ ἔχω ἔχειν, μήτε τι σοφὸς ὢν τὴν ἐκείνων
σοφίαν μήτε ἀμαθὴς τὴν ἀμαθίαν, ἢ ἀμφότερα ἃ ἐκεῖνοι ἔχουσιν ἔχειν. ἀπεκρινάμην οὖν ἐμαυτῷ καὶ τῷ
χρησμῷ ὅτι μοι λυσιτελοῖ ὥσπερ ἔχω ἔχειν. ἐκ ταυτησὶ δὴ τῆς ἐξετάσεως, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πολλαὶ μὲν ἀπέ-
χθειαί μοι γεγόνασι καὶ οἷαι χαλεπώταται καὶ βαρύταται, ὥστε πολλὰς διαβολὰς ἀπ’ αὐτῶν γεγονέναι, ὄνομα
δὲ τοῦτο λέγεσθαι, σοφὸς εἶναι· οἴονται γάρ με ἑκάστοτε οἱ παρόντες ταῦτα αὐτὸν εἶναι σοφὸν ἃ ἂν ἄλλον
ἐξελέγξω. τὸ δὲ κινδυνεύει, ὦ ἄνδρες, τῷ ὄντι ὁ θεὸς σοφὸς εἶναι, καὶ ἐν τῷ χρησμῷ τούτῳ τοῦτο λέγειν,
ὅτι ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη σοφία ὀλίγου τινὸς ἀξία ἐστὶ καὶ οὐδενός. καὶ φαίνεται τοῦτον λέγειν τὸν Σωκράτη,
προσκεχρῆσθαι δὲ τῷ ἐμῷ ὀνόματι, ἐμὲ παράδειγμα ποιούμενος, ὥσπερ ἂν εἰ εἴποι ὅτι οὗτος ὑμῶν, ὦ
ἄνθρωποι, σοφώτατός ἐστιν, ὅστις ὥσπερ Σωκράτης ἔγνωκεν ὅτι οὐδενὸς ἀξιός ἐστι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πρὸς σοφίαν.
ταῦτ’ οὖν ἐγὼ μὲν ἔτι καὶ νῦν περιιὼν ζητῶ καὶ ἐρευνῶ κατὰ τὸν θεὸν καὶ τῶν ἀστῶν καὶ τῶν ξένων ἄν τινα
οἴωμαι σοφὸν εἶναι· καὶ ἐπειδάν μοι μὴ δοκῇ, τῷ θεῷ βοηθῶν ἐνδείκνυμαι ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι σοφός. καὶ ὑπὸ
ταύτης τῆς ἀσχολίας οὔτε τι τῶν τῆς πόλεως πρᾶξαί μοι σχολὴ γέγονεν ἄξιον λόγου οὔτε τῶν οἰκείων, ἀλλ’
ἐν πενίᾳ μυρίᾳ εἰμὶ διὰ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ λατρείαν. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις οἱ νέοι μοι ἐπακολουθοῦντες, οἷς μάλιστα
σχολή ἐστιν, οἱ τῶν πλουσιωτάτων, αὐτόματοι, χαίρουσιν ἀκούοντες ἐξεταζομένων τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ αὐτοὶ
πολλάκις ἐμὲ μιμοῦνται, εἶτα ἐπιχειροῦσιν ἄλλους ἐξετάζειν· κἄπειτα, οἶμαι, εὑρίσκουσι πολλὴν ἀφθονίαν
οἰομένων μὲν εἰδέναι τι ἀνθρώπων, εἰδότων δὲ ὀλίγα ἢ οὐδέν. ἐντεῦθεν οὖν οἱ ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἐξεταζόμενοι
ἐμοὶ ὀργίζονται, οὐχ αὑτοῖς, καὶ λέγουσιν ὡς Σωκράτης τίς ἐστι μιαρώτατος καὶ διαφθείρει τοὺς νέους·
καὶ ἐπειδάν τις αὐτοὺς ἐρωτᾷ ὅτι ποιῶν καὶ ὅτι διδάσκων, ἔχουσι μὲν οὐδὲν εἰπεῖν ἀλλ’ ἀγνοοῦσιν, ἵνα δὲ
μὴ δοκῶσιν ἀπορεῖν, τὰ κατὰ πάντων τῶν φιλοσοφούντων πρόχειρα ταῦτα λέγουσιν, ὅτι τὰ μετέωρα
καὶ τὰ ὑπὸ γῆς καὶ θεοὺς μὴ νομίζειν καὶ τὸν ἥττω λόγον κρείττω ποιεῖν. τὰ γὰρ ἀληθῆ, οἶμαι, οὐκ ἂν
ἐθέλοιεν λέγειν, ὅτι κατάδηλοι γίγνονται προσποιούμενοι μὲν εἰδέναι, εἰδότες δὲ οὐδέν. ἅτε οὖν, οἶμαι,
φιλότιμοι ὄντες καὶ σφοδροὶ καὶ πολλοί, καὶ συντεταγμένως καὶ πιθανῶς λέγοντες περὶ ἐμοῦ, ἐμπεπλή-
κασιν ὑμῶν τὰ ὦτα καὶ πάλαι καὶ σφοδρῶς διαβάλλοντες. ἐκ τούτων καὶ Μέλητός μοι ἐπέθετο καὶ Ἄνυτος
καὶ Λύκων, Μέλητος μὲν ὑπὲρ τῶν ποιητῶν ἀχθόμενος, Ἄνυτος δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν δημιουργῶν καὶ τῶν
πολιτικῶν, Λύκων δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν ῥητόρων· ὥστε, ὅπερ ἀρχόμενος ἐγὼ ἔλεγον, θαυμάζοιμ’ ἂν εἰ οἷός τ’
εἴην ἐγὼ ὑμῶν ταύτην τὴν διαβολὴν ἐξελέσθαι ἐν οὕτως ὀλίγῳ χρόνῳ, οὕτω πολλὴν γεγονυῖαν. ταῦτ’
ἔστιν ὑμῖν, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, τἀληθῆ, καὶ ὑμᾶς οὔτε μέγα οὔτε σμικρὸν ἀποκρυψάμενος ἐγὼ λέγω
οὐδ’ ὑποστειλάμενος. καίτοι σχεδὸν οἶδα ὅτι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἀπεχθάνομαι, ὃ καὶ τεκμήριον ὅτι τἀληθῆ
λέγω καὶ ὅτι αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ διαβολὴ ἡ ἐμὴ καὶ τὰ αἴτια ταῦτά ἐστι. καὶ ἐάντε νῦν ἐάντε αὖθις ζητήσητε
ταῦτα, οὕτως εὑρήσετε. περὶ μὲν οὖν ὧν οἱ πρῶτοί μου κατήγοροι κατηγόρουν αὕτη ἔστω ἱκανὴ ἀπολογία

translation: provided for us everything that is good in life; and there is a time when I must be bold before you. <margin>Because he is someone who loves to learn</margin> Being someone who loves to learn, and having been very diligent with discourses concerning wisdom, at first I seemed to him to be very wise, and to many other philosophers; and finally even to myself. And then I tried to demonstrate to him that he believed he was wise, but was not. From there, I became hateful to this man and to many of those present; but as I went away, I reasoned with myself and thought that I was wiser than he. For even though this man thinks he knows something when he does not, just as I do not know, I also do not think [that I know]. I seem, therefore, to be wiser than he by this small thing: that I do not think I know what I do not know. From there, I went to another of those who seemed to be wiser than he, and the same thing appeared to me, and there I became hateful to him and to many others as well. After this, therefore, I went in order, perceiving and grieving and fearing that I was becoming hated, yet it seemed necessary to consider the matter of the god as of the highest importance. Therefore, I had to go to everyone who seemed to know something, while examining what the oracle says. And by the Dog <note>a typical Socratic oath, "by the Dog" refers to the Egyptian god Anubis or is simply a substitute for a stronger oath</note>, men of Athens, for I must tell you the truth, I suffered something like this: those who were most highly esteemed seemed to me to be almost the most deficient when I was searching according to the god, while others who seemed more common were better men regarding being sensible. I must, therefore, show you my wandering as one laboring through certain trials, so that the prophecy might be rendered irrefutable for me. For after the politicians, I went to the poets, those of the tragedies and those of the dithyrambs and the others, as if I would there catch myself being more ignorant than they. Taking up their poems, which seemed to me to be the most elaborately crafted by them, I would ask them what they meant, so that I might also learn something from them. I am ashamed, therefore, to tell you the truth, men, yet it must be spoken. For to put it simply, almost everyone present could speak better than they did about what they themselves had composed. I realized, therefore, also concerning the poets in a short time, that they do not create what they create by wisdom, but by a certain nature and while inspired, just like the divine seers and oracle-speakers. For these, too, say many and beautiful things, but know nothing of what they say. The poets appeared to me to have suffered some such experience, and at the same time I perceived that they, because of their poetry, believed themselves to be the wisest of men in other things, which they were not. I went away, therefore, even from there believing that I had an advantage for the same reason that I had over the politicians. Finally, then, I went to the craftsmen; for I was conscious of myself knowing nothing, so to speak, and I knew that I would find them knowing many and beautiful things. And I was not mistaken in this, but they knew things that I did not know, and they were wiser than I. But, men of Athens, they seemed to me to have the same fault as the poets and the good craftsmen: because they worked their craft well, each claimed to be wisest in other greatest things, and this very mistake of theirs concealed that wisdom. So that I asked myself on behalf of the oracle whether I would prefer to be as I am, neither wise in their wisdom nor ignorant in their ignorance, or to have both things that they have. I answered, therefore, to myself and to the oracle that it was profitable for me to be as I am. From this very examination, men of Athens, many hatreds have arisen for me, and such as are most difficult and burdensome, so that many slanders have arisen from them, and this name is spoken: to be wise. For those present each time think that I myself am wise in those things in which I refute another. But it is likely, men, that the god is truly wise, and that in this oracle he is saying this: that human wisdom is worth little or nothing. And he appears to be speaking of this Socrates, and to have used my name, making me an example, as if he were to say that this one of you, O men, is wisest, who, like Socrates, has recognized that he is worth nothing in truth regarding wisdom. These things, therefore, I still even now go about seeking and investigating according to the god, if I think anyone of the citizens or foreigners is wise. And whenever it does not seem so to me, I help the god by demonstrating that he is not wise. And because of this occupation, I have had no leisure to do anything worth mentioning for the city nor for my own affairs, but I am in ten thousand poverties because of my service to the god. In addition to these things, the young men who follow me, to whom there is most leisure, the sons of the wealthiest, do this of their own accord; they enjoy hearing men being examined, and they themselves often imitate me, and then attempt to examine others. And then, I think, they find an abundance of men who think they know something, but know little or nothing. From there, those who are examined by them become angry with me, not with themselves, and say that there is a certain Socrates who is most abominable and corrupts the youth. And whenever someone asks them what he does and what he teaches, they have nothing to say but are ignorant, but so that they do not seem to be at a loss, they say these ready-made things against all who philosophize: that he investigates the things in the heavens and under the earth, and does not believe in gods, and makes the weaker argument the stronger. For the truth, I think, they would not be willing to speak, that they become exposed as pretending to know, while knowing nothing. As, therefore, I think, they are ambitious and vehement and many, and speaking in an organized and persuasive manner about me, they have filled your ears, slandering me both long ago and vehemently. From these, Meletus set upon me, and Anytus and Lycon; Meletus, being distressed on behalf of the poets; Anytus, on behalf of the craftsmen and the politicians; and Lycon, on behalf of the rhetoricians. So that, as I was saying at the beginning, I would be surprised if I were able to remove this slander from you in such a short time, having become so great. These are the truths for you, men of Athens, and I say them to you without hiding or holding back anything great or small. And yet I know that I am hated for these same things, which is also proof that I speak the truth and that this is my slander and these are its causes. And whether you investigate this now or later, you will find it so. Concerning, then, what my first accusers were accusing me of, let this be a sufficient defense.

my own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved.

### Chap. 11.

1 Imitate me, just as I also imitate Christ.

2 Now I praise you, brethren, that you remember me in all things and keep the traditions just as I delivered them to you.

3 But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.

4 Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonors his head.

5 But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for that is one and the same as if her head were shaved.

6 For if a woman is not covered, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be covered.

7 For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.

8 For man is not from woman, but woman from man.

9 Nor was man created for the woman, but woman for the man.

10 For this reason the woman ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.

11 Nevertheless, neither is man independent of woman, nor woman independent of man, in the Lord.

12 For as woman came from man, even so the man also comes through woman; but all things are from God.

καὶ θάτερον ἐφαρμόττει· οἷον τῇ γραμμῇ ὑπάρχει καθ’ αὑτὸ τὸ μῆκος· ἐν γὰρ τῷ τί ἐστι κατηγορεῖται, καὶ οὐ μόνον γε καθ’ αὑτὸ ἀλλὰ καὶ ᾗ αὐτό. καὶ τὸ εὐθὺ πάλιν ὑπάρχει τῇ γραμμῇ καθ’ αὑτὸ καὶ ᾗ αὐτό· ὃ γάρ ἐστιν ὁρισμὸς τοῦ εὐθὺ δίχα τῆς γραμμῆς. ἆρ’ οὖν ἅπαντα καθόλου κατηγορεῖται, ὅσα ἐν τῷ ὁρισμῷ τινὸς παραλαμβάνεται; ταῦτα δ’ ἐστὶ τὰ γένη καὶ αἱ διαφοραί· ὑπάρχει γὰρ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὸ καὶ παντὸς εἶναι καὶ τὸ καθ’ αὑτό. ἢ δεῖ καὶ τρίτης προσθήκης εἰς τὸ ἀκριβῶς ὁρίσασθαι τὸ καθόλου; δεῖ γὰρ τὸ καθόλου, πρὸς τῷ παντὶ ὑπάρχειν καὶ καθ’ αὑτὸ ὑπάρχειν, ἔτι καὶ πρώτῳ ἐκείνῳ ὑπάρχειν καὶ οὐδενὶ ἄλλῳ προτέρῳ. <margin>Themist. f. 3 b.</margin>

ἀπαριθμησάμενος τὰ τοῦ καθ’ αὑτὸ σημαινόμενα καὶ ἀφορισάμενος τὰ χρήσιμα πάσης τῆς ἀποδεικτικῆς μεθόδου, μέτεισιν εἰς τὴν περὶ τοῦ καθόλου διδασκαλίαν. τρία δὲ οἶδε τοῦ καθόλου τὰ σημαινόμενα ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης, ἓν μὲν τὸ ἁπλῶς ὑποκειμένῳ παντὶ ὑπάρχειν τὸ κατηγορούμενον, κἂν μὴ καθ’ αὑτὸ ὑπάρχῃ, ὡς φαμὲν παντὶ Αἰθίοπι τὸ μέλαν ἢ παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ βαδίζειν· δεύτερον δὲ ὃ καθόλου τέ ἐστι καὶ καθ’ αὑτό, ὡς φαμὲν πάσῃ δεκάδι τὸ ἄρτιον· τρίτον δὲ ὃ καθ’ αὑτό τέ ἐστι καὶ ᾗ αὐτὸ καὶ πρώτως, ὅπερ νῦν καὶ παραδίδωσι καὶ ταῖς ἀποδεικτικαῖς παραλαμβάνειν μεθόδους, οἷον τὸ παντὶ τριγώνῳ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας εἶναι... τὸ γὰρ τοῦτο φησὶ τὸ καθόλου εἰς τὴν ἀπόδειξιν δεῖν παραλαμβάνειν. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, συμβήσεται μηδὲν εἶναι ἀποδεικτικὸν ἃ μὴ ἀντιστρέφει πρὸς τὸ κατηγορούμενον, χρὴ ἵνα συντόμως εἴπω, μόνας εἶναι τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς καὶ τὰ ἴδια ἀποδεικτικὰ διὰ τὸ ἀντιστρέφειν πρὸς τὰ ὁριστά, τὸ μέντοι ὅτι ὁ ἄνθρωπος ζῷόν ἐστι μὴ εἶναι ἀποδεικτόν, διότι μὴ πρώτως τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ τὸ κατηγορούμενον ὑπάρχει. καὶ φησὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ὁ Θεμίστιος ὅτι εἰ τὰ γένη καὶ αἱ διαφοραὶ τῶν ἀποδεικτικῶν, αἳ οὐ μὴ ἐξισάζουσι πρὸς τὰ ὑποκείμενα, ἀλλ’ οὖν ἐπειδὴ καθ’ αὑτό τε καὶ παντὶ τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ ὑπάρχουσι. καὶ δῆλον ὅτι ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης τὴν κυριωτάτην καὶ μάλιστα ἀπόδειξιν τὴν τῷ πρώτῳ πρέπουσαν φιλοσόφῳ διασκοπούμενος, ταύτην φησὶν εἶναι τὴν καθολικώτατα δεικνύουσαν. δῆλον οὖν ὅτι δευτέρα ἂν εἴη μέτρα ἀποδείξεως τὰ ἐπὶ τῶν γενῶν καὶ τῶν διαφορῶν παραλαμβανόμενα, πρῶτα δὲ ἃ μάλιστα ὅπερ αὐτὸς παρέδωκε. τινὲς δὲ πρὸς τούτῳ κἀκεῖνο ἔφασαν, ὡς ταὐτά φησιν ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης ὅτι ὅτι πάντα τὰ ἀποδεικτικὰ ὀφείλει ἀντιστρέφειν, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα τὰ συμβαλλόμενα πρὸς τὴν ἀπόδειξιν. οἷον ἐν τῇ ἀποδείξει τοῦ τὸ τρίγωνον τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν, παραληπτέον ὅτι ἐὰν εἰς δύο εὐθείας παραλλήλους εὐθεῖα ἐμπέσῃ, τὰς ἐναλλὰξ τρεῖς γωνίας ἴσας ἀλλήλαις ποιεῖ· καὶ ἔστι τοῦτο ἀντιστρέφον· ἐν ᾧ γὰρ αἱ ἐναλλὰξ τρεῖς γωνίαι ἴσαι ἀλλήλαις εἰσίν, ἐκεῖ εἰς δύο παραλλήλους εὐθείας εὐθεῖα ἐμπέπτωκε. τοῦτο δέ ἐσι ψεῦδος· οὐ γὰρ τοῦτό φησιν ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης, ἀλλὰ περὶ αὐτῶν τῶν ἀποδεικτικῶν τὸν λόγον ποιεῖται, ὡς ἐν τῇ λέξει ἐπισημειωσόμεθα... ἰστέον τοίνυν ὅτι ὁ μὲν Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τούτοις τὸ αὐτὸ φησὶν εἶναι τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ καὶ τὸ ᾗ αὐτό· εἰ τί μὴ ᾗ αὐτό, τοῦτο οὐ καθ’ αὑτό. οἱ δὲ περὶ τὸν Θεόφραστον διαφέρειν ταῦτα λέγουσι· καθολικώτερον γὰρ εἶναι τὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ τοῦ ᾗ αὐτό· εἴ τι μὲν ᾗ αὐτό, τοῦτο καὶ καθ’ αὑτό, οὐκ εἴ τι δὲ καθ’ αὑτό, πάντως καὶ ᾗ αὐτό. τῷ γὰρ τριγώνῳ ᾗ τρίγωνόν ἐστιν ὑπάρχει τὸ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθ’ αὑτό· τῷ δὲ ἰσοσκελεῖ καθ’ αὑτὸ μὲν ὑπάρχει, οὐκέτι δὲ ᾗ αὐτό· ᾗ γὰρ ᾗ ἰσοσκελὲς ὑπάρχει αὐτῷ τὸ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν· εἰ γὰρ τοῦτο, οὐκ ἂν τῷ ἰσοπλεύρῳ ἢ σκαληνῷ ὑπῆρχεν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἰσοσκελῆ, ἀλλ’ ἢ ἁπλῶς τρίγωνά ἐστιν. ταῦτα μὲν οἱ περὶ Θεόφραστον, ὁ μέντοι Ἀριστοτέλης εὑρὼν ἐπί τινων ταῦτα συντρέχοντα ταὐτὸν εἶναι ἔφη ἄμφω· τὸ γὰρ νῦν καὶ ἐπιστήμης δεκτικὸν καθ’ αὑτό τε ὑπάρχει τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ ᾗ αὐτό· εἰ γὰρ ᾗ ζῷόν ἐστι τὸ τῆς ἐπιστήμης δεκτικόν ἐστι, οὐδὲ ἡ ἵππος ἢ ἔμψυχον, ἀλλ’ ἢ ἄνθρωπος· δοκεῖ γὰρ τοῦτο μόνον τῶν ζῴων εἶναι καὶ καὶ ἐπιστήμης δεκτικόν. καὶ τῷ περιττῷ ἀριθμῷ τὸ μὴ εἰς ἴσα διαιρεῖσθαι δύνασθαι καθ’ αὑτὸ καὶ ᾗ αὐτὸ ὑπάρχει. <margin>Ioh. Phil. f. 17.</margin>

οὗτος οὖν ὁ τρίτος προσδιορισμὸς τοῦ καθόλου. τὸ δὲ "ἐπὶ τοῦ τυχόντος" <margin>32.</margin> τουτέστιν ὅταν τῷ τυχόντι τῶν ὑπὸ τὸ κατηγορούμενον αὐτῷ τὸ κατηγορούμενον ὑπάρχῃ, οἷον τῷ τυχόντι τριγώνῳ τὸ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν, καὶ μὴ μόνῳ τῷ τυχόντι ἀλλὰ καὶ πρώτῳ· ᾗ γὰρ πρώτως τῷ σκαληνῷ, ἀλλὰ τῷ τριγώνῳ ὑπάρχει τὸ τὰς τρεῖς γωνίας δυσὶν ὀρθαῖς ἴσας ἔχειν. <margin>id. f. 17 b.</margin>

σκοπεῖ πῶς σαφῶς διὰ τούτων τὰ εἰς τὴν ἀπόδειξιν χρησιμεύοντά φησιν εἶναι, ἀλλ’ ὅπερ ἔλεγον, τὰ ἀποδεικτικά· καὶ ἡ ἀπόδειξις γάρ, φησί, καθ’ αὑτὸ καὶ τοῦ καθόλου ἐστίν. <margin>id. ib.</margin> <margin>40.</margin>

δεῖ δὲ μὴ λανθάνειν ὅτι πολλάκις ἀπατώμεθα περὶ τοῦ καθόλου <margin>74a 4.</margin> καὶ οὐκ ἀποδεικνύντες αὐτὸ ᾗ δοκοῦμεν ἀποδεικνύναι καὶ μὴ δεικνύντες ἀποδεικνύναι νομίζομεν. τρεῖς δ’ αἰτίαι τῆς ἀπάτης εἰσίν, μία μὲν ὅταν τι τῶν καθ’ ἕκαστον ἢ καὶ ἄτομον ἐφ’ ᾧ ποιούμεθα τὰς ἀποδείξεις, οἷον ἥλιος σελήνη κόσμος· ἐπεὶ γὰρ οὐδέν ἐστιν ἀνωτέρω τῶν τούτων οὐδὲ κοινόν, ἀλλ’ ἐφ’ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἄτομον (εἷς γὰρ ἥλιος καὶ μία σελήνη καὶ μία γῆ καὶ εἷς οὐρανός), ὅταν τι τούτοις ὑπάρχον ἀποδείκνυμεν, ἢ τῇ γῇ τὸ ἐν μέσῳ κεῖσθαι ἢ τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ κύκλῳ φέρεσθαι, οὐκ οἰόμεθα καθόλου ὑπάρχον ἀποδεικνύναι, καίτοι μὴ καθ’ ὃ τόδ’ ἑκάτερον αὐτῶν καὶ ἄτομον ποιῶμεν τὴν ἀπόδειξιν. εἰ γὰρ καθ’ ὃ ἥλιος εἰς ἐκλείποντα αὐτὸν ἀποδεικνύομεν ὑποτρεχούσης τῆς σελήνης, ἀλλὰ τοιαῦταί εἰσιν αἱ γινόμεναι ἀποδείξεις ὡς εἰ πλείους ἦσαν, ὁμοίως ἁρμόσειεν. <margin>Themist. f. 3 b.</margin>

διδάξας περὶ τοῦ καθόλου, νῦν βούλεται παραδοῦναι τὰς αἰτίας τῆς ἀπάτης, καθ’ ἃς πολλάκις μὴ ἀποδεικνύντες τί τὸ καθόλου καὶ τὰ ἐνταῦθα παραδεδομένα ὅμως δοκοῦμεν καθόλου ἀποδεικνύναι. τρεῖς δέ φησιν αἰτίας εἶναι τῆς τοιαύτης ἀπάτης, μίαν μὲν ὡς ὅταν μοναδικόν τι ᾖ καὶ καθ’ ἕκαστα, ἐφ’ ᾧ ποιούμεθα τὰς ἀποδείξεις, οἷον ὅτι ἡ γῆ ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ παντὸς κεῖται ἢ ὅτι ὁ κόσμος σφαιρικός, ἢ τὰ τῷ ἡλίῳ ἴδια συμβαίνοντα συμπτώματα... οὐκ ἂν εἶεν καθόλου, διότι οὐκ ἐπειδὴ μία γῆ οὐδὲ ἐπειδὴ εἷς ἥλιος ταῦτα αὐτοῖς συμβέβηκεν, ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὴ ἁπλῶς ἥλιος καὶ ἐπεὶ ἁπλῶς γῆ, ὥστε εἰ καὶ πλείους ἦσαν, ταῦτ’ ἂν ἐπ’ ἐκείνων ἥρμοσεν. οὐκ ἄρα καθόλου δείκνυται τὰ ἐπ’ ἐκείνων δεικνύμενα. <margin>Ioh. Phil. f. 17 b.</margin>

δευτέρα αἰτία τῆς ἀπάτης, ὅταν ἔν τι κοινόν, ἀνώνυμον δὲ ἦται <margin>74a 8.</margin> τοῦτο, καὶ διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν κοινόν τι ὄνομα ἀναγκαζώμεθα ἐφ’ ἑκάστῳ

<meta>continues from previous page: and the other applies; for example, length belongs to a line essentially; for it is predicated in the "what it is," and not only essentially, but also as such. And straightness, again, belongs to a line essentially and as such; for it is the definition of "straight" without the line. Are, then, all things predicated universally, which are taken up in the definition of something? These are the genera and the differences; for both "belonging to every" and "belonging essentially" apply to them. Or is a third addition necessary to define the universal precisely? For the universal must, in addition to belonging to every instance and belonging essentially, also belong to that first subject and to no other prior to it. <margin>Themistius, fol. 3b.</margin>

Having enumerated the meanings of "essentially" and having defined those useful for the entire demonstrative method, he proceeds to the teaching concerning the universal. Aristotle recognizes three meanings of the universal: first, that the predicate belongs to every subject simply, even if it does not belong essentially, as we say "black" belongs to every Ethiopian or "walking" to every human; second, that which is both universal and essential, as we say "even" belongs to every decad; and third, that which is essential, as such, and primarily, which he now hands down and takes up for demonstrative methods, for example, that "the three angles of every triangle are equal to two right angles"... for he says that this is the universal that must be taken up for demonstration. If this is so, it will follow that nothing is demonstrative that does not convert with the predicate; it is necessary, to speak briefly, that only definitions and proper attributes are demonstrative because they convert with the defined, whereas the fact that "a human is an animal" is not demonstrable, because the predicate does not belong to the subject primarily. And Themistius says regarding this that if the genera and differences are demonstrative, which do not equal the subjects, they are so because they belong essentially and to every subject. And it is clear that Aristotle, examining the most authoritative and primary demonstration suitable for a philosopher, says this is the one that demonstrates most universally. It is clear, therefore, that the things taken up regarding genera and differences would be a second measure of demonstration, and those which he himself handed down are the first. Some, in addition to this, said that Aristotle says the same thing, that all demonstrative things ought to convert, but these are the things that contribute to the demonstration. For example, in the demonstration that "a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles," one must take up that "if a straight line falls upon two parallel straight lines, it makes the alternate angles equal to each other"; and this is convertible; for where the alternate angles are equal to each other, there a straight line has fallen upon two parallel straight lines. But this is false; for Aristotle does not say this, but makes his argument about the demonstrative things themselves, as we shall note in the text... One must know, therefore, that Aristotle in these passages says that "essentially" and "as such" are the same; if something is not "as such," it is not "essentially." But those around Theophrastus say these differ; for "essentially" is more universal than "as such"; if something is "as such," it is also "essentially," but if something is "essentially," it is not necessarily "as such." For to a triangle, as it is a triangle, it belongs to have three angles equal to two right angles, but it also belongs essentially; but to an isosceles triangle it belongs essentially, but no longer as such; for it does not belong to it as it is isosceles to have three angles equal to two right angles; for if this were so, it would not belong to the equilateral or scalene, since they are not isosceles, but are simply triangles. These are the views of those around Theophrastus, but Aristotle, having found these coinciding in some cases, said both were the same; for the capacity for knowledge belongs to a human both essentially and as such; for if it is as a living being that it is capable of knowledge, then not even a horse or any ensouled being, but only a human; for this alone of living beings seems to be capable of knowledge. And to an odd number, the inability to be divided into equal parts belongs essentially and as such. <margin>John Philoponus, fol. 17.</margin>

This, therefore, is the third determination of the universal. And "in any given case" <margin>32.</margin> means when the predicate belongs to any given instance of the subject, for example, to any given triangle it belongs to have three angles equal to two right angles, and not only to the given instance but also primarily; for it belongs to the triangle primarily, even if it belongs to the scalene, that it has three angles equal to two right angles. <margin>id., fol. 17b.</margin>

He observes how clearly he says through these that the things useful for demonstration are, as I was saying, the demonstrative ones; for he says that demonstration itself is also essential and universal. <margin>id., ibid.</margin> <margin>40.</margin>

One must not fail to notice that we are often deceived concerning the universal <margin>74a 4.</margin> and, not demonstrating it as we think we are demonstrating, we think we are demonstrating when we are not. There are three causes of this deception: one is when we make demonstrations about some particular or individual thing, for example, the sun, the moon, the cosmos; since there is nothing above these nor anything common, but the individual is in each case (for there is one sun, one moon, one earth, and one heaven), when we demonstrate something belonging to these, such as the earth lying in the center or the heaven moving in a circle, we do not think we are demonstrating it as belonging universally, even though we do not make the demonstration according to what each of these is as an individual. For if we demonstrate that the sun is eclipsed when the moon runs under it, such are the demonstrations that occur as if there were more, it would fit them likewise. <margin>Themistius, fol. 3b.</margin>

Having taught concerning the universal, he now wishes to hand down the causes of the deception, according to which we often think we are demonstrating universally when we are not demonstrating what the universal is and what is handed down here. He says there are three causes of such deception: one is when there is something unique and individual, about which we make demonstrations, for example, that the earth lies in the center of the whole, or that the cosmos is spherical, or the symptoms that happen specifically to the sun... these would not be universal, because it is not because there is one earth nor because there is one sun that these things happen to them, but because it is simply "sun" and because it is simply "earth," so that if there were more, these would fit them as well. Therefore, the things demonstrated in those cases are not demonstrated universally. <margin>John Philoponus, fol. 17b.</margin>

The second cause of deception is when there is something common, but this is nameless <margin>74a 8.</margin>, and because it does not have a common name, we are forced to [demonstrate] in each case

translation:
<header>THE PEACE, 1174-1192</header>

It is, he says, true Sardian tincture, <note>A high-quality, expensive red dye.</note>
Which they guarantee will not run;
But if ever it gets to fighting,
Though his scarlet coat be on,
He himself becomes as pallid
As the palest Cyzicene, <note>A reference to coins or people from the city of Cyzicus.</note>
Running like a tawny cockhorse,
He is the first to quit the scene;
His crests shake and quake above him:
I stood gaping while he fled.
Ah, but when at home they are stationed,
Things that cannot be borne they do,
Making up the lists unfairly,
Striking out and putting down
Names at random. It is tomorrow
That the soldiers leave the town;
One poor wretch has bought no victuals,
For he knew not he must go
Till he on Pandion’s <note>A statue in the Athenian marketplace where official notices were posted.</note> statue
Spied the list and found it was so,
Reading there his name inserted;
Off he scuds with a wry face.
This is how they treat the farmers,
But the burghers certainly
Somewhat better: godless wretches,
Rogues with neither shame nor—shield,
Who one day, if God be willing,
Strict accounts to me shall yield.
For they have wronged me much and sorely:
Very lions in the city,
Very foxes in the fight.
Hillo! Hillo!
What lots are coming to the wedding supper!

<summary>The speaker denounces the hypocrisy of officials who act brave in the city but are cowards in battle, and who manipulate military conscription lists to the detriment of the farmers.</summary>

The memory says that a bronze cow stood at this passage, having been set up by the Chalcedonians; for both this and those were the monument of the beautiful heifer. And this bull was called Thracian from the Thracian living around the place. Just as it was once called by the same name as this greater one. Dionysius <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer</note> says about this that its narrowest part ferries that whole thing, and those who have become sea-faring through the wave-swept [strait]; these are the prodigies who reveal such a Byzantine strait, and the historians use "heifer." But this geographer is accustomed to calling the Byzantine strait the "Thracian cow." And the prodigies call the Hellespont strait [the cow] over all the parents before the Thracian one came to be, and the geographer likewise records those on the stages in the strait, interpreting it. It must be noted that this, and all the local differences, the Thracian cow is what pours out toward the Pontus; the northern part is its own, the southern is that of the Propontis. And they know that the mouth of the Pontus will appear more accurately as the Hellespont of the Chalcedonians; for it is very close to the beginning of Dionysius, the waves and by Cyzicus, just as he himself says, and others not toward the whole place. But his scope of the Hellespont and that passage toward the Pontus is the remainder; therefore, let us also go to the widths themselves. Its northern [part] and the northern one toward the Pontus, that which is after the Hellespont; and after the Pontus, that which is toward the north is the mouth of the Pontus. These things have ambiguities because the ancients called the parts by Abydos the Hellespont, and the Pontus the Hellespont; others also [called] the whole Pontus. And the northern one is that toward the mouth of the Pontus; regarding this, those around Heracles despaired of the Hellespont. Others [call] the Aegean source of the Hellespont toward the north, as perhaps Homer does; the ocean toward the widths and the Hellespont. And I seem to follow Dionysius in these things, as it is necessary to divide [them] and [as] water of an exit; so that the Hellespont is the narrow channel, and the Pontus. And both are from the honor toward the Pontus, the one being the Thracian Bosphorus itself. And the one called personal, the Bosphorus is said to be the fugitive toward the Pontus itself, and the parts toward the shore the Hellespont; the chasm is greater, with the shore sources. And [it is] because Dionysius has also traveled well through both straits.

For immediately, indeed, because it was laid out before his eyes, he, if they should happen upon it. After these things, this king became one who, while living, went down to that which the Greeks believe to be Hades, and there gambled with Demeter, and sometimes winning, other times being unfortunate at her hands, and again coming up and arriving. He had a gift from her: a golden hand-towel. After Rhampsinitus' descent, when he arrived back, the Egyptians said he celebrated a festival. I know that even now they have it. They would not, however, celebrate for these reasons alone. The priests weave a robe for her every year on the day of the ceremony. After having the robe, they change into the road that leads to his temple, and they turn back. This priest, according to this custom of the religion, with his hands, or the wolf, is led to the temple of Demeter, which is distant by a few <term>stadia</term> <gloss>an ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</gloss>. And again, they lead the wolf back from the temple to the same place. Let these things be trusted by whoever finds such things persuasive.

The Egyptians say that I write the story as it is held by the hearing of each one. The Egyptians also say that the originators were Demeter and Dionysus. They are also the first Egyptians to speak the story that the soul of man is immortal. When the body wastes away, it enters into another living creature, always being born. And when it has traveled through all land creatures, and those of the sea, and the winged ones, it again enters the body of a man being born. The circuit of this happens in three thousand years. There are some of the Greeks who have used this story, some earlier, some later, as if it were their own. I know their names, but I do not write them. <note>Textual notes regarding the transcription of names and verbs (Perseus/Seriphos) and the rhythmic consistency.</note>

7. "Found"—22. "Found": by placing the same word at the beginning and the end of the story, the poet wittily marks the beginning and end of the myth; cf. Olympian I 93, Pythian X 51 — 10. "Flowing": cf. "they poured forth a wail" in Isthmian VIII 58 — 11ff. Pindar follows Hesiod's *Theogony* 274ff., except that here he makes Minerva a patron of Perseus, as also in Pythian X 45; in this, he is followed by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V 250, "Tritonia gave herself as a companion to her gold-born brother," and Apollodorus II 41 — 13. "Darkened": he blinded them by taking away the one communal eye which the daughters of Phorcys, that is, the Gorgons (so the scholia and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV 773; Apollodorus II 37 distinguishes between the Phorcides and the Gorgons), used alternately — 14. Perseus, son of Danae, turned the love of Polydectes, king of the island of Seriphos, for his mother Danae and the symbol he had demanded for his marriage to Hippodamia, into destruction; for, having brought the head of Medusa as a symbol, he turned the island and Polydectes into stone; cf. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V 242ff. — 16. "Beautiful cheeks": in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV 792, she is of the most brilliant beauty. From this, artists started wanting to portray the head of Medusa as an image of the highest beauty not extinguished even by death, and later poets imagined that Medusa had competed with Minerva for beauty — 17. "Son of Danae": placed with emphasis at the beginning of a new strophe, as in Olympian II 105, III 6, X 34, Pythian I 7, IV 185, XI 22, Isthmian VI 35, III 73 — 19. "Maiden": he placed this in the middle so it would be the subject of two verbs, "rescued" and "fashioned" — "All-sounding melody": cf. Olympian VII 12 — 20. "Euryale": the name of one of the Gorgons; he omitted the name of the third sister, Stheno — 22. "To mortal men to have": whether this alludes to the well-known myth about the goddess throwing away the flutes because they deformed her face is uncertain.

### IV 103, 2. 3. 104

...to the ground, having rounded leaves. And a third <term>phlomis</term>, the one called <term>lychnitis</term>, and by some <term>thryallis</term>, has three or four or more little leaves that are thick, hairy, and oily, useful for lamp wicks.

The root of the first two is astringent; for this reason, it is given in a drink with wine to those suffering from diarrhea, in the amount of an astragalus. Its decoction helps with ruptures, spasms, bruises, and chronic cough, and it relieves toothache when used as a mouthwash. The gold-colored one dyes hair and, wherever it is placed, it gathers cockroaches. The leaves, boiled in water, are applied as a poultice for swellings and inflammations of the eyes, and for necrotic sores with honey or wine; with vinegar, it treats wounds and helps those bitten by scorpions. The leaves of the wild one are a poultice for burns, and it is said that the leaves of the female type, when mixed with dried figs, keep them free from rot.

### 104 <term>Aithiopis</term> <gloss>Ethiopian herb</gloss>: this also has leaves similar to <term>phlomos</term>, but very hairy and dense, arranged in a circle around the base of the root.

*'Hokhmah* is on the active or male side; alternatively, it may be assumed that both *Binah* and *'Hokhmah* were emanated at the same instant and that each exists within the other. The letter of *Kether* is י (*Yod*), and the letter of *Binah* is ה (*Heh*); together they form *YaH*, the feminine Name (compare previous page 175). The third letter, belonging to *'Hokhmah*, is ו (*Vav*), making together יהו (*YHV*) of יהוה (*YHVH*), the Tetragrammaton, which contains the complete symbols of its power. The final ה (*Heh*) of this Ineffable Name is always applied to the six lower Sephiroth and the very last one—together forming the remaining seven Sephiroth. This name finds its resting place in the last Sephirah, *Malkhuth* (Kingdom), the 10th Sephirah, which is the harmony of all the Sephiroth. 

The first three Sephiroth, as we mentioned above, are called the Holy Upper Sephiroth. Together they form a Triad that is a Unity. In the Qabbalah, this is considered the most sacred of all the Sephiroth, as it includes all the others. It is termed the Upper Holy Triad, as well as *Olam ha-Moos'kal* <note>the Intellectual World or Condition</note>.

The *Zohar* says: "The *At-teek-ah Qadosha* <note>the Holy Ancient One</note>—May Its Name be Blessed!—exists with Three Heads, which together form only One Head, and that Head is Itself, which is the most elevated among the highest things. And because the *At-teek-ah Qadosha*—May Its Name be Blessed!—is represented by the Three, all the other Lights (Sephiroth) which enlighten us by their rays are equally comprised in the number Three" (*Zohar*, *Idrah Zootah* <note>Lesser Assembly</note>, iii, 288b). Another statement is: "There are Three Heads engraved one within the other, and one above the other. In this number, first count the mysterious Wisdom—that concealed Wisdom which is never seen without a veil. This Mysterious Wisdom is the supreme principle of all other Wisdom. Above that first Head is the Ancient One—May Its Name be Sanctified!—which is the most mysterious among the mysteries. Finally comes the Head which dominates all others; a Head which is not a Head. What it contains none know nor can know, because it escapes our knowledge and our ignorance. It is for that reason that the Ancient One—whose Name be Blessed!—is called *Ayin* <note>the No-Thing</note>." 

"Each point of matter has three directions: Length, Breadth, and Depth. There does not exist anything below whose root—that is, its perfect prototype—is not above. Therefore, it is necessary that these three have a spiritual root in the first point above. They are therefore called, in their spiritual nature in the primitive Upper Point: *Kether*, *'Hokhmah*, and *Binah*" (*Sepher Shepathal*, folio 49, column 3).

### 7. THE MAGIC CIRCLE IN THE PRAIRIE.—AN ALLEGORY.

A YOUNG hunter found a circular path one day in a prairie, without any trail leading to, or from it. It was smooth and well-beaten, and looked as if footsteps had trod in it recently. This puzzled and amazed him. He hid himself in the grass near by, to see what this wonder should betoken. After waiting a short time, he thought he heard music in the air. He listened more attentively and could clearly distinguish the sound, but nothing could be seen but a mere speck, like something almost out of sight. In a short time it became plainer and plainer, and the music sweeter and sweeter. The object descended rapidly, and when it came near it proved to be a car or basket of ozier containing twelve beautiful girls, who each had a kind of little drum which was struck with the grace of an angel. It came down in the centre of the ring, and the instant it touched the ground they leapt out and began to dance in the circle, at the same time striking a shining ball.

The young hunter had seen many a dance, but none that equalled this. The music was sweeter than ever he had heard. But nothing could equal the beauty of the girls. He admired them all, but was most struck with the youngest. He determined to seize her, and after getting near the circle without giving alarm made the attempt; but the moment they spied a man, they all nimbly leapt into the basket and were drawn back to the skies.

Poor Algon the hunter was completely foiled. He stood gazing upward as they withdrew till there was nothing left, and then began to bewail his fate. "They are gone for ever, and I shall see them no more." He returned to his lodge, but he could not forget this wonder. His mind preyed upon it all night, and the next day he went back to the prairie, but in order to conceal his design he turned himself into an opossum. He had not waited long when he saw the wicker car descend, and heard the same sweet music. They commenced the same sportive dance, and seemed even more beautiful and graceful than before. He crept slowly towards the ring, but the instant the sisters saw him they were startled, and sprang into their car. It rose but a short distance when one of the elder sisters spoke. "Perhaps," said she, "it is come to show us how the game is played by mortals." "Oh no!" the youngest replied, "quick, let us ascend." And all joining in a chant, they rose out of sight.

Its deductions are always logical, whether the premises are true or false. Hence the absurdity of many of our dreams; they are merely deductions from false premises.  The suggestions or impressions imparted to us during sleep being the result of accidental surroundings and stimuli, modified by the state of our health, our mental work during the day, and a thousand other things of which we can have no knowledge, and which are beyond our control, are necessarily of a heterogeneous character; and the deductions from such premises must of necessity be incoherent and fantastic to the last degree.

->BY THE LATE M.W. FRATER DR. W. WYNN WESTCOTT, IX°.<-

IT will not be necessary to detain you by any long statement as to the antiquity of the belief in the powers of a Divining Rod in the hands of a Diviner, or as to the universality of the recognition of these powers among all nations of which we have any records. The Old Testament contains many references to the power of a rod or wand in skilled hands, whether of divine prompting or of human magical art. The records of the Chaldeans, and of the Pharaohs of Egypt, show a similar use of a rod to produce super-normal results. The Arabs and the Negroes, the North American Indians, and the Maoris, alike used the Wand of the Adept, of the Voodooist, or the medicine-man. Throughout the history of mediæval and modern Europe we find references to the Divining Rod, in succession to the well-known classical allusions of the Greek and Roman authors to Rhabdomancy.

The uses of the Divining Rod have been to discover water-springs, to locate metals and their ores, and, at any rate in olden times, to discover criminals, murderers and thieves, dead persons and hidden treasure.

It is only with the question of the power of the rod in skilled hands to discover water and metals that it is proposed now to treat.

It has been the fashion of the Victorian age to decry and condemn all powers which the science of the day failed to explain. But our science is not absolute truth, it is progressive in its knowledge, and it corrects to-day what it supplied as true yesterday. When we find a thing believed in by some persons and scoffed at by others, we should pause to enquire if there be not an element of truth, as well as a share of falsity, in both the belief and the ridicule. ## Rushes.

**A**lthough there are many kindes of Rushes, yet I shall onely here insist upon those which are best known, and most Medicinal, as the Bulrushes, and other of the soft and smooth kindes ; which grow so commonly in almost every place of this Land, and are so generally noted, that I suppose it needlesse to trouble you with any Description of them: Briefly then take the Vertues of them as followeth.

<margin>*Government and Vertues.*</margin>
The Seeds of these soft Rushes, saith *Dioscorides* and *Galen*, toasted (saith *Pliny*) being drunk in Wine and Water, stayeth the Lask and Womens Courses, when they come down too abundantly : but it causeth Headach : It provoketh sleep likewise, but must be given with caution, lest the party that takes it wake not untill the Resurrection : *Pliny* saith, The Root boyled in water to the consumption of one third, helpeth the Cough.

Thus you see that Conveniences have their Inconveniencies, and Vertue is seldome unaccompanied with some Vices. What I have writen concerning Rushes is to satisfie my Country-mens Question, *Are our Rushes good for nothing?* Yes, and as good let alone as taken ; There are Remedies enough without them for any Disease, and therefore as the Proverb is I care not a Rush for them, or rather they wil do you as much good as if one had given you a Rush.

## Rye.

**T**his is so well known in all the Countries of this Land, and especially to the Country People who feed much thereon, that if I should describe it, they would presently say, I might well have spared that Labour :

<margin>*Its Vertues follow. Impostums Boyls & Swellings, pains of the Head, Chops of the Hands or Feet.*</margin>
*Government and Vertues.*] Rye is more digesting then Wheat ; The Bread and the Leaven thereof ripeneth and breaketh Impostumes, Boyls, and other Swellings : The Meal of Rye put between a double cloth, and moistened with a little Vinegar, and heated in a Pewter dish, set over a Chafingdish of coals; and bound fast to the head while it is hot, both much ease the continual pains of the Head. *Mathiolus* saith, That the Ashes of Rye straw put into Water, and suffered therein a day and a night, and the Chops of the Hands or Feet washed therewith, doth heal them.

is external of the church, and “commandment” what is inter-
nal of it. <note>The author differentiates between 'statutes'—the outward rituals and rules—and 'commandments'—the inward moral laws of the heart.</note>

**8364.** *All the disease that I have put on the Egyptians, I*
*will not put upon thee.* That this signifies that they are to be
withheld from the evils that pertain to those who are in **faith**
**separate** <note>The theological concept of believing in religious doctrines while living a life devoid of charity or moral action.</note> and in a life of evil, is evident from the signification
of “disease,” as being evil (of which below); from the represen-
tation of the Egyptians, as being those who are in faith sepa-
rate and in a life of evil (see n. 7097, 7317, 7926, 8148); and
from the signification of “not to put upon thee,” when said of
disease, by which evil is signified, as being that they are to be
withheld from evil; for Jehovah, that is, the Lord, does not
take away evil; but withholds man from it, and keeps him in
good (n. 929, 1581, 2256, 2406, 4564, 8206). <note>The author suggests that God does not delete human sin, but rather acts as a protective force that keeps a person from falling into it.</note> From this it is
that by “not to put disease upon them” is signified that they
are to be withheld from evils. [2] That “disease” denotes evil,
is because in the internal sense are signified such things as
affect the spiritual life. The diseases which affect this life are
evils, and are called **cupidities** and **concupiscences**. <note>Archaic terms for intense, selfish desires and lusts that corrupt a person's character.</note> Faith and
charity make the spiritual life. This life sickens when falsity
takes the place of the truth which is of faith, and evil takes
the place of the good which is of charity; for these bring this
life unto death, which is called spiritual death, and is damna-
tion, as diseases bring the natural life unto its death. Hence
it is that by “disease” is signified in the internal sense evil;
and by “the diseases of the Egyptians,” the evils into which
those cast themselves who had been in faith separate and in a
life of evil, whereby they had infested the upright, which evils
have been treated of in what precedes, where the plagues in
Egypt were treated of. <note>The 'plagues of Egypt' are here re-interpreted not as historical punishments, but as the inevitable spiritual consequences of a life without love or integrity.</note> [3] Evils are also meant by “diseases”
in other passages in the Word, as in *Moses*:—

> If thou wilt keep the commandments, and the statutes, and the judg-
> ments, which I command thee this day, Jehovah will remove from thee

To ensure there is no misunderstanding, let us clarify that suggestive therapeutics <note>The practice of using spoken affirmations or commands to influence a patient's physical health by speaking directly to their subconscious mind.</note>, in its simplest form, has no connection with hypnotic suggestion or hypnotism. Of course, there are some practitioners who combine the two, but there is no real benefit in doing so, and there are many reasons to advise against it. Hypnotism plays no actual role in the practice of suggestive therapeutics. 

Early hypnotists discovered that once they induced a hypnotic state, they could effectively suggest health to their patients. Because of this, they naturally assumed that hypnosis was a necessary requirement for treatment and recovery. However, researchers have since proven that suggestions are just as effective when given to a patient who is wide awake and fully conscious, without any attempt to produce a state of hypnosis. 

We strongly encourage our readers to separate the idea of hypnosis from that of suggestive therapeutics in their minds. There is no true connection between them, and there are many reasons why they should not be confused with one another.

¶ If her husband did not give her a **marriage settlement** <term>nudunnûm</term> <note>A gift given by a husband to his wife during the marriage, distinct from the dowry she brought from her father.</note>, they shall make good her **dowry** <term>šeriktum</term> <note>The property a woman brings from her father's house into her marriage.</note> for her, and she shall take a portion from the **goods** of her husband’s house equal to that of **one heir** <note>original: "kīma ablim ištēn", meaning she receives a share of the estate equivalent to what one of the sons would inherit.</note>. If her children **harass** <note>original: "uzahhamuši", meaning to press, annoy, or attempt to evict.</note> her in order to drive her out of the house, the **judges** shall investigate her **past record** <note>original: "warkaza", looking into her conduct and the circumstances of the case.</note>, and if they find the children to be at fault, they shall impose a **penalty** <term>arnum</term> upon the children. That woman shall **not go out** from her husband’s house.

### § 172A.—XXIX, 27–40.

¶ If that woman **sets her face to leave** <note>An idiom meaning she intends to move out or remarry.</note>, she shall leave the **marriage settlement** which her husband gave her to her children; she shall take the **dowry** from her father’s house and may marry the **man of her heart** <note>original: "mut libbiša", a phrase indicating a marriage of her own choosing.</note>.

### § 173.—XXIX, 41–50.

¶ If that woman, where she has entered <note>That is, in her second marriage.</note>, bears children to her **later husband**, and afterwards that woman **dies**, her former and later children shall **divide** her dowry.

### § 174.—XXIX, 51–56.

¶ If she does not bear children to her **later husband**, the children of her **first spouse** <note>original: "hāwirīša", referring to her first husband.</note> shall take her dowry.

¶ If either a **palace slave** <term>warad ēkallim</term> or the slave of a **commoner** <term>muškênum</term> <note>original: "MAŠ.EN.KAK", referring to a social class of state-dependents or citizens with fewer rights than the elite 'awīlum' class.</note> marry the **daughter of a free man** <term>mārat awīlim</term> and she bears children, the owner of the slave shall have **no claim** for **servitude** <note>original: "wardūtim", meaning the children cannot be claimed as slaves by the father's master; they are born free.</note> against the children of the daughter of the free man.

Water, followed by the vigorous rub, seems to be one of nature’s favorite remedies for gaining, retaining or restoring sexual vigor, or virility.

---

### CHAPTER XIII.

## CONSERVING SEX-ENERGY.

---

**T**HE ATTENTION of the thinking public of the several countries of the world is at present actively directed to the subject of the conservation of the great natural resources. The old habit of reckless waste and dissipation of these natural resources is being corrected, and a policy of “use but not waste” is being generally adopted by all civilized communities.

In the same way, the old idea of reckless, unbridled waste and dissipation of the vital sex forces, is being succeeded by a newer, saner, more scientific policy of “use but not abuse or waste.”

And this applies not only to the young man seeking dissipation in unlawful ways and channels, but also to the married man who is loyal to his wife. It is being recognized that marital excesses are just as harmful to a man as are those irregular excesses which are indulged in by many men. Marriage does not give a license to unbridled indulgence—it does not prevent one from suffering from the consequences of irrational and unwise over-indulgence.

It will be found that the average well-developed man of sound physique and strong healthy body is not the one who indulges in sexual excesses. Indeed, among such men one is apt to find, on the average, the greatest degree of self-restraint and sane regulation regarding sexual matters. And this not from any sexual weakness, remember—for such are the strongest normally sexed men—but rather because a healthy, sound, vigorous body is so well-balanced that it does not run to extremes at any point or phase of its being.

...in the digestion of quicksilver <note>argentum vivum</note>, the wateriness is separated and rises again. **Thus**, it is artificially united; for the "middle son" is an artificial product that proceeds to an equal sulfur through its black nature. In digestion and in full purification, it is placed <note>flourish at end of line</note> through the organs of nature and their artificial evocation. By artificial stiffness, it is poured into the cavities of the bodies, and finally, it lives by effect. Through a natural flow, it is joined and retained in the fire. **Because** the breaking of the form itself—a quaternary and a ternary without violence—does not fail; namely, by boiling and digesting in the native fire, by imbibing <note>imbibitio</note> and boiling with a little native water, and by gently exhaling. Such virtues of the metals are not asserted as living sulfurs, because they are weak at the beginning of their nourishment. It becomes heavy, and the virtues of nature are owed; the sulfurous virtues are overcome through much absorption and the imbibing <note>imbibitio</note> of water, and the sulfurous virtues dominate. The sulfur is weakened by its own dissolution and becomes a "sea of generation." **Thus**, the color of the spirit, boiled <note>elixatus</note> and mortified, will remain without bitterness. **Because** of this, the known blackness, and the strengthening and weakening of these things, is like taking mustard, even in that result. **Take** the juice then, and in this case, it fails somewhat in the manner we described in the sixth chapter. For it is necessary that the living sulfurous thing should seize the transmutation <note>transmutacio</note> itself, attract the powers of nature to itself, and drive them. **Indeed**, it is necessary that the spirit, resolved through its leading into the body, be congealed, and strength be gathered within it, being protected through the smallest parts. Regarding the greatest transformation that this reunification of fire with light can produce and has produced in the <term>animal nature</term> <gloss>the base, instinctual part of human nature</gloss> of man, before it is completely destroyed by temporal death, this transformation is represented a second time by a peacock. Its tail is now completely folded and lowered to the very ground. Its eyes are constantly fixed upon its black, unsightly feet and its front part, which is illuminated by certain rays of the great heavenly sun. For the rational and sensory part of man can in no way behold, in its true reality, the dark, weak, vain, and evil foundation upon which it stands, unless it is touched by some rays of the supernatural sun. Two things should still be noted regarding this peacock:

1. This peacock, which in the previous illustration was marked upon the whole frame or body of man as an essential part of himself, is now found in a special, separate half of the frame. It can easily be removed and taken away from the person by itself. This shows that after the reunification, the animal nature—and even more so the entire intentional, visible man—although still remaining in its own sphere, is no longer so closely, so inwardly, so truly, and so commonly united with the man. Instead, it is united with him only in external appearance.

2. This peacock in the previous illustration was presented with an intent within the darkest circumference of the dark world, which was located on the same surface opposite the circumference that formed the light world. But now that dark circumference has completely vanished from sight and is no longer visible in the present illustration. Only the brightest circumference of the light world is visible,

# FEBRUARY <term>Hornung</term> <gloss>February</gloss>.

<meta>An ornamental decorative initial D begins the first paragraph.</meta>

On February 1st, an <term>Oppositio Saturni Veneris</term> <gloss>opposition of Saturn and Venus</gloss> occurs, stirring up gloomy, frosty air with snow or rain, as also occurred on March 18th, 1513; November 16th, 1562; October 28th, 1589, and others. This significance is increased because around February 2nd, the <term>cauda Capricorni praecedens & sequens</term> <gloss>preceding and following stars in the tail of Capricorn</gloss> rise with the Sun in the morning. This rising commonly causes increasing cold, thick fogs, and subsequent fair weather with frost and sharp winds.

The Full Light <note>the full moon</note>, which falls on the Feast of the Purification of Mary and occurs on February 3rd, will for the most part cause foggy air with unstable sunshine. At that same time, the Sun rises <term>cum Apice Trianguli</term> <gloss>with the peak of the Triangle constellation</gloss>, giving unstable air or snow and sharp winds. Around the 8th, the <term>cauda Delphini</term> <gloss>tail of the Dolphin</gloss> sets with the Sun in the evening; this softens and dissolves the ice and snow, creating great floods of water and gloomy, foggy air with winds. On the 9th, a <term>Quadratus Martis Solis</term> <gloss>square of Mars and the Sun</gloss> takes place, bringing a release from the cold and gloomy weather, as happened on December 28th, 1556; December 4th, 1586; January 5th, 1589; and January 18th and 19th, 1574. On those last two days, such a cold was experienced as had not been seen for some time, but afterward, for several days, rain with soft snow followed, and the cold soon subsided. The last quarter moon occurs on February 10th. This will be moist and very windy. On February 11th, the Sun sets <term>cum Rhomboide delphini Australi</term> <gloss>with the Southern Rhomboid of the Dolphin</gloss>, as it also does on the 12th <term>cum Rhomboide delphini Boreali</term> <gloss>with the Northern Rhomboid of the Dolphin</gloss>; here the weather ends and rain or soft snow follows. On the 13th, a <term>Quadratus Martis Mercurij</term> <gloss>square of Mars and Mercury</gloss> occurs, giving strong winds, dark clouds, and unstable weather, as was experienced on January 23rd, 1591. Alongside strong winds, there is now snow, now rain, soon clouds, then clear sun-

translation:
forever and always. But we also cannot deny that he allows the persecution of his Church to test his elect for as long as it pleases him; this is in no way for us to fathom or criticize.

For as God is, so also must all those be who wish to be his servants—though not in all things, but according to his commandments and holy will: pure, clear, chaste, simple, pious, patient, holy, and just. For how can one show the way to salvation who does not walk it himself, but walks another? How can one teach rightly who denies such teaching with his own life? Although Christ commanded that one should follow what those say who sit in the <term>Stuhl Moysis</term> <gloss>Chair of Moses</gloss>, and not what they do. Yet, the indicated saying is to be directed such that the office of the scribes of that time, though not to be despised, did not earn them praise. Rather, because of the offense they gave and especially because of their contempt for Christ, they could not escape temporal and eternal punishment afterward. And at that time, before the total destruction of the Jewish Kingdom, the <term>Saducæer</term> <gloss>Sadducees</gloss> and <term>Esseer</term> <gloss>Essenes</gloss> had separated themselves from the <term>Pharisæern</term> <gloss>Pharisees</gloss> and raised sects in teaching, which afterwards taught factions in the <term>republic</term> <gloss>state</gloss>. Yet, all at once, under and through the just judgment of God, their blood came upon them and their children.

<margin>It is shameful for a teacher when his own fault refutes him. <note>original: "Turpe est Doctori, cum culpa redarguit ipsum."</note></margin>

<margin>Even the smallest things seem prefigured to be fulfilled in the New Testament. <note>original: "Minima etiã præfigurata videntur. Impleri in Nouo Testamento."</note></margin>

The Church, however, shall be cleansed in this manner and led through the <term>Probfewr</term> <gloss>trial by fire</gloss>. Trusting in Christ her Bridegroom and his promise, she shall be possessed and ruled by him until the end; of this there is no doubt at all.

<margin>Actual repentance is another; that is, it is in place of baptism, or a new birth and regeneration. <note>original: "Pœnitentia actualis est alter: hoc est vice baptismus, seu noua, & regeneratio."</note></margin>

# Gründliche Erklärung

Erkäntniß des HErrn werden erfüllet seyn; so ist doch nicht ein jeder unter denen/ die von Anbeginn sind Philister/ Tyrer und Mohren gewesen/ zu Zion gebohren. Darum muß solches in denen Ewigkeiten geschehen. Daß aber ein jeglicher unter denen/ die ehemals Philister/ Tyrer und Mohren gewesen sind/ zu Zion müsse gebohren werden/ erhellet aus der Grund-Sprache gantz deutlich. Denn in derselbigen heißt die Redens-Art/ Philistea dieser ist daselbst gebohren/ so viel/ als ein jeglicher unter allen/ die in Philistea gewohnet haben/ ist daselbst gebohren/ also heißt/ Tyrus dieser ist daselbst gebohren/ so viel/ als ein jeder unter allen/ die zu Tyro ehemals gewohnet haben/ ist daselbst gebohren. Und die Redens-Art/ die Mohren dieser ist daselbst gebohren/ heißt so viel/ als ein jeder unter allen Mohren/ die ehemals auf dem Erdboden gewesen sind/ hat sich zu GOtt gekehret/ und ist ein Heiliger worden. Mohren aber werden in der heiligen Schrifft nicht nur die genennet/ welche eine schwarze Haut haben/ sondern auch die/ welche ein schwarzes Herz haben/ das ist/ alle Kinder der Finsterniß. Dessen finden wir ein Exempel in dem siebenden Psalm/ allwo vers 1. von dem Simei/ der ein gebohrner Israelite/ aus dem Stamm Benjamin war/ um seiner schwarzen Sitten und Untugend willen gesagt wird/ er sey ein Mohr. Eben also sind alle Menschen/ die in der Finsterniß wandeln/ und Böses thun/ nichts anders denn Mohren. Diese Mohren haben zwar eine geraume Zeit einen rechten Greuel an Zion; es wird aber noch dahin kommen/ daß ein jeder unter ihnen seine alte Adamische Mohren-Geburt wird müssen verfluchen/ und von neuem aus Zion gebohren werden. Denn der HErr hat es gesagt.

Vers 5.

Und zu Zion wird gesaget werden/ ein Mann und Mann ist in ihr gebohren: Ein Mann und Mann/ heißt nach der Hebräischen Redens-Art so viel/ als ein jeglicher/ Niemand ausgenommen. So soll dann ein jeder Mensch/ er mag seyn wer er will/ und mag gelebet haben zu welcher Zeit/ und an welchem Ort er will/ noch endlich in Zion gebohren werden. Selig ist der und heilig/ welcher bald/ da er noch im Leibe lebet/ sich aus GOtt wiedergebären und erneuern läßt. Der wird mit Christo/ für GOtt/ in die Ewigkeiten derer Ewigkeiten/ ein Priester seyn. Wer aber zärtlich ist/ und die geistlichen Geburts-Schmerzen nicht ausstehen/ sondern nach dem Fleisch leben will/ der verscherzet das Recht der Erstgeburt/ und kan dennoch/ nach ausgestandener grosser Quaal/ an dem Leibe und an der Seelen/ denen geistlichen Geburts-Schmerzen nicht entgehen/ wie geschrieben stehet: Die

<column-break/>

Geburts-Schmerzen einer Gebärerin sollen ihm kommen: Er ist ein Sohn/ der nicht weise ist/ denn er stehet nicht die rechte Zeit in der Bär-Mutter der Kinder/ Hos. 13/13. Diß ist so viel gesaget/ als/ wer in dieser Welt/ die rechte Zeit/ in der geistlichen Bär-Mutter GOttes/ in welcher er zu einem ganz neuen und heiligen Leben soll wiedergebohren werden/ nicht ausstehen kan/ der soll die Geburts-Schmerzen/ vor welchen ihm in dieser Welt gegrauet hat/ in der Hölle fühlen. Von dieser geistlichen Bär-Mutter redet GOtt/ durch seinen Knecht Jesaiam/ wenn er spricht: Höret mir zu/ ihr vom Hause Jacob/ und alle übrigen/ vom Hause Israel/ die ihr von mir im Leibe getragen werdet/ und mir in der Mutter liegt/ Jes. 46/1. Gleichwie ein leibliches Kind/ das nicht seine rechte Zeit in der Mutter bleibet/ sondern ehe/ denn es zeitig ist/ abgehet/ eine unzeitige Geburt ist/ und nicht leben kan; eben also verhält sichs auch im Geistlichen. Wer GOtt dem HErrn nicht in der Mutter liegen bleibet/ biß daß er alle Glieder des neuen Menschen in gehöriger Vollkommenheit erlanget hat/ also daß er tüchtig ist/ für GOtt im Geiste zu wandeln/ der hat kein Theil an dem herrlichen Reiche JEsu Christi/ sondern muß so lange in der Hölle liegen/ biß er/ nach gnugsam ausgestandenen Geburts-Schmerzen/ wieder daraus erlöset wird. Wie dann GOtt spricht: ich will sie erlösen aus der Hölle/ und vom Tode erretten. Tod/ ich will dir ein Gifft seyn/ Hölle/ ich will dir eine Pestilenz seyn. Hos. 13/14. Daß in diesen Worten von keiner verblümten/ sondern von der recht eigentlichen Hölle gehandelt werde/ ist aus denen vorhergehenden Versen offenbar. Denn im siebenden und achten Vers sprach GOtt: So will ich auch werden gegen sie/ wie ein Löwe/ und wie ein Pardel auf dem Wege will ich auf sie lauren. Ich will ihnen begegnen wie ein Bär/ dem seine Jungen genommen sind/ und will ihr verstocktes Herz zerreissen/ und will sie daselbst wie ein Löwe fressen/ die wilden Thier sollen sie zerreissen. Und im zwölfften Vers heißt es: Die Missethat Ephraim ist zusammen gebunden/ und ihre Sünde ist behalten. Wer siehet hier nicht/ daß alle dieselbigen/ welche GOtt gefressen hat wie ein Löwe/ und denen die Sünde behalten ist/ in der recht eigentlich also genannten Hölle sind. Und dennoch heißt es: ich will sie erlösen aus der Hölle. Darum bleibet es dabey/ ein Mann und Mann/ das ist/ ein jeder Mensch/ muß in Zion gebohren werden. Diese göttliche Wahrheit gehöret unter keinen Scheffel/ und ist GOttes Wille durchaus nicht/ daß man sie verschweigen soll/ wie es dann heißt: Zu Zion wird gesaget werden.
