translation:
<meta>continues from previous page: the lake of fire. This is</meta> the second death. Then after that, death and hell are no more. Since the knowledge of the Lord shall be filled, yet not every one among those who from the beginning were Philistines, Tyrians, and Moors was born to Zion. Therefore, such must happen in the ages <note>original: "in denen Ewigkeiten," referring to the successive eons of time</note>. That every single person among those who were formerly Philistines, Tyrians, and Moors must be born to Zion is clearly evident from the original language. For in that language, the manner of speaking—"Philistia, this one was born there"—means as much as: every single one among all who lived in Philistia was born there. Likewise, "Tyre, this one was born there" means every one among all who formerly lived in Tyre was born there. And the expression "the Moors, this one was born there" <note>Referring to Psalm 87:4. The term "Moors" here refers to Ethiopians or those from the land of Cush</note> means as much as: every one among all Moors who were formerly on the face of the earth has turned to God and become a saint. In Holy Scripture, however, not only those who have black skin are called <term>Mohren</term> <gloss>Moors</gloss>, but also those who have a black heart; that is, all children of darkness. We find an example of this in the seventh Psalm, where in verse 1 it is said of Shimei—who was a natural-born Israelite from the tribe of Benjamin—that he was a <term>Mohr</term> <gloss>Moor</gloss> because of his black character and vice. In the same way, all people who walk in darkness and do evil are nothing other than Moors. These Moors, indeed, for a long time hold Zion in true abomination; but it will yet come to the point that every one among them must curse his old Adamite Moorish birth and be born anew out of Zion. For the Lord has spoken it.

### Verse 5.

And of Zion it shall be said, a man and a man is born in her. "A man and a man" <note>original: "ein Mann und Mann"</note> means, according to the Hebrew idiom, as much as: every single one, none excepted. Thus, every human being, whoever he may be and in whatever time or place he may have lived, shall finally be born in Zion. Blessed and holy is he who soon, while he still lives in the body, allows himself to be reborn and renewed by God. He shall be a priest with Christ, before God, into the ages of ages. But he who is delicate and cannot endure the spiritual birth pains, but wishes to live according to the flesh, forfeits the right of the firstborn. Yet even he, after enduring great torment in body and soul, cannot escape the spiritual birth pains, as it is written: The

<column-break/>

birth pains of a woman in travail shall come upon him: he is an unwise son, for he does not stand at the right time in the <term>Bär-Mutter</term> <gloss>womb or motherly source</gloss> of children <note>Hosea 13:13</note>. This is as much as to say: whoever in this world cannot endure the right time in the spiritual womb of God—in which he is to be reborn to a completely new and holy life—shall feel the birth pains in hell, the very ones he dreaded in this world. God speaks of this spiritual womb through his servant Isaiah when he says: Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb <note>Isaiah 46:1</note>. Just as a physical child who does not remain his proper time in the mother, but passes away before it is ripe, is an untimely birth and cannot live; so it is also in spiritual matters. Whoever does not remain lying in the mother for the Lord God until he has attained all the members of the new man in proper perfection—so that he is fit to walk in the spirit before God—has no part in the glorious kingdom of Jesus Christ, but must lie in hell so long until he is released from it again after sufficiently enduring birth pains. As God then says: I will ransom them from the power of hell and redeem them from death. O death, I will be thy plague; O hell, I will be thy destruction <note>Hosea 13:14</note>. That these words deal not with a figurative but with the actual, literal hell is obvious from the preceding verses. For in the seventh and eighth verses God spoke: Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I observe them. I will meet them as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps, and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lion: the wild beast shall tear them. And in the twelfth verse it says: The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hid. Who does not see here that all those whom God has devoured like a lion, and whose sin is retained, are in the place properly called hell. And yet it says: I will ransom them from hell. Therefore it stands: a man and a man—that is, every single human being—must be born in Zion. This divine truth belongs under no bushel, and it is by no means God's will that one should keep silent about it, as it is said: Of Zion it shall be said.

Der Candidat, wenn er vor den Meister gestellt ist, wird ungestüm gefragt; man prüft seine Beständigkeit, u. s. w. Dies ist ein abermaliges Sinnbild von der unmenschlichen Art, womit die Richter bei den Verhören der Tempelherren zu Werke giengen, und ihnen die Wahl anboten, zwischen Freiheit oder einem schmählichen Tode, um sie dahin zu treiben, daß sie den Orden verrathen und seine Geheimnisse entdecken sollten. Die Tempelherren, welche beständig in der Treue harrten, haben nichts entdeckt.

Der Freimaurer-Eid stellt das alte Gelübde vor, das ein Tempelherr bei seiner Aufnahme ablegte; eben so verbanden sich auch die Tempelritter alle eidlich, die Geheimnisse zu verbergen, die man ihrem Orden zugebracht hätte.

Nach dem Eide, führt man den Candidaten zurück bis an die Schwelle des Tempels, und dieses Zurückführen ist mit vielen Ceremonien begleitet: ein Bild der Gefahren, denen der Bruder durch seine eingegangene Verbindung mit dem Orden der Tempelherren ausgesetzt ist, und welche ihm Verfolgung, Verbannung und den Tod drohen.

Man nimmt dem Candidaten die Binde ab: er stutzt vor einem Lichtstrahle, der plötzlich wieder verlöscht, und in eben dem Momente sagt man ihm ins Ohr: sic transit gloria mundi! (also vergeht die Herrlichkeit der Welt!) Hierbei sieht er die Degen aller Brüder auf sein Herz gerichtet. Dies ist das Bild von dem Verschwinden alles äußeren Glanzes des Tempelordens, und aller Mordschwerter, die nach dem Blute des treuen Ritters dürsten. Es ist noch immer dieselbe Verfolgung, die uns durch das Blutmischen bei der Aufnahme eines neuen Freimaurers vorgebildet wird.

the carpet! <note>the tracing board or floor cloth</note> What happens during this signifies the unexpected news that spread regarding the persecution of all superiors of the Templar Order and the fatal blow dealt to it.

The candidate, when placed before the Master, is questioned impetuously; his steadfastness is tested, and so on. This is another symbol of the inhuman way in which the judges proceeded during the interrogations of the Templars, offering them the choice between freedom or a shameful death to drive them to betray the Order and discover its secrets. The Templars, who remained constant in their loyalty, discovered nothing.

The Freemason's oath represents the old vow that a Templar took at his admission. Similarly, the Knights Templar all bound themselves by oath to hide the secrets that had been brought to their Order.

After the oath, the candidate is led back to the threshold of the temple, and this leading back is accompanied by many ceremonies: an image of the dangers to which the brother is exposed through his newly entered connection with the Order of the Templars, and which threaten him with persecution, banishment, and death.

The blindfold is removed from the candidate: he is startled by a ray of light that suddenly disappears again, and at that very moment, someone whispers in his ear: <term>sic transit gloria mundi</term> <gloss>so passes the glory of the world</gloss>! At this, he sees the swords of all the brothers pointed at his heart. This is the image of the disappearance of all outward splendor of the Templar Order, and of all the murderous swords that thirst for the blood of the faithful knight. It is still the same persecution that is prefigured to us by the mixing of blood at the admission of a new Freemason.

translation:
### VII. Main Section §. 54.

Whoever has read some books of the Holy Fathers, and in particular such in which truths of faith are dealt with, cannot make this draft. I suspect it only among those who know nothing else than their schoolbooks. These I ask to answer a question: Is the teaching of the Holy Fathers without distinction also the teaching of the universal Church? If they answer yes: then I will convict them that the universal Church contradicts itself. I can bring forward propositions which are not accepted by the Church, but are taught by just as many, partly even more Church Fathers, than can be brought forward for the explanation of our prophecy. If they answer no: then I ask further: What does one have for a characteristic mark to distinguish in the writings of the Holy Fathers their teaching from the teaching of the universal Church? It cannot depend on the judgment of theologians: otherwise the sense of the Church would be tested not from the Holy Fathers, but from the pronouncement of living scholars. One must not seek the difference in the matter itself, whether it concerns the faith or not: because it is still doubtful, and it shall first be shown from the Fathers that a proposition, for example, that Isaiah prophesied of Christ in the seventh chapter, is a point of faith. The characteristic mark must be sought and shown in the writings themselves. The true one is if the Holy Father explicitly says: he does not assert it from his own sense, but he believes it: the opposite opinion is contrary to the general faith: let no one doubt it who confesses the general faith: that is what we have learned from Christ and the Apostles.

<summary>The author challenges the idea that all writings of the Fathers represent official Church doctrine, highlighting the need for explicit markers of "universal faith."</summary>
<keywords>Church Fathers, universal Church, doctrine, theologians, Isaiah, faith, Apostles</keywords>

# Biblical Names and Ph. Ph.

<meta>The catchword "e" refers to the first letter of the following page.</meta>

gave [her], saying she was his sister, but he was plagued by the LORD until he gave her back to her husband, Genesis 12. <note>This refers to the Pharaoh who took Sarah, Abraham's wife, into his palace.</note>

**The second** had a dream of seven fat and as many lean years, which Joseph interpreted for him. Because of this, he placed Joseph over the entire land of Egypt and treated all his relatives, the children of Israel, with kindness, Genesis 37, 39, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 50.

**The third** oppressed the children of Israel severely and commanded that all their newborn sons be killed, Exodus 1, 2.

**The fourth** would not let the children of Israel depart from Egypt according to the Lord's command. Instead, he hardened his heart even after he saw God's wonders. He hurried after the children of Israel as they departed from his land and was drowned in the Reed Sea <note>original: "SchilffMeer," commonly known as the Red Sea</note> along with all his people, Exodus 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15; 2 Kings 17; Psalms 134, 135; Romans 9. Eusebius calls this man Cenchrem in his *Chronicles* <note>original: "in Chronicis"</note>.

**The fifth** captured the city of Gezer. He married his daughter to King Solomon and gave her Gezer as a wedding gift, 1 Kings 3, 7, 9, 11.

**The sixth** was otherwise named Shishak. He supported Solomon's adversaries, Jeroboam and Hadad, 1 Kings 11. He marched against Rehoboam, Solomon's son, captured the city of Jerusalem, and plundered the Temple along with the royal palace, 1 Kings 14.

**The seventh** was called Pharaoh Necho. He slew the pious King Josiah and captured Josiah's son, Jehoahaz, 2 Kings 23; 2 Chronicles 35. He was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Babylon, Jeremiah 46.

**The eighth** was named Pharaoh Hophra. Jeremiah prophesied against him when he was led into Egypt by the remaining people of Israel during the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah 43, 44.

<column-break/>

**Phariseus, Pharisei,** <note>original Greek: "φαρισαῖος, φαρισάδης," translated as Pharisee</note>

**Pharisees** are "Separated Ones," distinct people, masters of the law, interpreters of the law, scribes, interpreters of scripture, and masters of scripture. This was the name given to the strictest sectarians among the Jews, Acts 26. They separated themselves from other common people and wanted to be regarded as teachers of the law. They interpreted the scripture according to the letter and according to the bare history, as Origen writes in his commentary *On Matthew* <note>original: "super Matthæum"</note>.

They sat themselves in Moses' seat, Matthew 23. They claimed the keys of the kingdom of heaven for themselves, Luke 11. They mixed the scripture with philosophy and held that the Messiah would begin a physical, earthly kingdom. They also wanted to declare what fortune or misfortune a person would have based on the hour of their birth, as Epiphanius writes in *Against Heresies* <note>original: "contra Hærefes"</note>.

They also said that whatever happened to a person, good or evil, was an unavoidable decree of God. Yet they allowed that man had a free will in some cases, according to Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews* <note>original: "Antiq. Iud."</note>, Book 13, Chapter 19, and Book 2. <note>Josephus was a first-century Jewish historian who described the different Jewish sects.</note>

They established many human laws so that they might nullify the commandments of God, Matthew 15, 23; Mark 7; Luke 11; Acts 15.

They honored the LORD with their lips, and with their mouths they drew near to him, but their heart was far from him, Matthew 15.

They placed heavy, unbearable burdens on the necks of men, but they would not move them with a single finger, Matthew 23.

They did all their works so that they would be seen by the people. They made their phylacteries <note>original: "Denckzettel," small leather boxes containing scripture worn during prayer</note> broad and the tassels on their clothes large. They loved to sit at the head of the table and in the synagogues, and they enjoyed being called "Rabbi" by men, Matthew 23; Luke 11.

selbst, sofern ein bestimmtes Quantum Arbeitszeit in ihnen ver-

Das Gold hat nicht wie Peter Schlemihl seinen Schatten ver-

wirkt daher nur, soweit es innerhalb des Prozesses den Preis
der einen Ware gegenüber der anderen oder jedem Warenbesitzer
gegenüber Gold vorstellt. Ein bestimmtes relativ wertloses
Ding, Stück Leder, Papierzettel u. s. w., wird zunächst gewohn-
heitsmäßig Zeichen des Geldmaterials, behauptet sich jedoch nur
als solches, indem sein Dasein als Symbol durch den allgemeinen
Willen der Warenbesitzer garantiert wird, d. h. indem es gesetz-
lich konventionelles Dasein und daher Zwangskurs erhält. Staats-
papiergeld mit Zwangskurs ist die vollendete Form des Wert-
zeichens, und die einzige Form des Papiergelds, die unmittelbar
aus der metallischen Zirkulation oder der einfachen Waren-
zirkulation selbst herauswächst. Kreditgeld gehört einer höheren
Sphäre des gesellschaftlichen Produktionsprozesses an und wird
durch ganz andere Gesetze geregelt. Symbolisches Papiergeld
ist in der Tat durchaus nicht verschieden von der subsidiären
Metallmünze, nur in weiterer Zirkulationssphäre wirkend. Wenn
die bloß technische Entwicklung des Maßstabs der Preise oder
des Münzpreises und weiter die äußerliche Umformung des Roh-
goldes in Goldmünze schon die Einmischung des Staats hervor-
riefen und damit die innere Zirkulation von der allgemeinen
Warenzirkulation sich sichtbar schied, so wird diese Scheidung
vollendet durch die Entwicklung der Münze zum Wertzeichen.

translation:
->— 110 —<-

themselves, insofar as a certain quantum of labor time is objectified within them. It therefore seems as if the value-sign directly represents the value of commodities, in that it presents itself not as a sign of gold, but as a sign of the exchange value that is merely expressed in the price but exists solely within the commodity. This appearance is, however, false. The value-sign is directly only a price-sign, hence a gold-sign, and only via a detour a sign of the commodity’s value. Gold has not sold its shadow like <term>Peter Schlemihl</term> <note>a literary character who loses his shadow</note>, but rather buys with its shadow. The value-sign therefore functions only insofar as it represents the price of one commodity against another or, to every commodity owner, against gold within the process. A certain relatively valueless thing, a piece of leather, a slip of paper, etc., first becomes a sign of the money-material by habit, yet only maintains itself as such in that its existence as a symbol is guaranteed by the general will of the commodity owners, i.e., in that it receives a legally conventional existence and therefore forced currency <term>Zwangskurs</term> <gloss>legal tender status</gloss>. State paper money with forced currency is the completed form of the value-sign, and the only form of paper money that grows directly out of metallic circulation or simple commodity circulation itself. Credit money belongs to a higher sphere of the social production process and is regulated by entirely different laws. Symbolic paper money is indeed not at all different from subsidiary metal coinage, only acting in a wider sphere of circulation. If the purely technical development of the standard of prices or the mint price, and further the external transformation of raw gold into gold coins, already summoned the interference of the state, and thereby the internal circulation visibly separated itself from general commodity circulation, then this separation is completed by the development of the coin into a value-sign.

<summary>This page analyzes the nature of value-signs, arguing that they are fundamentally price-signs (gold-signs) rather than direct representations of value, and that paper money with legal tender status is the logical evolution of this process.</summary>

Placing them upon the mandala: this is the sign that everything depends on wisdom. Furthermore, meditate on ten lunar mandalas on the palms of the ten fingers, and upon those, meditate on two sets of five syllables. That itself will be shown through mantra and mudra. Regarding the mantra and mudra that show the Great Self: the ten fathers and mothers arise from the ten syllables. By the mantra and mudra of the Vajra Rosary, the non-dual union of the Father and Mother is performed. By the mantra and mudra of Vajra Fullness, it refers to the swirling of Bodhicitta. By the mantra and mudra of Stable Commitment, the Bodhicitta is emanated and brought down through the mudra. The later part does not need to be explained. The "body of the recollection of hatred" means that by emanating the Bodhicitta as <term>Ar</term>, one holds in mind the subduing of all hateful ones gathered by the Buddhas, and it refers to arising in the body of a wrathful one. Now, the empowerment and blessing into the Great Self itself is shown. That too is the emanation of the mandala of me, the Karma Heruka...

<leaf-break/>

for the sake of empowering. "Might and majesty" refers to the radiation and absorption of Body, Speech, and Mind. "Sparks flying through the billion-fold universe" means possessing the Body, Speech, and Mind from the ritual dagger. The wrathful ones radiate through the billion-fold universe. It is the power and blessing that ensures all visualizations are accomplished. It refers to the ritual dagger itself becoming a wrathful one possessing Body, Speech, and Mind. "In the sky in front" means lifting the ritual dagger into the sky in front. "Abiding on the seat of <term>E</term>" refers to the triangular seat of <term>E</term>, which is the sign of relying on the basic space of phenomena <term>dharmadhatu</term>. "Striking with the King of White Mustard Seeds": between the sun and moon, meditate on white mustard seeds as tiny wrathful ones; this is for the purpose of showing them dissolving into the ritual dagger. "Fumigating with <term>guggul</term> incense": visualize <term>guggul</term> in the palms of the hands and burn it in fire. By the smoke, the ritual dagger comes to stay within a mass of wrathful fire; this is for the purpose of self-generation. Offering whatever inner and outer offerings are available is done to the ritual dagger. Then, offer praise with verses. Then, the yogi entrusts the activity that is held in the mind, saying "perform such an activity."

<leaf-break/>

This is the wrathful mantra. "One hundred thousand such as this" and so forth is the measure for the approach through counting. "If one desires the approach of emptiness" means "if it arises." "The ritual dagger itself" means the meditation on the ritual dagger as the wrathful one itself. By the word "also," it includes all the radiation, absorption, and the wrathful deities. Now, the fifth stage, the perfection of activity, is shown. Generally, this includes the perfection of one's own benefit and the benefit of others. First, the perfection of one's own benefit will be described. "Having found the ground to be examined at the very beginning" means having found it to be free of the "tastes" <note>faults/spirits</note> of the earth. "Expelling" means making a truthful statement: "For this many days, months, and years of practice, stay away from here," and thus expelling them. "Setting the boundaries" means entrusting the world-protectors to guard against obstacles and misleading spirits. Included in "and so forth" are the summoning of the Earth Goddess, taking the earth, and so on. Now, the boundaries of the three elements and the vajra boundary will be described. Through the concentration of a single instant...

རྫོགས་གཉིས་ལ་རྟགས་ཐོན་ཕར་རྗེས་བུའི་གསབས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཡང་དེའི་དུས་འདི་སྐད་གསུངས། ཉམས་རྟགས་མཚན་མས་མ་བཅིངས་པས། །འཁོར་འདས་གཉིས་ལ་མི་གནས་པར། །ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ། །ལམ་འབྲལ་མེད་སྒོམ་
པའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་བདེ། །ཅེས་གསུངས། གྲུབ་རྟགས་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཆེ་བ་ནི་ཡང་དུས་ཕྱིས་བླ་མ་ལ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལོ་བདུན་གྱི་དམ་བཅའ་ཕུལ་ནས་ནམ་མཁའ་སྤྲིན་གདིངས་སུ་བཞུགས་པས་ཞག་བདུན་སོང་བ་ན་ཡི་དམ་ཞི་ཁྲོའི་ལྷ་ཚོགས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནམ་
མཁའི་སྐར་ཚོགས་བཀྲམ་པ་ལྟར་ཞལ་གཟིགས། མི་དང་མི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་ཆོས་སྐྱོང་ཐམས་ཅད་དམ་ལ་ཐོགས་ཏེ་དྲན་བཞིན་དུ་བཀོལ། གཏུམ་མོ་ལ་རྟགས་ཐོན་ཅིང་སྲོག་བརྩོལ་ལས་སུ་རུང་བས་རྡོ་རྗེ་སྤུགས་སུ་ནུབ་ཅིང་དབུ་ལ་གཙུག་ཏོར་ཤར།
ཚེའི་རིགས་འཛིན་མཉེས་སྒྱུ་ལུས་འོད་གསལ་འབྱོངས་པས་ནམ་མཁའི་མཐོངས་སུ་དཀྱིལ་དཀྲུངས་མཛད་ནས་ཞག་བདུན་སོང་བའི་ཉིན་མོ་བླ་མ་རྗེ་བཙུན་ང་ལ་རྒྱབ་ན་མི་མ་ཡིན་ལ་ཆོས་གསུང་གི་བཞུགས་པའི་མདུན་གྱི་བར་སྣང་ལ་རས་གོས་ལ་

སྐྱོང་བྲན་བཞིན་ཉན། །རླུང་ལ་དབང་ཐོབ་དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན། །བླ་མ་རྗེའི་བཀའ་དྲིན་གྱིས། །མ་རྒྱུད་རྩའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཤེས། །རྩ་གསུམ་འཁོར་ལོའི་གདམས་ངག་ཡོད། །རྡོ་རྗེ་ལྔ་པ་སྤྲུགས་སུ་ནུབ། །སྤྱི་གཙུག་གཙུག་ཏོར་ནོར་བུས་བརྒྱན། །
རིག་པ་སྟོང་གསལ་དབུ་མར་ཐིམ། །གཞི་མེད་སྣང་བ་ཅིར་ཡང་ཤར། །ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དངོས། །ངོ་བོ་ངོས་བཟུང་མེད་པར་གྲོལ། །སྒྱུ་ལུས་འབྱོངས་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན། །བླ་མ་རྗེ་བཀའ་དྲིན་གྱིས། །རྩ་རླུང་དབྱེར་མེད་གདམས་ངག་ཡོད། །
རླུང་སེམས་རྩའི་འདུག་ཚུལ་ཤེས། །བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་སྐྱེད་ནས། །མ་བཅོས་ལྷུག་པར་སྒོམ་པ་དེ། །མ་ཡེངས་མི་བགག་དམ་ཚིག་ཡིན། །བྱ་བ་བཏང་བ་མན་ངག་སྟེ། །རིག་པ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ངང་དུ་གྲོལ། །ས་སྤྱོད་ཆེ་བ་དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན། །
གནས་ལུགས་གཉུག་མའི་མན་ངག་ཡོད། །འཁོར་བ་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པར་གྲོལ། །རིག་པ་ཐུག་ཕྲད་རང་ངོ་ཤེས། །དུག་ལྔ་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལྔ་རུ་རྟོགས། །བདེ་གསལ་མི་རྟོག་སྐུ་གསུམ་དེ། །དངས་མའི་ཐིག་ལེ་མཆོག་གྱུར་པས། །དྲུག་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་
ཆེན་དངོས། །ཚེ་ཅིག་སངས་རྒྱས་དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན། །འཕོ་བ་གྲོང་འཇུག་གདམས་ངག་ཡོད། །རང་བཞན་ལུས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཉིད་ཤེས། །རླུང་སེམས་ལུ་གུའི་ལུས་ལ་བཅུག །ལུ་གུ་གར་བྱེད་ཁྱུགས་སེ་ཁྱུགས། །འབད་སྒྲ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ངང་དུ་སྒྲོག །སྐྱེ་མེད་

protectors listen like servants. Such is the mastery over the winds. By the kindness of the Lord Guru, I know the natural state of the channels of the Mother Tantra. I have the instructions of the three channels and wheels. The five-pointed vajra is absorbed into the center. The crown of the head is adorned with the jewel of the ushnisha. Awareness, empty and clear, dissolves into the central channel. Unfounded appearances arise as anything at all. The actual co-emergent wisdom is liberated without an identifiable essence. Such is the mastery of the illusory body. By the kindness of the Lord Guru, I have the instructions on the inseparability of channels and winds. I know the way the wind-mind dwells in the channels. Having generated the supreme mind of enlightenment, meditating in an uncontrived and relaxed manner is the commitment of non-distraction and non-obstruction. To cast away worldly activities is the instruction; awareness is liberated into the state of reality. Such is the greatness of traversing the grounds. I have the instructions on the natural primordial state. Cyclic existence is liberated into Nirvana. Awareness meets its own face directly. The five poisons are realized as the five wisdoms. The three bodies—bliss, clarity, and non-conceptuality—are the supreme vital essence <term>bindu</term>. They are the actual sixth Buddha, Vajradhara. Such is the Buddhahood in one lifetime. I have the instructions for the transference of consciousness into another body. I know the suchness of the bodies of self and others. I placed the wind-mind into the body of a lamb. The lamb danced and frisked about. It sounded the cry of reality. The unborn—

<leaf-break/>

He did not falter, but gave his body and life to the practice. Abandoning a shrinking mind, he distanced himself from laziness and indifference. Without clinging to the ten signs, eight qualities, or other meditative experiences and marks, he meditated uninterruptedly like the flow of a river. Thus, signs of success arose in both the generation and completion stages, which repaid the father's kindness. At that time, he spoke these words: "By not being bound by experiences, signs, or marks, and not dwelling in either cyclic existence or nirvana, the yoga of meditating on the co-emergent Truth Body without separation from the path is blissful." Thus he spoke. Regarding his greatness in signs of accomplishment and qualities: Later, he offered a seven-year vow of practice to the Guru and stayed in the Cloud-Canopy of the sky. After seven days had passed, he had a vision of all the hosts of peaceful and wrathful meditational deities, spread out like the stars in the sky. He bound all the Dharma protectors to his command as if they were people, and they served him at his thought. Signs arose in his practice of Inner Heat <term>Tummo</term>, and his life-force and effort became workable; his energy was absorbed into the vajra-center and an <term>ushnisha</term> <gloss>crown protuberance</gloss> appeared on his head. Because he had mastered the illusory body and clear light of the long-lived Vidyadhara, he sat in the cross-legged posture in the expanse of the sky. On the day seven days had passed, while the Lord Guru was staying behind him teaching Dharma to non-human beings, he appeared in the space in front wearing cotton clothes—

<leaf-break/>

Regarding this: From the moment he met the Guru, he performed only prostrations and circumambulations, and applied himself solely to virtuous practices of body and speech. The Guru was very pleased. First, to purify karmic obscurations and accumulate merit, he was granted the instructions for empowerment three times. To clear away negative conditions and obstacles, he was granted the sadhana of Vajrapani in the tradition of Guru Walatsandra, including the instructions for the Garuda garment. To introduce the nature of mind, he was granted the three cycles of <term>Doha</term> <gloss>Spiritual Songs</gloss> in the tradition of the Nepalese Guru and Tiphu, including the instruction on resting in meditative concentration. To bring the channels and winds to the essential point, he was granted the Six Dharmas of Lord Naropa and the Nine Cycles of Mixing and Equal Taste. For the yoga of generation and completion, he was granted the Chakrasamvara and Varahi in the tradition of Guru Yerangwa, the Vidyadhara tradition. To accomplish the siddhi of long life, he was granted the Amitayus of the Siddha Queen and the Jinasagara Dakini Heart Practice. To protect the teachings and perform activities, he was granted the eight earlier protector deities of Guru Phur and the protector traditions of Khorlo Drilwa. He received all the heart-intentions without exception. From that time on, he practiced the yoga of the four sessions without interruption, regardless of body or life. Through continuous service and offerings of body and wealth, he pleased the Guru.

རིགས་ཀྱི་ཕྱག་མཚན་རྒྱན་ཞིང་དུར་ཁྲོད་ཆས༔ ༔རུས་པ་དང་ནི་རིན་ཆེན་རྒྱན་གྱིས་མཛེས༔ ༔ཡུཾ་ཡང་རུས་པའི་རིན་ཆེན་
རྒྱན་གྱིས་བརྒྱན༔ ༔རིགས་བཞི་ཁྲོ་རྒྱལ་དཀྱོིར་གསལ་བར་བསྐྱེད༔ ༔དེའི་ཕྱི་རིམ་པདྨ་འདབ་དྲུག་ནས༔ ༔རིམ་པར་ཞི་བའི་ལྷ་ཚོཌ་

འཁྲིལ༔ ༔ཕྱག་མཚན་ཨུཏྤལ་དྲིལ་བུ་མར་མེ་འཛིན༔ ༔སྒྲིབ་པ་རྣཾ་སེལ་ནིརྟི་མ་དང་འཁྲིལ༔ ༔ཕྱག་འཚན་པོ་ཏི་དྲིལ་བུ་

རྣམས་དབང་སྡུད་ཁྲོ་བོ་མཐིང་ནག་ནི༔ ༔ཞལ་གཅིག་ཕྱབགཉིས་དགྲ་སྟ་ལྕཌ་སྒྲོག་འཛིན༔ ༔ལྷ་རྣཾས་དབང་སྡུད་ཁྲཽ་དཀར་པོ་ནི༔ ༔ཞལ
གཅིག་ཕྱགཉིས་རྡོེ་དྲིལ་བུ་འཛིན༔ ༔ས་བདག་དབང་སྡུད་ཁྲོ་བོ་ནག་པོ་ནི༔ ༔ཞལ་གཅིག་ཕྱགཉིས་ཕུར་པ་འཁོར་ལོ་འཛིན༔ ༔དབུས

རིགས་ཀྱི་གདན་སྟེང་དུ༔ ༔བདུད་རྩི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལྷ་ཚོཌ་ལ༔ ༔ཞི་ཁྲོ་གཙོ་འཁོར་དྲུག་བཅུ་རྣཾས༔ ༔དུར་ཁྲོད་ཆས་སོགས་རྒྱན་དང་ལྡན

Six arms, body color blazing green. The center is green, right is yellow, left is red, and four legs are spread wide. The first two hands hold a curved knife and skull-cup of blood. The middle two hold a trident and a plow. The final two hold a crossed vajra and lasso. The green <term>Yaksha Kroti</term> clings to his body. Holding a curved knife and skull-cup of blood, she embraces the Father. All the fathers of the four families of wrathful kings possess wings of method and wisdom marked by vajras and so forth at the tips. They are adorned with the symbolic implements of their families and cemetery attire. They are beautiful with bone and jewel ornaments. The mothers are also adorned with bone and jewel ornaments. The wrathful kings of the four families are clearly generated in the mandala. Outside that, from the six lotus petals, the assembly of peaceful deities is generated in succession. From the east of the six petals, the deities are arranged: blue Samantabhadra holds a vajra and bell. Embracing Dharmadhatvi.
<leaf-break/>
The Muni of the Hungry Ghosts is red, holding a casket. The Muni of the Hell-beings is black, holding fire and water. Outside that, on the lotus petals, the Bodhisattvas and Consorts are generated in succession from the east: white Kshitigarbha embraces white Lasya. Symbolic implements are a lotus, bell, and mirror. White Maitreya embraces pale white Pushpa. Symbolic implements are a Naga-tree, bell, and flower. Red Samantabhadra embraces blue Aloka. Symbolic implements are a stalk of grain, bell, and garland. Blue Akashagarbha embraces Dhupema. Symbolic implements are a sword, bell, and incense. Avalokiteshvara embraces Girtima <note>Giti</note>. Symbolic implements are a lotus, bell, and lute. Orange-red Manjushri embraces Aloma. Symbolic implements are an utpala flower, bell, and lamp. Sarvanivarana-vishkambhin embraces Nirtima. Symbolic implements are a book, bell.
<leaf-break/>
Holding a wind-fan. The dark maroon wrathful one who subjugates the harmful spirits <note>Yakshas</note>, with one face and two hands holding a vase and lasso. The dark blue wrathful one who subjugates the obstacle makers <note>Vinayakas</note>, with one face and two hands holding an axe and iron chains. The white wrathful one who subjugates the gods <note>Devas</note>, with one face and two hands holding a vajra and bell. The black wrathful one who subjugates the earth lords <note>Shadags</note>, with one face and two hands holding a <term>kilaya</term> and wheel. In the four directions of the central great mandala: in the east is white Vijaya holding an iron hook. In the south is yellow Yamantaka holding a lasso. In the west is red Hayagriva holding iron chains. In the north is green Amritakundali holding a sword. Ho! Thus in the central mandala, upon seats of their respective families, in the assembly of deities of the Qualities of Nectar, there are sixty principal and surrounding peaceful and wrathful deities. They are endowed with cemetery attire and ornaments.

མའི་ངས་མ་རྟ་སྐྱར་ཀྱི་མེ་ཏོག་ལྟ་བུ་དྲན་འབྲུ་ཙཾ་སྐྱི་མ་འཚོར་བ་དང༔ ༢་འཕྲད་པ་ལས་ཞོ་དང་འཚལ་འདྲེས་པ་ལྟར་འདྲེས་ཏེ༔ མེར་མེར་ གོར་གོར་ ལྟར་ལྟར་ཡོ་གྱུར་བའི་དབུས་
སུ༔ མ་རིག་པའི་སེཾས་འཐུཾས་པས་ཕྲུ་ཆུ་འབྱུང་བའོ༔ དེ་ཡང་ཕ་མ་༢་ཀྱི་དངས་མ་དྲུག་མཉཾ་དུ་འདྲེས་ན༔ མི་དེ་སྟོབས་དང་གཟུར་བྱད་ཚལ་དང་ལྡན་པ་བསོད་ནཾས་ཆེ་ཞིང་རིག་པ་དང་
འདྲེན་པར་སྐྱེ༔ བཞི་མཉཾ་དུ་འདྲེས་ན་མི་འབྲིང་སྟོང་དུ་འབྱུང༔ གསུཾ་མཉཾ་དུ་འདྲེས་ན་འབྲིང་དུ་འབྱུང༔ ༢་འདྲེས་ན་འབྲིང་སྐུད་ རེ་རེ་འདྲེས་ན་ཐ་མའོ༔ ཕ་མའི་དངས་མ་མ་ཉཾ་དུ་འདྲེས
ན་ཕོ་མོ་གང་ཡང་སྔོན་གྱི་བསཌ་པས་སྒྱུར༔ ཕའི་དངས་མ་༡ མའི་དངས་མ་༢་ལྟེས་ན་བསེ་ཡོད༔ ཕའི་དངས་༢་ མའི་དངས་མ་༡་འདྲེས་ན་ཕོར་ཡོང༔ མཉཾ་པོ་ལ་ཕའི་

This is the white of the elements. Its essence: within this, the actual essence is white, blue, and radiant like sweat, with poisonous white mustard seeds. This is the cause for the arising of the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. The mother's essence is like the flower of a grey horse <note>unclear botanical reference</note>, the size of a mustard seed, not radiant. Through the meeting of the two, like the mixing of curd and vermilion, they become a soft mass, a round mass, and an oblong mass. In the middle, because the mind of ignorance is enveloped, the fetus arises. Furthermore, if the six essences of the father and mother are mixed equally, that person will be born with strength, a beautiful form, great merit, and will be led by intelligence. If four are mixed equally, an average person is born. If three are mixed, a middle-average person. If two, a lower-average. If one, a commoner. If the father and mother's essences are not mixed equally, whether male or female is determined by previous accumulations. If one part father and two parts mother, it is a daughter. If two parts father and one part mother, it is a son. If equal but the father's essence is stronger, the person has little flesh but strong bones. If the mother's is stronger, they have much flesh and are very virtuous. If the essence and the dregs are mixed, a confused, foolish, or mute person will come. If the parents have a chronic illness, the child will have a disease. If the essences are of equal strength at the time of conception, a hermaphrodite will come. If the essences are incomplete...

<leaf-break/>

...like one who performs a melt: for example, when performing a melt, if there is only fire and water, it will not melt; if the fire is too great, it will be consumed. Just as one adjusts the measure of the fire's heat, so too, at the time of entering into union with the <term>mudra</term>, if the conduct is too coarse, the <term>bindu</term> <gloss>vital essence</gloss> will wander and seek to escape. If it is not generated, bliss will be small, so generate it by adjusting the measure. Fix the awareness on each moment of bliss and remain in that bliss for a long time. If you cannot hold it, remain in the state of full awareness. Again, if you lose the bliss, generate it slowly, hold the bliss, and let it expand. By doing so, you will experience bliss and clarity. If you do not know these essential points, the <term>bindu</term> will escape and faults will arise. Third, being skillful in drawing up the <term>bindu</term> is like drawing water from a well: for example, if there is water at the bottom of a well, if it is not pulled up with a rope, it will not reach where the water is desired...

<leaf-break/>

...leaving activity in the state of the spontaneously present primordial purity, it is impossible not to capture it. If it is still not captured, block the path of the nectar's movement in the channels. If it is not captured thus, no qualities will arise, so one should persevere in the wind-yogas. Then, being skillful in distributing the <term>bindu</term> is like a generous donor distributing gifts: for example, a great universal monarch who gives gifts everywhere without hesitation—if he shows partiality, those people become angry. Similarly, if the yogi draws up the <term>bindu</term> but does not distribute it, faults will arise wherever it is not distributed. Therefore, guide the captured <term>bindu</term> to the joints of the body. First, send the <term>bindu</term> to the crown of the head, and as it stays there in a white mass, visualize it pervading all the channel-petals of the crown. Guide it with the seven physical movements. With the "laughing style of the <term>senmo</term> spirit," expel the wind three times. With the "gaze of the fox," inhale the wind three times. With the "churning method of the <term>tsame</term>," press down the upper wind and pull up the lower wind three times. With the "leaping of the wild animal," three times...

# The Practice of Suppressing the Loss-Demon
<note>The original title is God sri mnan pa'i lag len. A <term>God-sri</term> <gloss>Loss-demon</gloss> is a specific type of malevolent spirit believed to cause the death of livestock and the depletion of wealth.</note>

Act as the fierce and wrathful one! To the work of destroying the <term>God-sri</term>: <term>Am ghu sha jah</term> <gloss>a summoning mantra</gloss>!
Assemblies of wood deities of the East, to the work!
Assemblies of fire deities of the South, to the work!
Assemblies of iron deities of the West, to the work!
Assemblies of water deities of the North, to the work!
Kill the enemy! Kill the <term>Dre</term> <gloss>ghost</gloss>! Kill the <term>God-sri</term>!
Kill, kill the <term>Tri</term> <gloss>malevolent spirits</gloss>! Kill the <term>Zhung-zhung</term>!
Cut and kill the Wood! Cut and kill the Fire! Cut and kill the Iron! Cut and kill the Water!
Kill, kill! Cut, cut! Bind, bind! Press, press! Into dust, into dust! <term>Jah jah! Ya ya!</term>

Recite this mantra as many times as possible. Perform the <term>mar-gtor</term> <gloss>red torma or food offering</gloss>. Bring the torma and the ritual objects <note>original: "yas thabs"</note> to the threshold or suppress them at a crossroads. Seal them with the signs of Earth, Water, Fire, and the <term>Vajra-cross</term> <gloss>crossed thunderbolts</gloss>. The wrathful ones will burn them away.

<term>Om so ku ru ku ru mnan. Tri shi ku mnan. Zhi zhi ku ru mnan. Ku ru mnan svaha.</term> <gloss>Mantra for suppression</gloss>

Take some soil from beneath the right foot from inside the threshold and scatter it outward. This is the secret mantra for suppressing the <term>God-sri</term>.

There is also another tradition for this. When there is a great loss of wealth or livestock, write on the inside of the skull of the last animal to have died. Write: <term>Om ti phu mu la tse ra mnan</term>. Cut off the door of loss! Divert the door of loss! Turn back the door of loss!

On the right jaw, draw a <term>Vajra-cross</term>. On the left jaw, draw a <term>Yung-drung</term> <gloss>swastika, a symbol of eternity</gloss>. In the center of the skull, draw a wrathful cross. Inside the mouth, write: <term>Om ma ti</term>, cut the <term>Gong-sri</term> <gloss>demon of the upper realms</gloss>! Tie it in a black hair-cloth bag and suppress it at a crossroads.

Great is the essence of food, wealth, and enjoyments!
Do not take pleasure in wandering about this place!

Having said this, perform the dance of the four activities. Suppress it in the center of the livestock pen. May there be auspiciousness! May virtue and excellence increase!

The Commentary on the Images states: "The good fortune of the six-five line brings celebration."

Celebration means joy. However, the fifth line occupies the ruler's position, and what it accumulates is great; therefore, it is called celebration. This refers to the ancient saying: "When the sovereign possesses virtue, the realm rejoices."

Nine at the top: Carrying the highway of heaven, success.

This expresses the principle that accumulation reaches its extremity and dissolves into free passage. <term>He</term> <gloss>carrying</gloss> is pronounced as <term>he</term> <note>glossed here phonetically by the fanqie spelling hu-ke</note>, meaning to carry on the shoulder or bear on the back. <term>Dan</term> <gloss>to bear</gloss> is the same as the character <term>dan</term> <gloss>carrying pole / burden</gloss>, as in Yang Xiong's phrase <term>dan shi</term> <gloss>a peck and a stone of grain</gloss>. In the Book of Songs, the phrases "carrying a rain cloak" and "wearing a bamboo hat" both pronounce <term>he</term> in this tone. The Rhapsody on the Hall of Lingguang states: "Carrying the highway of heaven to attain primal success." Zhuangzi's phrase "bearing the blue sky upon one's back" shares this exact meaning. Zheng Kangcheng also explained that it means carrying upon the shoulder. The single yang line at the very top resembles a carrying pole, while the two yin lines hanging down on either side resemble loads suspended on both ends. This forms the visual image of carrying a shoulder pole. It signifies a single shoulder pole lifting up the grand highway of heaven. This is precisely what Chen Baisha meant when he wrote of making the bright moon and cool breeze into two loads suspended from a pole.

Musicians think of breaking the fingers of Bo Ya <note>a legendary master of the zither whose skill aroused envy</note>; charioteers wish to shove aside the hands of Wang Liang <note>a famous charioteer of antiquity</note>. Why is this? It is because they wish to monopolize the reputation for excellence and skill, and loathe seeing others surpass themselves.

For this reason, the beauty from Wei was exquisitely gorgeous, yet Zheng Xiu <note>the jealous consort of King Huai of Chu who deceived the newcomer into covering her nose and then had it cut off</note> had her nose severed; Chao Wu was loyal and steadfast, yet Wu Ji <note>a corrupt minister of Chu who slandered Chao Wu</note> drove him into exile. The afflicted hunchback is intensely jealous, and the deformed cripple is full of flattery <note>allusions to figures in the Classic of Poetry representing petty or resentful courtiers</note>. Therefore, on damp ground in a hall, dust does not scatter; beneath a low roof, the wind cannot be blocked. Things standing directly in the rush of the gale cannot grow to maturity; the banks where water rushes in a torrent cannot maintain steep cliffs.

Under such conditions, the imprisonment at Youli <note>where King Wen of Zhou was detained by the tyrant King Zhou</note> and the distress between Chen and Cai <note>where Confucius and his disciples were besieged and starved</note> can be understood, as can jumping into rivers or drowning in floods <note>as Qu Yuan did when driven to despair by slander</note>. To curry favor with the vulgar world using extraordinary talent, seeking to preserve unbroken fame and merit while serving a general or prince: if one escapes the disaster that befell Deng Xi <note>the ingenious legalist thinker executed by Zi Chan in Zheng</note> and avoids the execution suffered by Wu Zixu <note>the loyal advisor forced to commit suicide in Wu</note>, that is already sheer good fortune.

*Agn.* Without doubt you were charmed by this florid talker.

*Ang.* Yes, my pretty child, I was persuaded by this <term>quack</term><note>Here used to describe a religious hypocrite or false teacher.</note>. His words changed me in a moment; they snatched me from myself and made me eagerly pursue what I had constantly avoided. I became the most scrupulous person in the world, and because he had told me that I could not work my salvation outside the cloister, I imagined, until I was inside it, that I had all the devils about me. Since that time, he himself has endeavored to make me recover my right senses; he has given me such instructions as were capable of freeing me from the errors he had plunged me in, and it is to his morals that I owe all the repose and quiet of mind that I now possess.

*Agn.* Please tell me quickly who this man is.

*Ang.* It is Father Rancourt.

But she said to him, “I would be obliged to you if you would grant me a respite of a year and a day.” He said, “I will grant you that, hard though it is, if you will give me your unfailing promise that you will marry me at the end of the year.” And she gave the promise. Connachar obtained for her a female teacher and merry, modest maidens who would lie down and rise with her, and who would play and speak with her. Deirdre was clever in maidenly duties and wifely understanding, and Connachar thought he had never seen with his own eyes a creature that pleased him more.

Deirdre and her women companions were one day out on the hillock behind the house enjoying the scene and drinking in the warmth of the sun. What did they see but three men journeying toward them. Deirdre was looking at the men approaching and wondering about them. When the men neared them, Deirdre remembered the words of the huntsman and said to herself that these were the three sons of Uisnech, and that the one who carried himself above the rest was Naois, who was more noble than any other man in Erin <note>Ireland</note>. The three brothers went past without taking any notice of them, without even glancing at the young women on the hillock. What happened then but that love for Naois struck the heart of Deirdre, so that she could not help but follow him. CHAPTER III.
*Examination of the State of a Woman's Mind*

WHEN a man is trying to gain over a woman he should examine the state of her mind, and act as follows.

If she listens to him, but does not manifest to him in any way her own intentions, he should then try to gain her over by means of a go-between.

If she meets him once, and again comes to meet him better dressed than before, or comes to him in some lonely place, he should be certain that she is capable of being enjoyed by the use of a little force. A woman who lets a man make up to her, but does not give herself up, even after a long time, should be considered as a trifler in love, but owing to the fickleness of the human mind, even such a woman can be conquered by always keeping up a close acquaintance with her.

When a woman avoids the attentions of a man, and on account of respect for him, and pride in herself, will not meet him or approach him, she can be gained over with difficulty, either by endeavoring to keep on familiar terms with her, or else by an exceedingly clever go-between.

When a man makes up to a woman, and she reproaches him with harsh words, she should be abandoned at once.

When a woman reproaches a man, but at the same time acts affectionately towards him, she should be made love to in every way.

A woman, who meets a man in lonely places, and puts up with the touch of his foot, but pretends, on account of the indecision of her mind, not be aware of it, should be conquered by patience, and by continued efforts as follows:

In the beginning, says the best-known Egyptian version, the sun god Temu, whose name denotes the creator god, having awoke in the Nnu from a state of negative existence, appeared, as it were, upon the other side of the water, a figure of sunrise, and suddenly cried across the water, "Come thou to me!" (as spirits). Then the lotus unfolded its petals, and up flew the hawk, which represented the sun in mythology and a soul in the eschatology. Thus Tum the father of souls, being established in his spiritual supremacy, calls upon the race of men to come to him across the water in the track of sunrise or of the hawk that issued forth as Horus from the lotus. # Kohut’s Place in American Judaism

This is the year in which we of the progressive school have been celebrating the centenary of Isaac M. Wise, the virtual father of American Reform. None the less, our survey of Judaism as a whole should be sufficiently comprehensive to realize the value of Kohut's contribution to the cause in making for a more positive Judaism. Let us not forget that Dr. Wise was a staunch pleader for the sanctity of Bible law, and that his views would be classed as conservative today. Dr. Kohut, then, prepared the way for that genius, Solomon Schechter, who "came and saw and conquered." But that is another story.

If he were alive today, he would see a different line of cleavage. There are two camps still, but no longer those of Orthodoxy and Reform, but of Zionism on the one hand and anti-Nationalism on the other. We are not as keen as were our fathers as to the discriminating points of distinction in synagogue observance—as to the covered head in worship, the recital of prayer in Hebrew—the retention of some Orientalisms. We realize that "life fulfills itself in many ways." The vital question is, Which school makes for the best kind of Jew? Something can be said for both wings. The motive behind the action is everything. There is all the ethical difference in the world between ceasing to observe dietary laws because they are regarded as part of an ancient taboo, no longer accepted, or dropping them

3. Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and in that connection, convened a meeting of the Bhikkhu-samgha <note>The monastic community.</note>, and asked the Bhikkhus, "Is there, O Bhikkhus, in such and such an apartment, a Bhikkhu who is sick?"

"There is, Lord."

"Then what, O Bhikkhus, is the matter with that Bhikkhu?"

"He has a disturbance, Lord, in his bowels."

"And is there any one, O Bhikkhus, to wait upon him?"

"No, Lord."

"Why, then, do not the Bhikkhus wait upon him?"

"That Bhikkhu, Lord, is of no service to the Bhikkhus; therefore do they not wait upon him."

"You, O Bhikkhus, have no mothers and no fathers who might wait upon you! If you, O Bhikkhus, wait not one upon the other, who is there indeed who will wait upon you? Whoever, O Bhikkhus, would wait upon me, he should wait upon the sick.

He who otherwise prays this Psalm with reverence will be generally received with great favor.

**Psalm 16.**—This Psalm is important and can be profitably employed in different undertakings. As for example, 1st, If any one has been robbed, and wishes to know the name of the robber, he must proceed as follows: Take mud or slime and sand out of a stream, mix them together; then write the names of all suspected persons upon small slips of paper and apply the mixture on the reverse side of the slips; afterward lay them in a large and clean basin, filled for this purpose with fresh water from the stream—lay them in the water one by one, and at the same time pray this Psalm over them ten times with the prayer adapted to it keeping in mind at the same time the name of Caar, that is, Living, which name is found in the words of the sixth verse, as follows: Chabalim, and Alei, and if the name of the real thief is written upon the slips, that upon which his name is written will rise to the surface. The prayer is as follows: 
> Let it be thy will, Eel Caar, the Living God to make known the name of the thief, who stole from me (here name that which was stolen). Grant that the name of the thief, if it is among the names, may arise before thy eyes, and thus be made known to mine and all others who are present, that thy name may be glorified: grant it for the sake of thy holy name. Amen.—Selah!

2. Whoever prays this Psalm daily with reverence, and childlike trust upon the eternal love and goodness of God, directed to circumstances, will have all his sorrows changed into joy.
Finally, it is said, that the daily praying of this Psalm will change enemies into friends, and will disperse all pain and sorrow.

**Psalm 17.**—A traveler, who prays this Psalm early in the morning, with ardor, together with the proper prayer, in the name of Jah, will be secure from all evil for twenty-four hours. The prayer is as follows: 
> May it be thy holy will, Oh, Jah, Jenora, to make my journey prosperous, to lead me in pleasant paths, to protect me from all evil, and to bring me safely back to my loved ones, for thy mighty and adorable name’s sake. Amen.

The two letters of the holy name Jah are taken from the words, Shoddini, verse 9, and Mirmah, verse 1.

**Psalm 18.**—If robbers are about to attack you, pray this Psalm quickly but frevently, with the prayer belonging to it, with confidence in the holiest name of Eel Jah, that is, mighty, all-merciful and compassionate God, the robbers will leave you suddenly, without inflicting the slightest injury upon you. The letters necessary to make the holy name of God are contained in the words, Aisher, verse 1; Shoal, verse 1; Tamin, verse 33, and Haol, verse 47.
The prayer is the following: 
> “Mighty, all-merciful and compassionate God, Eel Jah! may it be pleasing to thy most holy will, to defend me against approaching robbers, and protect me against all enemies, opposers and evil circumstances, for thine is the power and thou canst help. Hear me for the sake of thy most holy name, Eel Jah. Amen.—Selah!

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Internal Support" strategy for treating sores and ulcers. The previous page established that tonifying the body is essential for pushing toxins outward and that treatment should begin before the wound even opens. This section focuses on specific herbal modifications for complications and distinguishes between the physical presentation of Yang-type and Yin-type ulcers.</meta>

If **Cinnamon bark** <note>original: 肉桂 (ròu-guì)</note> is used heavily, but there is itching and pain caused by **wind** <note>In Chinese medicine, "wind" (fēng) often refers to symptoms that move quickly or cause itching</note>, add **Saposhnikovia root** <note>original: 防風 (fáng-fēng)</note> and **Gastrodia rhizome** <note>original: 天麻 (tiān-má)</note>. If the flesh has become **necrotic** <gloss>dead or non-healing tissue</gloss>, add **Pubescent Angelica root** <note>original: 獨活 (dú-huó)</note> and **Cassia bark** <note>original: 官桂 (guān-guì)</note>.

For cases of extreme pain, add **Myrrh** <note>original: 沒藥 (mò-yào)</note> and **Frankincense** <note>original: 乳香 (rǔ-xiāng)</note>. These are all modified methods for treating the variations of **Yang syndromes** <note>Acute, red, and hot conditions</note>. 

However, if a **Yin eruption** <note>Deep-seated, cold-type sores that do not easily surface</note> transforms into a state of **deficiency and mental confusion** <note>original: 虛愦 (xū-kuì) — a state of physical exhaustion and delirium</note>, one must use large doses of **Ginseng** <note>original: 人參 (rén-shēn)</note>, **Astragalus**, and **Atractylodes** <note>original: 芪朮 (qí-zhú) — two primary herbs for boosting energy and the immune system</note>. To these, add plenty of **Honeysuckle flower** <note>original: 金銀花 (jīn-yín-huā)</note>, **Cinnamon bark**, **Aconite** <note>original: 附子 (fù-zǐ) — a potent warming herb</note>, and the like. By doing so, one may stabilize these extraordinary transformations. One must absolutely never stubbornly adhere to Yang syndrome treatment methods when attempting to treat the transformations of a **Yin-type ulcer**.

### Discourse on the Opening of Sores and Ulcers

In a **Yang-type sore**, once the pus has formed, it will certainly be pointed, firm, and **protruding** <note>original: 突出 (tū-chū)</note>. If a blade is used to open its head, the **pus and blood** <note>original: 膿血 (nóng-xuè)</note> will gush forth; once the opening is drained, the condition will immediately improve. It will certainly not spread further or rot without end. 

However, there are certain types of sores that do **not protrude significantly** <note>original: 突起 (tū-qǐ)</note>, though there is swelling and pain. The pain may be heavy or light. In light cases, there is **numbness and a lack of sensation** <gloss>the patient cannot feel the area</gloss>. If such a sore occurs on the back, it feels as heavy as a mountain. In severe cases, the sensation is exactly like being cut, pierced, or stabbed with a knife. After five to seven days, a head may emerge from the top...

<summary>This page provides specific herbal modifications for post-ulceration complications and emphasizes that Yin-type ulcers (characterized by numbness or deep-seated pain) must be treated with warming tonics rather than standard cooling methods used for Yang-type sores.</summary>
<keywords>Yang syndrome, Yin transformation, Internal Support (Netuo), Cinnamon bark, Ginseng, Suppuration, Necrotic tissue, Herbal modifications</keywords>

Sinking Silver and Floating Lead

<note>original: 內灼</note>
Emperor Wen of the Liu Song Dynasty <note>Bao Zhao</note> wrote in his Rhapsody on the Agate Bridle: The sunken light is like <term>gold and lead</term> <gloss>referring to hidden brilliance or density</gloss>, while the floating shadows are fresh on the exterior.

Four Burnings
<note>original: 四灼</note>
Lu Yun wrote in the Eulogy for Lord Xia: The splendor of fine jade and the <term>four burnings</term> <gloss>radiant light</gloss>, the reputation and news are intimately entwined.

Mirror Burning
<note>original: 鏡灼</note>
Zhi Pu wrote in the Rhapsody on the Ascent: Then returning to clarity and stillness, the reflected forms are identical and yet like a <term>mirror burning</term> <gloss>brightly reflected light</gloss>.

Ashamed and Burning
<note>original: 慙灼</note>
Bao Zhao wrote in the Memorial Declining the Position of General of the Chariots and Horsemen: Looking back on my own emptiness and shallowness, I have frequently failed my appointments. Looking up to meet the Heavenly Favor, I am inwardly prostrate with <term>shame and burning</term> <gloss>the heat of embarrassment</gloss>. Quan Deyu wrote in the petition for Wei Kuang to replace himself: Looking up and down, I am <term>ashamed and burning</term>, betraying the Emperor’s wisdom.

Increasing Burning
<note>original: 增灼</note>
Bao Zhao wrote in a letter: Respectfully receiving the Imperial Command, I am filled with grief, shame, and <term>increasing burning</term> <gloss>growing inner turmoil</gloss>.

Frying and Burning
<note>original: 煎灼</note>
In the Collection of Wang Rong, the Hymn of Pure Conduct states: <term>Frying and burning</term> in the fires of desire, longing for the clouds and dew.

Shaking and Burning
<note>original: 振灼</note>
Emperor Jianwen of the Liang Dynasty wrote in the Inscription on the Monk's Staff: The wonderful conduct and auspicious light follow the sage, <term>shaking and burning</term> <gloss>vibrantly radiant</gloss>.

Luminous Burning
<note>original: 耿灼</note>
Emperor Yuan of the Liang Dynasty wrote in a letter to Zhou Hongzheng: Since our correspondence has ceased, I am constantly <term>luminously burning</term> <gloss>filled with restless concern</gloss>.

Diligent Burning
<note>original: 勤灼</note>
Chen Zi'ang wrote in the Memorial on the Turks for Rectifier Qiao: Your servant has long been at the frontier, <term>diligently burning</term> <gloss>toiling with anxiety</gloss> day and night.

Glory and Burning
<note>original: 榮灼</note>
Li Yong wrote in the Stele of the Anluo Tree in Huaiyin County: At the beginning, the <term>glory and burning</term> occurred when the Way was realized; investigating its origin, it remains after the firewood of the Zhuangzi's master is exhausted <note>a reference to the death of a sage whose influence remains</note>.

Dry Burning
<note>original: 燥灼</note>
Fu Zai wrote in a Letter to the Grandee of Chu: Above, there is nothing to support the elders; below, nothing to comfort the orphans. Pacing back and forth, <term>dry burning</term> <gloss>intense internal heat or agitation</gloss> within like a disease.

Moxa Burning
<note>original: 艾灼</note>
Quan Deyu wrote in the Spirit Way Stele for Lord Wang, Scholar of the Jixian Institute: When the Emperor traveled west, the Duke protected the traveling palace. Captured by the rebels of Yan, the Duke said to his kin: To forget the Emperor's kindness to save one's life is not loyalty; to avoid the rebel's blade and escape death is not filial piety. Thereupon, he attacked his five internal organs with medicine and used <term>moxa burning</term> <gloss>cauterization</gloss> on his four limbs to exhaust his physical form and spirit, finally passing away. The gentleman considers the weight of such duty and the distance of the path to be difficult.

Guest at the Huainan Guesthouse
Yu Xin, from the poem Eight Taoist Guesthouses: Why must one <note>original: "何必"</note> linger there, climbing the branches of the cinnamon tree?

Magnolia Guesthouse
Yu Xin, from the poem Chanting on a Painted Screen: A thousand fathoms of <note>original: "千尋"</note> hundred-foot Hibiscus Halls.

White Crane Guesthouse
Liu Jun, from the poem Returning to Stone City from Jiangzhou: Gazing forward at the Azure Dragon Gate, looking slantwise at the <unclear>White Crane Guesthouse</unclear>.

Golden Pavilion Guesthouse
From the Song of the Perfected One of Mount Tongbai: Depicting my <note>original: "寫我"</note> fresh carriage in the realm of the Three Spiritual Herbs.

Purple Subtle Guesthouse
From the poem of the Lady of Purple Subtlety: Cloud-mists <note>original: "羈靄"</note> gather around the lush terrace, where the scattered light flickers.

Bright Truth Guesthouse
From the poem of the Lady of the Right Excellence of Yunlin: Holding sleeves <note>original: "擕袂"</note> and looking upward, awaiting the Supreme Sovereign.

Heavenly Grandchild Guesthouse
Xu Jingzong, from the Stele for Yuchi Gong, Commander-in-Chief of Bingzhou: The clear tower rises as a lofty structure, reaching afar to the ford of the Maiden Star; the yellow pavilion has frozen doors, closely bordering the <term>Tiansun Guan</term> <gloss>Heavenly Grandchild Guesthouse</gloss>.

Yellow Spirit Guesthouse
Wang Bo, from the Preface to the Ode on the Qianyuan Hall: Above, the Roc's expanse broadens, opening the courtyard of the Purple Emperor in the Jade Capital; below, the Turtle's records are cleared, opening the <term>Huangling Guan</term> <gloss>Yellow Spirit Guesthouse</gloss> in the precious wilds.

Directional Inspection Guesthouse
Wang Bo, from the Preface to the Ode on the Jiucheng Palace: The three ranks of officials descend everywhere, attending the Palace for Distributing Government; the six positions ride the seasons, yet the <term>Xunfang Guan</term> <gloss>Directional Inspection Guesthouse</gloss> has not been seen.

Long Happiness Guesthouse
Wang Bo, from the Rhapsody on Spring Longing: The rear riders are still divided at the <term>Changle Guan</term> <gloss>Long Happiness Guesthouse</gloss>, while the front banners already shine upon the Luoyang Palace.

Three Purities Guesthouse
Lu Zhaolin, from the text Relieving Sickness: Wandering <note>original: "彷徨"</note> about the <term>Sanqing Guan</term> <gloss>Three Purities Guesthouse</gloss>, dimly appearing as if on the Terrace of the Eight Winds.

Yanzhong Guesthouse
Lu Zhaolin, from the poem On the Lecture Hall of Wen Weng: The Brocade Neighborhood <note>original: "錦里"</note> of the Yanzhong Guesthouse; the Pavilion of Mount Min and Jixia.

Jieshi Guesthouse
Chen Zi'ang, from the poem on King Zhao of Yan: Climbing the <term>Jieshi Guan</term> <gloss>Jieshi Guesthouse</gloss> in the south, looking afar at the Golden Terrace. Gao Shi, from the poem Replying to Vice Director Pei: Writing a poem at the <term>Jieshi Guan</term> <gloss>Jieshi Guesthouse</gloss>, drinking freely at the Terrace of the King of Yan.

King of Yan Guesthouse
Shen Quanqi, from the poem Climbing Yingzhou: To the north is the <term>Yanwang Guan</term> <gloss>King of Yan Guesthouse</gloss>; to the east it connects to the Bridge of the Qin Emperor.

I fortunately obtained all these forbidden formulas. I, Yi, would not dare to pass them on to others recklessly even upon death. After living there for some time, I, Chunyu Yi, had a deep discussion about these formulas with Gongsun Guang while he was at leisure. He saw my words and remarked that they would be the essence of a hundred generations. Teacher Guang said happily: "You will surely be <note>character missing</note> <note>character missing</note>. I have a good friend named Yang Qing, a native of Linzi. He is skilled in formulas, and I am not his equal. His formulas are exceedingly marvelous, and not what the world has heard of. When I was in my middle years, I once wanted to receive his formulas, but Yang Qing would not agree, saying 'You are not the right person.' I shall go with you to see him; he should know you love formulas. The man is old now, and his family is wealthy." Before they could go, Qing’s son, Yin, came to present horses. Through Teacher Guang, I presented horses to the King. For this reason, I was able to become friends with Yin. Guang also entrusted me to Yin, saying: "Yi loves the arts, you must treat him with care." That man is a <term>Shengru</term> <gloss>Sage-Scholar</gloss>. He then wrote a letter to entrust me to Yang Qing. Because of this, I came to know Qing, and I served him diligently.

Because of this, he loved Yi.

The Emperor asked: "When you, Yi, examine illnesses and decide between life and death, can you do so entirely without error?" I, Yi, replied: "When I treat a patient, I must first feel their pulse and only then treat them. If the pulse is ruined or contrary, they cannot be treated. <note>character missing</note> <note>character missing</note> <note>character missing</note> <note>character missing</note> If the heart is not refined, and the pulse predicts life or death, even when one views it as treatable, one occasionally fails. I, Yi, am not <note>able to be perfect</note>."

The Emperor asked Yi, saying: "Have officials or commoners ever studied your formulas and completed their learning, obtaining everything? From which counties and villages are they?" I replied: "Song Yi of Linzi. Yi studied with me, and I taught him the <term>Wuzhen</term> <gloss>Five Examinations</gloss> for over a year. The King of Jibei sent his Imperial Physicians, Gao Qi and Wang Yu, to study with me, and I taught them..."

...the right course of VALENTINUS, 
and his more noble spirit. 
Which fills the fertile halls of his vivid breast 
with a more lofty seed: 
and with <term>ceris</term> <gloss>wax tablets or writings</gloss> which old age, 
foul with smoke and varied by a 
swelling belt, shall not hide; 
nor shall the mute offspring of the times 
put to sleep in a hidden garment. 
But those which, through the age of descendants 
and through the series of the flying year, 
scatter the lightning of a flaming spark: 
and may they shine more through the long 
starry day, through the losses of a 
slipping age, and through the 
midst of the darkness. 
Who does not know the times you spent 
through the circle of the Arts? How with 
watchful labors you have prepared 
this great glory of the sciences for yourself? 
When you were a youth, the <term>Musæ</term> <gloss>Muses</gloss> 
placed more shining charms on your lips, 
and they blessed your <term>genium</term> <gloss>natural talent or spirit</gloss>

res produxerunt, id est, ætherei.* Hæc autem anima in se vitalis, sed irrationalis per
acquisitionem portionis supercœlestis fit rationalis; Et tunc eam Augustinus
*lib. de anim. & spirit.* definit esse substantiam quandam rationis participem. Unde hæc
anima media, quatenus respicit superiora, habet virtutem intelligendi, & qua-
tenus inferiora, virtutem sentiendi: Similiter quatenus componitur hæc ani-
ma ex luce & spiritu, & quatenus mentem divinam cum cœli empyrei substan-

lucis hujus præsentia, à privatione sua liberatur & purgatur. Lucem autem

riam, quæ rationalitas inferior est intellectu. Nam in *Resolut. Theolog.* habetur,

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological investigation into the nature of the soul, the spirit, and the intellect, drawing heavily on Aristotelian and Scholastic definitions.</meta>

# On the Nature of the Soul and Spirit

In the treatise *On the Soul and the Spirit* <note>original: "de anim. & spirit."</note>, it is established that the distinction between these faculties is essential for understanding human nature.

Aristotle, in his *Book on the Spirit* <note>original: "lib. de spiritu"</note>, asserts that there are spirits <note>original: "esse spiritus"</note> which act as the primary instruments of the soul's power within the physical body.

In the *Theological Resolutions* <note>original: "Resolut. Theolog."</note>, it is further clarified that, insofar as the soul looks toward higher things, it is called the **intellect**; insofar as it looks toward lower things, it is called **reason**. <note>original: "quod, quatenus anima respicit altiora, dicitur intellectus, quatenus inferiora, ratio."</note>

The intellect of the foul <note>original: "fedi"; likely referring to the corrupted or base state of the mind</note> must be purified to perceive divine truths.

The physical seat of these movements often involves the **diaphragm** <term>diaphragma</term> <note>the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen, historically believed to be a center of emotion or "spirit"</note>, which regulates the vital breath.

Through the wild bearing <note>original: "ferationem"; referring to a state of wildness or animalistic impulse</note> of the passions, the spirit can become clouded, losing its orientation toward the higher intellect.

<summary>This page explores the hierarchical definitions of the soul, distinguishing between the intellect (focused on the divine) and reason (focused on the mundane), while noting the physiological role of the diaphragm.</summary>
<keywords>soul, spirit, intellect, reason, Aristotle, theology, diaphragm, Scholasticism</keywords>

Indeed, **Archimedes** once had the same plan; not content with leaving his discoveries to the pen, he also ordered that a sphere and a cylinder be placed upon his tomb as the glory of his invention, about which **Cicero** writes eloquently. <note>Cicero recounts in his *Tusculan Disputations* how he discovered Archimedes' neglected tomb in Syracuse by looking for these geometric symbols.</note> Meanwhile, I must not conceal that I have not yet found the *Emerald Tablet* among the Greek chemical writers, although I do not doubt it was regarded by them and passed down to the Latins. But truly, who has searched through all the Greek chemical manuscripts? Unless you prefer to agree with **Gaulmin** <note>Gilbert Gaulmin (1585–1665) was a French scholar who suggested that many Hermetic texts survived in Persian and Arabic before reaching Europe.</note> that the Tablet was found by the Persian victors either in Egypt or nearby, and was translated into Persian long ago, so that its name was unknown to the Greeks for a long time. However, in succeeding centuries, **Aristotle the Younger** <note>A pseudonym used by alchemical authors to borrow the authority of the Great Philosopher.</note> mentions the same tablet in his work *On the Perfect Mastery*; it is also mentioned by **Senior Zadith**, **Master Ortholanus** (or **Hortulanus**), **Avicenna**, **Arnald of Villanova**, **Isaac Hollandus**, **Albertus Magnus**, **Bernard of Trevisan**, and in the year of Christ 1330, **Petrus Bonus of Lombardy**, to say nothing of the almost infinite later writers. Let **Kircher** consider this, who contends that it was first shown to the world by the "Alchemist Canesius."

### III.

Besides the *Emerald Tablet*, various chemical works of **Hermes** [doubtless the later one] are extant, often cited by both Greeks and Latins, such as *The Physical Tinctures of Hermes* <note>original: τῷ ἑρμῦ Φυσικὴ βαφαὶ</note>, *The Primal Book of Hermes* <note>original: τοῦ ἑρμῦ Ἀρχικὴ βίβλῷ</note>, and likewise *Whatever was spoken by Hermes and the Philosophers*, written by **Olympiodorus**. <note>Olympiodorus of Alexandria was a late antique philosopher whose commentaries on alchemical lore are among the earliest surviving sources.</note> Finally, there are various Hermetic maxims praised in the ancient **Synesius**, in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum," a famous early Latin text where various pre-Socratic philosophers are depicted debating alchemical principles.</note>, in the *Precious Pearl* of **Petrus Bonus of Lombardy**, in the *Book of Secrets* of **Kalid**, in **Senior Zadith**, **Hortulanus**, the *Rosary*, **Rupescissa**, **Isaac Hollandus**, **Albertus Magnus**, **Arnald of Villanova**, the **Chemical Aristotle**, **Bernard of Trevisan**, and others. *Arguments of those who deny the Art concerning the mixing of hard bodies with hard, and soft with soft.*

### Chapter XXI.

Others, indeed, by combining hard bodies with hard ones and soft with soft due to their natural affinity <note>original: "convenientiam"; a philosophical concept suggesting that like substances should naturally combine or act upon one another</note>, wished for these bodies to be transmuted by one another and to effect transmutation. Yet they were unable to achieve this because of their own lack of skill. For instance, when mixing the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the Moon <note>Silver</note> with Venus <note>Copper</note> or any other of the metals, they did not see those metals transformed into the Sun or the Moon by a firm and true transmutation. Instead, it inevitably happens that through the intense action <note>original: "expressione forti"</note> of fire, each of those imperfect bodies is separated from the mixture and burned away, while the perfect body remains or returns to its former nature.

Indeed, some of these metals endure longer in a mixture, while others endure less, as shall be sufficiently determined by us in the following chapters. Therefore, all these delusions, which arise from ignorance, cause such men to completely distrust this Art and to argue that it does not exist. The very study of gold-making <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <note>The art of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> is such that, according to the testimony of Delrio and Valencia <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608) and Gregory of Valencia (1549–1603), Jesuit theologians who wrote on magic and moral philosophy.</note>, it hardly escapes the fault of vanity, while he who seeks profit from it does not easily escape the mark of imprudence. Since this happens to students of the gold-making art, they are deservedly, to put it most mildly, accused of simplicity. If Nature is difficult, one easily descends to seeking the help of the Demon through the hope of gaining wealth from meager means. For whenever Alchemy flourished among many, according to Delrio, then Sorcery and Divination also flourished; a loss of most precious time is made, and an account of its evil consumption and never-to-be-redeemed status must be rendered to God.

translation:
<meta>This page follows the title page of Crispijn van de Passe’s 1615 work. It serves as an introduction to the reader, explaining the historical and religious significance of the Sibyls and their prophecies regarding Christ.</meta>

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER.

<note>A decorative initial letter E contains an illustration of a seated man, likely a scholar or a saint, reading a book.</note>

Here for you, reader and kind observer of these plates, are the images of the Sibylline prophetesses, depicted, so to speak, according to their actual influence. In these images, the principal mysteries of our salvation shine forth. According to the testimony of Lactantius Firmianus <note>Lactantius was an early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who sought to use pagan prophecy to validate Christian doctrine.</note> in the first book of *On False Religion*, all female prophetesses were called Sibyls by the ancients because they announced the counsels of the Gods. This is because in the Aeolic dialect of the Greek language, they called the Gods *sious* and counsel *boule*. <note>original: "σιούς n. Deos, & consiliū βυλὴν". This is an etymological explanation: the word "Sibyl" is derived from the Greek words for "God's counsel."</note> Therefore, the Sibyl was named as if she were a *Theoboule*, or "Divine Counsel." The ancients established their number at ten, and no more, but more recent writers (whom I have followed) have made them twelve. Certain illustrious prophecies from all of these women regarding Christ and the future life are still read today. Whether these are all true, or whether some of them (as some have thought) were added by the first spreaders of the Christian religion to refute the errors of the pagans, they certainly deserve to be counted among the monuments of our piety. I strive to feed your eyes not only with empty and fleeting pleasure, but also to nourish your minds with deeper contemplation. Therefore, I now present these icons of the Sibyls in a more distinguished form and engraving. I previously published smaller and, in a sense, "silent" versions of them, but now I have attempted to reveal the secrets of the mysteries themselves through both sacred and common inscriptions, thus giving a living and breathing spirit to the images. Enjoy these with kindness, and embrace my efforts as I study to serve the public benefit to the best of my ability.

---

### I.
->THE DELPHIC SIBYL.<-

They claim that the Delphic Sibyl was the oldest of all the women who delivered oracles. She was said to be the daughter of Tiresias <note>A famous blind prophet in Greek mythology.</note> and named Artemis, and she lived long before the Trojan wars. It is said that Homer took many things from her verses and transferred them to the decoration of his own poems. Concerning this Sibyl, as well as those that follow, one should consult the writings of Varro, Lactantius, Pausanias, and other ancients, as well as Onuphrio Panvinio and Jean-Jacques Boissard, who left behind dedicated books on the Sibyls and their oracles. But it is most worthy of admiration that Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 3rd century BC.</note> is recorded to have handed down in his books on divination that she predicted a Great Prophet would arise, whose conception would be miraculous, occurring without male seed.

<meta>A decorative initial letter D contains an illustration of two figures, one seated and one standing, in a landscape setting.</meta>

### I.
->THE DELPHIC SIBYL.<-

The Delphic Sibyl lived before the destruction of Troy, so much so that Homer included several of her verses in his works. Chrysippus, a very ancient philosopher, speaks of her in his book on divination, saying she predicted that a great Prophet would be born whose birth would be miraculous and without male seed, a prophecy that concerns the greatest mystery of our salvation and religion.

<summary>The author explains that the twelve Sibyls were ancient prophetesses whose oracles are believed to have predicted the coming of Christ. This specific page focuses on the Delphic Sibyl, the eldest of the group, who allegedly inspired Homer and predicted the Virgin Birth.</summary>
<keywords>Delphic Sibyl, Lactantius Firmianus, Chrysippus, Tiresias, Homer, etymology, Greek prophecy, Virgin Birth, Christian mysteries, Crispijn van de Passe</keywords>
