<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the eternal nature of divine punishment. It transitions from the previous discussion on the lack of light for the wicked to specific scriptural proofs from the Gospels showing that once the debt of sin enters the afterlife, there is no further opportunity for repayment or forgiveness.</meta>

<page-num>20</page-num>

-># ON THE ETERNITY OF PUNISHMENTS<-

<meta>catchword: com-</meta>

"...until you have paid," <note>original Greek: *apodōs*</note> says Luke. However, it is most certain that the sinner is unable to pay, both from Matthew 18:25 and from the "analogy of faith" <note>the theological principle that any interpretation of a specific Bible verse must be consistent with the core truths of the faith</note>, due to humanity’s total inability to save itself and the fact that continued sin deserves punishment into all eternity.

XXIII. Nor can the strength of this argument be broken by the **"invention of a middle-ground,"** <note>original: *figmento temperamenti*</note> by which the sinner would pay in part through his own person, while that which remained to be paid would be wiped away through the grace of God and the **merit of Christ**. For both the text itself—which commands the debtor to pay the *last penny* <note>original Latin: *ultimum obolum*; a reference to the smallest denomination of coin used to symbolize a complete debt</note>—and the following passages confirm the opposite, as they completely overturn this middle-ground and forbid any mixing of Christ's merit with one's own satisfaction for sin. We assign the fifth category to those sayings that destroy the hope not only of Redemption but also of all the means toward Redemption in the future life. For Redemption to be granted, both the **Forgiveness of sins** and **Effective Conversion** are required. Sacred Scripture teaches us that both are sought in vain in eternity.

XXIV. It is evident from Matthew 12:32 that the hope for the **Forgiveness of sins** expires with the end of this life: *Whoever speaks a word against the **Holy Spirit** will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.* Whether "this age and the one to come" is understood as the **Dispensations of the Old and New Testament** <note>original: *Oeconomia*; the historical systems of God’s dealings with humanity</note> (as **Teelmann** <note>Henricus Teelmann (1694–1764), a Dutch Reformed theologian known for his "Sacred Exercises"</note> argues in his *Sacred Exercises*, p. 112 ff.), or as the present and future life (as the vast majority of interpreters <note>original: *interpretum integra inclinat sylva*; literally, "the whole forest of interpreters leans this way"</note> suggest), it is clear from Jewish usage that it signifies "never." This is also confirmed by Mark 3:29, which says: *he has no forgiveness forever, but is subject to eternal judgment.* <note>original Greek: *ouk echei aphesin eis ton aiōna, all’ enochos estin aiōniou krimatos*</note> Now, that phrase "forever" <note>original Greek: *eis ton aiōna*</note> is constantly used by the Savior and the New Testament writers to mean an eternity that never ends. Furthermore, our theologians have shown abundantly that even the defenders of **Purgatory** gain nothing from this saying. It is even more opposed to the defenders of absolute **Universal Restoration** <note>original Greek: *Apokatastaseōs*; the theological theory that all beings, including the damned and the devil, will eventually be reconciled to God</note>, especially when we embrace the simplest sense of the words. In the main point of this matter, we follow the rank and file of commentators, leaving the overly subtle observations of **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist who specialized in interpreting the New Testament through Jewish tradition</note> and others to their proper place, and

<summary>This page argues against the possibility of escaping eternal punishment through partial payment or divine grace after death. It uses Matthew 12:32 to demonstrate that forgiveness for certain sins is impossible in the future life, refuting the concepts of Purgatory and Universal Restoration.</summary>

<keywords>Eternity of punishment, merit of Christ, Forgiveness of sins, Effective Conversion, Holy Spirit, Dispensations, Purgatory, Universal Restoration, Teelmann, Lightfoot</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the pharmacological descriptions of medicinal substances, specifically finishing the entry for Schoenanthus (Camel grass) and moving into animal products, vegetables, and seeds. It maintains the categorical structure of the medieval medical tradition, likely following the "Canon of Medicine" or a similar herbal.</meta>

...with honey, and it consolidates deep ulcers. It is also applied dry upon them, or infused in water or wine. Its water is also extractive in this manner. **Organs of Breath and Chest.** When applied with a sponge and oil, it cures sharp pains and the spitting of blood <note>original: "spurū sāguīs"; likely hemoptysis</note>. **Organs of Expulsion.** A stone found in it <note>possibly a reference to a medicinal stone or the plant's effect on stones</note> breaks stones of the bladder. According to others and Galen, it should be burned so that it penetrates better to reach the stone.

### Scincus. What is it? <note>original: "Sı̄ncus"; referring to the Skink, a type of lizard</note>
It is an aquatic animal captured on the banks of the Nile. It is said to be a land-dwelling creature, for when it comes out of the water, it takes the form of a living animal <note>Medieval naturalists often categorized the skink as a "land crocodile" or a hybrid of fish and lizard</note>. **Selection.** The best kind is that which is captured in the spring and in places where they are fervent for mating. The larger it is, the better; the fatter it is, the better. Its fat should be taken with honey. **Instruments of the Joints.** It benefits cold diseases of the joints. **Organs of Expulsion.** Its salt excites sexual intercourse, but its flesh does so even more. Indeed, the flesh of this animal, specifically the parts near the kidneys and their fat, is used as an aphrodisiac.

### Spinach <note>original: "Pinacha"; from the Arabic 'isbanakh'</note>. 
**Nature.** It is cold and moist at the end of the first degree. **Operations and Properties.** It is softening and its nutrition is better for the body when it is well-digested. I say that its juice is [unclear], it washes the [unclear] and benefits the bile. It is eaten for its juice. **Organs of Breath and Chest.** It benefits breathing, the chest, and a hot lung. **Instruments of the Joints.** It is used for pains of the back caused by the blood. **Organs of Expulsion.** It is softening for the belly <note>meaning it acts as a mild laxative</note>.

### Flaxseed <note>original: "Semen lini"</note>. 
What is it? It is the primary companion to fenugreek. **Nature.** It is hot in the first degree, balanced in moisture and dryness. It is said that there is a great deal of superfluous moisture in it. **Operations and Properties.** It is maturing <note>it helps ripen abscesses or boils</note>, and it cleanses through its superfluous moisture. From it, that which is made [unclear] has a clear and balanced astringency in its essence. It is declared to be softening and a sedative for pain, much like chamomile. **Beauty.** From it, a plaster is made for the skin and nails. It benefits the [unclear] of the nails, cracks, and...

<column-break/>

...breaks in the nails, when mixed with an equal measure of watercress <note>original: "nasturtı̄"</note> and made with honey. **Abscesses and Swellings.** It holds back hot abscesses, both external and internal, and it opens those behind the ears. It also opens hard swellings. **Instruments of the Joints.** It heals [unclear] of the nails when mixed with wax and honey. **Organs of the Head.** Its smoke is used as a fumigation, as is the fumigation of the flax itself. **Organs of Breath and Chest.** It benefits a phlegmatic cough, especially when it is roasted. **Digestive Organs.** It is valuable for the [unclear] and for difficulty in digestion. **Organs of Expulsion.** When roasted, it binds the belly and its consistency is balanced. Its provocation is [unclear] if strengthened by roasting. When taken with honey and pepper, it excites sexual intercourse. When its decoction is used, it helps with [unclear] in the intestines. It also provides aid for ulcers of the bladder and kidneys. A decoction of flaxseed with [unclear] and oil helps greatly with ulcers of the intestines.

### White [Bird] <note>original: "Alua uis"; likely 'Alba avis', referring to the dung of a white bird like a stork</note>.
**Selection.** The kind that is similar to [unclear] is of strong operation. Its nature is hot. **Wounds and Ulcers.** It is effective for [unclear]. **Organs of the Eye.** It benefits the palpitation of the eyelid and white spots on the eye <term>albugo</term> <note>a white opacity of the cornea</note>. **Poisons.** It resists all venomous things, including serpents and scorpions.

### Animal Dung.
**Beauty.** Goat dung <note>original: "Stercus adib̄"; 'Adib' is likely the Arabic 'al-jadi' for goat or 'ad-dib' for wolf, but goat is more common in this context</note> benefits large spots and freckles through its cleansing property. Dog/Camel dung <note>original: "stercus caneli"; likely 'canis' (dog) or 'cameli' (camel)</note> cleanses and destroys warts, even large ones. **Organs of the Head.** Goat dung [unclear] through its cleansing property. Dog/Camel dung stops the flow of blood from the nose. When drunk with [unclear], it benefits epilepsy. **Organs of the Eye.** Goat dung binds the white spots of the eye. **Wounds and Ulcers.** Dog/Camel dung resolves swellings and ulcers. Similarly, the dung of a [unclear] animal for erysipelas <note>a skin infection causing red, swollen patches</note>. **Instruments of the Joints.** Dog/Camel dung settles [unclear]. **Abscesses and Swellings.** Dog/Camel dung resolves [unclear] strongly. Similarly, the dung of a [unclear] animal for erysipelas. **Instruments of the Joints.** Dung...

Ebion spread his poison before the Nicolaitans, as Irenaeus teaches in Book 1, chapter 23, around the year 44 after Christ's passion; although Tertullian writes that Ebion was a disciple of Cerinthus, but without sufficiently weighing the ratio of times and the variety of authors. Platina thinks he flourished under Clement the First, Bishop of Rome. Theodoret, in Book 2, places the Ebionites in the same time as Cerinthus. This heresy began, as Epiphanius says, first around Pella, a city of Syria in the village of Cochoba, which was later propagated more widely, and it very quickly pervaded the region of Basanitida, and then the neighboring Nabataea and Arabia, from which this unhappy shoot was transferred into Asia Minor, which infected and corrupted many with its pestiferous juice. Finally, it reached and tempted Rome itself. It persisted, however, longer in Armenia, as Epiphanius says, regarding the Archontics. But the men of this sect immediately severed themselves into various parts and divorces, one from another, so that a lie at length loses confidence in itself. It was nonetheless retained for a very long time, but with the prior name interpolated and changed, and that of the Sampsaeans and Elcesaens assumed, as Augustine teaches with Epiphanius in this place. translation:
These matters, although full of vanity, have been so buried by perpetual oblivion and general Amnesty that it is not permitted, for the sake or pretext of them or any other thing (whatever had been committed, secretly or openly, directly or indirectly, mutually or otherwise, on the occasion and during the storm of the Germano-Swedish war), to inflict hostility, enmity, or molestation, under penalty of broken peace to be incurred by the very law and fact. Certainly, to revive such causes, which have been extinguished and abolished, and to justify a war against Poland, which is included and finalized in the Münster records, the Swedes could by no means do so without great prejudice, or rather a rupture of the universal Peace.

However it might be, if the war had been brought into the vitals of the Kingdom of Poland from Sweden itself or from the Swedish dominion of Livonia, it would be one thing; but since it has had its origin and progress from Pomerania, a province of the Roman Empire; since the Swedish Army was recruited and commissioned in the said Pomerania, as well as in Bremen, Verden, Mecklenburg, and other lands, and does not cease to be recruited, supplemented, refreshed, and sent out against Poland, the fault for the disturbed Germany and the *broken Peace*, and all the atrocious and hostile [acts], and the greater evils that will follow (which God forbid), is to be attributed to the Swedes as the authors.

Added to this is the fact that the most unjust war in human memory, waged by Sweden against the Poles, has been promoted and sustained by the combined forces of both certain Princes and Imperial Cities, and is sustained even to this day by ready aid and continuous reinforcements (which His Sacred Royal Majesty of Poland and Sweden, my most Clement Lord, considers an injury and laments); so that Poland, which has deserved no such thing, is shaken not so much by the forces of Sweden as by those of Germany.

For this reason, I have deemed it fitting, in the name of the often-mentioned Sacred Royal Majesty and the Kingdom of Poland, to refer the whole matter decently to the Most Serene, Most Eminent, and Most Illustrious Electors, Princes, and Estates of the Holy Roman Empire, and to demand with the duty that is proper, that the invasion of the Kingdom of Poland, an associate of the Germano-Swedish peace, carried out by the Swedes, and the initial and further hostility from Pomerania and other lands of the Empire, and the subsidies of the Princes and Cities of Germany, and the daily military levies for the Swede, be not regarded with dissimulation and silence, but that the common cause be aided by common efforts, councils, and help, and that timely consultation be held for the maintenance of public and secure tranquility or for the repression of evil.

Moreover, there is some importance in the preservation and integrity of the Kingdom of Poland, because with this bulwark overthrown, like a broken embankment, it is to be feared that a flood of barbaric peoples (who have recently been moved to these very borders and are no further than one day's journey from Silesia, and who warn and terrify of danger for the future) may inundate neighboring Germany.

Which individual matters and all things must be prudently weighed by the Electors of the Holy Roman Empire.

translation:
**XXIII.**
But generally, in any *Hectic* [fever], the earwax is dry. Distillations are sharp and salty. Sweats [occur] on almost every night. Feces are generally dry, in some [cases] even liquid.

**XXIV.**
A changed quality is observed either in a part or in the whole.

**XXV.**
Thus, in a part, one encounters dry lippitude <note>inflammation of the eyelids</note> of the eyes (such as [that of] those who have completed a long journey in the sun and dust), concave eyes, collapsed temples, sharp nostrils, rigid ears and eyebrows. The vivid color of the face has perished; finally, the face is *Hippocratic* <note>a pinched, sunken, and pale facial expression indicative of impending death</note>.

**XXVI.**
In the whole, however, [there is] dryness and squalor, so that one appears as if a skeleton. For although digestion is poorly performed and the nourishment is depraved, cachexia <note>general physical wasting</note> does not occur, because it is consumed by the heat and dryness of the limbs: with apologies to Celsus, who seems to have listed cachexia among the species of Hectic. Heat is more distinct after food.

**XXVII.**
But if the Hectic [fever] is joined with a putrid [fever], it will have the signs of the putrid [fever] attached.

**XXVIII.**
To recognize an incipient Hectic [fever] is difficult, to cure one established is arduous, to know [one at its end] is easy. *Marasmodes* is immedicable, since the fibrous substance of the part cannot be restored.

Those who just now had snatched the Christians to punishments, soon sending word to their own error, underwent the same punishments with a joyful mind amid any sorrows. Shame remained for the enemies of the truth, while the greatest praise and glory remained for the Martyrs. Even today, not only Spain but the whole Christian world, as far as it lies open, execrates the former and admires the virtue of the latter, and honors them with deserved praises. Among them are those whom Spain affects with greater honors than they themselves would want if they were alive, for it pursues those, because of their zeal for religion, with religious worship. If they were to return to life, they would undoubtedly complain more about the excessive honors than about the most bitter pains they once suffered. Truly, it is neither wondrous to say nor difficult to believe that, among so many examples of true piety, there existed in Spain those who stained the sincerity of religion with new opinions. No century is fruitful in virtues that is altogether sterile of vices, nor does the wheat easily lack mixed tares. What wonder that these also were born in Spain? Especially the heresy of the <term>GNOSTICS</term> <gloss>those having secret knowledge</gloss> excited great disturbances there. It had its origin in Egypt. Soon its ruin also involved Spain. Marcus first introduced it into Spain; Helpidius and Agape pushed it further; finally, through the work of Priscillian, it permeated most of Spain. He was noble by birth, prompt in genius for speaking and disputing, and famous for learning that was neither vulgar nor common everywhere; moreover, he was not at all greedy for possessions, and he used what he had sparingly and moderately. Then indeed the appearance of humility, which he carried before himself both with his mouth and his habit, produced the greatest authority for him. When he had gradually reconciled men of various kinds, indeed even some from the order of Bishops to his sect, it was confronted by those who thought more rightly, but less circumspectly. Hence that spread more widely, which, if handled more cautiously, might perhaps have received a cure. Behold, you have from the princes of Dorothiel, from every order (that is, diurnal and nocturnal), 24 dukes, with a number of servants totaling ten thousand one hundred and sixty. And note that the operation through these is quite different from the others, just as we shall speak at length concerning the lord. For one must operate in this mansion according to the 12 hours of the day and the night, and four princes always preside over two hours, as much in the day as in the night; in such a way that it is not permitted for you to call another, except from the order that the hour concerns. If the operation is in the first or second hour of the day, call whichever of the first four presiding over the day you wish; if in the third or fourth, you will know the duke must be called from the second four. And so it must be done consequently through all orders and 24 hours, both in the day and in the night. When, however, you wish to operate in Steganography through the spirits of Dorothiel himself with the general premises accustomed to be placed at the start of the art, write whatever letters you wish, and turning yourself to that region of the orb which we commonly call Chorus by the wind, call one or more from the four who preside over the hour in which you operate.

Regarding Miltiades, Probus in his <term>Life</term> <gloss>of Miltiades</gloss>: 'Having been much occupied in commands and magistracies, he did not seem capable of being a private citizen: especially since he seemed to be drawn to the desire for command by habit.' <term>Bern.</term>

*Immoderate military license*] Thus, indeed, from the older editions, and that which Major cared for. Bongars and Berneccerus also retained that reading. Major, however, noted in the margin that a different reading exists, <term>militare</term> <gloss>military [adjective]</gloss>; and Bongars also warns in his <term>V. L.</term> <gloss>Variæ Lectiones/Variant Readings</gloss> that certain printed codices have it this way. I, however, would not hesitate to read <term>immoderatæ licentiæ militari</term> <gloss>of immoderate military license</gloss>; in that case, naturally, which the preceding 'accustomed' requires. <term>Vor.</term> I allow nothing to be changed here. For 'accustomed to license' is not more Latin than 'accustomed by license.' Cic. III. <term>de Orat.</term> <gloss>On the Orator</gloss>: 'Men accustomed by assiduous and daily labor.' Virgil: 'Opheltes, accustomed to wars.' <term>Schef.</term>

§ 9 *Which, even if they had been falsely announced*] It is difficult for the reading to be considered sound. I think Justin wrote either, *Q. e. falso n. f.* <gloss>which [was] indeed falsely announced</gloss> or *Q. e. falsa, apud timentes tamen*, etc. <gloss>which [was] indeed false, yet among the fearful</gloss>, etc. <term>Id.</term>

*False [things] taken for true among the fearful, etc.*] Sen. II. <term>de Ira</term> <gloss>On Anger</gloss> 22. 'What we hear unwillingly, we believe willingly.' Tac. IV. <term>H.</term> <gloss>Histories</gloss> 38. 3. <term>Bern.</term>

CHAP. II. § 1 *Silent, etc.*] Saxo XIV. p. 310. 6. 'Absalon ordered silence to be kept.'

§ 2 *Skilled*] I would prefer <term>paratum</term> <gloss>prepared</gloss>, which Bongars testifies is in all manuscripts. <term>Bernec.</term> One must entirely preserve what all manuscripts have, <term>paratum</term>. For I do not think 'skilled at looking forward' is even Latin. <term>Schef.</term>

*Prepared*] Not only did the manuscripts of Bongars prove this reading to Berneccerus and Scheffer, but the British, having found it in three codices, deservedly received it. <term>Graev. Engl. paratum.</term> Which reading, in my opinion, is the best. And I doubt whether 'skilled at' was in use among the Latins for 

<column-break/>

*taking precautions*. They would rather have said 'skilled in taking precautions,' as 'skilled in ruling the state,' 'skilled in arguing,' 'swimming,' and that type of thing. But 'prepared for taking precautions,' as in Cic. in <term>Orat.</term>: 'Prepared for speaking,' and in <term>Pro Milon.</term>: 'He was not sufficiently prepared for taking precautions,' using this very phrase. <term>Schef.</term>

*Adversity in prosperity*] The same was the custom of Roman constancy, 'to wear the face of favorable fortune in adverse circumstances: to moderate one's spirit in prosperous ones:' Liv. XLII. 62. 9. Add below XXXI. 8. 9. <term>Bern.</term>

§ 3 *Of the leaders*] Of the nobles, and the foremost of the people, i.e., of the senators. Thus Sen. <term>ad Helv.</term> <gloss>to Helvia</gloss> 11. pr. and 12. m. IV. <term>de LL.</term> <gloss>On the Latin Language</gloss>: 'Suprema [is] the height of the day; the twelve tables call this time the setting of the sun.' <margin>2</margin>is attributed to cattle: but it is wrong for the good to be mixed with evils, and it is not even common to many. And that pleasure is not the most powerful thing: but the good is the most powerful. And that it is an impediment to doing honorable things: for how can that which prevents one from doing honorable things be good? Therefore, we must first address the first point, regarding its origin, and dispel the argument that it is by no means true. Thus, in the first place, not every pleasure is a process of generation. For the pleasure that arises from looking is not a process of generation; nor is that 
<margin>10</margin>which arises from hearing and smelling. For they are not produced from a deficiency, as is the case in others, such as from eating or drinking. For these occur from a deficiency and a surplus, either by satisfying a deficiency or by removing a surplus: therefore, they seem to be processes of generation. But deficiency and surplus are a sickness: therefore, there is a sickness where there is a process of generation of pleasure. Yet, in looking, hearing, and smelling, it is not the case that sickness precedes it; for no one who takes pleasure in looking or smelling has been in distress beforehand. Likewise in thought: for there can be pleasure for the one contemplating some matter without a preceding distress; and consequently, there will be some pleasure which is not a process of generation. But if pleasure, 
<margin>20</margin>as their argument dictates, is not good because it is a process of generation, and there is some pleasure which is not a process of generation, then pleasure would surely be good. Yet pleasure is not a process of generation in its entirety: for the pleasures from eating and drinking cannot be called processes of generation. But those who claim that these pleasures are processes of generation hallucinate; they think, indeed, that since pleasure is generated when objects are brought forward (or while taking food), it is for this reason a process of generation. But it is not: for since there is a certain part of the soul by which we are delighted as soon as the things we needed are brought forward, that part of the soul is delighted insofar as it is exercised and moved. Yet the motion itself and the exercise is pleasure. Which, 
<margin>30</margin>when that part of the soul is exercised with the objects brought forward, they think is a process of generation because of its action, because the bringing forward of things is certain, but the part of the soul is uncertain, just as if one were to opine that a human being is the body, because it falls under the senses, and not the soul: but it is the soul. Likewise, it is also in this case. For there is a certain part of the soul by which we are delighted, which is exercised as soon as the objects are brought forward: therefore, no pleasure is a process of generation. But they say there is also a conversion into nature, which falls under the senses. For when they are not converting themselves into nature, there is no pleasure, since by converting, 
<margin>1205</margin>a saturation is made from the deficiency of nature. But, as we have said, it is possible for enjoyment to occur without any deficiency, since a deficiency is a sickness, but we say that someone can be delighted without sickness; and consequently, pleasure would not be the conversion of a deficiency. For there is nothing unworthy in such pleasures. Consequently, if pleasure is judged to be good because it is a process of generation, and no pleasure is a process of generation, then pleasure would indeed be good. Furthermore, they say that not every pleasure is good, which anyone might detect in this way: for because the good is said to be in all 
<margin>10</margin>predicaments, namely in essence, in relation to something, in quantity, in time, and in everything in all things, it is also manifest that some pleasure accompanies everything. Therefore, because the good is in all predicaments, pleasure also would be good. And consequently, since in these there are things good in themselves, pleasure would also be a good in itself. Yet pleasure is a pleasure of goods: therefore, every pleasure would be good. At the same time, it is certain from this that pleasures also differ in species among themselves, since the predicaments in which pleasure exists also differ. For it is not as it is in the sciences, 
<margin>20</margin>such as grammar or any other. If Lamprus possesses grammar, and this grammarian is affected by this grammar in the same way as any other person possessing grammar, there are certainly not two different grammars, the one in Lamprus and the one in Ileus. But it is not so in pleasure: for the pleasure that comes from drunkenness and that from sexual intercourse do not affect one in the same way; for which reason, pleasures will seem to be distinguished among themselves by species. Furthermore, because there are also evil pleasures, for this reason too, pleasure seemed not to be good. But that judgment is by no means proper to pleasure, but to nature and science. For there is also 
<margin>30</margin>an evil nature, such as that of worms, wasps, and utterly vile animals; yet it is not because of this that nature is evil. In the same way, there are also evil sciences, such as sedentary ones; yet it is not because of this that science is evil, but rather good in its genus, both science and nature. For just as a sculptor is not to be judged as to what sort of person he is from what he committed through error and did badly, but rather from what he did well, so neither is science 

<column-break/>

nor nature nor anything else to be judged as to what it is from its evils, but from its good qualities. Therefore, pleasure also is good in its genus. That indeed 
<margin>5</margin>there are also evil pleasures does not escape us. For there are also diverse natures of animals, good and bad, just as those of a human are good, but those of a wolf or any other wild beast are bad. Similarly, the nature of a horse is different from that of a human, and that of an ass and a dog. But pleasure is a conversion from that which is against nature, into the nature of each one; consequently, this also would be most sweet. Yet an evil nature has an evil pleasure. For what is for a horse is not for a human, and not even for others. But since there are diverse natures, there are also diverse pleasures. For pleasure is a conversion; and they say conversion, or restoration, restores to nature. Consequently, an evil nature has an evil conversion, just as a good one has a good one. Furthermore, those who contend that pleasure is not good are affected in the way that those are who are unfamiliar with nectar and think the gods drink wine, and that nothing is sweeter than that: they fall into this out of ignorance. A similar thing happens to those who assert that all pleasures are processes of generation, and by no means good. For because they ignore other pleasures besides 
<margin>20</margin>those of the body, they consider them to be processes of generation and not good: they do not think that pleasure in general is good. Since, therefore, there is both a pleasure of restoring nature and one of a nature already restored (the former are, of course, replenishments after a defect, but the latter are those which are perceived by the eyes and ears, and similar things), the functions of a nature that has been restored and obtains its own state, so to speak, seem to be better. For pleasures, spoken of in either way, are actions. Therefore, there is no doubt that pleasures from sight, hearing, and intelligence are by far the best, since those that fall under the body are produced from replenishment. Again, it was said that it is not even good, since that which is in everything and common to all is not good. That is certainly more proper to 
<margin>30</margin>the lover of honor and the desire for honor, for only the lover of honor wishes to have it and to surpass others in it. Should pleasure, therefore, if it must be good in itself, be of this kind, or not? Yet it is also in the opposite way. For it might seem to be good because all things seek it: for it is innate in all to seek the good. And consequently, if all things seek pleasure, pleasure would be good in its genus. Again, they denied that pleasure is good because it is an impediment, asserting that it is an impediment; which they do not seem to consider rightly. For it is not an impediment to the completion of matters, if there is any other impediment, as the pleasure of drunkenness might inhibit one from acting. Furthermore, in that way, science would also be an impediment to science: for it is not possible for you to exercise both at the same time. But why is science not good if pleasure is excited from science? And whether it is an impediment or not? Furthermore, it will act much more: for pleasure, once aroused, impels one to act more, because by doing what is right 
<margin>10</margin>it does what is from virtue, and does it sweetly. Will it not exercise much more those things that pertain to action? And if one acts while delighted, one will be good: but if one pursues honorable things while distressed, one is not good. For there is distress in those things that are from necessity. Consequently, if someone is affected by pain while pursuing honorable things, one performs them under compulsion: but one who is compelled to act from necessity is not good. Furthermore, no one can act in accordance with virtue without being affected by some pleasure or distress: for there is no middle ground. Why? Namely 
<margin>20</margin>because virtue is in an affection, and an affection is in distress and pleasure; nor is anything placed in the middle. There is no doubt, therefore, that virtue is with distress or pleasure. If anyone, therefore, pursues honorable things while sad, he is not good. Consequently, virtue would not be with distress: therefore with pleasure. It is, therefore, so far from being an impediment that it even exhorts one to act. And in total, it does not happen to be without pleasure, because it is produced by it itself. Another argument was that no science produces pleasure. That is not true either. For the builders of banquets and garlands, as well as perfumers, are producers of pleasure. Furthermore, for other sciences, pleasure is not the end, but it is with pleasure and not without pleasure. Therefore, there is also 
<margin>30</margin>a science that is a producer of pleasure. Again, it was said in another way that it is not the best thing. But in this way and by this reasoning, you would have lost the individual virtues, since courage is not the best thing. Is it, therefore, not good because of this? Or would that be absurd? # The good inspiration of the angel against vain glory.

<margin>John 15</margin>
<margin>Revelation 4 and 12</margin>
Against the fourth temptation of the devil, the angel gives a good inspiration, saying: "Wretch, why do you boast by ascribing to yourself constancy in faith, hope, and patience (which, however, is to be ascribed only to God), when you have nothing good from yourself?" The Lord says: "Without me you can do nothing." And elsewhere it is written: "Do not arrogate to yourself, do not boast, do not insolently exalt yourself, do not presume anything of yourself, do not attribute anything to yourself." And the Lord says: "Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled." And again: "Unless you become as this little child, you will not enter into the kingdom of heaven." Humble yourself, therefore, and you will be exalted, as the Lord says: "Whoever humbles himself will be exalted." And Augustine says: "If you humble yourself, God will descend to you. If you exalt yourself, God will recede from you." Turn, therefore, your mind away from pride, which once made Lucifer, the most beautiful of angels, the most deformed devil, and cast him from the heights of heaven to the depths of hell, which also was the cause of all sins. Whence Bernard: "Pride is the vanity of every sin and the cause of all perdition." The same: "Remove this vice, and all vices are cut away without labor." Wherefore it is uniquely to be noted that whenever a person dying feels himself tempted by <margin>Isaiah 14</margin> pride, he ought first to consider that pride so displeased God that, on its account alone, He banished the most noble of creatures, Lucifer, with all those adhering to him, from the heavens, damning them eternally. And thus, from such a consideration, he should humble and depress himself by recalling his sins, because he is ignorant of whether he is worthy of hatred or love. Whence he ought especially to take an example from Saint Anthony, to whom the devil said: "O Anthony, you have conquered me, for when I wish to exalt you, you depress yourself; when I wish to depress you, you raise yourself up." Second, he ought to think that humility so pleased God that, on its account, the glorious Virgin Mary conceived God and was exalted above the choirs of angels.

<margin>things that kill the embryo</margin>

**T**here are things that harm the embryo and not the mother, and conversely, and some harm both. Whence, wishing to establish a foundation, we say that the herb poppy and its seed harm both. The cause is that they induce sleep in both, and the herb stains the skin of the embryo with a spot that never departs. It should be known that the poppy and the white rose make a white spot, and the red one, a red spot. Whence a pregnant woman should not use them in food, lest the child become sleepy or spotted. The meat of the hare and the lion harms the embryo greatly because the former sleeps with its eyes open, and the latter similarly. Vinegar harms it, and suet, that is, the nerves of the feet of oxen, and milk and cucumber, in that they induce excessive coldness. Whence they carry danger to both. Lily and saffron harm the embryo and stain its skin a pale color. Leek, garlic, lettuce, and dill harm the embryo in that they deprive it of sight. Adel and alleum, that is, a large root in the bark, harm the embryo in that they corrupt the connection of the fingers of the hand, etc. The teeth grow late, and they are quickly deprived. Basil, wormwood, salt, and pepper harm the embryo in that through them it will be dry in flesh and becomes leprous from excessive heat, and it will have short nails. Pure cumin harms it on account of epilepsy. The meat of the pig and the eel harms it on account of the grime in the marrow of the bones and the dirt in the mouth. Salted meat, rustic cheese, and fried food harm it in that through them it becomes dry in flesh. And glutten, hyssop, caruca, dried figs, pine nuts, and morsels in wine, if not taken in excess, help the embryo and the womb, because they render it fat and bring color to the face. Sage, mint, fennel, and parsley are valuable to both because they generate good wind. Savory, pennyroyal, and borage kill the embryo. The smoke of an extinguished candle and lantern, the subtle steam of sulfur, and silver kill the embryo and harm the brain of the woman. When indeed the embryo moves, having hair, it causes pain to the woman in the belly or prickings. Also, it is to be known that the end of all humors in quantity, as much in time as in the person, when they are combined, becomes a sensory perception, as Galen says in his <term>Microtegni</term> <gloss>Small Art (of Medicine)</gloss>.

Next, I say that both human and divine authority must be attributed to the Augsburg Confession. Human, because the Confession did not proceed and originate immediately from God, but was written, published, and introduced into several churches by the labor of men, without revelation and a special impulse of the Holy Spirit. But it does not follow: This writing is of human authority; therefore, it is of no authority; unless you wish to strip all authority from the statutes and decrees of Emperors, Kings, and Princes. I also say the Confession has divine authority, not because it is properly <term>θεόπνευστος</term> <gloss>divinely inspired</gloss>, but because it is taken from the Sacred Scriptures and rightly embraces the sense of the divine word and the chapters of faith to be drawn solely from it. Therefore, if you look at the matters and subjects beyond the form and arrangement of the Confession, its authority is not merely human; and thus, with the accession of the consent of the Church, it can be proposed entirely as a symbol of doctrine and faith; but it cannot be referred to the Canon of Divine Scripture. I do not praise many masters; let there be one lord.
->One and Prince<-
The same poet calls them <term>diotrepheas basilēas</term> <gloss>Zeus-nurtured kings</gloss>, kings educated by <term>Jupiter</term>. Furthermore, the silent voice of nature is that monarchy is to be preferred. One king for bees, one for elephants, one ruler in the herd; cranes follow one leader; the one <term>Sun</term> presides over the day, the one <term>Moon</term> over the night, which is like the queen of the starry lights. In a ship there is one pilot, in a house one paterfamilias, in an army the sign of one. In the limbs the heart moves all things: in the parts of the soul reason presides: in the universe the one <term>God</term> is the creator and ruler of all. Although these things are most known, even to the bleary-eyed and the barbers <note>a classical proverb meaning things known to everyone</note>; yet there are those who both extol the mob and stir up mobs: there are those who prefer to be vexed by many than by one: there are, finally, those who admire, venerate, and embrace the womanly rule of a man. Not worthy of the name of men. I would wish that they also offered a fan and made a breeze. Since, however, it is certain by the judgment of the wise, by the calculation and suffrage of all, that women are unworthy to rule over men; let alone to claim for themselves a Majesty which they never had. It is shameful for the petticoat to command the toga; shameful for the distaff to command the sword. It is not the most unhappy servitude, by which the better sex is compelled to obey the worse, and he who ought to command is held to serve. And what is a <term>Woman</term>? Having forgotten her sex, she foams and the same one imitates huge bulls. Not so many serpents vomit poisons,

translation:
### EPITHALAMION.

<meta>A large printed initial letter C at the beginning of the first line of the poem.</meta>

O Christ, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> coming, who fell from the ether of the Father,
You enter the chaste womb of an untouched Virgin.
You are born into the world, promised to the fathers before,
You repair what perished through the serpent's wiles.
You destroy the devastating realms of horrific Satan,
You return thence as an everlasting Victor and Standard-bearer.
You carry with You the gifts which Your Victory produced,
These true blessings are birthed by Your blood.
You who send the paternal <term>Pneuma</term> <gloss>Spirit</gloss> into human minds,
So that hearts may truly please God.
Come here, Prince, to the holy Altar, while she is being led,
She who is to be the illustrious Spouse to the illustrious Duke.
With You as Leader, suggest the celestial breath from the Father's breast,
Which may join the two in chaste love.
Because the Hero has known You here from his tender years,
And has concern for pure religion.
Because this young woman has revered You with modest prayers,
And honors You with sincere piety.
And because You promise: "Whoever loves me alone,
And joyfully carries my words in his heart,
I shall meet him, and with the sacred Spirit,
We three wish to inhabit that house."
Then, because You approved of Marriage according to the custom of the fathers,
You also teach that You are its author.
Indeed, You were led to the Hymenæal joys,
And the cohort beloved with Your mother.

IN Concione, quae dixi publice, cum lectionem petant amici, fautores imperent; nec omnibus describendo par sim, a prelo subsidium peto, quin per compendium describo.

Si proinde peregrinas in manus devenerit; sciant: non orationem; verum orationis *Ideam*, quam prolixiorem conscripseram; sed in hanc *Epitomen* redegit diei, quo dicta, *solennitas*. Legitur tamen, ut est *dicta, verbis conceptis*. Non est *Confessio*, quam scripto probavi Venerando Ministerio, priusquam data fuit huic professioni libertas; sed EXITUS ex BABYLONE defensio. EXODUM nomino, praevideo *desertum*: *serpentes* in illo, plurimos adversantes. Sed securus de *Columnis; Nubis*, quae tegat; *ignis*, qui luceat, ad Canaan coelestem contendo.

Rationes hujus *Exodi* per *Epitomen* indigito, quas in *oratione copiosius explicaveram*, nec divina destituuntur authoritate, tot ab orthodoxis demonstratae.

Romana dici debuerunt lingua, sed explicari vernacula, quo sciant Germani, germanae fidei meae sensum, quin et constantiam propositum.

Vides igitur, B. L. quae sunt auribus dicta, quia sic expetis, oculis legenda, quibus animo Tuo, mentis arcana commendo. Quae dicta sunt CORAM TE, dicta velim CORAM DEO, cui intima mei cordis in hac professione probo. Sunt brevia quidem, sed sufficiunt candidis, qui malunt veritatem sine multiloquio, sine fuco. Scis igitur, qua de causa prelum premat haec IDEA, ne premat me, vel scribendo pluries, vel negando pluribus. Sit idea: si vel amici vel inimici efflagitaverint, nec orationem, cujus haec est idea; nec confessionem, cujus est caput, denegabo. *Nam pati, mori quidem possum pro Veritate, non vero tacere.*

## To the Benevolent Reader. Greetings.

<meta>An ornate woodcut initial letter I features floral and scrolling foliate designs.</meta>

SINCE friends request a copy of the sermon I delivered in public, and patrons command it, and since I cannot keep pace with everyone by copying it out by hand, I seek the assistance of the printing press to record it in a condensed form.

If it should fall into foreign hands, let them know: this is not the speech itself, but rather the *Idea* <note>original: "Idea"; concept or outline</note> of the speech, which I had written out at greater length. However, the *solemnity* of the day on which it was spoken reduced it to this *Epitome* <note>original: "Epitomen"; summary</note>. Yet it is read as it was *spoken, in the very words conceived*. It is not the *Confession* <note>original: "Confessio"; a formal statement of faith</note> which I approved in writing before the Venerable Ministry before liberty was granted to this profession; rather, it is a defense of the EXIT from BABYLON. I call it an EXODUS, and I foresee the *desert*: there are *serpents* in it, and many adversaries. But being secure in the *Columns; the Cloud* that covers, and the *fire* that shines, I strive toward the heavenly Canaan.

I point out the reasons for this *Exodus* through an *Epitome*, which I had explained more copiously in the *speech*. These reasons are not lacking in divine authority, having been demonstrated by so many orthodox writers.

It should have been spoken in the Roman <note>i.e., Latin</note> tongue, but it was explained in the vernacular so that the Germans might know the sense of my German <note>a play on the words "Germani" and "germanae," meaning "true" or "genuine"</note> faith, and indeed the constancy of my purpose.

You see, therefore, Benevolent Reader, what was spoken for the ears, because you seek it, is now to be read by the eyes, to which I entrust the secrets of my mind and your own soul. What was said BEFORE YOU, I would have said BEFORE GOD, to whom I prove the innermost parts of my heart in this profession. It is brief indeed, but it suffices for the candid, who prefer truth without loquacity and without pretense. You know, therefore, for what reason the press prints this IDEA: lest it weigh upon me, either by writing it many times or by denying it to many people. Let this be the idea: if either friends or enemies demand it, I will not deny either the speech, of which this is the idea, or the confession, of which this is the head. *For I can suffer, and indeed die, for the Truth, but I cannot remain silent.*

->Y. H. <note>An abbreviation for "Your Humble servant" or similar respectful closing.</note><-

->M. Ostrovvski.<-

<note>The circular red ink library stamp of the Berlin Royal Library reads: "From the Royal Library, Berlin."</note>

<summary>Martin Ostrowski explains his decision to publish a condensed summary of his public sermon, framing his departure from his previous religious stance as an "Exodus from Babylon" and expressing his willingness to suffer for his stated truths.</summary>
<keywords>Exodus, Babylon, sermon, confession, German faith, religious defense, Martin Ostrowski</keywords>

<header>IVSTINI</header>

Moreover, they say that Geryon himself was not of a triple nature, as reported in fables, but that there were three brothers of such great harmony that they seemed to everyone to be ruled by one mind; nor did they bring war upon Hercules of their own accord, but having seen their herds being plundered, they sought to recover what was lost by war.

CHAPTER V. After the kingdoms of Spain, the Carthaginians were the first to occupy the empire of the province. For when the Gaditani, at the command of a dream, had transferred the sacred rites of Hercules from Tyre—whence the Carthaginians also trace their origin—to Spain and had founded a city there, the neighboring peoples of Spain envied the growth of the new city and, for that reason, harassed the Gaditani with war. The Carthaginians sent aid to their kinsmen. In a successful expedition, they both vindicated the Gaditani from injury and added the greater part of the province to their own empire. Later, encouraged by the auspices of the first expedition, they sent the commander Hamilcar with a great force to occupy the province. After achieving great things, while Fortune followed him too incautiously, he was led into an ambush and killed. His son-in-law, Hasdrubal, was sent into his place, and he too was killed by a slave of a certain Spaniard, who was avenging the unjust death of his own master. Hannibal, the son of Hamilcar—greater than either of them—succeeded him. Having surpassed the deeds of both, he subdued all of Spain. From there, having brought war upon the Romans, he exhausted Italy for sixteen years with various disasters. Meanwhile, the Romans sent the Scipios into Spain, who first drove the Carthaginians from the province and later waged grave wars against the Spaniards themselves. Nor could the yoke of Spain be accepted by the province until Caesar Augustus, having subdued the world, transferred his victorious arms to them and, having led the barbarous and fierce people to a more cultivated habit of life through laws, reduced the region to the form of a province.

# SILI ITALICI
<note>Silius Italicus</note>

Amidst this, the consul, ejecting the blood flowing from his lacerated mouth: "Well done, O paternal virtue! Nor are hopes narrow, when such hearts remain for the Romulean kingdom. Take the horse away with spurs, where the wound permits, and from here: let the gates of the city be closed quickly, this pestilence will rush to these walls, say, I pray; let the reins of affairs be handed over to Fabius. My fury fought with our warnings. What more of life remains, except to show the blind plebeians that Paulus knows how to die? Am I carried into the city consumed by wounds? For how much would Hannibal wish to buy it, so that he may see our backs turning? Not such are the hearts to Paulus, nor do we enter the image of the spirits so small. I myself—but why do I delay you, Lentulus, with vain complaint, sick as I am? Proceed and quickly rescue the horse, exhausted by the spear, from here." Then Lentulus seeks the city, carrying great commands; nor does Paulus allow what is left of his light to go unavenged. Just as a tiger, yielding at last to a lethal wound and having thrown its body, struggles with death and opens a languid gap in vain bites, nor being sufficient for its anger with its blows, licks the hunting spears with its final tongue. And now, he had fixed his sword, rising unexpectedly, into the man who was bringing his weapon closer, glittering and secure from the slaughter of Ierta <note>a specific soldier or location</note>, and he was looking around for the Sidonian leader, wishing to place his struggling soul into that right hand. But they conquered the man with weapons gathering from all sides, both the Nomad, and the Garamantian, and the Celt, and the Moor, and the Asturian.

( भवनेषु रसाधिकेषु पूर्वं क्षितिरक्षार्थमुशन्ति ये निवासम् ); cf. वष्टिभागुरिरलोपं &c. Sid. Kau. निस्वा वष्टि शतं &c. S'āntis'ataka. ब्रह्माङ्गभ्वः—It is difficult to know what this exactly means. Different commentators have given different interpretations. The meaning that would readily suggest itself to the mind is—'born of Brahmā' (as some commentators, as quoted by Mr. Despande take it. ब्रह्मणः अङ्गभूः, ब्रह्मणोद्भूत मूरतपत्तिर्यस्य ); see our note on रुद्र: II. 26. and cf. स रुद्रो यो रुद्रः स ईशानो य ईशानः स भगवानमहेश्वरः । Atharvas'ira-upanishad. Or the source of the Vedas and their Upāngas. Chār. says—ब्रह्मा अङ्गभूः पुत्रो यम्य. Malli. understands by this—Who is the repository of the Mantras सद्योजात and others, by having made the Nyāsa, i. e., touching the six parts of the body हृदय and others and assigning deities to them by repeating the proper Mantras; cf. अथ वा ब्रह्मांगानि पञ्च शैवसिद्धान्त प्रोक्ता मन्त्रविशेषास्तेषा-मुत्पत्तिस्थानम् । आयातः-ईशान-वामदेव तत्पुरुष-सद्योजातलक्षणानि पञ्चाङ्गानि । Sukhāvabodhatikā, as quoted by Mr. Despande, who further says—"ब्रह्म is a prayer or any pious expression in the worship of gods or a mantra used as a spell for averting evil influences. सद्योजात &c. are simply शिवमूर्तिभेदs."

ब्रह्मन्—ब्रह्मन्, the one supreme Ens, is, according to the Vedantins, the material and efficient cause of the universe. It is नित्य 'ever-lasting', शुद्ध 'pure', बुद्ध 'intelligent' and मुक्त 'unfettered by any conditions' ( अस्ति तावन्नित्यशुद्धबुद्धमुक्त-स्वभावं सर्वज्ञं सर्वशक्तिसमन्वितं ब्रह्म । S'ār. Bhā. ). The two great texts ( Mahāvākyas ) setting forth the nature of Brahman are सत्यं ज्ञानमनन्तं ब्रह्म ( Tait. ) and सत्यं विज्ञानमानन्दं ब्रह्म ( Brh. ).

# The Gairi Kamboola and Khallasara Yogas

But the Moon desires to go to the sign of Libra. Libra is the sign of exaltation for Saturn. Therefore, because of its fast motion <note>original: *shighragamitva*</note>, the Moon moves to that other sign—Libra—and forms a **Mutthashila** <term>an aspect indicating the completion of an event</term> with Saturn, who is situated there. This specific planetary arrangement is known as **Gairi Kamboola**. 

Now, its result is stated: It grants gain in the form of the fulfillment of the desired task through the assistance of another, a third party.

An example chart <note>referring to the diamond-shaped diagram</note> is provided for this. In this same configuration, if Mercury or other planets were in the sign of Libra, but lacked even a single dignity <note>original: *adhikara*, referring to essential dignities like domicile or exaltation</note>—whether favorable or unfavorable—and the Moon, having gone there, formed a **Mutthashila** with Mercury or the others, then that **Gairi Kamboola** should be understood as yielding undesirable results. In this example, there is no consensus because it was not mentioned by Samarasimha <margin>original: *Samarasimhenapyuktatvat*; However, some copies suggest it *was* mentioned by Samarasimha.</margin> ॥ 58 ॥ 59 ॥ 60 ॥

Now, the author explains the characteristics of the **Khallasara** yoga. In the verse "Void," the word "by any one" should be supplied.

->If the Moon enters its exaltation or another sign and forms an **Itthashala** <term>an applying aspect</term>, it is **Gairi Kamboola**; it grants gain through help from others. ॥ 60 ॥<-
->If the Moon is a **Void-Traveler** <note>original: *shunyadhvaga*; a planet making no aspects in its current sign</note> and forms no **Itthashala** or connection <note>original: *yuti*</note> with either [of the two main planets], it is **Khallasara**. This is inauspicious and destroys the results of a **Kamboola**. ॥ 61 ॥<-
->If a planet that is set <term>combust by the sun</term>, in debilitation, in an enemy’s sign, or retrograde is weak and forms a **Mutthashila**, it is unable to carry the matter forward. Because its light is at its end or in its "face" <note>original: *mukha*; referring to its current degree-position</note>, it does not accomplish the task. ॥ 62 ॥<-

<margin>Or because of the lack of logic, it destroys the result of the Kamboola yoga. ॥ 61 ॥</margin> A **Mutthashila** yoga between the Lord of the Ascendant <note>representing the querent</note> and the Lord of the Matter <note>representing the object of the question</note> is indeed expected. In that context, according to the previously mentioned characteristics, the Moon is a "Void-Traveler" on a void path. Such a Moon does not possess a **Mutthashila** yoga with either the Lord of the Ascendant or the Lord of the Matter. Alternatively, if such a Moon does not even have a connection <note>original: *vayu* or *yuti*</note> with those two, the yoga is known as **Khallasara**. This is not auspicious. In what way? It "destroys the result of the Kamboola." When there is a **Mutthashila** or just a simple yoga, the **Kamboola** is fulfilled. But here, due to the lack of a **Mutthashila** with anyone, it destroys the result. ॥ 61 ॥

Now the characteristics of the **Radyoga** are explained. "Set" etc.: If a planet is set <term>invisible due to the Sun's proximity</term>, or in its sign of debilitation, or in the house of its enemy, or is retrograde, or has "diminished light"—meaning it is devoid of brilliance—such a planet is considered "weak." If a weak planet forms a **Mutthashila** with any lord of a house, that planet, whether at the "face" <note>beginning of a sign</note> or the end, is not a fulfiller of that house's task...

These women burn their left breast, in order to be more hardened in shooting. Their weapons are bows and arrows; they are agile, fast, skillful, brave, and accurate shooters, and above all, they are very steadfast and do not let themselves be put to flight easily. In battle, they use this ruse: they act as if they want to flee, after which they turn around quickly, then doing great damage to their enemy with their shooting. When they then notice that the enemy thinks they have overcome them and breaks their order, they turn around unexpectedly and fall boldly upon the enemy, killing and shooting down everyone who comes before them, so that they are also feared everywhere because of their agility and accurate shooting.

<margin>And inhabit a separate region; their nature and custom, described.</margin>They inhabit a separate region granted to them by the Emperor, and at certain times they join the men, whom each chooses according to her own preference, in order to beget children so that their lineage will not die out. When they then bear boys, they send them to the men in their land, but when they are girls, they keep them with them, rearing them so that, having reached their years, they may also go to war.

(Stallb.). Rettig objects that this rendering is inconsistent with ἠρέμα φιλίους, and explains by "oculis prope admotis intueri, also scharf ansehen," cp. *Phaedo* 103 A, *Rep.* 531 A. Ast gives "oculos in aliquid immotos habere intentos": Reynders, τὸ βλέμμα ἄνω καὶ κάτω κινεῖν: Jowett, "rolling his eyes."

**ἠρέμα παρασκοπῶν.** This verb is ἅπ. εἰρ. in Plato, and perhaps conveys a literary allusion: Rückert explains it to mean "oculis quasi comitari, observare, ut omnes motus lento oculorum motu notare videaris."

**δῆλος...πόρρωθεν.** "Similiter Apollodorus, qui Socratis incessum imitatus est, τῶν οὖν...πόρρωθεν ἐκάλεσεν κτλ." (Hommel).

**ὁ ἑταῖρος.** So Jahn, after Aristides t. II. p. 72: the more definite term is preferable, as Rettig argues against Teuffel. For confusion of the two words in the codd., cp. 183 C (*crit. n.*), and see Schanz, *nov. comm.* p. 59.

**221 C προτροπάδην.** "In headlong rout"—an Epic (*Il.* xvi. 304) word, ἅπ. εἰρ. in Plato. For the sense, cp. Tyrt. 11. 11—13 οἳ μὲν γὰρ τολμῶσι... παυρότεροι θνήσκουσι κτλ.: Seneca, *Ep.* 94 audentes fortuna iuvat (see Bergk, ad Simon. *fr.* 227): *Il.* v. 531 f. αἰδομένων δ’ ἀνδρῶν πλέονες σόοι ἠὲ πέφανται· | φευγόντων δ’ οὔτ’ ἂρ κλέος ὄρνυται οὔτε τις ἀλκή: *ib.* xv. 561 ff.

**Πολλὰ...καὶ ἄλλα κτλ.** Cp. 195 B, 201 D. Hirschig's θαυμάσαι gives us (as Rettig argues) "einen matten Gedanken."

**θαύματος.** "Of wonder" (the subjective feeling), cp. *Phil.* 36 D, *Laws* 967 A: elsewhere in Plato θαῦμα means "quod mirum est."

**οἷος γὰρ κτλ.** For Achilles, see *Od.* iv. 267 ff.; and cp. 179 E f.

**Βρασίδαν.** For this famous Spartan leader, who fell fighting at Amphipolis in 422 B.C., see Thuc. II. 25, 85 ff., v. 6; Bury, *Hist. Gr.* pp. 445 ff.

The time, when Eucritus and I were walking toward the Hales
From the city; and Amyntas was with us as the third.

Poplars and elm trees showed a shady grove;
Overarched and thick with green leaves.
And we had not yet finished half the road; nor had the tomb
Of Brasilas appeared to us, when we found a certain traveler,
A noble man skilled in the Muses, a Cydonian.
His name was Lycidas; and he was a goatherd; nor would anyone
Have failed to recognize him upon seeing him; for he looked exactly like a goatherd.
For he wore the tawny skin of a shaggy goat upon his shoulders,
Smelling of fresh rennet.
And an old tunic was fastened around his chest
With a woven belt; and in his right hand he held a curved staff of wild olive,
And he spoke to me quietly, his face
Wearing a smiling look; and a laugh clung to his lip.
Simichidas, where do you drag your feet at high noon,
When even the lizard sleeps upon the stone walls?

### XXX. To make Manmene <gloss>g</gloss>.

Take the thighs <gloss>h</gloss> or the flesh of capons, boil <gloss>i</gloss> them, and carve them small into a mortar. Take milk of almonds with broth of fresh beef and put the flesh into the milk or the broth. Place it on the fire and mix it together with flour of rice or of wheat, thickened like the 'blanc de sure', and with the yolks of eggs to make it yellow, and saffron. When it is dressed in dishes with 'blanc de sure', sprinkle upon it cloves <gloss>k</gloss> and sprinkle upon it powder of galantine, and serve it forth.

### XXXI. To make Bruet of Almayne <note>German broth</note>.

Take roasted partridges, chickens, and roasted quails, and larks boiled. Dismember them and make a good caudle <note>a warm, spiced drink or sauce</note>. Dress the flesh in a dish and sprinkle powder of galantine thereupon. Stick in cloves and serve it forth.

translation:
...[believ]ed, not studied. And I act thus as if I were providing a defense for eloquence against its detractors, which is greater than my purpose. For we are writing not about this, but about the elegance of the Latin language, from which, nevertheless, a step is made toward eloquence itself. But if anyone is not eloquent, he should only then not be rebuked if he was unable to emerge as such, not if he fled from this labor. He, however, who knows not how to speak elegantly and commits his thoughts to writing, especially in theology, is most impudent; and if he says he does this deliberately, he is most insane—though there is no one who would not wish to speak elegantly and fluently; but since this does not fall to their lot, they wish (perverse as they are) to seem unwilling, or certainly that they ought not to speak so. And therefore they say that the pagans spoke in this manner, and that it is not fitting for Christians to speak in the same way—as if those whom I have named spoke in the manner of these men, and not in the manner of Cicero and the rest of the pagans, whose manner of speaking they have neither recognized nor experienced. Not the language of the pagans, not grammar, not rhetoric, not dialectic, and the other arts are to be condemned (since the apostles wrote in the Greek language), but the dogmas, the religions, and the false opinions concerning the practice of virtues, through which we climb into heaven.

The other sciences and arts, however, lie in a middle ground, which you may use both well and badly. Wherefore, I beseech you, let us strive to arrive there, or at least very near, where those luminaries of our religion arrived. You see with how wondrous an ornament the garments of Aaron were distinguished, how the Ark of the Covenant, how the Temple of Solomon: by this, eloquence seems to me to be signified, which (as the noble tragic poet says) is the queen of things and perfect wisdom. <margin>Euripides in Hecuba.</margin> And so, others adorn private houses—these are those who study civil law, canon law, medicine, philosophy, contributing nothing to divine matters; let us adorn the house of God, so that those entering it may be moved to religion not by the mold of neglect to contempt, but by the majesty of the place. I cannot restrain myself from saying what I feel. Those ancient theologians seem to me like certain bees flying even into distant pastures...

# FIFTH ACT.

Heaven no longer awaits from us
A human victim.
It is no longer a time of vengeance and wrath,
But of grace and love. Today commands
Our Goddess, that in place
Of a horrible and mortal sacrifice,
Happy and fortunate weddings should be made.
But tell me, how much of the day remains?
Mon. An hour, or little more. Tir. Is evening coming so soon?
Let us return to the temple, and there immediately
Let the daughter of Titiro, and your son,
Give each other marital faith, and spouses
May they become from lovers, and let one lead
The other very soon to the paternal houses.
Where it is fitting, before the Sun sets,
That the fortunate heroes be joined.
So commands heaven. Give me back, son,
Him whom you have taken from me; you, Montano, follow me.
Mon. But look well, Tirenio,
That without violating the holy law
She cannot give to Mirtillo
That faith which was once given to Silvio.
Car. And to Silvio will be given
Likewise the faith: for Mirtillo
Had such a name from his birth;
If the truth was told to me by your servant;
And he was pleased,

The body is heavy and phlegm is abundant. The body is lethargic, sleep is excessive, the tongue is white, and vomiting occurs. One feels intoxicated and heat arises gradually. Mostly, the disease settles in the joints <note>literally: joint-four</note>.

When the condition arises from wind and bile in the late summer, the symptoms are body heat and vomiting. The head and bones ache with a cold, dull sensation. There is insomnia, dizziness, and the mouth and tongue are dry. One feels as if being scorched by the sun and has great thirst. There is confusion, much talkativeness, and the upper pulses are empty. It mostly settles in the locations of the lungs and heart.

When phlegm-wind heat arises in the spring, the symptoms are low fever and loss of appetite. The body trembles, sleep is heavy, and the tongue is grey and coated. The mouth is thirsty, phlegm is abundant, and breathing is uncomfortable. There is constipation, dizziness, and the brain and joints ache. The body and neck feel heavy and dull, and digestion is weak. It mostly settles in the areas of the kidneys and waist.

When phlegm-bile heat arises in early winter, the symptoms are alternating heat and cold. The body sweats, phlegm is abundant, and thirst is great. The mind is dull, the mouth is bitter, and there is much impurity. Appetite is poor and the stomach aches. Specifically, the head aches and the eyes and tongue are yellow. It mostly settles in the stomach.

When a combination of factors arises, mostly in late winter, the symptoms of all the types appear. There is heavy sleep during the day and little sleep at night. The eyes are red and teary, and thirst is great. The calves, heart, ribs, and bones ache. Dizziness occurs and the tongue... <note>sentence ends mid-leaf</note>

<leaf-break/>

When phlegm seizes the seat of the bile, it is called a "lingering epidemic of diarrhea." Detailed explanations depend on oral instruction.

As for the temporary signs of the epidemic settling: When it settles in the skin, the body trembles. The body hair stands on end and the head aches. This is considered the time of unripened heat. When it settles in the flesh, heat and thirst are great. When it settles in the vessels, the pulse is fast and the urine is red. The vessels are distended and elevated. When it settles in the bones, the teeth feel cold and ache. The facial hair and skin ache.

When it settles in the solid organs, the general signs are taught through specific symptoms. When it settles in the hollow organs, the general signs are suppression and blockage. Specifically:
Settling in the lungs causes coughing.
Settling in the heart causes intoxication, muteness, and much chest agitation.
Settling in the liver causes yellow eyes and the dripping of dark blood. This particular sign is called <term>Lep-gan</term> <gloss>the great flat one</gloss>.
Settling in the spleen causes hiccups, abdominal distension, and rumbling.
Settling in the kidneys causes urinary retention and pain in the small of the back.
Settling in the stomach causes vomiting and loss of appetite.
Settling in the small and large intestines causes diarrhea and blockage.
Settling in the bladder causes urinary suppression.

By knowing these unmixed signs of the <term>rmugs-pa</term> <gloss>dullness/fog</gloss> epidemic, one should apply the temporary healing treatments in accordance with the time.

Regarding the five types of epidemics that descend like rain: In the "madness epidemic," the patient is agitated and shouts. They speak much nonsense, have no sleep, protect their eyes, and cry out "I am dying" as they rise up. The heat of the bile... <note>sentence ends mid-leaf</note>

<summary>This page details the diagnostic symptoms of various epidemic fevers according to their seasonal onset and their manifestation in specific organs and bodily tissues. It classifies these conditions based on the balance of the three humors: wind, bile, and phlegm.</summary>

And write the first, second, and third seals <note>Talismanic symbols or diagrams often found in the margins of these manuscripts.</note> upon it, and recite the invocation <note>The "Invocation of the Shaking of the Abyss" mentioned in previous pages.</note> over it twelve times. Bury it under a blacksmith’s anvil or under a grinding stone, and you shall see a wonder.

### (Chapter Forty-Eight)
**For ophthalmia** <note>Original: *ramad*. A term for acute eye inflammation or conjunctivitis.</note> **to afflict one of your enemies** — If you desire this, take the skin of a mouse and write the third seal upon it. Place it in a clay jug along with onion skins and garlic skins, and place it in the chimney of an oven or a coffee house, and you shall see a wonder.

<margin>H</margin> ### (Chapter Forty-Nine)
**For the splitting of the eye of one of your enemies** — If you desire this, take an apple and recite the invocation over it three times. Place it where the wind and air blow, and write upon it the name of the intended person and the name of his mother; you shall see a wonder.

### (Chapter Fifty)
**To set the Jinn** <note>Supernatural spirits in Islamic cosmology who can be commanded by a sorcerer to harass a victim.</note> **upon one of your enemies** — If you desire this, take the collar of a blue shirt and write the seven seals upon it. Recite the invocation sixteen times and bury it in a ruined place; he shall be afflicted quickly.

### (Chapter Fifty-One)
**For the stoning of the house of one of your enemies** <note>Historically, "stoning" (*rajm*) in a magical context refers to poltergeist-like activity where stones are seemingly thrown by unseen hands.</note> — If you desire this, take a raw pottery shard and write the second seal upon it. Recite the invocation over it ten times and bury it under the threshold of the intended house; you shall see a wonder as long as the shard remains buried under the threshold of that place.

<margin>+</margin> ### (Chapter Fifty-Two)
**To set the *Ammar*** <note>The specific class of Jinn believed to inhabit and "colonize" human houses.</note> **upon one of your enemies** — If you desire this, take ashes from an oven and recite the invocation over them nineteen times. Sprinkle them in the place where you desire this to happen, and it shall immediately become inhabited by Jinn.

### (Chapter Fifty-Three)
**For the separation of enemies** — Write the second seal for them on a black rag and recite the invocation over it seven times. Bury it in the place where the work is intended, and they shall be separated from that moment.

### (Chapter Fifty-Four)
**For displacement from one place to another** — If there is an oppressor and you wish for him to depart from his place, write the fourth seal for him in a *sukkuruja* <note>A small ceramic bowl or saucer.</note> and recite the invocation over it nineteen times. Erase the writing with water from a bathhouse and sprinkle it in the house you desire, and they shall depart.

### (Chapter Fifty-Five)
**To break the millstone of an oppressor** — If you desire this, take some flour and recite the invocation over it fifteen times. Throw the flour into the heart of the millstone, and it shall break at that very hour and moment.

### (Chapter Fifty-Six)
**To disable the oven of an oppressor or break its stone** — If you desire this, take a piece of paper and write the second seal upon it. Place it inside a loaf of dough and throw it into the oven; the bread shall not bake and the stone shall break.

<margin>H</margin> ### (Chapter Fifty-Seven)
**For the harm of enemies** — If you desire this, take some bran and recite the invocation over it ten times. Sprinkle it in the place intended for the work, and you shall see a wonder.

<margin>✻</margin> ### (Chapter Fifty-Eight)

### Records of Things Heard, Volume 3: Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate

○ Even if a thing or affair is large, it is "below form" <gloss>physical</gloss>. Even if a <term>Principle</term> is small, it is "above form" <gloss>metaphysical</gloss>. <term>Principle</term> cannot truly be described as large or small. Here, calling <term>Principle</term> "small" is only to contrast the <term>Principle</term> found in a single small object with a very large thing, such as Heaven and Earth. It is like saying: "Heaven and Earth are indeed large, but they are 'below form.' The <term>Principle</term> of a single thing is indeed small, but it is 'above form'." This also must be looked at with flexibility. ○ Master <term>Huang Mianzai</term> asked: "The <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> cannot move or be still by itself. Since these are already <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, how can we say it 'produces' <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>?" The answer was: "Producing <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> is like <term>Yang</term> producing <term>Yin</term>," and so on. Since <term>Confucius</term> said the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> produces the <term>Two Modes</term>, and Master <term>Zhou</term> said the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> produces <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, the Sages and Worthies clearly did not mind saying that <term>Principle</term> produces <term>Energy</term>. Today, why do some people hate this theory and avoid saying it, insisting instead that <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> produce themselves without originating from the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>? What is their intention? 

<column-break/>

The statement "We see the movement of the millstone because of the movement of the ant" <note>an analogy where the millstone is the universe and the ant is the Supreme Ultimate</note> is also an "inverted" way of speaking. It is correct to say: "Because of the movement and stillness of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, we can see the movement and stillness of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>." But it is incorrect to say: "Because of the movement and stillness of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>, we see the movement and stillness of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>." Perhaps the two characters for "mill" and "ant" were swapped by mistake. Also, looking at the context, after the phrase "cannot move or be still by itself," there should be more words about "movement and stillness" that have been lost. ○ One must look at the word "observe" <gloss>guan</gloss>. It means I go inside the thing to take it apart and look at it. It does not mean the thing itself has "two faces." <term>Principle</term> and <term>Energy</term> are definitely two separate things, but they cannot be separated. This is <term>Master Zhu</term>'s teaching. One is hidden and one is manifest; they are clearly "two faces." But if the thing itself did not originally have two faces, how could I "take it apart" to look at it? ○ "Benefit and Firmness <gloss>Li-zhen</gloss> are <term>Nature</term> and <term>Emotion</term> <gloss>Xing-qing</gloss>." "When movement reaches its limit, there is stillness; when stillness reaches its limit, there is movement again." After "Nature and Emotion," there should be the sentence: "This is the stillness of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>." Otherwise, the text does not make sense. This matches the context. ○ Master <term>Cai Jiezhai</term> said: "Form <gloss>xing</gloss> means it moves and can be seen..."

a black object is black, that by which a thing is such a thing, <term>tode ti</term> <gloss>a "this-something," or a particular individual thing</gloss> ¹. It is the principle by which the substance is in its actual state and not in another state; it is the substance considered as being *in act*, <term>hōs energeia ousia</term> <gloss>substance as actuality</gloss> ².

But the things that we study are subject to change. The object of which we speak can be sometimes black and sometimes white; that is to say that when it has white as its actual tint, it is possible for it to become black; when it is actually black, it is possible for it to become white. At the same time, therefore, that we conceive what it is actually and, consequently, its form, we must conceive what it is in potentiality; and this potentiality to be something else is precisely what remains in the substance while it is actually such a thing; it is by this potentiality that the substance is matter. "I name it matter," says Aristotle ³, "in that it is not actually this thing, but that it is potentially this thing. <term>Hylēn de legō hē mē tode ti ousa energeia dynamei esti tode ti</term>."

Matter is therefore opposed to form as potentiality (<term>dynamis</term>) is opposed to act (<term>energeia</term>). This opposition is the essential character of the Physics of Aristotle.

We have seen that in every substance susceptible to generation, change, and destruction, there is matter; such a substance, indeed, has the potentiality to be what it is not in act; while it is actually such a substance, it is in potentiality to become, through corruption, such another substance; while it is actually in such a state, it is in potentiality to receive such another state.

Is there matter in beings incapable of generation, alteration, and corruption, as the celestial bodies will be, according to the preference of Aristotle? Assuredly, if these substances are susceptible to changing place. Indeed, while such a being is actually in such a place, it is in potentiality to find itself in other places. This potentiality of finding itself in a place other than its actual place, even while it exists outside of any potentiality to receive another state or to transform itself into another substance, constitutes a matter, but a matter of a particular kind—
